en: Preface, Spring of the Wuyin Year. Master Chongfu Hui-gong completed the *Vajra-piṇḍārtha* (Essential Summary of the Diamond Sūtra). With single-minded devotion, he refined his work and discarded all extraneous commentaries;
I was already deeply moved by this. Before long, he further produced the *Lengyan Zhengjian* (Correct Vision of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra). His contemporaries—
In selecting the meanings and dividing the sections, there is a distinct judgment that arises entirely from his realization. Observing his words, he states:
"The Sūtra takes the Perfect Ultimate as its primary principle and the definitive meaning as its goal; it requires a wondrous awakening to leap directly into it.

How, then, can this be fully exhausted by mere names, phrases, and syllables? Previously, I heard that you, my lord, received the full precepts at Gaoteng, studied under Lingyin, and resided at Mount Jing.
Later, he retired from public life at Xingfu Monastery in Loudong. The Master was preeminent in character and possessed a stable and profound realization.

Furthermore, he was highly gifted with elegant thought, which manifested as deep talent; taking the exhortation of others as his own responsibility, he delighted in receiving visitors and guiding them according to their capacities.
Thus, within the teaching that does not rely on words, he instructed people through words in this manner. This concludes the collection.
The questioner requested a preface from me. I reflected: The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* is the supreme teaching, its ultimate meaning being unsurpassed.

Even the Venerable One, who was the primary recipient of the teaching, still harbored doubts regarding his realization; how then could I, with the limited knowledge and views of an ordinary person, dare to attempt a mere partial assessment?

Having no other recourse, there exist the discursive commentaries of the various predecessors from the Tang and Song dynasties onwards. Indeed, since the time the Minister Fang took down the oral teachings in writing, [the tradition at] Chongfu...
Master Kuò composed a commentary on the scripture’s case-binding; this was the beginning of its exegesis. Master Zhèn of Guǎntáo divided it into eight sections and seven categories;
this was the beginning of its topical analysis (*kēpàn*). Master Yuán of Zīzhōng composed a commentary asserting that the three dharmas correspond to the three contemplations;
this was the beginning of the Tiantai school’s interpretation of the sutra by Gūshān and others. As for its connection with Chan...

Regarding those who provide doctrinal interpretations of the sutras, it began with Master Yan of Changqing’s composition of the *Shuowen*. This [Master] Wengleng and others are the patriarchs of using Chan to adjudicate the teachings (*jiao*).
Furthermore, in the early Song dynasty, there was Master Xuan of Changshui, who emerged from the Xianshou school and synthesized it with the Tiantai school.

The commentaries he compiled comprehensively encompass both the teachings and contemplative practice; scholars regard them as the core doctrine for a hundred generations and may rightly call them the synthesis of all preceding schools.
Nevertheless, while the masters prior to the Song dynasty shared a single, unified lineage, the scriptural exegeses following the Song era diverged into various branches of agreement and difference.
For instance, although Master Jì of Shìmén—like Dǐngfǎ—held that the realization of one's nature was the primary tenet, he nonetheless differed from Língyuán...

These views conflict with one another. Furthermore, there is the criticism that Changshui held a biased interpretation of the teachings, similar to Master Yuan of Gushan, who applied the "Three Stills and Three Contemplations" (san-zhi san-guan) as a commentary for the entire sutra.
Master Yue of Wuxing expanded upon this theory, yet some have labeled it as the "School Outside the Mountains" (shan-wai yi-jia), which is not a comprehensive or orthodox view.
As for Master Zhengmo of Jiaoguang, he exerted great effort in refuting its errors, as did Master Huan of Wenling.

Regarding the section outside the "Platform" (Taitang), he separately delineated the four categories beginning with the Path of Vision (darśanamārga). These stand out as independent works, sufficient to serve as a guide for the world.
Yet, to claim that masters such as Xuanyue and Yuanzhao were all insufficient to serve as standards of judgment is likewise an excessive argument.

For instance, Master Weikong of Shizi Lin compiled the commentaries of nine masters from the Tang and Song dynasties into the *Huìjiě* (Comprehensive Explanation); for a hundred years, this work was the standard followed at lecture halls throughout both the North and South. Thus, [the aforementioned claim] is unfounded.

Furthermore, there is the lament of "the boat being marked at Yanjin. For all such cases, where factions engage in mutual strife, treating their own side as masters and others as slaves, how can one rectify these matters without the instruction of the final teaching?

Judging by my humble opinion, although the various schools are numerous, it is only through the Chan school’s interpretation of the scriptures that one truly accords with the investigation of the mind and the discernment of nature found within them.

This is the meaning; this constitutes the True Dharma. Now, observing the eminent masters of the Ming dynasty, such as Master Hanguang of Caoxi and Master Huai of Xuelang, both were hailed as great craftsmen of the Dharma.
However, regarding this scripture, Master Huai spoke in accordance with its nature, his exposition being lucid and unimpeded, as if he wished to sweep away all scholastic categories;
thus, he did not compose further treatises. There remains only Master Hanguang’s *Xuanjing Gangyao* (Essential Outline of the Suspended Mirror), which is brilliantly...

Nevertheless, it was worthy of transmission. He then sat in meditation for three years until, one night, he attained profound awakening. He integrated his realization within the "One Mind and Three Contemplations" (*ekacitta-trivipashyana*) and freely composed this work to expound upon them.

What he described—the essence of contemplation, the characteristics of contemplation, and the function of contemplation—collectively explains the entire scripture rather than assigning specific sections to individual parts.
This is truly one who has transcended words to produce words; when the Chan school speaks of the scriptures, this work should certainly be regarded as their fundamental canon.

Examining the Dharma lineage of Caoxi, both Jingshan and Lingyin are of the orthodox tradition of Nanyue. Considering that you, Master, once resided at these two mountains, you are truly a scion of this school.
Now, you shall further propagate the teachings in the Loujiang region and once again expound the ancestral style.
In widely proclaiming the vehicle of the Dharma, what is there that is insufficient for those who radiate light from the Ocean-Seal Samādhi?

Successors have transmitted this from one to another, mutually verifying this wondrous realization of direct, transcendent entry. Even when Confucian schools expound their classics, they frequently employ Chan principles to judge and categorize the teachings.
This is entirely consistent with Zongtong of the former Cibu, Ruyue of Jingling, and the *Menglun Zhigui* by Qian Yushan;
there is nothing that does not accord. These were all those whom I have long revered as my teachers. It was once while I was in the mountains of Dengwei...

I have previously composed ten treatises on delusion as well as a "Summary of Essentials. I myself regret that these are merely the words of a pedant, for I am utterly devoid of any realization of the truth.

Now, having been able to follow and contemplate the Right View, my speech will surely proceed from the heart. This shall serve as a means to seek correction from others in the future, so that I may settle my mind and clear my vision.
To silently realize the true dharma, one should offer ten handfuls of incense and reverently strike the *ghanṭā* before the ritual vase and whisk.
Written on a winter day in the Jia-mao year of the Kangxi era by the Dharma-brother from Kunshan, Sheng Fusheng, at the age of eighty-five.

The introductory draft of the solicitation states: "The First Patriarch came from the West not to establish written words, but to point directly to the human mind, so that one may see one's nature and become a Buddha.
Yet Yantou also said: "One cannot give a real dharma to others. Furthermore, at the assembly of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the World-Honored One said: "I have [forty]..."
For nine years he preached the Dharma, yet never uttered a single word. Thus, even within the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, it is said:
"Where there is only verbal expression, there is no real meaning at all. One can see that the successive transmission from Buddha to Patriarch has never followed a divergent path;

it is like a great mass of fire or a drum smeared with poison, leaving no lingering traces and admitting no conceptualization. Should one hesitate for even a moment, one immediately falls into a pit or a ditch.

How could there be any room for mere verbal discourse? Yet, observing the great masters of antiquity throughout the ages, there were none who did not profoundly clarify the vehicles of the teachings and extensively master the internal scriptures.
They gave voice to subtle words regarding the essential tenets and entrusted profound principles to their deep and far-reaching discourses.

Although they upheld the pivotal mechanism of the "Direct Transmission Above," they also comprehensively mastered the keys to both Nature (xìng) and Characteristics (xiàng). This was because they deeply understood the future generations.
Those who are狂誕 (frivolous and arrogant) take blind acupuncture and blind moxibustion as the "Direct Pointing" and coarse fists and chaotic clubs as their "gate and courtyard.

Not only do they fail to investigate the underlying principles, but they are even ignorant of the terminology. Therefore, I deeply pity such people and have secretly bestowed these expedient means before them.
If this is so, how could one not study the ocean of the teachings? I, Lou Xingfu Chan [Master].
The temple is an ancient site of practice. The Abbot, the Great Monk Huìgōng, is the son of Línghǐn Jùgōng and the grandson of Sānfēng Hàn'wēng.
He has mastered the strategy of "seizing food and driving the plow" and wields the skillful means of "cooking Buddhas and forging patriarchs.
He concealed his horns and tusks by the waterside and beneath the forest trees, yet he revealed his claws and fangs amidst fragments of paper and worn-out manuscripts before the Dharma Hall.
Even though the weeds may grow as deep as ten feet, he truly maintains the legacy of the ancient masters. He never uses the bustle of his gate to ensnare the monastics of this age.
Having resided here for many years, he does not inquire at all about matters outside his door; he is truly an outstanding figure among all quarters.
My family has served the Buddha for generations, and my late father devoted himself to the study of the Buddhist scriptures; although I myself am utterly ignorant in this regard—

Kui remarked, "However, by nature I delight in associating with those beyond the secular world. I have long admired the lofty character of the Master, yet I have not had the fortune to receive his personal guidance.
Recently, a guest brought a scroll and showed it to me, saying it was 'The Correct Vision of the Śūraṅgama,' composed by Master Hui.
As I read the first fascicle with deep reverence, I involuntarily raised my hands to my forehead and exclaimed: 'This is indeed the Supreme Vehicle of all Buddhas...'"
O Wise Life! This is the primary cause for sentient beings, the grand framework of the scriptures, and the essential gateway of the Chan school.
Those who wish to clarify the mind and perceive their nature should all devote themselves to this with utmost sincerity.

Some may say that since Master Hui was a successor to Sanfeng and Lingyin, he ought to have greatly revitalized the secrets of the Five Houses and the source of the Three Essentials; yet instead, he applied himself minutely to these [minor matters].
Regarding these words and phrases: why are they here? I know there is a profound intention behind them.
It is likely because [the Master] observed that those today who call themselves scholars merely clench their fists and point their fingers, following established conventions like the wind;

therefore, he used these to manifest the luminosity of his own original ground and stood out preeminently among the crowd. However, as for those who have interpreted this sutra, from the Tang dynasty until the present day...
The number of such individuals is beyond counting. Among those most renowned are Changshui, Wenling, Tianru, and Juefan. In sum, each saw his own strengths;
yet when one examines their ultimate aim, they are largely the same with only minor differences. They may be compared to diverse streams that all flow back into the sea.
Now, having read this collection, it perfectly accords with the Buddha’s mind and elucidates profound meanings. It does not merely repeat the leftover words of predecessors;
rather, every phrase flows forth from the depths of the author’s own heart. Truly, every word captures the very marrow, and every character probes for the pearl.

This is indeed a bridge and a ferry for sentient beings of the final age who study the Buddha-dharma. Reading this, one further understands that the Master’s practice and realization were in perfect accord, and how he taught others—without fail.
I am weary. There are those who are beyond my reach; how can they be compared to those who are merely called "knowledgeable" friends?
It is only fitting that this be entrusted to the woodcarvers to be spread throughout the realms of dust.

However, as the volumes are vast and my resources for alms are limited, unless great donors and faithful believers generously contribute the funds for carving, by what means could this superior cause be accomplished? Although I am...

Preface. I venture to offer these few words as an exhortation, briefly recounting the sincere hardships endured in the pursuit of the Dharma, in order to encourage my fellow practitioners who delight in goodness to empty their purses and provide assistance.
I am confident that there will surely be those who nod in agreement and grant their consent, not regarding my words as mere empty rhetoric.
This serves as the preface. Written with prostrations by the Elder Wang Suian of Taiyuan.
The Scripture on the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, the Ultimate Meaning of the Secret Cause for Cultivating and Realizing Enlightenment of the Tathāgata’s Great Uṣṇīṣa,
and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas: Volume One, *Zhengjian* (Correct Vision),
composed by the Śramaṇa Jishi, residing at the Ancient Xingfu Chan Monastery in Lousong.

Among the three titles in the heading, they are: Buddha, Tathāgata, and Bodhisattva. Among the three meanings within the Dharma, they are: the Summit (*mūrdhan*), the Cause (*hetu*), and the Practice (*caryā*).
Practice refers to function; cause refers to meaning; and the summit refers to the ultimate, the pinnacle—the designation for that which is unsurpassed.
Furthermore, "Buddha" means awakening (*bodhi*); this awakening is not the awakening of a phenomenal event, but rather primordial awakening (*mūla-bodhi*).
Awakening (*jue*). Because original awakening (*ben-jue*) is unsurpassed, it is called the "Crown" (*ding*). "As-it-is" (*ru*) means non-coming;

since coming must have a cause, it is called the "Cause" (*yin*), which refers to the subtle selection of the tainted mind (*lou-xin*). "Realization" (*zheng*) is a designation for the definitive meaning (*liao-yi*);

that is to say, because the cause is subtle, one is able to come, and because realization is exhaustive, one is able to be as-it-is. Now, "as-it-is" is also awakening, and "coming" is also awakening. Why is it not called "awakening" here, but rather...?
The term "Tathāgata" signifies the meaning of the Dharma as it truly is; it refers to that which is realized through the profound mystery.
The term "Bodhisattva" is a designation based on both awakening and application. The awakening and application of ordinary beings are not true awakening; they are deluded awakening.
The awakening and application of a Bodhisattva is true awakening, not deluded awakening. Delusion is empty, while truth is real. Because it is real, it follows [the nature of reality].

Conditions do not change; yet because they are empty, they cause stagnation wherever one encounters them. Therefore, when a Bodhisattva realizes this ultimate awakening, they give rise to function from that awakening.
Function does not lose its essence, and essence does not obstruct function. Thus, it is manifested in every head and penetrates through every object;
though undergoing a thousand transformations and ten thousand changes, it is inexhaustible. Hence it is said: "The practitioner is the function. This is the single phrase of the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*.
This summarizes the three meanings mentioned above. In the Sanskrit language it is *śūraṅgama*; here it is translated as "all-pervasive ultimate solidity.

This means that it is ultimately solid in its essence, ultimately solid in its function, ultimately solid in principle, and ultimately solid in phenomena. In short, there is nowhere that is not *śūraṅgama*.
This refers to the Great Samādhi of the Śūraṅgama; thus it is said: "The nāga is always in samādhi; there is no time when he is not in samādhi. This is precisely that meaning.

Furthermore, as a general rule for all sūtras, they are explained by dividing them into three parts: the introductory section (nidāna), the main body (samyak-siddhānta), and the dissemination section (parīndanā).

The introductory section (nidāna) and the concluding section (parīndanā) will be evident from the text itself. As for the main body of the teaching (saddharma), the text is divided into five major sections.
The first is *miao shemotuo* (妙奢摩他); in Sanskrit, this is *śamatha*, which here is translated as "quiescence" (*jijing*) or "calming" (*zhi*).

This is the explanation of the single phrase "Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa. The passage in the Sūtra from the seven investigations and ten demonstrations, through the refutation of the delusions of the three aggregates and the revelation of the nature of the seven elements, constitutes its textual content.
As for the *samāpatti*, the Sanskrit term *samāpatti* means "wondrous concentration" (*miaoding*) or "contemplation" (*guan*); this is the explanation of the Tathāgata’s secret cause.

A single phrase: in the sutra, from Subhūti’s objection based on grasping at characteristics to the nature, up until the teaching of the two definitive meanings—where the six dissolve and the one perishes—this constitutes the textual passage.
As for the third *dhyāna*, the Sanskrit term *dhyāna* means "cultivation of tranquil contemplation" (*jìjìng sīwéi xiū*) here;
it is also called the "Middle Way. This explains the single phrase regarding the myriad practices of the Bodhisattva. In the sutra, from... [text continues].
The twenty-five sages set forth their accounts of perfect penetration, culminating in the instruction for Mañjuśrī to select the most suitable faculty; such is the text.
Regarding the fourth, the "Initial Expedient Means": the Sanskrit term is *upāyakauśalya*, which is translated here as "expedient means" (*fangbian*).

This refers to the final five hundred years, when one is very far removed from the Buddha. Since there is no longer the opportunity to present oneself before the Sage’s face, and furthermore, a lack of guidance to set one on the path...
The Way is profound and its depths are mysterious; by what means can it be realized? Therefore, one must provisionally establish methods to serve as gateways for beginners to enter into virtue.

Within the sutra, the passage from the three gradual stages, through the construction of the altar and the recitation of mantras, up to the detailed exposition of the fifty-five stages of true Bodhi, and finally Mañjuśrī’s request for the title and the conclusion of the scripture—these are the texts that constitute this method.
As for the remainder of these five expedient means (*upāya*), it is truly because upon the essence of the one truth, there are originally no provisional names of "sentient beings" or "Buddhas.
Yet, within the myriad gates of phenomena (*dharmamukha*), there appear to be distinctions of grade regarding ascent and descent.

If one has not yet exhausted the three emptinesses (*śūnyatā*), how can one attain the perfect fusion of the single reality? Therefore, following the primary teaching, the sutra does not decline to employ the mind of expedient means.

From the internal divisions within the middle section, extending to the "Ten Habits" and "Six Interactions," it explains the three good destinies, the three evil destinies, and the seven realms of existence including the *asura*s; such is the text.
The five major sections mentioned above constitute the *zhengzongfen* (the main body of the teaching).
The subsequent section of the sutra, which specifically elucidates the fifty kinds of *skandha-māras* until its conclusion, belongs to the *liutongfen* (the dissemination portion).

Generally speaking, regarding the fundamental purport of this entire sutra, its scope and timing, and its divisions and flavors, all schools of thought hold settled views; these shall not be described in detail here. However, since this sutra...
The Perfect Ultimate of the One Vehicle is the primary tenet; the definitive meaning is the goal. How could one seek it merely within the traces of the teachings or the literal words?
One must necessarily possess wondrous awakening, leaping directly across in a single stride to sweep away the fragmentation of intellectual views and penetrate the Dharma-eye of perfect luminosity.
Only then can one erect the great banner of the Dharma, perpetuate and honor the Triple Gem, and become a true bearer of the Dharma.
This accords with the Buddha’s intent. Next, there are those who have resolved to attain the Great Mind and study the Way, yet because of past obstructions they cannot enter awakening.
They must follow the Buddha’s grand regulations and train through the three gradual stages, reciting the *Buddhōṣṇīṣa-prabhāsa-dhāraṇī*.

By hollowing out the mind to enter into principle, and as this entry into principle becomes profoundly deep, the mind naturally opens and one perceives the Way. Therefore, the first half of this sutra...

The first half opens the gate of the Sudden Teaching, while the latter half opens the gate of the Gradual Teaching. The divine mantras spoken by the transformation Buddhas from the light on the crown of the head manifest inconceivable and wondrous efficacy.
Throughout the middle section as well, expedient vehicles are briefly indicated to accord with the grand principle of the Great Vehicle.

This is called the teaching of non-fixed [categories]. All who apply their minds to study this—regardless of whether they are great or small, comprehensive or limited, partial or perfect—once they enter this school, shall all reach the shore of the Way. By this one knows that this sutra exhausts all essential natures;
it analyzes and clarifies with such brilliance as a south-pointing chariot for one traveling across the ocean, or like a standard of trust held by a general leading his army.
If scholars obtain this, what could they not master? Therefore, I exhort those who sincerely study the Way:
you should devote your whole hearts to it.
The Preface is divided into three parts: 1. The Constant Preface (Cháng xù). 2. The Specific Preface (Bié xù). 3. The Circumstantial Preface (Yīnyuán xù). First, the Constant Preface.
"Thus have I heard: at one time the Buddha was [staying] together with one thousand two hundred and fifty people.

These are the words used at the time of the compilation (*saṃgīti*). Generally, all sūtras are explained according to the "sixfold perfection" (*ṣaḍ-ākāra-sampad*), and therefore this shall not be further explained here.
Regarding the present context, from "Thus have I heard" down to "at such-and-such place" should be read as a single sentence; thus it constitutes the *nidāna* (introduction).
[The power of] force. Why? Is the city of Śrāvastī not a defiled realm of great wealth and desire?
Is the Jetavana Monastery not a sublime place of detachment from desire and tranquility? Where does the Buddha reside right now?
Does he reside in the pure, or does he reside in the defiled? Long ago, when the Tiantai Master Zhizhe was reading the *Lotus Sūtra*...
Sutra: "To reach this point is true diligence; this is called the true Dharma-offering to the Tathāgata.
At this, one attains thorough awakening and personally beholds the single assembly on Vulture Peak as if it were still present, never having dispersed.

If you can now truly grasp this meaning with complete penetration, I know that such a person has come directly from the Jeta Grove and can say: "Such a Dharma as this, I have heard from the Buddha. Do not...
Mistaken.
All are untainted Great Arhats.
The phrase "all are untainted Great Arhats" serves as a general heading. To praise such people and yet have this...
Virtue. Virtue consists of six phrases, namely: body, speech, and mind; precepts, concentration, and wisdom. Furthermore, these six phrases may be condensed into three, namely:
body, speech, and mind—which are themselves precepts, concentration, and wisdom. Moreover, when these three phrases are minutely examined, they are one:
that is, a single person who possesses this body, speech, and mind, as well as these precepts, concentration, and wisdom. Thus, a single person possesses this one [set].
"Three times six" means that each of the one thousand two hundred and fifty followers individually possesses this "three times six.
That we now single out six individuals and their six virtues is merely a matter of mutual manifestation and mutual concealment. Therefore, they are collectively praised with these titles.
All of them were great Arhats free from outflows. Furthermore, "Arhat" is translated as "Worthy of Offerings" (應供).
Such persons are capable of wandering to transform others and are capable of receiving offerings. Is it not the case that Ānanda lacked this virtue and possessed a mind still subject to outflows?
"The Buddha-sons abide in their office and skillfully transcend all realms of existence" (up to "together with those at the initial stage of resolve, they come to the Buddha's presence").
The section beginning with "Buddha-sons" lists them individually. Regarding "The Buddha-sons abide in their office and skillfully transcend all realms of existence":

this indicates the virtue of the body (*kāya-guṇa*), for which Śāriputra serves as the representative. Śāriputra is also called "Son of Śārī"; he possesses the virtue of the body, and furthermore, [he received it] from the Buddha’s own mouth.

Born from the Dharma through transformation, he is called a "Son of the Buddha. Because he is well able to transcend the twenty-five realms of existence and is well able to uphold the Buddha-Dharma, he is designated by this title.

Second, regarding "one who can achieve dignified deportment within the land," this indicates the virtue of intention (*āśaya-guṇa*), for which Maudgalyāyana is the representative. This is because Maudgalyāyana possesses supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), which constitutes his virtue of intention.

Therefore, he was able to achieve dignified deportment within the realm. As for "dignified deportment," it refers to attaining mastery and composure within the four modes of conduct—walking, standing, sitting, and reclining—and is thus designated by this term.

Third, regarding "one who follows the Buddha’s wheel-turning and is wonderfully worthy of being entrusted with final instructions," this indicates excellence in oral virtue, exemplified by Mahākauṣṭhila. This is because Kauṣṭhila...
Eloquence. Possessing the power of oratorical skill—this is the inconceivable wheel of his mouth.
Therefore, he is capable of assisting the Buddha in turning the wheel of Dharma and is capable of receiving the final entrustment; for this reason, he is so titled.

Regarding "The fourfold purity of the *vinaya* establishes a broad model for the three realms," this indicates the excellence of his preceptual virtue, and Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra is assigned to this role. As for Pūrṇa:

He is translated as Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra. His father’s name was Pūrṇa and his mother’s name was Maitrāyaṇī; thus, his fellow practitioners of the holy life called him "the son of Pūrṇa and Maitrāyaṇī.

Because he was fully endowed with the virtue of the precepts, he was able to strictly purify the Vinaya and was able to propagate the model for the three realms, acting as a teacher for humans and devas;
therefore, he was designated by this title. Fifth, as for the immeasurable deliverance of sentient beings through the five response bodies:

The designation of the virtue of merit (*guṇa*) is represented by Subhūti. Subhūti is translated as "Born of Emptiness" (*Kūṭastha*). He truly cultivates the meditative concentration of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*).

Because this concentration can give rise to functional application, he is able to manifest immeasurable response-bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*). Because emptiness can deliver one from suffering, he is able to liberate sentient beings; for these reasons, he is so named.
Sixth, regarding "rescuing the future and transcending all worldly burdens," this designates the virtue of wisdom (*prajñā*).
He is designated by the name Upānisaḍa. "Upā" here is translated as "dust-nature" (rajas).
Because he was able to realize that the nature of dust is empty, and because this emptiness is his wisdom, he was able to rescue and deliver future beings, transcending all worldly defilements;
therefore, he is so named. The six persons and their six virtues mentioned above are the pillars of the assembly, and furthermore, they are... [the text continues].
The fundamental principle of the sutras is precisely what is referred to as the simultaneous presentation of both person and dharma. However, the Dharma cannot exist as a mere abstraction;
it must rely upon a person to uphold it. Likewise, a person cannot exist as a mere individual; they must abide by means of the Dharma.
Whenever a sutra designates a person or highlights their virtues, it is truly for the purpose of indicating the assembly of dharmas. Reflect on this. II. The Specific Introduction (Nidāna).
Regarding the passage from "The bhikṣus concluded their summer retreat and performed the *pravāraṇā* ceremony" up to "with Mañjuśrī as the leader":

outside of the standard introductory sequence, the sūtra author separately introduces the characteristics of what is to be remedied by the Three Vehicles. The single phrase "concluded their summer retreat" generally indicates the time;

the section from "the *pravāraṇā*" onwards concerns the characteristics of what is to be remedied. This means that the fruit of Buddhahood remedies the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and therefore [this section exists].
The posture of spreading out a seat signifies the state of peaceful composure; because Bodhisattvas govern their hindrances, there is the posture of freely resolving doubts.

Because Śrāvakas govern their outflows (*āsrava*), there is the posture of freely examining one's own faults. These are the postures governed according to the specific tenets of each of the Three Vehicles.
If one looks at them from the perspective of other schools (*tīrthika*), it is likewise no different. Thus, there are [postures as numerous as] the sands of the Ganges.

This section on the Bodhisattvas gathering at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) is composed as such because, for the most part, those of the Three Vehicles abide according to their respective teachings.
However, if one seals this with the principle of the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), there is not even the designation of "Two Vehicles" or "Three Vehicles."
How could there be any distinction between one’s own school and other schools?
For this sutra takes the wondrously luminous true awakening as its essence and the perfectly bright, quiescent wisdom as its function; therefore, it designates Mañjuśrī alone to embody them.
This is the skillful method of the sutra’s prologue, which one must understand. △ III. The Prologue of Causes and Conditions.

while the body has coming and going, the nature has no movement or stillness. The Buddha approved all of this. If so, it seems there is a certain comprehension.
Therefore, it is likened to suddenly encountering one's compassionate mother. Nevertheless, I simply do not know which of these is the true reality.
If you recognize that this very body and this very mind are the truth, they are nonetheless phenomena subject to arising and ceasing before your eyes.

If you recognize that this very body and this very mind are delusion, the Buddha manifest before you is nevertheless permitted to be the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing. Thus, one hesitates between these two pillars:
is what is before one ultimately true or false? Are the body and mind subject to arising and ceasing, or are they not?
"Is it extinguished? Therefore, we pray that the Tathāgata will reveal the true and the false, the real and the unreal of body and mind, and manifest before us the two natures of luminosity:
that which is subject to arising and ceasing, and that which is neither-arising-nor-ceasing.
At that time, King Prasenajit rose and addressed the Buddha, saying: "All those who possess outflows likewise desire to hear this."

Now, teachings consist of the inner school and the outer school. The inner school does not transcend the single mind; the outer school does not depart from the two views of annihilationism and eternalism.
These two views are not identical to the single mind; rather, they arise erroneously from without, deviating from and confusing true permanence.
Therefore, they are called "outer. Even if the inner school is indeed the single mind, if one lacks right view, one will instead become attached to it.
Deluded views have caused confusion within our own school, making it appear as though we were outsiders; therefore, this must be clarified.

Now, Ānanda has been cornered by the Buddha’s inquiry until he is at a loss for words—unable to speak of the mind, unable to speak of nature, unable to speak of seeing, and unable to speak of not seeing.
This is precisely the point of difficulty. For this reason, Śāriputra steps forward from the side to apply a sudden pressure, seeking to...
To revitalize Ānanda’s potential, he clarified the distinction between the internal and the external. Regarding Puṣya (Pó-sī-ní), this is translated as "Harmonious Joy" or "Victorious Army.
"King" (*rāja*) carries the meaning of being sovereign and is a title for one who holds mastery.
The Buddha’s intention was that a person who studies the Way attains mastery over the five aggregates; such a person is indeed a "Victorious Army" amidst birth and death.
Only when one attains great mastery within can one truly be called harmonious and joyful. Observing this, the "hidden" (the ultimate reality) is precisely like this;
therefore, I have borrowed these words to manifest its meaning. Generally speaking, when language reaches its limit, it is extremely difficult to express.

For this reason, I establish an image to clarify its intent, requiring people to take responsibility for what lies beyond words, so as not to fall into views of annihilationism, eternalism, arising, or ceasing.
This is precisely where one gains strength in the study of the Way. Kātyāyana is his clan name; his personal name is Kālodāyin. He maintained that all phenomena both exist and do not exist.
Vīrāḍhiputra—Vīrā being the name of his mother—is his alternative designation, Śanayin. He maintained that all phenomena possess an inherent nature.
These are all the doctrines of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) characterized by the view of annihilationism. Later, Ānanda [will explain] this through causes...
Regarding the objection concerning the nature of spontaneity (*svabhāva*), this is the original text of that chapter:
"The Buddha said to the Great King: 'Your body exists now... [omitted] ...therefore, know that my body will ultimately undergo transformation and extinction.'"

From the passage beginning with "The Buddha said" onwards, the Buddha intends to dispel the *saṃjñā-skandha* (aggregate of perception) and point out the true permanence. First, he establishes two great pillars:
one to represent the adamantine eternal abiding, and one to represent birth-and-death and transformation-and-destruction. Now, first, he describes birth-and-death and transformation-and-destruction.

From the passage beginning with "World-Honored One, as for me now," he provides a general outline; from the passage beginning with "The Buddha said, Great King, you have never before ceased," he provides a specific analysis.
This describes the characteristics of arising and ceasing. The passage beginning with "The Buddha said, 'It is thus'" specifically describes the state of transformation and decay.

Furthermore, the passage beginning with "Moreover, Great King" again describes two kinds of birth and death: first, birth and death by stages (*pariccheda-maraṇa*); second, birth and death through transformation (*pariṇāma-maraṇa*).
From the King’s words below, the *pariccheda-utpāda-vināśa* (segmented birth and death) is described.

If I were further to describe the *pariṇāma-utpāda-vināśa* (transformative birth and death) below, generally speaking, transformative [death] is termed "momentary" (*kṣaṇa*), whereas segmented [death] is limited by years. Transformation and decay are spoken of in terms of form;
arising and ceasing follow the shifting of thought. This single period of arising, ceasing, transformation, and decay constitutes the entirety of sentient experience from beginning to end.
The outward form does not exceed this, yet the momentum of the writing possesses extreme cadence and restraint. Within the great there is the small;
within the coarse there is the fine; within the fine there is the subtle; and the subtle reaches its limit in the soundless.

It is like the transformative power of spring’s warmth, causing the myriad plants to flourish in fragrance, such that one is unaware of it until every flower has its own unique character, reaching its limit in the formless.
Furthermore, it is like a master painter who first lays out the composition and instructs his disciples to apply the colors;
they proceed until, without realizing it, they reach a point where they can no longer continue. One should know that the meaning of this passage is likewise so.

Simply observe that the World-Honored One questioned and Sāṇavāsin answered; the World-Honored One led the way first, and Sāṇavāsin followed behind, also without realizing it, yet the truth was attained.
This refers to a further layer of meaning beyond the words.
From the passage where the Buddha says to the Great King, "Do you see these transformations? down to the King’s reply, "No, World-Honored One," the text first addresses the transformations;
subsequently, it demonstrates that the Vajra is eternally abiding and indestructible. However, there are points of selection and emphasis.
First, King Ajātaśatru recounted that Kātyāyana claimed that the annihilation of this body after death is called *nirvāṇa*. The Buddha now challenged him, saying:
"Great King, at what age did you see the waters of the Ganges? The King replied: "When I was three years old, I passed by this stream and immediately knew it was the water of the Ganges.
[The Buddha then said: "King Ajātaśatru, I have previously described to you my observation of the present moment, moment by moment (*kṣaṇa-kṣaṇa*)."
Arising and ceasing; new and new, it does not abide. One must decisively know that this body shall eventually reach total extinction.
The Buddha now asked, "Great King, you said that at twenty years of age, when you were ten, you saw the waters of the Ganges River at the age of three.
When you reached thirteen, what was that water like? The King replied, "It was exactly the same as when I was three years old; there was no difference whatsoever. [At present, six...]

The tenth [point] is likewise without difference. Previously, King Nimi described how when I was a young child, my skin and flesh were smooth and lustrous, whereas now that I am advanced in years and pressed by decrepitude, my end is near. The Buddha then asked him:
"As you look at this Ganges River now, does the vision of the river you had in your childhood possess any quality of youth or old age? The King replied, "No."
World-Honored One, judging by this evidence: since the perception of the river remains unchanged from childhood to old age, is not King Ajātaśatru’s fear of death merely a futile exertion?
Moreover, if the nature of the river’s perception does not even undergo change, is King Ajātaśatru’s anxiety over its destruction not surely groundless?
Furthermore, at the age of three, he already recognized it as the waters of the Ganges.
Reflecting on this now, it remains vividly clear: is not the nihilistic view of the non-Buddhists a false and erroneous conception?
Judging from this, I do not believe that if one claims the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), it can be accepted as such.
The Buddha said, "Great King, although your face is wrinkled... [and so on] "...you leap for joy, experiencing what you have never had before.
This strikes away [the notion of change] to reveal the nature of true permanence. If one speaks in terms of worldly appearances, it seems as though there is decay and transformation;

yet if one observes with the Buddha-eye, it is truly identical to the diamond-like, eternally abiding, and indestructible. Therefore, he now strikes away [delusion] by saying: "That which is wrinkled..."
That which undergoes transformation yet does not wrinkle is non-transformative. If examined according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), there clearly appear arising and ceasing;

if investigated through ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), there is in reality no arising and ceasing. Therefore, it is now refuted: that which transforms undergoes cessation, while that which is unchanging is fundamentally free from arising and ceasing.
Discussing it thus, the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) are not true, whereas the nature of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is.
In reality, it is identical to the diamond-like [nature], eternally abiding and indestructible. How could the nihilistic doctrine of the non-Buddhist Makkhali Gosāla be worthy of belief?

The above has analyzed that the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is itself wondrous. What His Majesty King Ajātaśatru has described throughout this entire passage is the aggregate of perception; it is that which arises.
The Dharma of cessation taught by the World-Honored One is, throughout its entirety, the eternal principle; it is the Dharma of neither arising nor ceasing.

Whether as a single warp or a single woof, it is like weaving brocade. Yet, when one contemplates the intent of the World-Honored One, it is like a water-clearing jewel cast into the mud, or the light of the bright moon returning to a secluded valley—it cannot but be luminous, it cannot but be pure.
The exquisite fingers and their resonant tones cause people to listen with undiminished interest. △ Fourth, the movement itself is sublime.
Ānanda immediately rose from his seat... [until] "...I pray that you will arouse compassion to wash away my defilements."
This is because it was previously stated that while I see the Tathāgata’s hand opening and closing, it is not the nature of my seeing that has opening and closing.
Furthermore, while my head moves, the nature of my seeing does not even have stillness; what, then, could be shaking?
Yet the Buddha said all such things as if to acquiesce to me. But when it comes to the final reprimand, he asks: "Why do you now [regard] movement..."
"Taking the body as the self and movement as the object, one undergoes birth and extinction moment by moment, losing the true nature and acting in delusion.
Such profound censure seems almost like a refusal to accept me. Now, having come to see the Buddha, I hear that this perception of the river’s flow is fundamentally without arising or ceasing;
it is exactly the same as my own previous way of seeing. Because of this, a dispute has arisen."

[Ananda] held [the bowl]. He requested again, saying: "If this nature of seeing is necessarily neither born nor extinguished, why do you say that I have lost the true nature and act in a state of delusion?
Alas! If it is so, Ānanda, you not only do not know where you yourself are situated,"

Furthermore, you do not recognize the Buddha’s words; you fail to realize that the Buddha’s two instances of "thus" (rushi) were actually the setting of a trap for a tiger, and moreover, a point where the Buddha himself withdrew his own mechanism.
For if the tiger were not trapped, the mechanism would not be profound; and if the mechanism were not withdrawn, one's own school (zong) would remain unpenetrated.
Furthermore, the so-called "theory of the hidden king" is like a rider lying in ambush within the forest, anticipating [the enemy] in advance.
Ānanda held such a view. At that moment, as the Tathāgata lowered his golden arm, [Ānanda] did not realize that his body and mind were in a state of inversion.
The Buddha has but one arm, yet Ānanda perceived it as falling in two places; when the Buddha’s hand pointed downward, he called it "inverted."
When the Buddha points upward with his hand, it is called "correct. Yet, when asked where the names of its "inversion" reside, one is again utterly bewildered and knows not where they fall.
This reality is truly strange! One does not know from whom "correctness" was transmitted, nor from whom "inversion" was transmitted.
If you can understand this clearly, you will see that your own body and the Buddha’s body are but a single interval apart. What, then, is inversion? What is correctness?
How can this be described?
The Buddha, arising in compassion and pitying Ānanda... (up to)... "The Tathāgata says he is one who should be pitied.
Within the preceding inquiry by Ānanda, there are two points: first, an inquiry into the reality or falsity, and the truth or unreality, of body and mind; second, an inquiry into the present...
The case of King Pāyāsi regarding the nature of arising-and-ceasing versus non-arising-and-non-ceasing was intended to verify that arising-and-ceasing;
the episode of hanging down his arm was intended to examine its reality or unreality. Furthermore, what King Pāyāsi asked concerned the characteristics of arising-and-ceasing.
That which the Tathāgata points to is the meaning of non-arising and non-ceasing;

that which Ānanda has responded to is nothing other than inversion, while that which the Tathāgata has shown is nothing other than reality. Now, observing the Tathāgata’s examination in this manner, [it is clear].
Thus he pointed it out; yet Ānanda was entirely ignorant of the distinction between arising-and-ceasing and non-arising-non-ceasing, or between the real and the inverted.
For this reason, the Buddha gave rise to great compassion and revealed [the truth] (as follows). The text has two parts: first, a general explanation from the words "I have always said" onwards;
second, a specific explanation from the words "Obscured darkness becomes space" onwards. Regarding the first, the general explanation, [it concerns] form...

The two characters "mind" (citta) collectively refer to the triad of sense organs, objects, and consciousness. "Various conditions" refers to the grasping after wholesome and unwholesome karma and so forth.
"That which is driven" refers to the twenty-five states of existence within the three realms, including the seven destinies of humans and devas.
These karmic consciousnesses and mental compulsions do not exist in some separate location; they manifest solely upon one's own mind. Now, Ānanda does not understand this.

Regarding the true and the false, the real and the unreal of body and mind: it is because you have hitherto clung to the false while neglecting the true, and clung to the unreal while being deluded regarding the real.
You have never known that your body and your mind are both objects manifested within the wondrously luminous, essential, and marvelous mind.
To awaken is for the whole to be entirely true; to be deluded is for the whole to be entirely false. The false is precisely the unreal; the true is...
This is indeed so. It is like water forming ice, and the ice returning to water; they are of one essence by the very nature of things—how could there be anything else?

Why, then, do you below reproach him for his failure? This refers to his neglecting his own original, wondrous, and perfect mind, instead clinging to the delusory, illusory mind of the sense organs and objects;
failing to recognize awakening while recognizing delusion—this is a great error. Second, the specific explanation.

The three phrases beginning with "That which is obscured and darkened constitutes emptiness" re-explain the preceding character *se* (form). The two phrases beginning with "Form is intermingled with false conceptualization" re-explain the preceding character *xin* (mind).
The two phrases beginning with "Gathering conditions, it stirs within" re-explain the preceding character *yuan* (conditions).

The three phrases beginning with "A state of turbid and restless appearance" re-explain the preceding character *shi* (driving forces). The three phrases beginning with "Not knowing the physical body" are a re-explanation of the preceding phrase "it is solely mind."
To discuss these two characters in general terms: within the wondrously luminous mind, a single moment of non-awakening is called ignorance (*avidyā*).
Because of this lack of clarity, it results in the dark and obscure void. This void, characterized by the obscuration of form, is called "stolid emptiness" (*jaḍa-śūnyatā*).

When the mind is ensnared by form, it is called "deluded thought" (*vikalpa*). Following the influence of karma, thought gives rise to a body; from this, the faculties of seeing, perceiving, hearing, and so forth become differentiated.
[He] knows that it agitates its own nature. The six faculties of reception rush headlong toward their objects;
having disturbed the source, they lose sight of the root. Setting aside other matters for a moment, consider Ānanda this very day:

he takes the Buddha’s hand as his mind, takes the *tūla* cotton as his form, takes the white, pure, soft, and smooth as the condition, and reckons the pointing up and down of the fingers as [the object].
Driven by the mind, at such a time, if you grasp for the Buddha’s hand, you lose your own mind; if you grasp for your own mind, you lose the Buddha’s hand.
Since neither can be attained, you do not know where the name of this delusion resides.
You fail to realize that from the physical body outward to the mountains, rivers, space, and the great earth—all are objects within the wondrously luminous true mind, like reflections in a mirror.
The image contains the mirror; the image is still the mirror. It is formed by a single dharma and does not exist externally. This is like the following analogy used to reprove delusion:
the bubble is the ocean, and the ocean is the bubble. Yet people today know only the bubble and do not know it is the ocean;
they know only that this lump of flesh is the self, without realizing that both your body and your mind are entirely within the ocean.
It is like a bubble on water or a reflection in a mirror; one does not know which to point to as real and which as false, nor which is empty and which is substantial.
Therefore it is said: "You all are people who are doubly deluded within delusion.
You are no different from my hanging down my hand; you are truly objects of pity."

The above analysis of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is thus complete. Question: Since this is the aggregate of formations, why is it discussed in connection with the five aggregates?

Answer: The aggregate of formations is the chief minister among all the aggregates; without it, the other aggregates would not arise. It is because the aggregate of formations arises that the continuity of the various aggregates is established.
Therefore, this section treats the various conditions of form and mind, as well as the mental factors (*caitta*) and secondary afflictions (*anuśaya*).
"Indication" refers precisely to the discourse on the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). △ Fifth, consciousness itself is the wondrous.
Ānanda, having received the Buddha’s compassionate rescue and profound instruction, [said: "...uprooting my root of doubt, I shall return to the unsurpassed Way."
Ever since Ānanda first received the Buddha’s instruction, he has recognized that fundamental enlightenment (benjue) is without awareness.

Yet, if he were to grasp at this "absence of awareness," he fears falling into the view of nihilism (uccheda-dṛṣṭi), and thus he does not dare to acknowledge it. He has also recognized that initial enlightenment (shijue) possesses awareness.

Yet, if he were to grasp at this "presence of awareness," he fears falling into the view of eternalism (śāśvata-dṛṣṭi), and thus he does not dare to acknowledge it. If he relies on both, he falls into the extremes; even a middle position would then be a mere empty fabrication.
In all cases, you have fallen into external views; therefore, you dare not recognize it. If there were no seeing-consciousness at all, you would again have nowhere to emerge.

Now, hearing the sound of the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma, you have awakened to this wondrous clarity that was originally perfect and complete, this湛然 (zhanran—tranquil and lucid) awareness and realization as being your own mind.
Yet, you still dare not recognize it because Ānanda has been taking empty steps from the very beginning.
This was merely to invite the World-Honored One to bear witness. This Ānanda did not realize that the mind of conditions is an object of inference (anumāna);
he mistakenly took it to be of the nature of direct perception (pratyakṣa), and thus made such a statement. Question: What is the distinction between direct perception and inference?
He said: "When the five sensory objects first reach the sense organs, they have not yet entered the realm of the mental consciousness; this is the object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
It passes away in a single moment—how could there be any room for deliberation or conjecture in that interval?
What Ānanda has now presented is merely inference (*anumāna*), not true direct perception. Therefore, the Buddha distinguished it for him, saying: 'You all still use the mind of conditions...'"

Hearing the Dharma—this mind also takes it as an object, yet it does not attain the nature of dharmas (dharmatā). What is called "taking as an object" refers to the mind relying upon an objective realm;
how could this be anything other than the inferential cognition (anumāna) of the aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha)?
Therefore, it is clear that what Ānanda has presented is merely inferential cognition belonging to the aggregate of consciousness, and is certainly not true direct perception (pratyakṣa).
The Buddha told Ānanda: "You and others [should understand that] even up to the point of being free from the conditions of all dharmas, there is a nature devoid of discrimination.
The two metaphors in the text are clear and can be understood. However, Ānanda did not observe the moon but observed the finger;
he did not realize the truth but realized the false. This was an error in his application of mind. Furthermore, the innkeeper is not like a temporary guest who comes and goes. The Truth...

How could the nature follow conditions through the mind’s discrimination? Since there is discrimination, it is clearly the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), not the path of true permanence.
Suppose they offer this defense: "When my present mind encounters conditions, I do not grasp at the characteristics of sound; therefore, there is no arising or ceasing.
If, because one does not grasp at the characteristics of sound, there is no arising or ceasing, then true nature itself must possess discrimination. This is not so.
It arises in dependence upon conditions. Now, apart from the characteristic of sound, how could there be a nature devoid of discrimination?

It is not only the characteristic of a single sound that is thus; the characteristics of all six sense objects are likewise so. Apart from the conditions of all phenomena, there is no nature devoid of discrimination.

While the nature itself is non-discriminative, it can be said that there is a mind that conditions it—is this not a matter concerning the limits of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*)? When compared with this...
The non-Buddhists [rely on] the *Kośa* (Abhidharmakośa), yet they do not understand that it regards the *mūlaprakṛti* (primordial nature) as the ultimate truth.
While their nature is no different from that of Ānanda, they falsely calculate that there is a mind conditioned by objects; to explain them as being otherwise is impossible.
"Then the nature of your mind each has its place of return... (up to)... I pray you will deign to show compassion and explain this for me.
The World-Honored One pointed out that Ānanda’s mental nature exists only through the convergence of conditions; when conditions disperse, it ceases to exist.
"How can this be your true master? This single question alone seizes away all one's private property. Furthermore—
He presented his objection, and Ānanda then spoke with stubborn persistence: "The natures of my various faculties each have their respective objects to which they return.

When the Tathāgata speaks of the wondrous, luminous, primordial mind, how can it be said that it has no place to return? Looking at this, although their words were as sharp as the meeting points of two flying arrows, [it was a subtle exchange].
Little do you realize that your entire body is already within the bowstring’s range.
The Buddha said to Ānanda: "Furthermore, as for what you see me [do]... now I shall show you the ground where there is no returning."
This point is made by addressing the guest in order to reach the host. Why? When the Buddha was before Ānanda, Ānanda himself should have seen the Buddha.
Although "your seeing of my seeing" is not the original nature—being like a second moon produced by pressing [the eye]—it is certainly not the seeing of another; it is truly Ānanda’s own.
That which is seen by the essence of your own seeing need not be returned. How do we know this? It is like a reflection of the moon that emerges from the true moon;
one can say there is a principle of it returning back. Now, your seeing of me is like a second moon;
it is produced by Ānanda himself through pressing [his eyes]. To whom, then, could it return? Furthermore, if it were not...
“Have faith! I now show you the ground from which there is no returning.
Ānanda, this great lecture hall opens wide toward the east... for this reason, the Tathāgata is called ‘the Compassionate One.’”
The World-Honored One, wishing to demonstrate the ground of no-return, first enumerates the characteristics of that which does have a place of return.
From "Ānanda, from this great lecture hall downward" to "enumerate the eight places of return," and from "Ānanda, you look at all these things below" to "marking the locations of the eight returns":
since these eight characteristics each have a place of return, you should examine the essential nature of the clarity of seeing within these eight kinds.

"When you wish to return something, to whom would you return it?"—this single question was intended to lead Ānanda to realize for himself that the nature of his own seeing is without anything to return.
As for the passage beginning "Why is this?", it provides a separate explanation of the absence of anything to return.

This demonstrates that although the characteristics of things that *can* be returned may differ, your seeing that is *without* anything to return is no different. Therefore, the conclusion states: "All those things that can be returned are naturally not you. It does not...
That which returns to you is none other than Ānanda’s own fundamental nature. Thus, you should know that your mind below [this] rebukes Ānanda for having lost his own fundamentally wondrous,
bright, pure, and non-returning nature, instead following these eight kinds of deluded thoughts and their returning objects,
drifting and drowning in the cycle of birth and death all day long— a state truly to be pitied.
The above has clarified that the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is itself subtle. The mind that takes conditions as its object is precisely the aggregate of consciousness.

Consciousness is able to differentiate various forms and appearances (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*), for if it were separated from forms and appearances, it would lack a nature of differentiation. The mind that differentiates sounds differentiates my own appearance.
All of this is the functioning of the conscious mind. Therefore, when the eight kinds of material forms are returned, there is nothing left to return—could this not be Ānanda’s own mind?
4. Opening the Eye of My Way (5 sections): 1. Opening form to realize the Way; 2. Opening sensation to realize the Way; 3.
Opening perception to realize the Way; 4. Opening mental formations to realize the Way; 5. Opening consciousness to realize the Way.
The first [case] is attaining the Way through the manifestation of form.
Ānanda said, "Although I recognize that this nature of seeing is without anything to be returned, how can I know it to be my true nature?

Previously, having received the Buddha’s instruction, Ānanda recognized that the characteristics of consciousness have things to which they return; these all belong to the conditions of sensory objects and are subject to return. It is only the nature of seeing that is without return.

Its nature is simply oneself; this is truly beyond doubt. However, since this essence of vision is said to be "me," yet now that it is separated from external conditions, it lacks the capacity for discernment.
Even regarding its state of non-return, it is difficult to accept as one's own.
Thus, having given rise to doubt, he asks: "Ultimately, how can I know that this is my true nature?"
The Buddha said to Ānanda, "I now ask you" (up to) "you should herein distinguish between self and other.
Ānanda did not know the true nature. The Buddha’s intention was to examine him through three stages: first, instructing him to examine himself; second, the Buddha examining him;
third, the teacher and disciple examining together. Regarding the first, the examination by himself, from the passage "The Buddha said to Ānanda" onwards, [the text] first sets forth [the inquiry].
Regarding the person who is able to see: starting from Ānanda and continuing down to myself, I shall now delineate the objects seen. You should issue a command to examine them yourself;

that is to say, there are differences among the three vehicles and the five eyes regarding the seer, and there are distinctions between the clarity and obscurity of material images regarding the seen.
If they differ, they differ from the object, not from the seeing. If they vary, they vary from...
Humanity does not deviate from its nature. Now, the nature of humans and the nature of things are clearly distinct and manifest before you;
you must discern them for yourself: "This is a certain person," "This is a certain view," "This is a certain thing," "This is a certain characteristic.
You must distinguish these clearly: is this the self-nature, or the nature of things? Is it one's own view, or the view of things? You must certainly...
This is clear. This is the teaching for Ānanda to personally discern [the fruit]. *Amala* translates as "difficult to distinguish.
A certain fruit resembles a peach but is not a peach; it resembles a crabapple (*nai*) but is not a crabapple.
"Now I shall lead you to discern [the nature] within seeing" (up to) "this is the subtle, wondrous, luminous, and sincere nature of your seeing.
Next, the Buddha selects [the true from the false]. First he establishes the standard, then he performs the selection. "Now I shall lead you..."—these two lines provide the general standard.

"Ānanda, exhaust the source of your seeing..."—this provides the specific selection. Now, by selecting the palaces of the sun and moon and so forth, [he shows that] these are all the natures of external objects; they are not seeing.
Nature. Why is this? To raise up a category is to refer to an object; within objects there is no nature of seeing. Therefore it is said: "All are objects, not you.
From the passage beginning with "Ānanda, these things near and far," [the Buddha] distinguishes that all things near and far are the nature of seeing, and not the nature of objects.
Why is this? To raise up the eyes is to refer to seeing; within seeing there is no nature of objects. Therefore it is said: "Truly..."
"You perceive the nature. Thus, although there are a thousand differences among these various objects, the nature you now perceive is without distinction.
I shall set aside the preceding objects; it is entirely Ānanda’s perception of the nature.
Why do you doubt yourself and fail to recognize your own true nature? This is the method by which the Buddha makes his selection.
"If you see this object, then you too [are the seer]... naturally [the object] is not the thing; why then would it not be you?
The three masters and their disciples together examined this. The Buddha’s intention was that my seeing of things such as blue or yellow is a "seeing of existence.
If your seeing were also of blue or yellow, it would constitute the same kind of seeing. To allow for your seeing me would be like the moon producing a second moon. Why?
Therefore, there is something within your nature that perceives my perception; hence it is said: "If one perceives in the same way as I do, this is called 'perceiving me.
If I do not perceive blue, yellow, and so forth, this is non-perception. Why do you not perceive my state of non-perception?
If you were to perceive non-perception, it would constitute a divergent perception, because perceiving me would be non-existent—just like the moon appearing with a halo. Why is this?
Therefore, because you see the Buddha within your own nature yet do not see him, it is said: "If you see, you do not see.
This is naturally not the characteristic of that non-seeing. Even if I have no seeing, you likewise have no seeing; this is precisely me having no you before my eyes.
Before you, there is no self; this constitutes true vision. Because the self is non-self, it is like the solitary moon in a tranquil night.
Why is this? Because within your nature there is no arising. Since your nature is without arising, it is without artifice.
What else could it be but Ānanda’s true nature? Therefore it is said: "If you do not see the ground of my not seeing, it naturally is not a thing. Thus it is spoken.
"What is it that is not you? Jia Shan said, "Before your eyes there is no master; here there is no old monk.
This is precisely the commentary on this passage of scripture.
Furthermore, when you now see an object (up to) "your nature is not true," you are seeking reality from me.
This concludes the summary of the preceding three meanings for the sake of discernment. Furthermore, from "Moreover, you now... onwards, the first meaning is analyzed.
When objects compete with the self and the mind opposes its objects, one is simply incapable [of realization]. Therefore, it is said: "Since you see objects, objects also see you;
their essential natures become confused and intermingled, such that they cannot be established in stability. Thus, I previously instructed you to [regard] objects...
Return the categories of things; see them returned to your side. By discerning them in this way, clarity will arise of its own accord. The second meaning is the same as this.
Next, the two lines following "Ānanda" distinguish the aforementioned third meaning: namely, "I" is my own view, and "you" is your own view.
Within my view there is no you; within your view there is no me. Even if each possessed the other, it would simply be non-identity.
It is established. Therefore it is said: "If you see at that time, it is you and not me; my seeing is non-existent, while you possess the act of seeing.
Thus, I previously distinguished this: if you see where I do not see, it naturally is not that which is characterized by non-seeing.
Why is this? Because within your nature there is the act of self-seeing (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*). The final two lines of the verse on the nature of seeing (*dṛṣṭi-svabhāva*) distinguish its true nature.
Furthermore, phenomena abide in their fixed positions; their characteristics are fundamentally empty from the start. If there is no clinging mind, the essence of nature is naturally all-pervasive;
hence it is said that "seeing the nature is universal pervasion. If it is not you, then who is it? Even if you do not accept this, whose fault would it be?
Therefore, I previously distinguished that if one does not see the ground where neither "I" nor "not-I" exists, it is naturally not a thing. How could it not be you? Because...
By this one knows: seeing only non-self is precisely Ānanda’s true nature. Why do you harbor doubts? This concludes the reprimand.
Previously, Ānanda asked: "Although I recognize that this seeing-nature has nothing to return to, how can I know it is my true nature?
Therefore, he now concludes by reprimanding Ānanda for doubting his own true nature, saying: "Your nature is not true."

"Take me and seek the truth. Formerly, the Sixth Patriarch asked Huiming: "Neither thinking of good nor thinking of evil—what is the original face of Elder Huiming? At these words, Huiming attained great enlightenment and said:
"Beyond this secret and profound discourse, is there still another secret meaning? The Patriarch replied: "That which I have spoken to you is not it."
It is secret. If you were to reflect back upon yourself, that secret would be right beside you. Now Ānanda does not turn his own light back to reflect and awaken to his original face;
instead, he seeks it outwardly, grasping for me and seeking the truth from others. Is this not the height of delusion and confusion?
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One... [omitted] ...I pray that you will bestow your great compassion and expound this for me.
Generally speaking, birth and death arise from the perception of impurity; it is simply because one clings to the shadows of both the holy and the profane."
Therefore, the World-Honored One first removed for him the shadows of external objects to purify his ordinary perceptions.
Once ordinary perceptions were purified, his noble perceptions still remained; thus, he further removed the shadow of the Buddha to purify those noble perceptions.

When both ordinary and noble sentiments were exhausted, the true and eternal essence was revealed, enabling Ānanda to uniquely awaken to the reality of his own nature—this is precisely the intent of the Buddha.

Now, Ānanda, it is not so. Although ordinary and holy beings may forget their distinctions, they still remain separated by the barrier of views. You claim that this seeing-nature must be yours alone and not that of others;
yet when you looked upward from here to the Hall of the Four Heavenly Kings and reached as far as the Sahā world—so vast in extent—and then returned to this vihāra, it filled only a single room.
Was it that the great was contracted into the small? Or was it that the walls and buildings cut it off?
Yes. This error arises because the Buddha’s words state that the nature of seeing is all-pervasive; from this, the thought "if it is not you, then who? is raised. Consequently, another doubt arises:
[this statement] is merely intended to smooth away the steepness of the waves of "seeing" for the sake of the subsequent text.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "All the worlds... [down to] 'furthermore, excluding the location of the characteristics of empty space.
From the point where the Buddha spoke downward, he generally refutes what is erroneous. Why? Because that which was previously shown by the World-Honored One is the true seeing of the mind;
whereas that which Ānanda now clings to is merely the shadow of material objects. If one calculates...
Objects are shadows. Not only are the palaces of the Four Heavenly Kings and the like shadows;
even your physical body and all the activities performed within the world are nothing but shadows. Why is this? Because they all belong to the external objects of perception.

Below, an analogy is raised to clarify this. The vessel is a metaphor for the physical body (the sense organs); the squareness and roundness are metaphors for the shadow; and empty space is a metaphor for true seeing. From the passage "Following the analogy... onwards:
first, the analogy is presented and its significance is questioned; second, from "If it were fixed as square... onwards, the nature of squareness and roundness is analyzed;

third, from "As for your statement that you do not know... onwards, the dharma and the analogy are combined to reveal the truth; fourth, from "Ānanda... onwards, the meaning of the analogy is reconciled and explained. The text is explicit.

This can be understood. It is because empty space has neither squareness nor roundness; rather, squareness and roundness reside in the vessel, and thus empty space appears square or round accordingly.

Ultimately, empty space possesses neither squareness nor roundness, nor does it possess the characteristic of being "without squareness or roundness. Therefore, it is said that the nature of its meaning is thus.
To claim now that empty space has squareness and roundness is merely the attachment of those who deal with vessels. This is what is called "seeing" [the truth].
There are distinctions of large and small; this is Ānanda’s clinging. Because Ānanda possesses clinging views, his perception expands or contracts accordingly.
Ultimately, true seeing has no expansion or contraction, nor does it have any measurable quantity of expansion or contraction. Therefore it is asked: "How can it be said to be 'within'?
If you do not cling to the vessel, then there will be no appearance of squareness, roundness, expansion, or contraction; thus it is said that it does not exist [therein].
Squareness and roundness have no expansion or contraction; nor do they exist apart from your grasping at your vessel and speaking of them.

How could true emptiness and true seeing possess squareness, roundness, expansion, or contraction that could be eliminated? Therefore it is said: "One should not speak of the location of the characteristic of squareness."
As for your question regarding the time of entering the room—whether there could not possibly be a continuation of the tracks—this interpretation is incorrect.
This analogy is cited to refute Ānanda’s doubt. That one sees something small upon entering the room, yet sees it as large when observing the sun, is what the deluded nature clings to;
the true nature possesses nothing of the sort. A wall can block [the path], but a hole must allow it to continue; this is merely what deluded vision perceives.
This is a delusion; in true vision, it does not exist. Therefore, he rebukes it, saying: "This interpretation is not so. This means that such a principle is absolutely non-existent.
All sentient beings, from beginningless time... [up to] ...are universally able to contain the lands of the ten directions.

All sentient beings will subsequently understand the convergence of the Dharma and its metaphors: just as space has no squareness or roundness, yet what we now perceive as square or round is merely the limitation imposed by the vessel;
so too, true nature is free from the view of self, yet that which we now perceive as a self-view is merely a delusion.
This is merely that sentient beings are deluded. Sentient beings are deluded because they are turned by external objects. Once turned by objects, they falsely perceive things as large or small;

this is the inevitable nature of affairs. If one can lower oneself and directly manifest the fundamental wondrousness, such that the emotions do not cling to objects, then all sentient beings are identical to the Tathāgata.
When the nature does not cling to views, the body and mind are fundamentally perfect and luminous.
Since the nature is already perfectly luminous, it universally encompasses the ten directions; seeing is identical to the awakening of the Buddha, and even a single speck of dust is wondrous.

Observing in this way, what nature would not be manifest, and what thing would not be true? However, the expression "transforming objects" is merely used in response to the conceptual attachments of sentient beings.
From Ānanda’s words: "Although I recognize that this nature of seeing has no place of return, how can I know it to be my true nature?
This passage marks the point where form is opened up to reveal the Way. Previously, the seeing was analyzed in relation to objects; here, the objects are analyzed in relation to the seeing.
When objects are analyzed in relation to the seeing, the objects are no longer mere objects; they are the wondrous functioning of the nature.
Distinguishing the nature of objects to clarify vision: what is seen is not truly "seeing. This seeing is the wondrous clarity of the fundamental nature.

Sentient beings inherently possess this wondrously luminous true nature, yet they remain unenlightened because they are constrained by the aggregate of form and falsely engage with external conditions.

Therefore, the Tathāgata employs the method of the golden probe to open their innate luminosity and restore them to their true nature. Once the nature has returned to its truth, there still remains "seeing."
Being obstructed, one can only resort to further metaphors to clarify it. The metaphor is that within emptiness there are no signs of squareness or roundness;
within seeing there is no sentiment of "self" or "other. If there is no self or other, what nature would not be true?
If one does not grasp at the vessel, what light would not penetrate? Thus, one function is a thousand functions; a thousand essences are but one essence. Xuan Sha said: "Exhausted..."
In this great earth, there is no second person. To whom, then, could the teaching be entrusted? This is precisely the meaning. II. Opening the Acceptance and Attaining Enlightenment.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One... (omitted)... I only pray that you will bestow your great compassion to reveal and awaken those who have not yet understood."
