Ānanda, pressed by the Buddha, realized that the nature of seeing does not reside within objects; if it were within objects, then one’s seeing would be attached to objects.
Nor does it reside within the body; if it were within the body, then one’s seeing would be attached to the self, which is untenable.

He then understood that the mountains, rivers, the great earth, the Hall of the Four Heavenly Kings, and so forth—all things encountered wherever they may be seen—are themselves none other than the self.
This wondrous nature, when one turns back to observe oneself—whether body or mind—is seen as being no different from external objects;
hence it is said: "Now this wondrous nature is present before me; what I see must be my true self. Furthermore, he shifts his calculation, saying:
"That seeing-nature cannot distinguish between 'me' and 'other,' whereas my current body and mind are indeed capable of discrimination and possess substantial reality. If one were to say...
That [object] sees me, yet the body is not me. If the body were me, then that [object] would not see me. This is not so; for that which sees is also seeing, and the view of self is also seeing.

Since both are seeing, how can it be as the Tathāgata previously objected—that because you see an object and the object also sees you, their essential natures would be confused, and thus establishment would be impossible? Alas! Ānanda!
How profoundly subverted! One’s own master, yet one makes such distinctions; this is still to be possessed by a ghost.
Though one may be able to respond, it does not issue from oneself. Alas! Such is the harm wrought by the aggregate of sensation.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "As for what you have just said... [down to] "...the Buddha said: 'So it is, so it is.
The passage beginning with "The Buddha told Ānanda" below criticizes his error. The passage beginning with "If it were truly yours" below generally interrogates the nature of his vision.

The passage beginning with "Furthermore, right now, for you" below specifically interrogates the characteristics of that which possesses vision. The passage beginning with "The Buddha again told Ānanda" below interrogates it separately.
As for the nature of that which is without seeing, the World-Honored One had previously pointed directly to his own mind;

yet Ānanda did not recognize the fundamental principle and erroneously claimed that this nature was currently before him. Therefore, the Buddha severed his delusion for him, saying, "This meaning is not real.
This single phrase is like a sharp blade; one need not worry that Ānanda would not die. Nevertheless—
This matter cannot yet be let pass; it is necessary to inquire as to the origin of his vision. He then asked Ānanda:
"As you sit here now in the Jeta Grove, observing all manner of objects and forms, there is nothing with shape that you do not point to. Ultimately, what among these is your nature of seeing?
Furthermore, fearing that he might evade the root of the question, the Buddha first presented him with the two terms "emptiness" and "vision."
The Buddha then separated his eyelids and asked him for an account of what he saw. Ānanda replied, "As I look out from here with my eyes wide open, everything I point to is an object;
there is no 'seer' [among them]," and so forth. The Buddha then confirmed this, saying, "It is so.
He further asked Ānanda, "While you sit in the Jeta Grove, you observe various distinct forms; surely..."
"I have no way to perceive the essence of seeing as you point it out. Furthermore, among all these objects, I cannot discern which one ultimately is not seeing.
Ānanda replied again, "I have indeed looked throughout this Jeta Grove, yet I do not know which among them is not seeing.
I have also reflected upon these myriad phenomena, searching for the subtlest manifestation of light, but I find none."
"It is not one who sees. The Buddha again confirmed this, saying, "It is so. These two instances of "it is so" are precisely the trap for tigers.
Here, can it be said that there is seeing? Or can it be said that there is no seeing? Such is the subtle and wondrous point.
"Even though his wisdom were like that of Śāriputra, he would still not know where the Buddha has gone.
Therefore, the great assembly consists of those who are no longer learners... [you] must contemplate this with earnest attention so as not to disgrace our sorrowful longing."
This concludes the preceding two views in order to encourage Ānanda to press forward.
His state of being startled and terrified, his appearance of trembling and apprehensive fear, was such that he lost what he was guarding and lost what he was grasping.
At that time, the great assembly saw Ānanda in this condition and did not know where he had fallen; thus, they manifested an air of anxiety, fear, and trembling. When the students saw him thus—
Not knowing the meaning of this permission, he was filled with alarm and trepidation;
consequently, he lost his composure and found it difficult to proceed. Thereupon, the Tathāgata, feeling compassion for him, comforted him, saying:
"You all think that the Path has vision, yet that is not so; nor is it that the Path lacks vision.
Rather, it is the Buddha-dharma that possesses deception and falsehood. Yet the Buddha-dharma is not deceptive or false; it is spoken according to reality as it is."

If you were to think that the Tathāgata permits the view that the path exists, or permits the view that the path does not exist, this would imply that the Tathāgata has two distinct statements. Yet, the Tathāgata has no such dual statements; these are words of truth.
Some may doubt that the World-Honored One is like the heterodox teacher Makkhali Gosāla, who engaged in fourfold equivocation in his discourses. However, [this is not so].
The World-Honored One’s discourse does not resemble the deceptive and confused arguments of the non-Buddhists; it is a discourse on the true primary meaning.
This is because the Tathāgata perceived that Ānanda and the great assembly were not reflecting deeply, harbored fear and trepidation, and were not diligently engaged in investigation.
Yet, out of my own shame and sorrowful longing, I have thus offered words of consolation to encourage Ānanda and the great assembly.
At that time, Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince—from [the point where he spoke] until the end—there was neither "is" nor "is not" within that interval.

Mañjuśrī’s inquiry has three intentions: first, to reproach Ānanda for his lack of skillful realization; second, to analyze the point of difficulty; and third, to formally state the purpose of the question.
Generally, those of the Hīnayāna hold that when there is an object, one can see; when separated from the object, one does not see.
If it is the Mahāyāna, one opens the eye of the true reality (*dharmatā*). Upon seeing any form, one sees one's own mind;
thus, one can see the Way in every instance and perceive the absolute truth in every object. This is the distinction between the Small and the Great Vehicles.

Now, Ānanda has reached the ultimate limit yet cannot turn [his realization]; consequently, his mental faculties grow dim and withered, and his spirit becomes terrified and cowed. For this reason, Mañjuśrī appears.
I have come to ask from the side, seeking to manifest the natural scenery of our own original ground;
it is not a matter of making a livelihood based on whether one sees or does not see. From the passage "Thereupon, the great assembly...

onwards, [the text] first rebukes Ānanda and the assembly for their failure to properly awaken to the Tathāgata’s intent, which was precisely a point where their wisdom was exhausted and their emotions withered. From the passage "The World-Honored One... onwards, it distinguishes that...
This is a difficult point. For images such as form and emptiness are the locus where the mind and its objects contend; each side claims "this is right" and "that is wrong.

If these images of form, emptiness, and so forth were the seeing itself, they should be something that can be pointed out. Yet, now, these images of form, emptiness, and so forth cannot be pointed out as being the seeing.
Conversely, if these images of form, emptiness, and so forth were not the seeing, there should be nothing gazed upon. Yet, now... [the text continues].
"Images such as emptiness are all that I perceive. Observing from this perspective, both mind and objects are obstructed, and right and wrong are entangled;
this is precisely the point of difficulty. Thus, one does not know where the meaning of these phenomena ultimately leads.

This is for no other reason than that their roots of goodness from the past were slight and meager. From the words 'I only pray' onwards, the intent of the question is properly set forth, saying: 'As for these various objective images...'"
As for this essence of seeing, what is it fundamentally? Within it, there is neither "is" nor "is not. This question employs the method of the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Regarding the four propositions: for example, the object-image is a phenomenon that "exists," while my seeing of it is a phenomenon that "does not exist.
The object-image exists and the seeing does not; this is the proposition of both existence and non-existence. As for the object-image...
It is not existent, yet it is seen as not non-existent; this is the dharma of neither existence nor non-existence.

Ānanda had fallen entirely into the dharmas of the four propositions and was ultimately unable to discern [the truth]. Therefore, Mañjuśrī took up these four propositions and combined them into a single question, asking solely:
what are these various material forms and this essence of seeing fundamentally? Within that, there is no "is."

It is not so. It is also like when a monk asked Mazu: "Transcending the four propositions and cutting off the hundred negations, I pray that you will directly point out the meaning of the Westward Transmission.
This question shares the same essential intent as the one at hand.
The Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī and the great assembly... [up to] "...this Mañjuśrī is no Mañjuśrī. The intent of the Buddha’s response is also threefold:
first, a re-explanation of the preceding four lines; second, a direct demonstration of his original nature; and third, a series of questions directed at Mañjuśrī.

Regarding the initial passage from "seeing and the conditions for seeing" (*jìng yǔ jiàn yuán*) downward: the upper character "seeing" (*jiàn*) refers to the faculty (*indriya*), while "conditions for seeing" refers to the objects (*viṣaya*).
The characteristic of perception is consciousness. These three—root, object, and consciousness—explain the meaning of the four preceding lines.
As for these four lines of doctrine, they are extracted from within the roots and objects. This extraction of the root-source exists when grasped and is non-existent when not grasped;
it is not a difference between a true essence that sometimes has seeing and sometimes lacks seeing, but is entirely created by the minds of sentient beings themselves.
It is like flowers in the sky. The flowers are the sky, and the sky is the flowers. They appear to one with diseased eyes, but vanish once the disease is cured.
It is not that there is any difference between the sky having flowers or being without flowers; it is entirely what is falsely perceived by the diseased eye itself. Therefore it is said:
"This seeing and its objects, along with the characteristics of thought, are like flowers in the sky; they have never existed."
Next, following this view and its conditions, [the text] directly points to that which is primordial.
Ānanda, this "pinching of the root" is the path of seeing; it is also Ānanda who does not see. It is Ānanda who says "it is";
it is also Ānanda who says "it is not. One’s own mind grasps one’s own mind; it is certainly and definitively nothing other than this. It is merely Ānanda...
If that which is difficult to perceive—namely, the provisional form within the faculties and objects—is not the case, then the whole body is truly real.

How could there be such a thing as "seeing" or "not seeing," as you have explained to me? Question: Since this is one's own wondrous, pure, and luminous essence, how can there be delusion and reality?
Answer: It is like when a person is fast asleep and hears the sound of a pestle, yet perceives it to be the ringing of a bell. If a person who is awake hears it...

The sound of the pestle is indeed the sound of the pestle. Yet there is another person who hears the sound of the pestle but does not perceive it as the sound of a pestle, nor is he separate from this sound of the pestle.
These three people are identical in their nature of hearing; they differ only in their awakening to delusion.
What is now said—that "this seeing and its objects are originally Bodhi"—is spoken only in contrast to those who are awake. If it were for those who are [already] awakened...

"One person still remains far away. From "The three follow Mañjuśrī" down to "I now ask you," the separate inquiry directed at Mañjuśrī is intended to mean that herein there is originally no mark of right or wrong, nor any doctrine of right or wrong.
Now, Mañjuśrī’s statement that "there is no right or wrong" has not yet reached a definitive eradication. Suppose you were Mañjuśrī; would there still be "is"?
"Is it Mañjuśrī? Or is it that there is no Mañjuśrī? This single question from the Buddha completely cuts off Mañjuśrī's heels; he intends for him to meet him beyond words.
"Thus, World-Honored One, I am truly Mañjuśrī"—up to—"within this there is truly no duality of 'is' and 'is not.
The Buddha poses this question; had it been anyone else, they would have seen it as fragmented. Now Mañjuśrī is a master;
he directly assumes responsibility, saying, 'I am truly Mañjuśrī. This first establishes his own footing, and only then does he cast everything open."

He said: "There is no such thing as Mañjuśrī. Why? Within one’s own single, wondrously luminous essence, if there were such a thing as Mañjuśrī, there would necessarily be a non-Mañjuśrī, and thus they would become two. Therefore it is said: 'If there is such a thing [as Mañjuśrī], then there are two Mañjuśrīs.
Observe how he establishes and refutes, how he picks up and lets go; yet first, he takes up the duality of 'is' and 'is not.'"
The characters are opened. Then, revealing his true face, he said: "Today, it is not that I lack Mañjuśrī.
Is this not him treading upon solid ground, employing his own spiritual nature to manifest his fundamental function?"
The Buddha said: "This seeing is wondrously luminous... (down to) in between there is naturally neither this moon nor that which is not the moon.
This borrows the sphere of activity of Mañjuśrī to serve as the conclusion. One should know that the sphere of Mañjuśrī’s activity is precisely the wondrously luminous true seeing;
and this wondrously luminous true seeing is precisely Mañjuśrī. Furthermore, one must know the wondrously luminous true...
It is seen that there is no wondrously bright true seeing apart from empty objects; nor is it the case that empty objects themselves are the wondrously bright true seeing.
As the ancient masters said: "It is like throwing a sword into the air—one need not discuss whether it reaches its mark or not.
Manjusri’s application of this principle was precisely like this; hence it is said: "This seeing is wondrously bright, and [as for] all empty objects..."
It is likewise so. From the passage "From this fundamental wondrous clarity" downward, the text rebukes their delusion and falsehood. Why?
It is a pity that they do not awaken to their own single segment of wondrously luminous true vision, yet instead speak of hearing and seeing upon the basis of empty space and sensory objects.
Even if they were to speak correctly, it would be like a second moon; and since it is already a second moon, how can one even discuss whether it is truly a moon?
Is it not the moon? Descending from Mañjuśrī, he distinguishes and determines the true moon. Now, that which is bright and limpid when one raises one's head is the true moon;
that which appears when one presses upon the eyes is the "second moon. That which is bright and round at the bottom of the water is the reflection of the moon.

If it is the reflection of the moon at the bottom of the water, one cannot say it is either this or that. If it is that which appears when one presses upon the eyes, one likewise cannot say it is either this or that.
It is not that one cannot discern it. If the clarity and stillness of the light above the head are present, this too is said to be beyond the scope of "is" or "is not.
Why is this so? If the clarity and stillness of the light above the head are the true moon, then what need is there to deliberate upon its being or not being so?

If the [reflection] at the bottom of the water or that which is squeezed out is the false moon, then since it is a false moon, what need is there to deliberate upon its being or not being so? Therefore it is said: "But..."
The month is real; within it, there is inherently neither "this month" nor "not this month.

Therefore, when you now observe the visual faculty and its objects (up to the point where it can cause you to distinguish between pointing and not pointing), it is able to lead you to discern what is the pointing finger and what is not.
This is the detailed account of how truth and falsehood become entangled.

It is because Ānanda did not realize his own wondrously enlightened and luminous nature, but instead gave rise to cognition and vision upon empty objects and sensory dust. To say "this is seeing" and to say "this is not seeing"—is this not his deluded conceptualization?
Due to these deluded conceptualizations, he is unable to transcend the duality of "is" and "is-not" within that state. However...
This deluded thought is not some other thing; it is none other than your own wondrously enlightened and luminous nature.

It is because of this wondrously enlightened and luminous nature that you are able to give rise to cognition and vision within empty space and amidst sensory objects, pointing to something as "this is seeing" and to something else as "this is not seeing.
Is this not your wondrously enlightened and luminous nature? Because of this wondrous clarity, it is able to cause you to emerge.
"Fingers are not fingers.
From this point, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, if this essence of seeing... This is the passage concerning the opening of the faculties and the accomplishment of the Way.
Once Ānanda focused on objects, and once he focused on seeing; the World-Honored One gave his seal of approval in both instances.
"One who acts in this manner is precisely opening the way for the reception of the aggregates. Mañjuśrī said, "I am truly Mañjuśrī;
there is no such thing as 'Mañjuśrī. Yet, today I am not without being Mañjuśrī—this is precisely what demonstrates the Way."
Observe how Manjusri, with a single stroke, turns [the mind] around; he does not fall into "this place," nor does he fall into "not this place.
He truly possesses the power to push over mountains and suck up the sea. One can perceive this through contemplation. △ Third, opening thought to achieve the Way.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One... [up to] "...attaining the wondrously enlightened nature of the true mind.

Ānanda’s doubts and difficulties are twofold: first, the difficulty regarding the confusion between the internal and external; second, the difficulty regarding the mutual conflict between causes-and-conditions and spontaneity.
Although Ānanda was young in years, he had already attended many assemblies and remembered that the World-Honored One was at Mount Laṅkā.
At that time, the non-Buddhists maintained that all phenomena possess an inherent nature and do not arise from causes and conditions. Why?
Because causes and conditions are not inherent. The World-Honored One taught that all phenomena arise from causes and conditions and do not exist inherently. Why?
"It is because it is spontaneous and not due to causes and conditions. As I now contemplate this nature of awareness, it appears to be spontaneous and not due to causes and conditions.

If that were so, World-Honored One, there would be the fault of contradicting your own words. This objection concerns the mutual conflict between the concepts of "causes and conditions" and "spontaneity.
Furthermore, Ānanda was by nature intelligent and acute, having read extensively across many books; he had previously encountered the teachings of the Brahmins.
The True Self pervades the ten directions; its nature is neither arising nor ceasing. Today, the Dharma King has taught that awakened cognition pervades the ten directions;
its nature is neither arising nor ceasing. If the Brahmin [teacher] and the Dharma King thus share the same intent, then in the Buddha-dharma, what is noble and what is inferior?
If this were so, the Dharma King would incur the fault of his position not being universally established (*aprasiddha*). This is the objection.
The internal and external have become confused and indistinguishable. Alas! Ānanda truly fails to maintain his proper station; instead, he wanders amidst discursive thoughts.

Why is this? Today the World-Honored One directly points out the primary truth (paramārtha-satya), yet Ānanda fails to realize it and instead records the details of Mount Laṅkā as being such-and-such. Is this not merely the wandering of his thoughts?
Today the Tathāgata has pointed directly to one's original nature to show it, yet Ānanda failed to receive it; instead, he spoke of how the former brahmins were or were not.
Is this not his own wandering in confusion? This is what is meant by "many mistaken paths before the Precipice of the Withered Tree," as exemplified by Ānanda.
"Brahmin" (梵志) is a general term for non-Buddhist practitioners (*tīrthika*). "Śveta-karṇa" (娑毗迦羅) refers to one with yellow hair.

"Ultimate Truth" (*tattva*) refers to the notion that within the profound obscurity there exists a sovereign controller; this is precisely what is meant by the "Self" (*ātman*). "Casting ash on oneself" refers to the ascetic practices of the non-Buddhists, as explained in detail in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (唯識論).
The Buddha told Ānanda: "If I were now [as you describe], such that the nature of seeing were severed and extinguished, how could one see light?
'Expedient means' (upāya) refers to speaking in accordance with principle and phenomena, and through analogies and dharmas; such speech is called expedient means."
Furthermore, all words and phrases are skillful means (*upāya*). An ancient worthy said: "It is solely for the sake of compassion that there are 'discourses that descend into the weeds.
To descend into the weeds is itself a skillful means. Now the World-Honored One says: "I have now thus revealed and instructed through skillful means, and I have told you the truth;
yet you still do not awaken, deludedly regarding it as something spontaneous (*svabhāva*). This, too, is [a descent into the weeds].

This concludes the provisional discourse on "nature. From the passage beginning with "You should now observe this" below, he investigates its natural essence. From the passage beginning with "Ānanda," he refutes the meaning of that nature.
In the middle, the four characters "zhōng jiāng míng àn děng fǎ" (in the midst, about to clarify the dharmas such as light and darkness) form a structural unit.
This means that if a nature of spontaneity existed, it could not accommodate dharmas such as light and darkness. Why? Because there would be no dual substance. That is to say, [light...]
If phenomena such as darkness exist, their inherent nature (*svabhāva*) cannot be admitted. Why? Because multiple entities are not one;
if they were to coexist, there would be mutual obstruction, and the existence of even one would be impossible. Examining it in this way, no inherent nature exists;
thus, your adherence to such a notion is refuted.
Ānanda said: "If this wondrous vision [extends] to empty space, how can it be grasped according to your insistence?
This concludes the previous refutations to demonstrate the fundamental dharma. The Buddha said: "As for what you have said," and so forth, he interrogates him regarding its causes and conditions.

Ānanda, the following section refutes the meaning of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*). The manner of this refutation is the same as before. That which is called the "Original Dharma" is neither cause nor condition;
it is neither spontaneous (*svabhāva*) nor non-spontaneous. Why is this? Because if there were something that is "is," there would necessarily be something that is "is not.
Therefore, it is said: there is no "is" and no "is not"; there is no "is not" and no "not-is not. Furthermore, it is like empty space, which cannot contain anything.

[The text discusses] marks (*lakṣaṇa*). Nevertheless, it does not reject the manifestation of various marks; this matter is likewise so. One does not grasp at a single dharma, nor does one abandon a single dharma. Why is this?
If one grasps at a single dharma, then there will be a surplus in the mental dharmas. If one abandons a single dharma...
Then the mental dharmas would not be all-pervasive. Therefore it is said: "To be free from all marks is itself all dharmas.
Why do you now reprimand him for his delusion? That which neither grasps nor rejects is original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*).

Because original enlightenment is free from names and marks and free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), to grasp at causes and conditions or to grasp at spontaneity (*svabhāva*) constitutes names and marks. If one speaks...
To say "it is" or "it is not," or to say "it is neither not-is nor not-not-is," is nothing but frivolous conceptualization (*prapañca*).
To employ the names and signs of such conceptualization to approximate the most subtle awakening is clearly seen to be of no benefit.
It is like using the palm of one's hand to grasp empty space; since empty space cannot be grasped, would it not be a mere waste of effort for a person to attempt to do so? By means of...
The subtle awakening cannot be grasped; yet if a person should grasp it, is this not false conceptualization?
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "It is truly as the Dharma King has taught. This passage marks the point where the opening of thought leads to the realization of the Way.
As for Ānanda’s recollection of the former brahmin and Mahāmati, and so forth... [as previously mentioned].
This is the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*). The World-Honored One said:

"One should know that such wondrously bright and subtle awareness is neither caused nor conditioned, nor is it spontaneous, yet it is not non-spontaneous; this is the opening of perception. He further said:
"There is no 'not' and no 'not-not'; there is no 'is' and no 'is-is. To be free from all marks and yet identical with all phenomena" is precisely what demonstrates its nature.
This is the Way. The meaning of the text resides beyond the words; you should reflect upon it thoroughly. △ Fourth, opening up practice to achieve the Way.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One... [up to] ...the characteristics of all causes and conditions are not the primary truth.”
To discuss this fully, there are nine conditions; here only four are presented for the sake of literary convenience.

It is because, according to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), causal nature exists as described by worldly characteristics, whereas it does not exist within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Now, Ānanda has been overturned by the Buddha’s rebuke.
To speak of spontaneity is untenable; to speak of causes and conditions is untenable. Where conceptualization fails to operate, the mind has no destination.

Thus, you invoke the nature of causes from the gradual teachings to raise an objection, saying: "Since the Tathāgata does not permit causes and conditions, for what reason did the World-Honored One tell the bhikṣus that the seeing-nature possesses four kinds of conditions—namely, space as a condition, light as a condition, the mind as a condition, and the eye as a condition?"
[The questioner asked: "Is there such a thing as equality? The Buddha said: "What I have spoken regarding the various causes and conditions of the world is not the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

Now, however, I am pointing directly at Ānanda’s original nature. If it is Ānanda’s original nature, it is not something to be sought after by means of spontaneity, nor is it something to be attained through the conjunction of causes and conditions.
One must accept it beyond words and see the original source directly. [The text continues: "Not..."
The path is obstructed and winding; only then will it be thoroughly penetrated.
"Ānanda, I ask you again" (up to) "seeing is not an obstruction"—these four meanings are established.
From "Ānanda, I ask you again" onwards is the double interrogation. The Buddha’s intention is that for the time being, he shall not speak further.
Regarding the ultimate truth: according to your own adherence, how do you define "seeing" and how do you define "not seeing"?
Ānanda replied: "In the world, people call it 'seeing' when there is the sun and so forth; they call it 'not seeing' when there is no sun and so forth.

Based on this, if one defines "seeing" as being dependent upon the sun and so forth, then it becomes a nihilistic view (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*). Why? Because the sun and so forth are merely worldly phenomena. This is...
Because it is impermanent. If one holds that there is "non-seeing" when the sun and so forth do not exist, this would result in the fault of eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*).

Why? Because the non-existence of the sun and so forth constitutes non-seeing; thus, seeing is [defined as] the absence [of those things]. To claim that seeing exists or does not exist is the tenet of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), which results in the faults of superimposition and denial (*samāropa-apavāda-doṣa*).
From the passage beginning "Ānanda, when it is dark," the following double refutation is made, namely, that [seeing] depends upon the sun and so forth.
"Existence is visibility; the absence of the sun and so forth is invisibility. This is not correct.
According to your own tenet, when it is bright, one should not perceive brightness, and when it is dark, one should not perceive darkness. Why?

Because at the time of darkness, the characteristic of brightness has already ceased, and since it should not exist at the time of darkness, [it follows that] if one necessarily perceives darkness, this is merely the absence [of light].

[The Buddha] said: "What is meant by 'no seeing'? Based on this, if one sees light when it is light, and upon reaching darkness one still sees darkness, then it would be both existent and non-existent, which constitutes the fault of contradiction. [The text] from 'Ānanda, if in the time of darkness' onwards presents a double thesis:
if light is due to the sun and so forth, and darkness is the absence of the sun and so forth, then in the time of darkness there would be no light."
It is called "not seeing" when darkness is present; it is also called "not seeing" when, at the time of dawn, there is no darkness. Thus, these two conditions are both termed "not seeing.
Furthermore, if there were "seeing" in the presence of light, then there would also be "seeing" in the presence of darkness. Thus, these two conditions would both be termed "having seeing."
Thus, in a time of clarity, darkness cannot exist; in a time of darkness, clarity cannot exist. These two characteristics mutually supplant one another:
if they coexist, their natures persist, and both are termed "seeing"; if one supplants the other, their natures are lost, and neither sees.
Furthermore, in a time of clarity one does not see darkness, and in a time of darkness one does not see clarity; thus, they are neither existent nor non-existent.
This would result in the fault of frivolous conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). Therefore, Ānanda, the following two lines provide the explanation:
When people of the world see the sun and so forth, they call it "light"; when they see the absence of the sun and so forth, they call it "darkness. Now, this is not the case.

One should know that at the time of seeing light, the seeing itself is not the light, because there is no light upon the seeing. At the time of seeing darkness, the seeing itself is not [the darkness]... [text fragment ends].

Darkness. Because one perceives that there is no darkness above it, the same applies to empty space and obstructions. Question: Since there is currently light and there is currently darkness, how can you say they do not exist? Answer:
That which exists in the present is precisely True Suchness (tathatā) remaining unchanging while following conditions;
thus, it causes you to perceive light and perceive darkness. Because True Suchness follows conditions while remaining unchanging, it causes you to perceive emptiness and perceive [obstructions].
Obstruction. By reasoning from this, one should know that when seeing light, the seeing is not the light, for it is the luminosity of its own nature (*svabhāva*).
When seeing darkness, the seeing is not the darkness, for it is the obscurity of its own essence (*svadeha*). The same applies to emptiness and obstruction.
If one clings to them, they become delusion; if one does not cling, they become dharmas. Therefore, it is said that the four meanings are established: luminosity is not an external object.
It is for your sake that I have established [the distinctions of] light and darkness and so forth.
You should further understand that when seeing sees, [it encounters] conditions, spontaneity, and the characteristics of conjunction.

The preceding was explained according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); therefore, existence and non-existence oppose one another, and light and darkness define each other, thus clearly forming the four views. Hence...
There are many contradictions [in such views]. Now, speaking according to the True Dharma (satyadharma), neither existence nor non-existence is established;

both light and darkness are forgotten. Only when one-pointed mind (ekacitta) is directly revealed will there be no further dispute. Nevertheless, although light and darkness are both forgotten, the faculty of seeing still remains;
although existence and non-existence are not established, the mind still remains. Because the mind remains, right and wrong are clearly distinct; thus, it is not yet the true mind.
Because there is a "seeing that exists," the duality of subject and object remains manifest;
thus, it is not true seeing. Therefore it is said: "At the time of seeing the seeing, this seeing is not seeing. This is because true seeing is without seeing, and the true mind is without dwelling.
Because it is without dwelling, it cannot be grasped through deliberation; because it is without seeing, it cannot be described by metaphor. Even if there were a description, it would also...

It cannot be described by words; even if one were to attempt to conceptualize it, such conceptualization would fail to reach it. Thus it is said: "Even seeing is detached from seeing, for seeing cannot reach it.

Panshan said: "The moon of the mind is solitary and perfect; its light swallows the myriad phenomena. The light does not illuminate objects, nor do objects exist; when both light and objects are forgotten, what is this?
From this we know that once mind and objects are forgotten, words— *Note: The provided text ends abruptly. This translation reflects the available portion.*
My thoughts cannot reach this. How can you further speak of causes and conditions, spontaneity, and their conjunction?
To speak of causes and conditions, spontaneity, and conjunction is truly like speaking of dreams within a dream.
"You disciples are narrow-minded, inferior, and ignorant (up to: you have not attained [the realization that] the path to wondrous Bodhi is free from weariness and indolence.
You lowly ones are deluded; I urge you to advance toward the pure true reality (*dharmatā*).

This very nature inherently possessed by Ānanda, he failed to awaken to, yet instead clung to causes and conditions and clung to spontaneity (*svabhāva*). How narrow-minded and ignorant! Your delusion and inversion are extreme."
Question: Previously it was said that the true mind has no abiding and that true seeing has no seeing;
why can it now be called the pure real mark (*dharmatā*)? Answer: It is not so. For example, if one points to the substance of the sun and moon, it is called the real mark;
if one points to their light, it is called the markless (*animitta*). Why? Because the sun is a single mark, and within its light there are no various marks. Furthermore...
It is like a mirror: if one points to its substance, it is called "true reality" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*); if one points to its reflectiveness, it is called "signlessness" (*animitta*). Why?
Because the mirror has but a single characteristic, and within its light there are no various characteristics; the nature that is primordially present is likewise so.
To point to its essence, it is called the "true mark" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*); to point to its function, it is called "marklessness" (*alakṣaṇa*). Why is this? Because the nature is a single mark;
within that nature, there are no deluded conceptions of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*). Indeed, the absence of the five aggregates within the nature is the true mind (*tathatā-citta*).
Since the true mind has no abiding, it is called "pure. The absence of deluded marks within the nature is true vision (*tathatā-darśana*).
True seeing is non-seeing; therefore, it is called the "true mark" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). This pure true mark is both name and reality.
One invokes the essence by means of the name, and through the realization of the essence, one attains the Way. Once the Way has been illustrated, even the name no longer exists.
As the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "I merely use provisional names to guide sentient beings. This is precisely that meaning. Alas for the śrāvakas!
Being narrow-minded and lacking wisdom, they are unable to penetrate the pure reality-mark (*dharmatā*).

Therefore, the Buddha reveals it to them, enabling them to personally realize the truth of their own nature and avoid falling into fragmented views. Thus it is said: "One should contemplate well. Were it otherwise, [the purpose would not be achieved].
To speak of "mind" and "nature," and to recognize names and grasp at appearances, is unwholesome reflection; it is merely conventional worldly thought and is not the fundamental intent.
From Ānanda’s address to the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, the wondrous enlightened nature must be neither cause nor condition," up to this point—
This is the passage that explains the practice leading to the realization of the Way. How is this clarified?
"Relying on emptiness, relying on clarity, relying on the mind, and relying on the eyes" refers precisely to the characteristics of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations).

Because of these, there is constant agitation and disturbance, which causes the human heart and mind to be unsettled, much like one suffering from malaria; alternating between cold and heat, it causes the body to be restless. This is the *saṃskāra*.
The aggregates (*skandha*) are likewise: one light and one dark, capable of causing people’s deluded thoughts to be restless.
The Tathāgata analyzes and refutes each of them individually, so that the four views are all eliminated. When the two truths are not established, both medicine and disease are discarded.
This is not a sudden severance; rather, it is the opening of its practice. As for the moment of "seeing seeing," that seeing is not [ordinary] seeing.
Seeing is already detached from seeing, such that seeing cannot reach it. Since seeing does not reach it, the mind does not dwell [upon it].
What else could this be but the true essence? This is the demonstration of its Way. The principles are as clear as looking at black and white.
Why do scholars not awaken? △ Fifth, the opening of consciousness to achieve the Way.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: [From "World-Honored One" to] "with tears of compassion, he prostrated at the Buddha's feet and received the holy instructions."
That Ānanda’s mind has not yet been opened is for a reason. Previously, in the refutation of causality and spontaneity, it was concluded:
"One should know that this wondrously enlightened nature of clarity is neither caused nor conditioned; it is neither spontaneous, nor is it non-spontaneous. There is no 'not' and no 'is-not';
there is no 'is' and no 'is-not. Is and is-not are both not-is. Thus, through four negations, one arrives at non-existence—non-existence.
"Is this my mind? If my mind were thus non-existent, then what is this thing that now appears before me?
Thus, I am once again bewildered and distressed. Now the Buddha further says: "When seeing is seen, that seeing is not seeing."
To see this as "no-seeing" results in that no-seeing becoming empty. If my mind were thus empty, then what would become of me who now clearly sees?
Therefore, this only serves to further increase one's confusion and distress.

Based on this, Ānanda’s state of confusion and his failure to open his mind are entirely due to the functioning of the discriminating consciousness; it is not the realization of the Way. (From the *Yuanjue jing*)
The Awakening says: Because there is deluded karma, there is the deluded vision of saṃsāra. Those who loathe saṃsāra have the deluded vision of nirvāṇa.
Due to this, they cannot enter pure awakening. It is not that awakening rejects those who would enter; rather, it is because there are those [who perceive] as entering.
Because it does not enter through the gates of cognition, both the movement of thought and the cessation of thought alike result in delusive confusion. Ānanda is precisely like this;

I humbly pray that you will grant a further request. When the awakened mind is bright and pure, it stands in contrast to the aforementioned delusive confusion; it is because of that delusive confusion [that this state is obscured].
One cannot enter awakening; therefore, I request that you bestow the great eye of wisdom and reveal it to us.

The underlying meaning is that once the eye of wisdom is opened, the mind of awakening becomes pure, and one may then perceive the Way without further effort. This intention lies beyond the literal words and can be contemplated.
At that time, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for Ānanda (and so forth), [taught] the *dhāraṇī* whereby all those with outflows (*sāsrava*) may attain the fruit of Bodhi.
*Dhāraṇī* is the general name for the three trainings (*triśikṣā*). This term is translated as "total retention" (*zongchi*).

*Samādhi* is translated as "right reception" (*zhengshou*), or alternatively, "right concentration" (*zhengding*). However, it is not merely a name for meditative concentration; therefore, the character "one" (*yi*) is included throughout the various terms. In truth...
This is a general indication of the function of the Buddha’s fundamental tenets. The compiler of the sutra abbreviated the text, hence composing such a preface.
As for the passage where the Buddha addresses Ānanda, he again enumerates the names of the three contemplations;
the omission of *dhyāna* (meditative absorption) therein is not due to a textual deficiency. For once the Buddha has rebuked Ānanda for his failure to skillfully employ his mind, how could he...
Could it be that there is a mind subject to outflows? Certainly not. Consider this, Ānanda:
all sentient beings revolve in the world... (up to) how much less could one distinguish between that which is neither the lamp nor the seeing?

"Ānanda, below 'all sentient beings,' the names are listed to provide a general indication. When examined through principle, these two false visions do not come from without, nor do they exist inherently;
it is clear that they are formed by the delusive vision of sentient beings. They arise according to karma and flow on according to karma.
Yet, when one considers the single character 'delusive' (妄), they have never existed from the beginning; when one considers the single character 'flowing' (轉),"
Thus, sentient beings truly suffer; this is what is called the perversion of sentient beings.
As for what is meant by "inferior," in explaining the first type—the delusive vision of individual karma—it first employs a metaphor to clarify its falsity:

it is like seeing circular halos due to an eye ailment. Yet these circular halos are seen only by those with diseased eyes. Why is this? Because to a person without such an ailment, they do not appear.
Because this shadow does not exist [independently], this false perception is produced by the individual karma (*bipākakarma*) of sentient beings.

Why? Because within true vision, such a perception does not exist. Regarding the phrase "What do you think? and below, [the text] refutes the identity of the lamp and the vision. Suppose the opponent offers this defense:
"The color resides in the lamp, while the shadow is seen by the eye. Therefore, the present refutation states: "If it were the color of the lamp, then a handsome person..."
Why do you not observe them together? If this were color, the person with the visual disorder (*taimirika*) should not see it.

Inferring from this, your claim that it is "identical to the lamp" is incorrect, and your claim that it is "identical to the vision" is also incorrect. Why? Because the lamp and the vision are substantial entities (*dravya*).
Furthermore, [the text] below, beginning with "Ānanda," refutes the notion of being separate from the lamp and separate from the vision. To address a possible defense: "This shadow..."

[The opponent claims: "The shadow exists upon the lamp; it exists separately from the lamp. Yet color does not exist upon the eye; it exists separately from the act of seeing. Therefore, we now refute this:
If the shadow existed separately from the lamp, why would there be no circular shadow on a screen, a curtain, a table, or a seat?

If color existed separately from the act of seeing, it should not belong to what is seen by the eye. Observing this, your assertion that [the shadow] exists separately from the lamp is also untenable.
This is so. To say that it is apart from seeing is also not correct. Why? Because the shadow and the visual aberration are the lamp’s seeing.
Therefore, one should know that what follows refutes [the view] that it is neither the lamp nor seeing. Since the lamp originally has no circular shadow, it is said to be "not the lamp.

Since those without the aberration do not see it, it is said to be "not seeing. Therefore, one should know that when there is no aberration, there is no circular shadow; yet one sees the circular shadow.
This is indeed the case with diseased eyes. To see circular shadows is the experience of diseased eyes; to see no shadows is the experience of healthy eyes.
If one has healthy eyes, one should neither say "it is" nor say "it is not. Why? Because seeing the optical aberration (*timi*) is not itself a disease.
If one has diseased eyes, one likewise should neither say "it is" nor say "it is not. Why? Because [the shadow] is... [an aberration].

Because both the seeing and the cataract are illusory, it is like a second moon appearing below. This is a further metaphor for its falsity: both the shadow and the seeing are cataracts, just like a second moon.
If it were truly a second moon, one could not say whether it exists or does not exist. Why? Because it is merely a perception of a second [moon].

It is neither substance nor reflection; it is produced by pressing upon the eyes, and therefore should not be spoken of. If it were produced by pressing upon the eyes, one might still say that it is distinct from what is not so obtained.
Why? Because this pressing upon the sense organ is neither form nor vision; it truly lacks any essential nature, and thus should not be spoken of.
"This is also like this" and below, both the phenomenon and the metaphor are simultaneously discarded; for it is merely produced by pressing upon the eyes.
It is like a second moon; since it has no substance, it should not be spoken of. Why? Because its form lacks substance, what is seen is illusory.
If one wishes to speak of it, with what else could one do so? This circular reflection is produced by a cataract in the eye;
it too is without substance, and thus should not be spoken of. Why? Because the reflection lacks substance, that which is seen is...
It is delusion. If one were about to speak of it, whom else could it be named? Thus, one comes to know that "separation" and "union" are both empty, and "is" and "is not" do not exist.
What the world now clings to—whether as the view of a self or as its non-perception—is entirely a single void delusion.

How can anything be said of it? Generally speaking, the eye is originally clear and bright; it is only due to illness that cataracts appear. A lamp has no circular shadow; it is the cataract [that creates the illusion].
One sees the overlapping layers; the shadow does not leave the lamp, yet it does not belong to the lamp. The cataract does not leave the eye, yet the eye originally has no shadow.
The eye is a metaphor for true seeing; true seeing is devoid of seeing. The cataract is a metaphor for delusion; the shadow does not exist by virtue of the lamp, so false seeing is not established.
True seeing is free from cataracts; thus the seeing of the shadow is ultimately empty. If this is so, then based on delusion, there is both seeing and the shadow.
Relying on the truth, there is neither seeing nor cataracts. Judging by the reality, the fundamental substance is one true essence; how could cataract-induced shadows be divided?
Observing it from this perspective, the nature is originally one, and thus the lamp and the seeing have no source.
Now, as for seeing the circular shadow, is this not due to the diseased eyes of sentient beings? Now, as for seeing its falsity, is this not due to the discrimination of sentient beings?
How profound is this karmic principle! From this it may be said: when the seeing sees, that which is seen is not itself the seeing. At this point, everything becomes clear;
there is no need for further inquiry or interrogation, and one naturally has no more room for idle comment.
What is meant by "common delusory vision" (sabhāga-viparyāsa-darśana)? [This continues] up to thirty, forty, or fifty.
What is meant by "inferior"? To explain "common delusory vision," it is generally defined in terms of external retribution (*vipāka*) to clarify its delusive nature.
Roughly speaking, although the dimensions of this Sahā world are vast, they do not extend beyond a single ocean; such are the worlds and lands.
Although extensive, it does not exceed the realm of Jambudvīpa; this is the general outline.

As for the great continents, they are counted by the thousands, and the small continents by the hundreds—whether one or two, three, five, or ten—all vary according to their respective boundaries in such a manner.
Now, if one takes the near to illustrate the distant, and the few to illustrate the many, and judges it by reason, then it is thus explained.
The three thousandfold great thousandfold world-system is, without exception, a single delusory realm. It is only because the karma of sentient beings differs that their retributions vary in degree.
Nevertheless, in essence, these do not exist within the fundamental nature; therefore, they are called "external retributions.
Jambudvīpa refers to the southern continent of Aparagoyānī (Jambūdvīpa). Furthermore, it is named after the Jambu tree, which exists upon this continent.
There is a tree called *jambū*. In this grove there is a river whose bed yields golden sand; furthermore, the sap of the tree can be dyed gold, and is thus named Jāmbūnada-gold.
Generally speaking, a level land within the ocean that is habitable is called a continent (*dvīpa*);

when sentient beings are born therein and it is demarcated as a distinct territory, it is called a kingdom (*rāṣṭra*). Is this not indeed so? It is nothing other than [the perception of] sentient beings themselves.
It is thus created by delusion. To discuss this in detail: the ocean represents the nature of original existence, while the continents represent the nature of non-awakening.
Because of this non-awakening, karma arises within them; since karma has fixed divisions, they are partitioned into realms and become nations.
As it is for one person, so it is for many; as it is for one nation, so it is for all nations.
Thus it is: through successive transformations and successive dependencies, how could there be an end?
Therefore it is said that these are all external retributions, existing because one encounters delusory objects.
Ānanda, if among these there is even one small continent (up to) which he has neither previously seen nor heard of.
Previously, external retributions were cited; here, karmic conditions are shown. How do we know that these are karmic conditions? Let us not discuss them at length for now;
let us speak briefly of what is most immediate. For instance, a single continent may have two kingdoms—this is a case of what is most immediate.
Yet when an entire nation sees all manner of portents— such as two suns or two moons,
things that the people of that nation have never before seen nor heard— is this caused by an interval or gap in the yin and yang?
If it were caused by an interval in the yin and yang, then even the entirety of heaven and earth would be unable to contain such a phenomenon.
Indeed. Why is this? Each thing has its own substance; each thing acts of itself. How could it admit another?
Since things themselves have no fixed substance, we know that yin and yang cannot be held responsible for blame. This is certain.
Nevertheless, the ill omens currently manifesting are created by the deluded minds of sentient beings. Because the deluded mind stirs from below, calamities and portents arise.
These manifestations appear above. How do we know this? It is like a cauldron of water: if one adds fuel and increases the fire, it becomes hot;
if one removes the fuel and extinguishes the fire, it becomes cold. Water itself cannot cause cold or heat; cold and heat depend upon the person.
These inauspicious phenomena are the result of the people of that nation collectively creating evil karma; therefore, they experience such inauspiciousness in that country.
It does not exist. It is naturally unseen; it is not merely that it is unseen, but furthermore, it is unheard of. Why is this?

It is because purity and defilement do not interpenetrate. From this we know that the Pure Land is the dwelling place of the sages, whereas the defiled land is where the sentient beings of the five turbidities reside.
This is truly because they are steamed by the five turbidities, and thus inauspicious signs manifest.
This is the mark [of such perception], yet the Sage is free from it. Does the *Lotus Sūtra* not say: "While the perceptions of the multitude are consumed by fire, my Pure Land is not destroyed"?
From this, one gains even greater conviction. Nevertheless, two kingdoms within a single continent are still far apart.
Now, the Jeta Grove—could this not be a single location? The Buddha and the great assembly dwell together; the Buddha is without such perceptions, while Ānanda...
To cling to the view of causes and conditions, or to cling to the view of spontaneity, is no different from the inauspicious sights perceived by the sentient beings of those lands.
Therefore, it is said that this is explained in terms of what is most immediate and proximate. Halos and solar or lunar eclipses are the portents of the sun and moon;
comets, meteors, and falling stars are the portents of the constellations; and the "burdened ear," rainbows, and halos are the portents of yin and yang.

These are portents of calamity. When bright, it is called a rainbow (*hóng*); when dark, it is called a *ní*. When it faces the sun as if bearing it on its back, or is beside the sun as if an ear, with rays like a broom, it is called a comet (*huì*).
When light radiates out in all directions, it is called a *bèi*. When it vanishes without a trace, it is called "flying. When the lights connect, it is called "flowing.

When an oblique vapor encircles the sun, it is called a halo (*yùn*). When the sun or moon undergoes an eclipse, it is called an occultation (*shì*). As for the jade pendants and rings, their shapes are like those worn by humans.
"The pendants on my girdle are also like this; they are all images transformed by the sun, moon, stars, yin and yang, and the cycles of cold and heat.
Ānanda, I now explain these two matters to you [up to] that which appears before you as an objective realm is, in fact, originally my own enlightened awareness."
Ānanda, I shall now provide both the teaching and the analogy. To apply the analogy to the teaching is called "progression";
to apply the teaching to the analogy is called "regression. In this manner, through one progression and one regression, it is clarified that what is seen is actually non-seeing.

Ānanda, as in that previous example of the retreating [eye-disease], this is a metaphor for shared karma; as in the following example of advancing, this is a metaphor for the delusion of individual karma.
Applying this to the Dharma: why is this so? When one with impaired vision sees a circular shadow, although it appears to be an external object, it is not produced by material form (*rūpa*).
Rather, it is formed by the fatigue of the eye-disease. All wise people know that this circular shadow is merely the result of such ocular affliction.
Once this is accomplished, one will no longer cling to the distinction between seeing and not seeing. One knows that the shadow is produced by a cataract.
Having known that the shadow is produced by a cataract, even the act of seeing is without fault. One knows that the cataract is a diseased eye. By this analogy, one may understand [the rest].
Nowadays, when people of the world observe with their eyes the mountains, rivers, lands, and all sentient beings, these appear as present objects;
yet they are not created by form (*rūpa*). Rather, they are produced by the beginningless delusion of seeing.
Those who possess wisdom know that these mountains and so forth are produced by the sickness of seeing, and thus they do not cling to either seeing or not seeing. Knowing the mountains...
The rivers and so forth are false perceptions. Once one knows that these perceptions are produced by delusion, then both the perception and its source are seen to be without fault.
Knowing that the root of false perception is my own enlightened clarity (*jñāna-prakāśa*), if this is so, then even when speaking of seeing, there is no seeing.
Since seeing itself is without seeing, how can one say that "I see" or "I do not see"? Seeing an object is itself a visual aberration;
awakening to this seeing is immediately the cessation of the aberration. (Up to: How, then, can it again be called awakening, hearing, knowing, or seeing?
Generally, people of the world refer to the mountains, rivers, and so forth as that which is seen; they refer to themselves as "I" who see these mountains, rivers, and so forth as the seer.
If one clings to this seer as being the true seeing, it is merely the cataracts and visual distortions afflicted within the eyes.
If one clings to that which is seen as the seer, it is precisely the circular shadow seen within that cataract. Therefore it is said: "The object of vision is the cataract;
awakening to the vision is itself the cataract. One fails to realize that one's own fundamentally awakened, luminous mind—were there awakening, it would not belong to the subject that perceives;
were there seeing, it would not belong to the object perceived. Why? Because fundamental awakening is without [dualistic] awakening. Were there...
That which possesses awareness is self-awareness; true seeing is non-seeing. Were there to be seeing, it would be merely self-seeing;

therefore, it is called the "originally enlightened luminous mind. Awareness of conditions is not a cataract; thus we know that whatever is perceived is not true awareness, but rather deluded awareness.
Deluded awareness constitutes a shadow; hence it is said, "The awareness of what is perceived is a cataract. In reality, original enlightenment is without [delusion].
Awakening. If there is awakening, it is self-awakening; self-awakening is not an ailment. Therefore it is said that awakening does not exist within an ailment.
Awakening in this manner is called true awakening; seeing in this manner is called true seeing. Thus it is said: "This is truly the seeing of seeing.
Since even seeing does not reach [the ultimate], how can one speak of "my seeing"? Since awakening itself cannot be established, how can one...?
It is called "I have heard. Yet, when people of the present day say, "I see" or "I hear," or "I perceive" or "I know," these are truly the words of one who is asleep;
they are merely verbal expressions and possess no real meaning whatsoever.
Therefore, when you now see me and yourself—up to the point that their nature is not a visual defect—it is not called "seeing.
This [passage] aligns the dharma with its metaphor. It is like being afflicted by a visual defect (a cataract) due to failing to realize for oneself while clinging to false awareness.
It is like a circular shadow due to failing to see for oneself while clinging to false seeing. Seeing a circular shadow because of a visual defect is just like...
As for this, people of the world cling to the view of self (*ātman*). Let us set aside other matters for a moment;
consider only this: you see me before you as a Buddha and as a teacher, and I see you before me as Ānanda and as a disciple.
As it is between me and you, so it is with the ten classes of sentient beings in the world: each clings to a self, each clinging to their own.
One sees it. Furthermore, this is not merely the case today; from time immemorial, it has always been thus.
To cling to a self and cling to views—is this not entirely the formation of a single delusion? How does it differ from that optical illusion of a circular shadow seen by one with cataracts?
Therefore, it is said that all are simply the seeing of a cataract. Yet, how could these illusory shadows exist for one with healthy vision? For one with healthy vision possesses none.
This cataract is precisely what is called true seeing; therefore it is said that "it is not the seeing of the cataract.
Because a healthy eye lacks this circular shadow, it is called "non-seeing"; therefore it is said that "that seeing is the true essence, whose nature is not the cataract.
By this one knows that because the healthy eye lacks the cataract, its seeing is itself non-seeing. Because the diseased eye possesses the circular shadow, therefore...
To see this is false seeing. The preceding section, through both dharma and metaphor, establishes the principle with perfect parity.

In responding to Ānanda’s prior doubt regarding the nature of seeing—that when one sees seeing, that seeing is not [true] seeing—it can be said that the matter has been explained with exhaustive detail and thoroughness. Students must not fail to investigate it deeply and contemplate its essence.
Ānanda, it is like the deluded vision shared by those sentient beings (up to) "deludedly born together and deludedly dying together.
In the preceding passage, the commonality was set aside to advance to individual karma as an analogy for the Dharma.

For example, the case of one person with impaired vision due to individual karma is used to illustrate Ānanda’s deluded vision; furthermore, Ānanda’s deluded vision is equated with that of the ten classes of beings in the world.
Sentient beings now advance through their commonality (*sabhāgatā*) and retreat through their individual karma (*pṛthag-karman*). To illustrate this by means of the Dharma:

it is like the deluded vision of the commonality of ten classes of sentient beings, which in turn illustrates the individual karma of a single person. Furthermore, one person with diseased eyes is analogous to that single country;
again, that single country is analogous to all the contaminated countries throughout the ten directions. Thus, by successive analogy, one comes to know [the truth].

This means that advancing and retreating are both in accord with the clarity of this Dharma. How does the circular shadow seen by a single diseased eye differ from what an entire nation sees as all manner of ill omens?

How does the false vision arising from the pestilence and evil of a single country differ from the false birth and false death produced through the combination of conditions in the tainted lands of the ten directions? Furthermore, these sentient beings are...
The leakage of awakened clarity: the lands of the ten directions are formed from this circular reflection.

Because the clarity of awakening is so extreme, it exceeds the capacity of comprehension and thus reverses into ignorance (*avidyā*). This ignorance is precisely the disease and the optical aberration.

Taking luminous awareness as a visual faculty, yet being unable to fully discern it, one consequently forms false vision; this false vision is precisely the circular reflection. Therefore, know that within the wondrously luminous mind—
Half, possessing cognition, becomes sentient beings; half, lacking cognition, becomes the world. The world is the circular shadow;
sentient beings are the pathological vision. Thus they evolve successively into a basis and evolve successively into delusion.
When investigated and observed, these realms of outflows and these sentient beings are not created by form; they are, in fact, the awakening-mind itself.
This clarifies the untainted, wondrous mind: it exists through the conjunction of delusive conditions.
If one can distance oneself from all conjunctive conditions, one will reach the pure fundamental mind, wherein original enlightenment is eternally abiding.
It was previously stated that through false conjunction one is born, and through false conjunction one dies; therefore, it is now concluded and demonstrated:
"If one can distance oneself from all conditions of conjunction as well as non-conjunction, then one will further eliminate the causes of birth and death. Question:
How does one distance oneself from conjunction and non-conjunction? Answer: Because True Suchness (Tathatā) arises and ceases in accordance with the deluded mind, there exists [conjunction].
Regarding birth and death: if one realizes that the nature of true suchness (*tathatā*) is empty, one will no longer be in conjunction with birth and death;
hence it is said, "to remain far removed from conjunction. However, the very existence of this "remaining far removed from conjunction" implies the existence of a state of non-conjunction.
Furthermore, the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* states: "All bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age should remain far removed from all..."
Illusory transformations and false objects are abandoned by means of a mind that resolutely maintains detachment. When the mind itself is like an illusion, it too is abandoned.
That which abandons is abandoned as being illusory; even the abandonment of that illusory abandonment is further abandoned.
When one attains the state where there is nothing further to abandon, all illusions are eliminated. This is also the case here: one abandons all composite conditions and their opposites.
In harmony, they naturally eliminate the causes of birth and death and perfect the nature of bodhi that is neither born nor extinguished.
Ānanda, although you previously awakened to the wondrous clarity of fundamental enlightenment (up to the point where it is said) that all various obstructions are likewise so.
In the previous section on Ānanda’s request, there was doubt regarding whether causes and conditions are naturally harmonious or not, as well as the nature of seeing and non-seeing.
By means of the two analogies of the "same" and the "different," the Buddha has already resolved the matter of seeing and non-seeing;

thus, one should no longer harbor confusion therein. Next, we shall refute the notions of harmony and lack of harmony. If [it were argued that] causes and conditions are natural... [the previous section] opened this discussion.
Regarding the section on "conception" (*saṃjñā*), it has already been fully analyzed; there is no need to speak of it again. Therefore, it is said:

"Although you have previously realized that fundamental enlightenment is wondrously luminous, its nature is neither caused by conditions nor is it a spontaneous nature. This refers to the passage beginning from "Now, Ānanda, although you have previously realized... and so forth.
This first provides a general indication of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and non-conjunction. Next, from the passage "Ānanda, I now... onwards, it specifically refutes the meaning of conjunction.
Within this refutation, it again employs the four previous principles to examine the matter; through this, one will come to understand that there is no underlying principle for conjunction.

Why is this? Since the four sense-objects are already provisional, with what thing could they be conjoined? If clear vision and the object were two distinct entities, they would be separate and thus could not constitute conjunction.
If one clearly perceives them as one, then there is no differentiation, and thus perception is not established. If you say it is not seeing, then clarity is likewise non-existent.
If you say it is identical to seeing, then by what would one see that seeing? As for the term "perfectly complete," this refers to the meaning of mutual parity:
if seeing is equal [to clarity], then there is no clarity; if clarity is equal [to seeing], then there is no seeing. Together, they constitute clarity...
Both views are lost. Who knows what constitutes their harmony? That which is dark and that which is pervasive, as well as all the various obstructions, are likewise destroyed in this way.
Furthermore, Ānanda, you who are now [present], up to and including all the various obstructions, are also like this.
From the passage beginning "Furthermore, Ānanda," below, the refutation of the "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) is presented; the meaning of the text is clear and need not be further analyzed.

However, since this "conjunction" involves my self uniting with another, it is examined through the two terms "intermingling" (*miśra*) and "alignment" (*sāma*). Regarding intermingling, there is no true conjunction;
regarding alignment, there is no perception. The former point has already been established. As for the present refutation of conjunction, "conjunction" refers to the formation of a single unity.
Therefore, one distinguishes them by means of the two entities of light and darkness. If it were conjoined with light, one would not see darkness when it is not appropriate for light;

if it were conjoined with darkness, one would still see light when it is not appropriate for light. Since what is seen is a single characteristic, there can be no doctrine of its being conjoined with light or conjoined with darkness.
Darkness pervading various obstructed categories is to be understood in this same way.
Ānanda said to the Buddha, “World-Honored One... [omitted] ...and the various *piśācas* are likewise so.
Since the previously mentioned ‘conjunction’ has been refuted, then conjunction cannot be established. Now you further calculate that there is ‘non-conjunction.
If it were non-conjunction, then there would be a distinct boundary that could be pointed out; this must be distinguished. Following the Buddha’s words, you now further...”
Under these words, first the non-harmony is refuted. One must further examine it by means of the four meanings, such as light and so forth; there must necessarily be boundaries.
This essence of non-harmony—does it reside at the limit of light, or at the edge of seeing? If it resides at the edge of seeing, then it would not itself know light.
If it resides at the limit of light, then seeing would not reach it. Since seeing does not reach it, how can a boundary be established?
Since brightness is not known, how can its boundaries be distinguished? That darkness permeates the various obstructions;

if one examines each of them, there is no substance that is not of the nature of harmony (*sāmagrī*). Furthermore, regarding the "wondrous seeing-essence" below, it refutes the notion of non-conjunction (*asaṃyoga*):

if one were to rely on non-harmony, then the substances would not interpenetrate, which could still be explained. But if it were non-conjunction, then the light and the seeing would not reach one another; how then [could they function]?
This is discernible. Why? Because their natures and characteristics are at odds, and their faculties and objects are mutually opposed;
they are like the ear and light, which do not touch one another, or like vision and its objects, which do not reach one another. How can they be distinguished as being non-conjoined?
The preceding analysis of identical and distinct false visions serves to resolve Ānanda’s doubt regarding whether the "seeing of seeing" is itself seeing. Now, [I shall address this].
To break the conjunction is precisely to eliminate Ānanda’s delusion of still being separated from seeing. Furthermore, conjunction and non-conjunction are analogous to spontaneity;
both collective karma and individual karma do not transcend causes and conditions. Ānanda would have naturally understood this through his own insight, and thus the Buddha did not speak further.
"Ānanda, you have not yet clearly understood that all floating dust [of phenomena]... (down to)... delusion and enlightenment, birth and death, are utterly unobtainable.
This is the summary of the general meaning. From "Ānanda, you have not yet clearly understood" onwards, it concludes the discussion on the false vision of individual karma (*bipākakarma*).

It means that seeing the sun and so forth is considered "light," while the absence of the sun and so forth is considered "darkness"; this is similar to the way a diseased eye perceives circular shadows. This...

When the sun and so forth encounter the sensory faculties of the floating dust, they truly become illusory and delusory phenomena; they arise in their respective locations and perish in those same locations.
How could your own wondrously enlightened and luminous essence also be like these illusory appearances and thus non-existent? It is simply that you have not yet understood the meaning within this.
This concludes the reprimand regarding Ānanda’s doubt concerning the "seeing of seeing. From [the passage] beginning with "As such... [it continues].
This extends down to the formation of the commonality of the same class (*nikāya-sabhāga*) through deluded vision.

Within this commonality, the miasmic evils that arise and the observation of various inauspicious signs are no different from the circular shadows seen by one with diseased eyes. These diseased eyes constitute a single sense organ;

likewise, when the five aggregates (*skandha*), six sense bases (*āyatana*), twelve spheres (*dhātu*), and eighteen elements (*dhātu*) are confronted by the clarity of awareness, they are in reality illusory and false.
"It is not real. Through the combination of causes and conditions, there is illusory birth; through the separation of causes and conditions, what is called 'extinction' is likewise illusory.
How could your own fundamental true nature also be like this illusion and delusion, being empty and false? It is simply that you have not yet awakened to the principle within this.
This passage rebukes Ānanda for his doubt regarding "seeing" and "not seeing. From this point on, [the text] is utterly unable...
"Know that 'below' refers to the meaning of non-union. You perceive the conjunction of the aggregates, bases, and fields as 'arising,' and their lack of conjunction as 'ceasing.
Yet you do not realize that within the Tathāgatagarbha there is fundamentally no arising or ceasing; it is originally wondrously luminous and eternally abiding.
When you perceive the presence of light and so forth, you call it 'coming'; when you perceive the absence of light and so forth, you call it 'going.'"
Little do you realize that within the nature of True Suchness (tathatā), there is truly no coming or going; it is fundamentally immovable and all-pervading.

It is because you do not understand this essential meaning that you remain in ignorance. This concludes the reprimand for Ānanda’s doubt regarding the statement, "the seeing is still separate from what is seen.
You perceive the light of the sun and such as "coming," and you perceive the darkness when there is no sun and such as "going"—this is to cling to delusion.
This is delusion; to realize the nature is awakening. When the aggregates exist, there is birth; when the aggregates perish, there is death.
Yet one fails to realize that within the true permanence of the nature, if one seeks coming and going, delusion and awakening, or birth and death, nothing at all can be found.
This profound meaning within is something you truly cannot fathom. This concludes the reprimand for Ānanda’s doubt regarding his inability to perceive this.

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, although the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has for our sakes proclaimed the nature of causes and conditions, as well as spontaneity, the characteristics of harmony and disharmony, my mind remains unenlightened.

Now, having further heard of 'seeing seeing' and 'not seeing,' my confusion and distress have increased even more. To reach this point is precisely the opening of consciousness and the realization of the Way."
This is the *vijñapti* (representation). In the middle section, there is an extensive clarification of the two inverted views of common karma and distinct karma;

this is precisely the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). The Buddha said: "If one can remain far removed from all conditions of conjunction as well as non-conjunction, then one further eliminates the causes of birth and death, and fulfills the nature of bodhi that is neither arising nor ceasing. This then opens up the [nature of] consciousness. It continues until it says:
Within the true and eternal nature, one seeks for coming and going, delusion and enlightenment, birth and death, yet finds absolutely nothing to be obtained.
Is this not the perfection of its subtlety? However, the momentum of the text is like a long wind blowing forth, causing ten thousand apertures to roar in fury;

it is also like the shadows of clouds and objects flickering, while a single orb shines alone in clarity. Readers must contemplate in this manner before they can perceive the subtle artistry of the author’s guidance.

Furthermore, the previous refutation of the five aggregates was precisely the arousal of the wondrously luminous mind; the subsequent analysis of the five aggregates is precisely the opening of the eye of the Way.
