From the beginning of the first fascicle up to this point, the attachment to the person (*pudgala-grāha*) has been extensively revealed; from the following three categories and the seven elements (*dharmadhātu*), the attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) will be extensively clarified.
This shall be discussed in the relevant passages. Question: Since the five aggregates are already wondrous, why is there further mention of "opening" them?
"Is this not overly cumbersome? He replied, "It is not so. Suppose pearls are hidden in Hepu and jade is buried in Mount Jing.
When jade comes from Mount Jing, it does not mean that Mount Jing is itself the jade; when pearls come from Hepu, it does not mean that Hepu is itself the pearl.
The essential point is that one must await their emergence from the palm before their reality can be seen. The mind contains the five..."
The aggregates (*skandhas*) are not inherently marvelous; it is only when the Buddha displays them upon his palm that their marvel is perceived.
Thus we know that the previous refutation of the five aggregates refers to things such as the Mount Jing mountains or the Hepu pearls [which are hidden and require effort to find].
The subsequent analysis of the five aggregates and the statement that they are "opened" refers to displaying them upon the palm. Therefore, the Buddha has no need for prolixity.

...the fault thereof. △ Second, the analysis of the division of clinging to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*), which has five parts: first, the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*); second, the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*); third, the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*);
fourth, the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśadhātu*); fifth, the seven great natures. First, the five aggregates.
Ānanda, how is it that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha, the wondrous nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*)?
This serves as a general heading for the five aggregates. "Aggregate" (*skandha*) signifies the nature of obscuration; its meaning is that which veils True Suchness.

When the five sense objects encounter the five sense faculties, if one does not engage in false conceptualization, they are originally one with the dharma of True Suchness, fundamentally free from all affairs. This is truly because...

True Suchness (Tathatā) does not abide in its own nature. Because one erroneously calculates that characteristics such as blue, yellow, long, and short obscure True Suchness, they are called "aggregates" (skandhas).
If one investigates and contemplates them thoroughly, those five aggregates are none other than the Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrous nature of True Suchness;
they do not exist separately from it. 1. The Aggregate of Form (Rūpaskandha).
Ānanda, it is as if there were a person with pure eyes... (up to) the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*); you should know that it is likewise so.
Ānanda, below [this], in the first section distinguishing the aggregate of form, he first cites a metaphor to clarify its origin.

"With pure eyes seeing the clarity of the sky" is a metaphor for the aggregate of form. This is because True Suchness (*tathatā*) does not abide in its own nature, but rather gathers [the conditions].
Form constitutes the aggregate (*skandha*). That which is but a single empty eye-sphere, utterly devoid of anything, is a metaphor for non-awakening (*abodha*).
Because True Suchness (*tathatā*) is non-awakened, it perceives that which is non-existent; this non-existence is precisely ignorance (*avidyā*).

That person, having no cause, does not move his eyes but stares fixedly until they become fatigued; this is a metaphor for the development of conceptual proliferation (*vikalpa*). This refers to staring without cause.
The pupils of the eyes now move and give rise to fatigue; this is because there is a latent cause. To know that there is a cause is itself a conceptual transformation.
Thus, seeing distinct floating flowers within empty space is a metaphor for the characteristics of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).

Using floating flowers as a metaphor for the aggregate of form is like True Suchness (*tathatā*) not maintaining its own nature, whereby it transforms through conceptualization into blue, yellow, and so forth, thereby establishing [the phenomenal world].
These are false appearances. Therefore it is said: "The aggregate of form should be known to be likewise.
Ānanda, these various frantic flowers do not come from space [nor go anywhere]. How then can the clear sky be called the "clear and bright eye"?
Below [the section on] Ānanda, there is a separate refutation of his shifting arguments regarding such characteristics as these illusory flowers.

These flowers do not come from space, nor do they emerge from the eyes. If one were to say that space possesses flowers that enter and exit it, then space would no longer be empty; it would instead be a substantial entity.
How could a substantial entity accommodate other appearances? It would be like Ānanda being unable to accommodate another Ānanda, for Ānanda is a substantial reality.
Because it is the substance [of the eye]. Furthermore, if there were flowers entering or exiting the eyes, there should be instances where one sees them and instances where one does not;
there should not be a cataract. How then could the empty eye be called "clear and pure"? Thus we know that both the void and the eye are devoid of flowers.

That we now see "wild flowers" (floating hairs) — is this not their delusory appearance? This is analogous to how True Suchness (tathatā) has no appearances such as blue or yellow, yet now they appear.
Is it not the case that the seer is a false construction resulting from conceptual proliferation?
Therefore, one should know that the aggregate of form is empty and false; fundamentally, it is neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.
Therefore, the following section concludes both by means of the Dharma and its analogy. One must know that the "wild flowers" have no source; they are merely the eyes staring in exhaustion.
Likewise, the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) has no source; it is simply the self-nature of True Suchness (*tathatā-svabhāva*) undergoing a transformation through conceptualization.

Thus, when one realizes that the self-nature of True Suchness is without arising, one immediately knows that the aggregate of form is likewise without arising. Originally, it is the wondrous True Suchness of the Tathāgata.
Nature. How could there be causes and conditions for this natural, deluded vision of yours? △ Second, the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*):
Ānanda, it is like a person whose hands and feet are at ease... (up to) you should know that the aggregate of sensation is likewise so.
Below, Ānanda: Second, the analysis of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*). First, a metaphor is raised to clarify its origin. "The hands and feet are at ease;
the hundred bones are harmoniously adjusted" is a metaphor for the aggregate of sensation.

To recognize the field of empty clarity and peace because True Suchness (*tathatā*) does not maintain its own nature is precisely the objective realm of the aggregate of sensation. Suddenly, as if forgetting one's birth-nature, there is no conflict.

"Following" (shùn) is a metaphor for lack of awareness. Wàngshēng said: "Now that I have lost my self, I have reached the state of withered wood and extinguished ashes, yet I do not realize it"—this is his folly.
That person, for no reason, rubs his two palms together against the void; this is a metaphor for shifting calculations.
"For no reason" means at a time when there is no business [to attend to]. Because there is no business...
Therefore, they suddenly rub their two hands together, and immediately [the sensation] exists. Because it exists, is this not a further conceptualization?

To falsely give rise to various characteristics such as roughness, smoothness, cold, and heat is a metaphor for the characteristics of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*). True Suchness does not maintain its own nature;
instead, it further conceptualizes tranquility, peace, and non-action as bliss, taking the extinction of wisdom and the quenching of the mind to be the ultimate.
This clarifies that it is illusory and false. Therefore it is said: "You should know that the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) is likewise so.

Ānanda, these various illusory contacts do not come from space [nor go anywhere]; they exist only when there is a meeting [of conditions]. What need is there to wait for their union to be known? It is precisely this [meeting] that is designated as "contact" (sparśa).
Ānanda, let us analyze this separately. These illusory touches do not come from space, nor do they emerge from the palm. Why is this?
If space possessed touch, it would not need to be selected as the source of contact. If the palm possessed touch, it should not depend upon conjunction with another object.

There is a single entity that comes and goes within the body; why must it necessarily be known through conjunction? By this, one knows that both the empty space and the palm lack the characteristic of tangibility.
If one now perceives roughness, smoothness, and so forth, is this not a false delusion? Likewise, True Suchness (Tathatā) likewise lacks characteristics such as non-awakening (anabodha).
If one now perceives a state of tranquil ease and the absence of affairs as being "non-awakening," is this not merely a shifting conceptualization? And...
Is it not, then, a false fabrication?

Therefore, one should know that the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is a false fabrication; fundamentally, it is neither caused by conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) nor is it of spontaneous nature (*svabhāva*).

Thus, below, both the teaching and the metaphor are concluded together: to realize that qualities such as roughness and smoothness are without source is to emerge from [the realm of] characteristics (*nimitta*).
Mo. The aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is likewise without origin; it is simply the transformation of the self-nature of True Suchness (*tathatā-svabhāva*).
When consciousness realizes the self-nature of True Suchness, the aggregate of sensation is not some other entity; it is originally the wondrous True Suchness-nature of the Tathāgata.
How could there be causes and conditions or spontaneity for you to receive this as sensation? △ Third, the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).
Ānanda, it is like a person talking about eating sour plums... you should know that the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is also like this.
Ānanda, below [this], the third section distinguishes the aggregate of perception. First, a metaphor is raised to clarify its origin:
though there is no actual substance in the mouth’s speech, water flows; though there is no precipice, the feet ache. This is a metaphor for the aggregate of perception. Perception...

These are mental images. Because True Suchness (tathatā) does not abide in its own nature, it manifests in accordance with conditions; thus, all single thoughts and mental images are transformations of one's own mind.
How could they be external things like plum blossoms or cliffs? Therefore it is said: "One should know that the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) is likewise so."
Ānanda, this analogy of the sourness not arising from the plum (up to the point where he imagines treading on a precipice) is similar to the explanation.
Ānanda then descends to refute it at length: "The plum does not speak of itself, nor does the mouth hear anything. Yet, hearing someone speak of the plum, the mouth subsequently flows with saliva.
Why is this so? The sourness of the precipice is like this. From this, one knows that True Suchness is unchanging yet follows conditions.
To further calculate this as a characteristic—surely it exists!
Therefore, one should know that the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) is empty and false; fundamentally, it is neither caused by conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.
Thus, below, both the dharma and the analogy are concluded together: the plum cliff has no substance, which is to say that the sourness of the water is likewise empty.

What is habitually practiced through delusion—the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha)—is likewise so. It is entirely the self-mind grasping at the self-mind; it has no substance that can be clung to.

This is precisely the Tathāgata’s wondrous true suchness (tathatā). How could there be causes and conditions or spontaneity for you to conceive as such? △ Fourth, the aggregate of mental formations (saṃskāra-skandha).
Ānanda, it is like a violent torrent where waves succeed one another... (up to) the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*); you should know that it is likewise so.
Ānanda, below [this], the fourth section distinguishes the aggregate of formations: it is like a violent torrent where waves succeed one another.

If one speaks of the characteristics of the waves, there is a sequence of before and after; if one speaks of the nature of the water, they do not overstep one another. This is a metaphor for the aggregate of formations.
Because True Suchness does not maintain its own nature, it flows and shifts according to conditions; it does not stop for a single moment, and in each new instant it fails to abide.
Ultimately, it cannot emerge from its own substance, being no different from the shifting flow of waves.
Ānanda, this nature of flowing does not arise because of space (and so on, until) space does not exist outside of water, nor is there flow outside of water.
Ānanda, the following provides an extensive refutation: this nature of flowing does not arise because of space, nor does it exist because of water.

That is to say, if space could produce it, then all ten directions would simultaneously suffer from being swept away; if water possessed flow, its essential nature would remain distinct and divided into two.
It is illustrated that True Suchness has no marks of activity; rather, such marks are merely the continuous conceptual constructions of sentient beings.
Therefore, one should know that the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) is empty and false, fundamentally being neither produced by causes and conditions nor arising spontaneously.

Therefore, below, both the Dharma and the analogy are concluded together. In emptiness and water, there is truly no characteristic of flowing; likewise, True Suchness (Tathatā) has no characteristic of movement.
That which is now seen as the shifting and changing characteristic of movement is merely what has been displaced by the conceptual constructions of sentient beings.

If one realizes that True Suchness is immovable, then that aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) is itself the wondrous enlightened nature of the Tathāgata, which exists without causes or conditions.
"Indeed, it is for your sake that I have performed this practice. V. The Aggregate of Consciousness (vijñāna-skandha):
Ānanda, it is as if there were a person who took a *pingala* jar... [as previously described] ...you should know that the aggregate of consciousness is likewise thus."
Below, Ānanda: Fifth, the analysis of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). Regarding the metaphor of the *piṅgala* (the *kalaviṅka* bird):
taking its form, it is said to have a beautiful voice; taking its vessel, it is in fact impermanent.

"Plugging its two holes" refers to being plugged by good and evil karma, thereby constituting a false existence. According to principle, good and evil are fundamentally empty; they are originally impermanent.
Therefore, it is spoken of by means of two apertures; this is what is meant by "one metaphor through which many principles are understood.
To carry empty space filled to the brim as provisions for another country is a metaphor for sentient beings maintaining their karma as they travel back and forth through the six realms.

How is this different from True Suchness not abiding in its own nature, but following karma to entrust itself to consciousness as it travels between the three realms? Thus it is said: regarding the aggregate of consciousness, one should know that it is likewise...

It is likewise. Ānanda, this space does not come from that direction. When one opens the empty vessel or turns it upside down, one should see space emerge. Ānanda, [the Buddha] then extensively refutes [this view]:
if one were to lift up space and serve it to someone far away, that [space] would not increase; if one were to store space and carry it away, then this [space] would not decrease.

It does not diminish. This is illustrated by the fact that True Suchness (Tathatā) neither decreases among ordinary beings nor increases among sages; it is neither existent in birth nor non-existent in death.

That we now perceive the increase and decrease of sages and ordinary beings, or the existence and non-existence of birth and death, is merely the conceptual proliferation of the sentient beings' emotional consciousness.
How could such things exist within True Suchness?
Therefore, one should know that the aggregate of consciousness is empty and false, fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor arising spontaneously.
Thus, [the text] below concludes with both dharma and analogy: while space has no characteristic of coming or going, True Suchness likewise has no characteristic of coming or going.
That we now see the bustling confusion of the three realms and the turmoil of the six destinies is merely the delusion of sentient beings.
This is a delusion. If one perceives True Suchness (*tathatā*), that aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) is itself the Tathāgata’s wondrous nature of awakening.
How could there be causes and conditions or spontaneity by which you might recognize it as "your own"?

The Third Fascicle of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*: The Ultimate Meaning of the Secret Cause for Cultivation and Realization of the Tathāgata’s Great Buddha-Crown, and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Jishi, residing at the Ancient Xingfu Chan Monastery in Lousong.
△ Second, the analysis of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
Furthermore, Ānanda, how are the six sense bases fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha, the wondrous nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*)?
That which is called "entry" (*āyatana*) refers to the entry of mutual interpenetration. For True Suchness has no boundaries; thus, the six faculties...
Because all [dharmas] can enter [it]. This is not the same as the Hīnayāna’s adherence to them as being existent.

Since the Hīnayāna dogmatically maintains that external objects and other such signs exist and give rise to the sense organs, it is not like this. What is now called "entering" refers to True Suchness itself, its self-awakened self-characteristic;
it is not something that can be entered by means of external objects. Therefore it is said: "The six entrances are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrous..."
The Nature of True Suchness (Tathatā). △ First: The Sense Base of the Eye.
Ānanda, that very eye-organ which, when stared fixedly, gives rise to fatigue—[this extends] until: the two objects of light and darkness ultimately have no substance.

First, regarding the explanation of the sense-base of the eye: first, an analogy is presented to clarify its falsity. The preceding analogy concerned the exhaustion of the eyes, whereby one sees phantom flowers;

these phantom flower-appearances are not external objects. Rather, they arise from the exhaustion of the wondrously enlightened and luminous nature, which, through being strained, gives rise to this madness.
One falsely perceives the appearance of flowers; yet these delusory flowers are ultimately without substance apart from the mind.

Because of the subsequent indication of the nature of non-arising, and because the faculty of vision is triggered by the two objects of light and darkness while situated between them, this nature of vision is likewise not an external thing.
Because True Suchness does not maintain its own nature, it draws in these phenomenal images; this is termed "seeing the nature.
However, this seeing-nature, when separated from phenomena, ultimately has no substance, being identical to those flowers in the sky seen by one with cataracts.
Thus, Ānanda, you should know that this seeing—[extending to] "furthermore, when empty space itself observes, what concern is it to your faculty?"—is thus extensively refuted below.
You should know that this seeing does not come from light or darkness; it does not emerge from the faculty;
nor is it produced from empty space. Why is this? If seeing were identical to light and darkness, there would be no room for its arising or ceasing. If it were identical to the faculty...
If there were seeing, then there would be neither light nor darkness. If space were capable of seeing, it would likewise see its own root.
Furthermore, since space observes itself, what concern is that for your sense-faculties? When one investigates these four locations, there is no seeing at all.

Judging from this, when we speak now of "having seeing," it is truly the self-awakening and self-characteristic of True Suchness (Tathatā); how could there be any external objects? Even if there were external [objects]...
Objects that enter through the eye are merely false and delusory, like the visual fatigue of one staring fixedly.
Therefore, you should know that the eye-faculty is false and illusory; it is fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.
Therefore, the following concludes the meaning of the Dharma: If one calculates that there is a "seer" within the eye when encountering objects such as light and darkness, this is false and delusive.
One fails to know that the nature of this seeing is fundamentally the Tathāgata’s wondrous True Suchness-nature.
How could it be seen by you through causes and conditions or through spontaneity? 2. The Ear-entrance.
Ānanda, it is like a person who, with two fingers, [moves back and forth]—the two objects of movement and stillness ultimately have no substance.

Second, regarding the analysis of the ear-entrance (*śrotra-āyatana*): first, a metaphor is raised to clarify its falsity. It is like the fatigue of the ears, which causes sounds to arise within the head.

This characteristic of sound is not an external object; rather, it is because the wondrous, enlightened, and luminous mind, through staring and fatigue, gives rise to acute hearing, and thus this delusion occurs.
There is the characteristic of sound; however, this characteristic of sound is ultimately without substance apart from the mind.

Because of the following indication of the nature of non-arising, it is now shown that while the two objects—motion and stillness—trigger the faculty of hearing which abides within, this very nature of hearing is likewise not an external thing.
Because True Suchness does not maintain its own nature, it draws in these sensory objects; this is called the faculty of hearing.
However, this faculty of hearing has no essence whatsoever apart from its objects, just as that which produces sound has no essence apart from the sound itself.
Thus, Ānanda, you should know that this hearing—from [the point of] "again, emptiness hears itself" on—has no concern with your sense-faculties.
Thus, the following section provides an extensive refutation. You should know that this nature of hearing does not come from movement or stillness, nor does it emerge from the sense-faculty.
It does not arise from empty space. Why? If hearing existed when [space] was still, it should not exist when it is moving;
if hearing existed when it was moving, it should not exist when it is still. If the sense organ had hearing, there would necessarily be no movement or stillness;

if empty space had hearing, it would no longer be empty space. Furthermore, if empty space itself hears, what concern is that for your faculty of hearing? When one investigates these four possibilities, none of them apply.
This is known through the nature of hearing. Thus we know that those who now possess the nature of hearing are simply the True Suchness itself, hearing within its own mind;
how could there be any external objects? Even if there were external objects entering through the ear, they would be illusory and false, identical to that which was blocked by the finger.
Therefore, you should know that the ear-entrance is empty and false; it is fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.
Thus, the following concludes the meaning of the Dharma: if one calculates that characteristics such as movement and stillness enter the ear and there is hearing, this is merely empty falsehood.
One does not realize that this nature of hearing is originally the Tathāgata’s wondrous true thusness-nature. How could there be any cause?
Is it by natural conditions that you have been able to hear? △ Third, the Nose Faculty.
Ānanda, it is like a person who suddenly pinches his nose... [until] the two objects of obstruction and penetration are ultimately without substance.
Third, regarding the analysis of the sense-base of the nose: first, an analogy is raised to clarify its falsity. It is like the case of eye-strain:
when one hears of cold sensations, various fragrances, or foul odors, these characteristics of cold sensations and so forth are not external objects.

Because the wondrously enlightened and luminous mind is strained by staring, the false appearances of cold sensations and so forth arise. However, these appearances of cold sensations and the like are ultimately [non-existent] apart from the mind.

It has no substance. Because it is based on the following characterization of the nature of non-arising, this faculty of hearing now arises in response to the two objects—openness and obstruction—while residing in the middle.

This nature of hearing is truly not an external thing; for True Suchness (Tathatā) does not abide in its own nature, but rather draws in these sensory images, which is called the "olfactory-hearing nature.
However, this olfactory-hearing nature is ultimately without substance when separated from its objects, being identical to the sensation of cold touch.

You should know that this hearing does not come from the open or the obstructed; it exists inherently within emptiness itself—what concern is it to your faculty? This shall be extensively refuted below.
You should know that this hearing does not come from the open or the obstructed; it does not emerge from the faculty, nor is it produced from emptiness. Why is this?
If there were hearing when there is openness, then its nature would be extinguished at the time of obstruction. If there were hearing when there is obstruction, then...
If hearing were not distinct from time, then if the faculty of hearing existed, there would necessarily be no such thing as being open or obstructed.

If space itself could hear, it would naturally smell your own nose; furthermore, if space itself hears, what concern is that for your sensory faculty? When examined across these four locations, there is nowhere at all where hearing exists.
Speaking from this perspective, that which possesses the nature of hearing is precisely the self-hearing nature of True Suchness (tathatā) itself;
how could there be any external objects? Even if there were external objects entering through the nose, they would be merely false and illusory, identical to the exhausted toil of those beasts.
Therefore, you should know that the nose-faculty (*ghrāṇāyatana*) is empty and false; it is fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.
Thus, the following concludes the meaning of the Dharma: if one calculates that there is hearing within the nose based on the faculties of openness and obstruction, this is empty and false.
One does not realize that the nature of smelling and hearing is originally the Tathāgata’s wondrous True Suchness-nature (*tathatā*). How could there be any cause?
Is it by natural cause that you are able to smell? △ Fourth, the tongue-base (*jihvā-āyatana*).
Ānanda, it is as if there were a person who licks his lips with his tongue... (up to) ...and the two objects of taste, sweet and bland, which ultimately have no substance.

Fourth, regarding the analysis of the tongue-sense base (*jihvā-āyatana*): first, an analogy is raised to clarify its falsity. It is like the fatigue of the tongue, which gives rise to the appearances of sweetness, bitterness, and so forth.

These qualities of sweetness and bitterness are not external objects; rather, they are falsely produced through the fatigue of the wondrously enlightened and luminous mind when it is stared at intently.
Yet, these qualities of sweetness and bitterness are ultimately without substance apart from the mind. Because of sweetness and bitterness...

The preceding section established the nature of non-arising. Now, because cognition arises from the two objects of sweet, bitter, and bland flavors while abiding in the center, this nature of knowing taste is not an external object.
Because True Suchness does not maintain its own nature, it absorbs these sensory images; this is termed the "nature of knowing taste.
However, this nature of knowing taste has no essence whatsoever apart from the objects; it is identical to those tastes of sweet and bland.
Thus, Ānanda, you should know this (up to): furthermore, since empty space knows for itself, what does it have to do with your faculty of taste?
Thus [the text] refutes [the opponent's position] extensively below. You should know that this tasting of bitter or bland is known as not being the arrival of sweet or bitter;

it does not arise because of the blandness, nor is it produced from the sense organ, nor does it emerge from empty space. Why is this? Because if this nature of knowing flavor were derived from the sweet...
When bitterness arises, the nature of sweetness ceases. If sweetness were to possess cognition, then the nature of sweetness would already be lost.
If the faculty possessed cognition, there could be no sweet, bland, or bitter objects. If emptiness had flavor, it would not be within the reach of the nature.
Furthermore, if emptiness knew itself, what would that have to do with your faculty? Examining these four possibilities, there is nowhere a nature that knows flavor. From this it may be said:
All that possesses the nature of knowing taste is simply the self-experiencing essence of True Suchness (tathatā) itself;
how could there be any external object? Should there be an external object entering through the tongue, it is merely a delusion, equivalent to that "licking of toil."
Therefore, you should know that the tongue-base (*jihvā-āyatana*) is empty and false; it is fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.
Thus, the following concludes the meaning of the Dharma: if one calculates that characteristics such as sweetness and bitterness arise from the tongue-base, this is empty and false.
One does not realize that this nature of knowing taste is originally the Tathāgata’s wondrous True Suchness-nature (*tathatā*). How could there be any cause?
"Did you naturally experience this for yourself? △ Fifth, the entry of the body.
Ānanda, it is like a person who, with one cold hand... [until] ...the two objects of opposition and compliance ultimately have no substance.

Fifth, regarding the analysis of the body-sense base (*kāyāyatana*): first, an analogy is presented to clarify its falsity. It is like the fatigue from touching; this reveals the cognition of separation.

As for "cognition of separation," it refers to moving away from cold toward heat, or moving away from heat toward cold—all of which are spoken of in terms of momentum; hence, it is called the "cognition of separation.
Furthermore, the essence of this cognition of separation is not an external object, for it arises from the delusion of the wondrously enlightened and luminous mind when it is fatigued by staring.
There is the nature of cognition. However, this nature of cognition is ultimately without substance apart from the mind.

Because of the subsequent indication of the nature of non-arising, it is now shown that because the two objects—separation and conjunction—arouse awareness within the center, this awareness is not some other entity.
Because True Suchness does not maintain its own nature, it draws in these sensory objects; this is termed the nature of cognition.
However, this nature of cognition is ultimately without substance apart from sensory objects, just like that hand-touching.
Thus, Ānanda, you should know that this awareness—[from "to" "emptiness"]—is self-aware; what concern does it have with your sense-faculties? Thus, below, there is an extensive refutation.
You should know that this awareness does not come from separation or union; it does not exist through opposition or conformity;

it does not emerge from the sense-faculties, nor is it produced from emptiness. Why is this? Because when this nature of awareness confronts the moments of separation and union, if [the sense-faculty] were to unite...

If there is cognition, then at the time of separation, the nature of cognition must have already ceased. If there were cognition during separation, then the nature of cognition would vanish at the time of contact.

The same refutation applies to the states of opposition and conformity. Furthermore, if the sense organ possessed cognition, it would necessarily lack the four characteristics of separation, contact, opposition, and conformity.
If space possessed cognition, what would it have to do with your sense bases (*āyatana*)? Examining these four locations, the nature of cognition is found to be entirely absent. Therefore...
To discuss this: whatever possesses the nature of cognition is precisely the *tathatā* (suchness) of one's own mind perceiving its own mind;
how could there be any external objects? Even if external objects were to exist, should they enter through the sense gates of the body, they would be merely false and illusory.
It is identical to that [feeling] in being apart from cognition.
Therefore, one should know that the body-base (*kāyāyatana*) is empty and false; it is fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.

Thus, the following concludes the meaning of the Dharma: if one calculates that there is a characteristic of tangibility (*spraṣṭavya-lakṣaṇa*) within the body through the conjunction or separation, or the opposition or compliance [of objects], [it is likewise false].
This is precisely false and delusory. You do not know that this characteristic of sensation and touch is fundamentally the Tathāgata’s wondrous, true Suchness-nature.
How could there be any causes and conditions or spontaneity by which you might come to know it? △ Sixth, the sense-base of the mind.
Ānanda, it is like a person who, when weary, falls asleep—[and so on, until]—the two objects of arising and ceasing ultimately have no substance.
Regarding the sixth, the faculty of the mind (*manas*), first a metaphor is raised to clarify its falsity:

just as the mind is weary, there arise such matters as waking, sleeping, remembering, and forgetting. These states of waking and sleeping are not external objects; they exist because of the wondrously enlightened and luminous mind.
Through staring and fatigue, there falsely arise matters such as waking and sleeping, remembering and forgetting, and birth and extinction; these habits return to the mind.
Yet, apart from the mind, these states of waking and sleeping ultimately have no substance. This is because [the text] below marks their nature as non-arising.

Now, due to the two objects of birth and extinction, the gathered cognition abides in the center. This nature of gathered cognition is likewise not an external thing, for True Suchness does not maintain a fixed state.

As for its intrinsic nature: it flows along with whatever is seen or heard until it reaches the limitlessness [of experience]. The mind (*manas*) then encounters this flow. "Mind" here refers to an "image";

it takes on the image of those phenomena, and thus it is called the faculty of mental cognition (*manovijñānendriya*). This "mental cognition" is precisely "awareness. Now, as for this nature of awareness:
Being devoid of dust, it ultimately has no substance; it is like that which occurs during waking and sleeping.
Thus, Ānanda, you should know that such [consciousness], up to its very self, is empty awareness; what concern does it have with your sense-faculties?
Thus it is extensively refuted below. One should know that this faculty of cognition does not come from waking or sleeping;

it does not exist through arising or ceasing; it does not emerge from the sense-faculties, nor is it produced from emptiness. Why is this? If this faculty of mental cognition exists during the state of waking, it is then non-existent upon reaching the state of sleep;
by what means, then, could there be sleep? The nature of sleep is the opposite of this. If it exists during the state of birth... [the text continues].
When it reaches the point of extinction, it simply ceases to exist; what then can be used as the "nature of extinction"? The opposite is true for that which emerges from the faculties:
its waking and sleeping, its opening and closing, belong solely to the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) and have no connection whatsoever with the mind-faculty (*manas*).

Yet, those who now claim there is a "mind-faculty that knows" are ultimately like flowers in the sky. Furthermore, if emptiness were to possess cognition, what would it have to do with your sense-bases (*āyatana*)? Search for it in these four locations.
There is no intention whatsoever. Judging from this, that which is called the faculty of mental cognition is simply the true suchness (tathatā) itself remembering and awakening by itself;
how could there be any external objects? Even if there were external objects entering through the mind, [they would be nothing other than suchness].
This, then, is false and illusory, like that [state of] staring-induced fatigue.
Therefore, one should know that the mental sense-base (*manāyatana*) is false and illusory; it is fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.

Thus, the following concludes the meaning of the Dharma: those who calculate that the nature of the mind which perceives arising and ceasing enters the mental sense-base and possesses cognition— [End of fragment]
This is precisely delusion. You do not know that this awakening and this cognition are fundamentally the wondrous true suchness-nature (tathāgatagarbha) of the Tathāgata.
How could there be causes and conditions, or spontaneity, for you to conceive of as "your own mind"? △ Third, the analysis of the twelve bases (āyatana).
Furthermore, Ānanda, how are the twelve bases (āyatana) fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrous nature of True Suchness?
As for what is called a "base," a base refers to a locus. These twelve bases are precisely the loci of the mind. Thus it is asked.
Perfectly pervasive and boundless, the true realm has no form. How, then, could there be any location? It is said: For example, it is like a person dreaming of a fine house;
they immediately give rise to feelings of pleasure. Not only do these feelings of pleasure arise, but they further give rise to the notion of a self. Yet, upon waking, [these vanish].
Upon awakening, there is nothing at all to be found; let alone that which follows waking, how could even that dream-house be an external object?
One does not realize it is entirely produced by one's own mind, manifesting as perceptions of pleasure and sensation. The twelve bases (*āyatana*) are likewise so. Therefore, it is said:
This is precisely the Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrous nature of True Suchness. △ First, regarding the object of form:
Ānanda, you should observe this Jeta Grove (up to) the arising of form through the seeing of the eye, and the arising of the appearance of form through the eye.
First, the analysis of the object-field of form (*rūpa*). To begin, a case is cited to raise the inquiry:
"The Jeta Grove and its various springs and ponds—these are the objective domain of the eye. Yet, the eye has never actually reached the location of those groves and springs. Why?

Because when the eye were to reach the groves and springs, there would necessarily be the phenomenon of entering and exiting; however, within the eye, no such phenomenon of entering and exiting exists. Therefore...
The forest and springs have never reached the place where the eyes are; yet the forest and springs do not reach above the eyes either.
For when the forest and springs arrive, the eye has no space for planting trees, nor does it have ground upon which to receive the springs;
thus, they have never reached above the eyes. Nevertheless, as for what we now see—the Jeta Grove and its various springs and ponds—why is this?
Is it that form arises and is seen by the eye? Or is it that the eye arises as the appearance of form? The analysis of this vision will be discussed below.

Ānanda, if it were the case that the faculty of the eye gives rise to the appearance of form, then when the eye perishes, that appearance would be utterly non-existent; who then would perceive empty space and form?
Ānanda proceeds to refute the nature of non-arising. First, regarding the refutation of the eye producing the characteristic of form:

if the eye perceives a substantial entity that is form, you may concede that it possesses characteristics; however, if it perceives space, this is not form. Since it is not form, the nature of the perceived characteristic has already dissolved.
Once dissolved, it is entirely non-existent. Who then knows of its non-existence? Next, he refutes the production of the eye’s seeing by means of form.
If you maintain that a substantial entity of form reaches the eye and thus allows for seeing, then suppose space were not form;
since it is not form, the very nature of seeing space would also perish. If it perishes, then it is utterly non-existent. Who could know its non-existence?
By this reasoning, even the nature of seeing does not exist; how, then, could there be a location?
Therefore, you should know that seeing and form are empty (up to: they are fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor by spontaneous nature).
Thus, the conclusion below establishes the meaning of the Dharma: seeing emptiness is non-seeing; seeing form is also non-seeing.
Since both emptiness and form are non-existent, the locus [of perception] cannot be established. That there is now visible form is merely a delusion. It is not real.
One should know that this form and these characteristics are fundamentally the Tathāgata’s wondrous nature of True Suchness (tathatā).
It can be seen that they are originally neither produced by causes and conditions nor are they of a spontaneous nature. △ Second, the sense object of sound.
Ānanda, listen further to this: within this Jeta Grove, [the sound] comes to the side of the ear, or the ear goes to the place of the sound.

This is the second analysis of the auditory object (*śabda-viṣaya*). First, a case is cited to raise the inquiry: although the bell and drum are objects of the ear, they cannot be the locus of the mind.
Why? Because sound possesses no characteristic of coming or going. Since sound is thus [without such a characteristic]...
If there is no coming or going, then what does the ear grasp from its object? This is because the ear likewise lacks the characteristic of coming or going.
Since the ear has no coming or going, then what does it grasp from the location of the sound? Therefore, we now ask:

when food is prepared, the drum is beaten, and the assembly gathers, and the bell is struck—is it that the sound comes to the side of the ear, or is it that the ear goes to the place of the sound? Distinguish this!
See the following passage:
"Ānanda, if this sound were to come from outside to the side of the ear... (until) if there were no coming or going, there would likewise be no hearing.
Below this, Ānanda refutes the nature of non-arising. First, he refutes the notion that the sound comes to the side of the ear: "Suppose, for instance, that I go out to beg for alms..."
Within the city, at the Jeta Grove, there is no self. To use an analogy: when a sound reaches Ānanda’s ear, then the place where the bell or drum is located is without sound;
if that were so, one would have no hearing at the Jeta Grove. But now it is not so; the sound of the bell [is heard].
With one strike, they come together at the place of eating; by this, it is clear that sound does not come to the side of the ear.
Furthermore, the following passage refutes the notion that the ear goes to the place where the sound is: suppose I return to the Jeta Grove; while I am in the city, I would no longer exist [there].
This is analogous to the ear having already gone to the place where the drum was struck; then, the nature of hearing would no longer exist within the faculty of the ear. Great!
The multitude would then remain unaware [of it]. Now, however, when the bells are struck simultaneously, they are heard by all at once;
even elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep each have their own sounds. From this, it is clear that the ear does not travel to the location of the sound.

Furthermore, if there were no mutual coming and going, the principle of hearing could not be established. By this we know that since hearing itself is not established, how could there be a location for it?
Therefore, you should know that hearing and sound (up to the point of their cessation) are fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.
Thus, the following concludes the meaning of the Dharma: Sound does not come to the ear, and thus there is no nature of hearing;
the ear does not go to the place of sound, and thus there is no characteristic of sound. That there is now sound which can be heard is merely a delusion; one does not realize this.
This sound is heard; fundamentally, it is the Tathāgata’s wondrous true thusness-nature. Originally, it cannot be heard as being either produced by causes and conditions or arising spontaneously.
△ Third, the sense-object of fragrance.
"Ānanda, you should again smell this sandalwood in the incense burner... [does it] arise in your nose, or does it arise in space?

This third section distinguishes the object of fragrance (*gandha-viṣaya*). First, he raises a matter to pose a question; for although fragrance is indeed the objective domain of the nose, [it must be examined as to its locus].
However, within the nose there is no scent of sandalwood; in the sandalwood there is no nature of smelling; and in empty space there is likewise no substance of fragrance.
When these three locations are examined, each is found to lack the nature of arising. Therefore, I now ask:
if one ounce of this incense is burned, those who smell it simultaneously across forty *li* is truly a marvel. Does this fragrance arise from the wood? Or does it arise...
Does it arise in the nose? Or does it arise in space? This is refuted in the following passage:
"Ānanda, if this fragrance were produced in your nose [and so forth], how could you have smelled it from within forty li?"
Ānanda then proceeds to refute the nature of non-arising. First, he refutes arising from the nose:

if the nose were to produce the fragrance when it encounters a scent, then that fragrance ought to emerge from within the nose itself. But this is not the case; the nose is not sandalwood, yet there is the scent of sandalwood.
To say that you "smell" the fragrance makes it clear that it comes from the outside; thus, the claim that the nose hears [perceives] it is illogical. Next, he refutes arising from space.
If emptiness possessed fragrance, its substance should be ever-present; however, this is not the case. When wood is burned, it becomes fragrant, but when unburned, no scent is perceived.
Third, regarding the production of fragrance from wood: when wood is burned, smoke rises; yet if the nose were merely to encounter the smoke, one should not perceive fragrance.
Now it is not so. Before the smoke has traveled far, it is heard by everyone within forty li;
from this we know that the nature of fragrance is without arising—how could it have a location?
Therefore, you should know that the fragrance, the nose, and the act of smelling—from the beginning—neither arise through causes and conditions nor by way of spontaneous nature.
Thus, the following concludes the meaning of the Dharma: the nose does not produce sandalwood, and sandalwood lacks the nature of a nose.

That there is now a fragrance to be smelled is but a false construction; it is a failure to understand that the smelling and the object of smell are fundamentally the wondrous [nature] of the Tathāgata.
The nature of True Suchness (tathatā) is fundamentally not produced by causes and conditions; it is not something that can be smelled of its own accord. △ Fourth, the object of taste:
Ānanda, when you are among the assembly holding your alms bowl at the two times [of morning and noon]... (up to) does it arise within the tongue, or does it arise within the food?
Fourth, the analysis of the sense-object of taste (*rasa*). First, an example is raised to provoke inquiry: although taste is the domain of the tongue, the tongue does not produce taste;
food does not produce taste; and space does not produce taste. When examined across these three locations, each lacks the nature of production.
From where, then, does taste come? Therefore, it is now asked: "When you constantly carry your alms bowl, you may encounter ghee, curd, or clarified butter (*ghṛta*)."
Regarding this "supreme flavor of ghee": does this flavor arise from space? Does it arise from the tongue? Or does it arise from the food?
This will be refuted in the following passage:
"Ānanda, if this flavor were to arise from your tongue... [omitted] ...there would necessarily be no cognition; how then could it be called 'flavor'?"

Ānanda now refutes the nature of non-arising. First, he refutes production from the sense organ: if this flavor were produced in the tongue, the tongue would not consist of multiple entities, as there is only a single tongue;
since it has already distinguished the flavors of ghee and curd, it should not then taste honey. If it does not undergo transformation, [it cannot perceive different objects].
How do you know taste? Next, [I shall] refute its arising from food: if taste were produced from food, then if the food possessed consciousness, it would not depend upon your tasting;
since food does not possess consciousness, how can you call it "taste"? Third, [I shall] refute its arising from space:
if this taste were produced from space, then if space possessed taste, what kind of taste would it be? If it were a salty taste, then the people of this realm would all be [salty].
As for sea fish, once they have become accustomed to saltiness, how could they know what it is to be fresh? Since they do not know what freshness is, how can one speak of "flavor"?
Judging from this, flavor is fundamentally unarisen; how, then, could there be a location for it?
Therefore, you should know that taste, the tongue, and the act of tasting (up to this point) are fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.
Thus, the following concludes the meaning of the Dharma: the tongue has no inherent nature of tasting; food likewise has no inherent nature of being tasted.
That there is now a taste to be tasted is merely a false construction. Not knowing that this taste and this nature are originally the Tathāgata.

The wondrous nature of True Suchness (Tathatā) is fundamentally not produced by causes and conditions; it cannot be experienced as something that arises spontaneously. △ Fifth, the sense-object of touch:
Ānanda, when you regularly rub your head with your hand in the early morning, [is the sensation] located in the hand or is it located in the head?
Fifth, the analysis of the object of touch (*spraṣṭavya*). First, a question is raised by citing an example. Speaking in terms of the body:
although touch is indeed the objective domain of the body, the head itself has no touch; the hand likewise has no touch; the subject has no touch, and the object has no touch.
Investigating these four locations, each is found to lack the nature of arising. Who, then, constitutes this contact? Therefore, I now ask:
when you regularly rub your head with your hand in the early morning and perceive contact as being the body, does it reside in the agent or the object?
Does it reside in the hand or in the head? The refutation of these views follows in the text below.
If it were located in the hand, there would be no cognition [of it elsewhere], up to the point that it should not be the case that space comes into contact with you.
Below, in the discussion on the nature of non-arising, first the mutual existence and mutual non-existence are refuted:

if this nature of contact were both existent and non-existent in one place, then contact would not be established; if it were separately existent in each, then two distinct bodies would result. Next, the identity [of the two] is refuted.
Regarding this nature of touch: if the head and hand were produced by a single touch, they would constitute a single entity without depending on mutual friction.
This refutes the three [positions] and establishes two entities. In this nature of touch, both the head and the hand possess their respective capacities as subject and object;
that which is the subject is not the object, and that which is the object is not the subject. From this, it is known that even this nature of perceiving touch does not exist in its location.
From what could it arise? It is not possible for empty space to constitute a tactile object for you.
Therefore, you should know that the perception of touch and the body—from their very origin—are neither caused by conditions nor are they of spontaneous nature.
Therefore, the following concludes the meaning of the Dharma: the head and hands have no nature of tangibility, and space likewise has no nature of tangibility.
That there is now a perception of touch is merely false and illusory. One does not realize that this perception and this touch are fundamentally the Tathāgata’s wondrous True Suchness-nature;
they are originally neither produced by causes and conditions nor known through spontaneity. △ Six: Mental Objects (dharmas).
"Ānanda, as for the objects of good and evil that you constantly perceive within the scope of your mind—do they exist apart from the mind in some other location?
This sixth section, the "Analysis of Mental Objects," first raises the inquiry by citing examples:

although phenomena such as good, evil, and neutral states are the objective domains perceived by the mind, they cannot serve as the locus of the mind, because all phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
It merely takes as its object the *nimitta-bhāga* (perceived aspect) of one's own mind;

since this *nimitta-bhāga* of one's own mind also lacks substantial reality, it is like flowers in the sky or images in a mirror. Upon thorough investigation, one finds that neither the sky nor the mirror has ever been produced.
All dharmas have the same characteristic: in reality, they are without arising. Therefore, it is now asked:
do dharmas such as good and evil arise from the mind itself, or do they exist separately apart from the mind? This will be refuted in the following text.

Ānanda, if [the object] were identical to the mind, then dharmas would not be external objects (*viṣaya*). (Up to: Since the mind is not a locus of objective support (*ālambana*), from whom could it be established?

Ānanda, the following section refutes the nature of non-arising. First, he refutes the position that [the object] is identical to the mind: because that which is identical to the mind is itself non-arising. Why is this?

Because the mind only takes conventional dharmas as its objects of perception, and does not take real dharmas as its objects. Real dharmas are precisely the external objects (*viṣaya*). As it is said:
Fire and wind: wind possesses the nature of coldness, while fire possesses the nature of burning; therefore, they are called real dharmas (*dravyadharma*).

A conventional dharma (*prajñaptidharma*) is not a sensory object (*viṣaya*). It is like water and waves: the wave is a distinct characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), whereas the water is the common characteristic.

Therefore, they are called provisional phenomena (*prajñapti-dharma*). Now, regarding phenomena such as good and evil that arise from the mind: the mind itself is a provisional phenomenon, not a sensory object (*viṣaya*). Thus it is said:
"If it is not an object of the mind, how can it constitute a sense-field (*āyatana*)? Next, [the text] refutes [the view of those who] maintain that [phenomena] exist apart from the mind.
Because that which is apart from the mind is likewise unarisen. Why is this? If the mind were apart from the mind, would it possess cognition or not?
If it possesses cognition, then cognition is what constitutes the mind; thus, it remains its own essence.
Since its own essence is unarisen, it differs from your [position] regarding non-objects and becomes identical to another's mind. And since another's mind is also unarisen, [your position] is not so.
If there were another mind apart from your own that knew for you, it too would be unborn. If it were not a knower, it would not be a knowing mind;
it would be devoid of all sensory objects and activities, and thus entirely without manifestation. Since it lacks manifestation, it is unborn.
Even if one were to remove the human realm, there would be no place outside of space that could serve as an object of cognition.
That which constitutes your mind is likewise non-arising. Discussed from this perspective, the mental faculty (*manas*) is truly non-arising; from what, then, could its locus be established?
Therefore, you should know that dharmas and the mind (up to the point of their ultimate nature) are fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor are they of spontaneous nature.
Therefore, the following concludes the meaning of the Dharma: neither the mind nor consciousness has any arising; the locus of dharmas likewise has no arising.
To claim now that there is a "mind" acting as the object-field of dharmas is merely a false fabrication. Not understanding this, one fails to realize that the mind is itself the dharma.

The original is the Tathāgata’s wondrous nature of True Suchness (tathatā). Fundamentally, it is neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it spontaneously so; it is to be understood as the Dharma.
△ Fourth, the analysis of the eighteen realms (dhātus).
Furthermore, Ānanda, how are the eighteen *dhātus* fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha, the wondrous nature of True Suchness?
Furthermore, below is the general heading: that which is called a "realm" (*dhātu*) refers to a boundary or limit. For example, the ear governs hearing and the eye governs seeing;
they do not transgress one another's domains. Thus, by adding the six consciousnesses to the six faculties and the six objects, the eighteen realms are formed.

Question: Why is consciousness (*vijñāna*) considered a constituent element (*dhātu*)? Answer: It is like an infant whose speech is not yet clear; when seeing objects, it can do no more than utter indistinct sounds such as "da-da" or "ha-ha. This is purely the functioning of the mind (*citta*). Once the child grows up and learns to speak the dialects of Qi or Chu, upon seeing objects, he immediately recognizes whether they are green or yellow, long or short, beautiful or ugly; and upon seeing people, he knows them as Zhang San or Li Si. This is the same principle. Consciousness is the same: though its essence is originally one, its functions differ according to the distinctions of the six sense bases (*ṣad-āyatana*). Therefore, it is established as a separate element. Furthermore, because it serves as the basis for the arising of all phenomena, it is called a "constituent element" (*dhātu*). Thus, it is said that consciousness is the seed of all phenomena. Just as an infant’s speech is indistinct, so too is the function of consciousness at the initial stage of birth. When it encounters conditions, it gives rise to various mental states, just as the infant’s speech becomes distinct through learning. Because it is the foundation for the arising of all phenomena, it is called a "constituent element. Moreover, because it is the basis for the continuity of rebirth, it is called a "constituent element. Just as the infant’s speech is the basis for subsequent verbal expression, so too is this consciousness the basis for the continuity of future existence. Therefore, it is established as a separate element. Furthermore, because it is the basis for the differentiation of the world, it is called a "constituent element. Just as the infant’s speech differentiates between various words, so too does this consciousness differentiate the various realms of existence. Therefore, it is established as a separate element. Finally, because it is the basis for the manifestation of the world, it is called a "constituent element. Just as the infant’s speech manifests various meanings, so too does this consciousness manifest the various worlds. Therefore, it is established as a separate element. For these reasons, consciousness is established as a constituent element.
