In this way, disturbances interact and give rise to weariness; as weariness persists for a long time, dust is stirred up, and their own characteristics become turbid.

These five knots demonstrate the nature of delusion. "In this way" refers to the aforementioned identity and difference between subject and object, as well as their mutual distinction and non-distinction.
This is because these factors are inextricably mixed and confused within the essence of awakened clarity, agitated and unsettled. Why is this? As soon as there is a single...

Where there is an object of characterization (*lakṣya*), there must be a subject of characterization (*lakṣaṇa*). As soon as there is a common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), there is a distinct characteristic (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*).
Thus, the subject and object, the common and the distinct, mutually depend upon one another without ceasing. When this dependence does not cease, the characteristic of weariness (*klama*) arises.

Therefore it is said: "In this way, through mutual dependence and disturbance, weariness arises. Weariness is precisely weary deliberation (*pariśrama*). When weary deliberation persists for a long time, the spirit becomes darkened and obscured.
Dust arises naturally. Dust is a thing that is dark and devoid of cognition. When the mind-ground possesses dust, how could it not become turbid? Therefore it is said:
"Through long labor, dust is produced, and they mutually obscure one another. To examine this closely, it is the causal characteristic of the three delusions (*trividha-moha*). How is this known?
That which is supremely luminous and supremely awakened, while the ordinary is neither luminous nor awakened; it is not luminous.

This is precisely what is called ignorance; how could it be anything other than the delusion of ignorance? That which is illuminated and that which is awakened must necessarily have that which illuminates and that which awakens.

This duality of subject and object—how could it be anything other than the delusions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges? Furthermore, that which is awakened stands in opposition to that which is illuminated as something distinct.
It is not that non-illumination corresponds to non-awareness as being identical; rather, identity and difference mutually serve as causes and conditions for one another.
How could this be anything other than the afflictions of views and thoughts? Indeed, within the essence of awakened illumination, these three delusions act as the cause.

It is because of this that the karmic fruits of worldly sentient beings come to exist. Question: If that is so, does the wondrously bright essence of awakening possess these three delusions? Answer: No.

However, the Buddha said: "The nature of awakening is inherently luminous. Delusion constitutes the act of perceiving through that luminosity. Awakening itself is not an object of perception; yet, because of this luminosity, an object is established.
To establish both the luminosity and its object—is this not delusion? Once delusion has been formed, one falsely perceives mountains, rivers, and the great earth;
one falsely perceives sentient beings undergoing flux and transformation, even down to the animate and inanimate, whether as supports or as primary entities—there is nothing that is not so."
All are equally formed by delusion. It is like a person dreaming: in the dream they see mountains, rivers, and lands;
they see "self" and "other," right and wrong; they see the lofty and the wealthy; they see the lowly and the ugly.
Although such appearances exist, while dreaming the person does not know them to be false. Yet upon waking, nothing at all can be found.
Thus we know that the dreamer is the cause; upon the substance (the mind), there are such false effects.
The effect does not transcend the cause, and the cause does not emerge from anything other than falsehood. Falsehood has no basis of its own, but dwells solely by depending on ignorance.
Therefore it is said: "These three delusions are the causes upon the substance. From the following section onward, the characteristics of the effects are explained. △ Fourth: Clarification.

The characteristic of arising within the *tathāgatagarbha* nature gives rise to the defilements and afflictions... (up to) "therein there is neither sameness nor difference; truly, conditioned phenomena do not exist.
The first part provides a general outline. From "By this" (*youshi*) onwards, the three characteristics are briefly explained. "By this" (*youshi*) means "for this reason. Awakening...

Regarding the essence of clarity (*prabhāsvara*): from these three delusions, worldly toil and affliction (*kleśa*) are incited. Now, as for the nature of "dust" (*rajas*), its meaning is that of obscuration by darkness.
As for the nature of "toil" (*lao*), its meaning is that of frequent movement. "Affliction" (*fan*) refers to feverish heat; "distress" (*nǎo*) refers to opposition and friction.
Because the clarity of awareness fails to realize [itself], it is obscured by darkness, thus it is called "dust. This is what is meant below by "the clarity of awareness within emptiness."
The obscuration of the four wheels and so forth constitutes their characteristic. Because they are able to illuminate and awaken, yet repeatedly agitate the mind, they are called "toil.
This clarifies that delusion is not something else; the six delusions and so forth constitute their characteristic. Furthermore, it clarifies what is not illuminated.
To be awakened to that which was not yet awakened, the mind-ground becomes conflicted and obstructed; because of this, there is feverish distress, hence it is called "affliction" (*kleśa*).
This is identical to the subsequent attachment to conceptualizations and desires; its specific characteristics are the three roots: killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct.

This is merely a general indication, which is why their specific meanings are not yet explained here. Regarding the phrase "arising as the basis for the following," first provide a brief explanation to clarify the intent of its induction. This is the fundamental [text].
The nature of original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*) either does not arise, or if it arises, it is delimited by that which is illuminated and awakened.
For example, if a single thought arises, it is immediately delimited by the three periods of time; thus it is said that "arising constitutes the world.

The nature capable of illuminating and awakening either does not sink, or if it sinks, it becomes trapped in that which is neither illumination nor awakening—this is what is meant by "a single thought."
Lacking awareness, one is trapped by stubborn emptiness; hence it is said that "stillness becomes empty space. For this reason, when there is knowing and seeing, there is movement;
when there is no knowing or seeing, there is sinking. To sink is to be identical with empty space; to move is to differ as the world.
Thus it is said: "Empty space is identity; the world is difference. The following two lines provide a minor conclusion, stating that in those [states], there is identity.

To establish "neither identical nor different" based on difference is the eternal principle (*nitya-dharma*). This is just as establishing "neither birth nor death" based on the perception of birth and death;

this is nirvana. Yet, when viewed from the perspective of the ultimate reality, even that establishment of the eternal principle—neither identical nor different—and the establishment of nirvana as neither birth nor death, are themselves conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) within the true essence.
What, then, could be permanent and real? Therefore it is said: "Therein is neither sameness nor difference.

Truly, conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) arise through the mutual dependence of awakening and clarity against emptiness and dullness, resulting in agitation... (up to) by these causes and conditions, the world continues in succession.
Next is the detailed explanation. First, the world is specifically elucidated. Regarding the passage beginning with "The clarity of awakening": first, the wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*) is explained.
Now, when the nature of ultimate clarity and ultimate awakening is mistakenly identified as a void that is neither clear nor awakened, one remains in ignorance and complacency.
Through this mutual dependence, cold arises; through its agitation, wind is formed. Thus, there exists a wind-circle that sustains the world. For wind is, by nature, movement. The world...
The realm (*dhātu*) is so called because it is the nature of abiding. Following the discussion of space, we next clarify the Golden Wheel (*kāñcanacakravāṭa*).
Space is fundamentally immovable; movement and agitation are merely ignorance (*avidyā*). Because of the movement caused by ignorance, the obstruction of manifest awareness (*vidyā*) arises.
That which is naturally firm and luminous is supreme; thus, there is the Golden Wheel that sustains the land. This land is precisely that which is produced by ignorance. Gold...
Because the jewel is firm and bright, it can be maintained; hence it is said that one "maintains" it. Below the firm awakening, there is the third [element], the fire-wheel.

However, since it has already been established through firm and clear awakening, it cannot help but be shaken by the winds of objects. One is firm and one is moving; as these two substances rub against each other, the fire-element prevails.
Thus, the nature of transformation is expressed by means of the fire-element. Now, to speak of transformation in terms of its fundamental nature is precisely—
A manifest fire possesses the nature of burning; when it burns, that which is solid loses its solidity, and that which is moving loses its movement.

Thus, fire prevails over these two substances. Regarding the "Jewel Radiance," the following four radiances represent the water wheel. Because luminous awareness gives rise to craving, it flows downward with moisture;
because ignorance opposes and obstructs, it blazes upward. It is like sweat breaking out when one is oppressed by summer heat; when the mind craves, [it flows down].
Saliva flows. Because these two substances do not overcome one another, there is a water-wheel that contains the worlds of the ten directions.

Roughly speaking, all ten dharma-realms possess the natures of seeing, craving, opposition, and friction; therefore, water is able to contain and soak them. These four wheels mentioned above truly follow a sequential order.
When the nature of awakening fails to awaken, emptiness is formed. Emptiness can give rise to wind, and wind overcomes non-awakening.

Because of awakening, wind is placed next as the first. Space moves and awakens to obstruction; obstruction is solidity, and solidity is superior to wind; therefore, metal is placed next as the second.
That which can awaken and that which is awakened—the opposition between subject and object—are two forms of superiority; fire can transform them, so fire is placed next as the third.
That which can illuminate and that which is illuminated—flaming upward and moistening downward—are two forms of non-superiority; water [is placed next].
It is able to contain [them]. Therefore, water is placed fourth. These four wheels are such that they arise from one another in succession and each excels the one preceding it in its qualities.
To clarify how they arise sequentially: the mountains, seas, grasses, trees, and so forth do not exist apart from what is produced by these four wheels.
Just as both mountains and seas rest upon the earth, and the earth is itself soil, this soil arises from fire.

Regarding "arising": if it concerns grasses and trees, they arise from water; therefore, this is explained separately. However, while worldly discourse discusses the five elements (*pañca-mahābhūta*), wind is not included therein.

This is likely because that [worldly view] speaks according to the aspect of manifestation (*siddha-lakṣaṇa*), whereas this [treatise] discusses them according to the aspect of arising (*utpatti-lakṣaṇa*).
Arising must depend on the True to give rise to the delusory; from that which is produced by delusion, such phenomenal results (*phala-lakṣaṇa*) come to exist. Therefore, first...
First clarify the four wheels, and only thereafter address the mountains, seas, grasses, and trees. From the fire ascending and descending, one clarifies how delusions arise in succession:
water flows to moisture; fire seeks dryness; this is the nature of things. Sometimes they interact and ignite one another, with fire preceding water.
Fire is superior; therefore, dry land forms islands and sandbars. Water precedes fire; therefore, moisture forms the great ocean.
If you do not believe this, consider that within the great ocean fires constantly arise, while rivers and streams constantly pour into those islands and sandbars—is this not proof?
Furthermore, regarding the mutual overcoming of water and fire, sometimes water overcomes it.
If fire does not prevail, the power of water is inferior, and fire then mounts it, forming high mountains. It is as if one were to believe this implicitly;
yet when the stones of these mountains are struck, they produce flames, and when melted, they become water—is this not its proof?
Furthermore, regarding the mutual containment of earth and water: if the earth retreats to cover the water and does not prevail, then the power of the earth is inferior.

Water then mounts it; it is drawn forth as grasses and trees. If you do not believe this, consider now how forests and thickets, when burned, become soil, and when squeezed, become water—is this not its proof?

"Intermingled delusion" concludes the preceding meaning, stating that the various phenomena mentioned above do not arise without cause, but result from the aforementioned lack of awareness, which produces the state of obscurity and darkness.
Emptiness. Within emptiness, ignorance gives rise to delusion; delusion establishes the subject and object, and delusion perceives identity and difference.
Thus, movement and stillness alternate as seeds for one another. For this reason, the world is able to arise and continue in succession.
Furthermore, Pūrṇa, it is explained that delusion is not caused by another [until] "by these causes and conditions, sentient beings continue in succession.
This second section specifically clarifies sentient beings. Previously, the characteristics of the world’s arising were clarified; now, the arising of sentient beings is clarified.
Judging by this principle, the characteristics of the world’s arising are born of non-awakening (*abodhi*); the arising of sentient beings arises from deluded capacity (*mṛṣā-śakti*). The former...
The text says: "The nature of awakening is inherently luminous; delusion constitutes the 'luminous awakening. Can this luminous awakening not be delusion? It further says:
'Awakening is not that which is illuminated; it is because of luminosity that an object is established. Is that which is illuminated not deluded luminosity?
Thus, within the pure and tranquil mind, this single thought of deluded luminosity arises without cause, agitating its source; because of this agitation, there comes to be [the world].

The characteristic of capability: sentient beings are born within it. If one investigates and observes this, is it not ultimately the fault of cognitive clarity that causes sentient beings to undergo birth and death, death and birth, without end?
Therefore it is said: "This delusion of clarity is none other than the fault of cognitive clarity.
Yet, this capability cannot exist independently of its own nature; it must depend upon the characteristic of the objectified. That objectified characteristic is not...
Its self-establishment must depend upon that which enables its formation. The "enabler" belongs to the category of attributes, while the "enabled" belongs to the category of realms.

Once both the enabler and the enabled are established, the karma created by sentient beings and their subsequent experience do not transcend these. Therefore it is said: "Once the false has been established, the principle of clarity does not exceed it.
What is meant by "not exceeding" is that it does not go beyond its own domain; this is precisely like the nature of sentient beings.

Within the constituent parts [of the sense organs], there is deluded capacity; therefore, the ear can hear sound. Within the constituent parts of the realm of sentient beings, there is deluded clarity;
therefore, the eye can see form. Thus it is said: "For these causes and conditions, hearing does not go beyond sound, and seeing does not transcend form.

These two members [ear and eye] arise independently; therefore, they apprehend their objects through separation. The subsequent three members involve a mutual confrontation between subject and object.

They arise in succession; therefore, they collectively apprehend objects. As for the mind (*manas*), it follows the sense organs to distribute its harvest, rather than being restricted to a single faculty.
Thus, the six delusions are established. However, one must know that their ultimate convergence does not exceed a single, overarching delusion capable of this.
It is precisely this single delusive capacity that differentiates seeing, sensing, hearing, and knowing, thereby forming the divisions of nature and the divisions of boundaries.

The meaning [of this]. Therefore it is said: "From this they are divided into seeing, hearing, awareness, and cognition. From the phrase "bound by common karma" (*tong-yeh xiang-chan*) downward, the text clarifies the causes and conditions of sentient beings.
Although the preceding section clarified why sentient beings arise, it did not explain how sentient beings differentiate from one another.
Now, the causes and conditions thereof are explained in detail; the phrase "common karma" and below provides a general enumeration of their categories. This general enumeration...

"Categories" refers to the four modes of birth: womb-born, egg-born, moisture-born, and transformation-born. When the karma of the parents and that of the self coincide, one is reborn as a womb-born or egg-born being.
When there is no dependence on parents but rather arises solely from the karma of the self at the point of conjunction, one is born as a moisture-born being.

Alternatively, by departing from its former location to accord with that [object], it immediately transforms into a class of beings. This is also the fundamental cause for the arising of the four modes of birth (*yoni*).
This is explained in detail below in the section on "Seeing and Luminosity. "Seeing" refers to the subject that sees; "luminous seeing" refers to the object seen.

Furthermore, this subject and object are distinguished as being either identical or different. If they are identical, one feels attachment based on conceptualization (*saṃjñā*); if they are different, one forms aversion based on conceptualization.

Aversion serves as the distinct condition (*pratyaya*), while craving serves as one's own seed (*bīja*). If the parents share the same thoughts and the same craving, conception occurs upon their union.

Generally speaking, common karma (*sabhāga-karma*) acts as the cause (*hetu*) and the parents act as the condition. Through these causes and conditions, the *kalala*, *arbuda*, and so forth are produced.
*Kalala* means "coagulated mucus," and *arbuda* means "fetal vesicle. Within the womb, there are five developmental stages.
The preceding two weeks constitute the initial cause before the differentiation of stages. From the womb and egg downward, this clarifies the categories of sentient beings:

the union or separation of emotion (*ch'ing*) and perception (*hsiang*). Originally, all four modes of birth (*catur-yoni*) possess these equally; however, for the sake of generalization, it is said that where emotion predominates, one is born from a womb;

where perception predominates, one is born from an egg; where attachment is heavy, one is born by coagulation (*saṃsvedaja*); and where there is dispersal, one is born by transformation (*upapāduka*).

Their dwelling is by way of miraculous birth (*upapāduka*). These categories—sentiment (*sneha*) and perception (*saṃjñā*), their conjunction and separation, and their lightness or heaviness—are each distinguished according to what is appropriate for them.
Furthermore, they undergo mutual transformations: either the bonds of sentiment do not reach their end, or the threads of perception lack constancy. Where there is conjunction, perception arises;
where there is transformation, sentiment becomes attached. When sentiment is heavy, one sinks downward; when perception is light, one follows the flight [of thought]. This...

Furthermore, although the specific nature of the retribution experienced by these various types of beings is not fixed, none fail to arise with emotional conceptualization and karma as their causes and conditions.
For this reason, the birth and continuity of sentient beings proceed without end.
Pūrṇa’s conceptual attachment is the same as the bond of craving; one cannot be separated from it. (Up to: Because of this falsehood, one ends and begins again.
Third, the specific clarification of karma and its fruit. There are three types of karma. First, from "Pūrṇa" downwards, it clarifies those who possess desire and greed.
Thus, the arising of sentient beings occurs through ideation (*saṃjñā*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*). When ideation and craving do not cease, they mutually form fetters (*bandhana*).

These fetters cause beings of a similar class to aggregate together. Through this aggregation driven by the fetters of ideation and craving, parents and children are born in succession without interruption.
If one examines this through principle: these [states] arise from within a pure mind. When consciousness is extremely clear and bright, it perceives the emergence of luminous forms;
as this luminous seeing becomes conceptualized, the mind of desire is stirred. Yet one fails to realize that the objective realm of form has already vanished in an instant.
Yet, as their emotions continue to accumulate without ceasing, they engage in conjecture and mental projection, giving rise to various forms of defiled attachment; thus, the mind of desire is born.
From this, we know that for the sentient beings of the world who experience mutual birth and mutual affection, desire and greed constitute the very root.

Next, following the section on greedy attachment, the text clarifies the nature of the greed for killing: one must understand that sentient beings are fundamentally not of a single kind. [The text continues with] perception...

Affection is likewise not of a single kind. Because one establishes oneself as "I" and "mine," one takes the food of others; because others establish themselves as "they" and "theirs," they take one's food.
Among those born from wombs, eggs, moisture, or by transformation, each acts entirely out of self-interest according to its relative strength, devouring one another;
each acts entirely out of self-love, killing one another. When observed through reason, these beings, due to their [ignorance],...
Within the pure mind, the clarity of awakening becomes a fault. When views are shared, it results in attachment; when views differ, it results in hatred. Thus, the intent to kill arises.

One fails to realize that there is no distinction between self and other, yet by forcibly establishing the opposition of subject and object, all manner of private interests are formed, and thus the intent to kill is born.
By this, one knows that for worldlings and sentient beings to engage in mutual birth and mutual killing is itself the act of killing.
Greed is the root of this. The third section, beginning with "Following others to eat sheep," clarifies the thief and the greedy person.

Now, greed arises because of desire, and killing is accomplished because of greed; this necessarily implies the existence of the distinction between self and other. Once the distinction between self and other is established...

One must expand upon this point. Why? Because today, while sheep are weak and humans can eat them, in another day humans may die and become sheep, and sheep may die and become humans, such that they too can eat one another.
Yet it does not stop at a single sheep or a single human; all ten kinds of living beings are like this because of their evil karma.

Born together at the same time, they are able to devour one another; likewise, through death and rebirth, birth and death continue until the very end of the future, for by reason of their evil karma, they are able to devour one another—how could there ever be an end? To observe this through principle:
These arise from the false establishment of cognitive awareness within the pure mind. Once cognitive awareness is established, the subject and object are divided.

Consequently, the mind of "self" and "other" arises, and one secretly consumes [the other]. Not knowing that self and other are but a single interval, one is still born by oneself and killed by oneself;
one secretly steals for oneself and eats for oneself. Because the awareness of luminosity differentiates between subject and object, it thereby brings this about.
This is theft. By this, one knows that for the sentient beings of the world who take the form of being born and eat one another, it is precisely greed for theft that serves as the root.
From the phrase "Because you have taken my life" onwards, he explains the establishment of cause and effect.

Indeed, killing, theft, and sexual misconduct are in reality of one and the same root; they become three only through the sequence of karmic actions. Why is this? It is because greed seeks to satisfy its desires.

The mind becomes killing; because of killing, one sees the thieving of views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*). This is what is called the causal characteristic of deluded karma within the luminous awareness of the mind.
It is just as if you had taken my life—that is, you once killed me—and now that we have met, it is your duty to repay me.
Thus, I would repay you, and you would repay me, compensating for one another in this way for hundreds of thousands of kalpas. Constantly...
"Within birth and death, if you wish for them to end: suppose that my love for your mind and your affection for my form cause us to linger together;
thus bound, we would remain entangled for hundreds of thousands of kalpas—how could there ever be an end?

This is what is called the manifestation of the fruit of deluded karma within the awakened, luminous mind. The fruit must rely upon the cause, and the cause must be requited by the fruit. Thus it is said.
Such causes produce such effects. Within the mind of awakened clarity, one gives rise to deluded birth and death, continuing in this cycle without weariness;

these three alone constitute the root. From the point where Pūrṇa’s discourse on these three kinds of inversions concludes, he summarizes the three preceding inversions. The phrase "such as these" refers to the aforementioned various worldly characteristics.
Regarding the characteristics of arising and the characteristics of karmic fruition: why are these three types of characteristics called "inversions"?

It is because the nature of awakened clarity originally possesses the faculty of knowing, yet it cannot maintain itself; from the locus of knowing, characteristics arise, and through those characteristics, seeing is obtained.
Is this seeing not delusory? Is the locus of knowing not delusory clarity? Since they are termed "delusory," then as for the nature—
Within the essence itself, these things do not exist. Since they are inherently non-existent within the nature-essence, yet now appear to exist, what else could this be but perversion?
From the continuity of this perversion, there arise the mountains, rivers, and the great earth; there arise the various classes of sentient beings;
and there arises the retribution of karmic fruits. When all conditioned phenomena are examined in their actual reality as they successively flow and change, these [things] exist...
These inverted appearances exist upon the substance of awakened clarity; how could they possibly be real?
They are nothing more than the deluded awakening of ignorance. Yet this realm of deluded awakening does not occur but once;
it begins again after it ends, and ends again after it begins, revolving in succession through kalpas as infinite as space—how could there ever be an end to it? △
The fifth section provides a fivefold explanation to resolve doubts and difficulties. First, the objection is set forth:
Pūrṇa said, "If this wondrous awakening [is thus], how could the outflows of conditioned habitual tendencies ever arise again?"
The initial presentation of the doubts raised by Pūrṇa contains two points of difficulty: first, the doubt that awakening (*bodhi*) and non-awakening (*abodhi*) are distinct;

second, the doubt that permanence (*nityatā*) and impermanence (*anityatā*) are separate. Why is this? It is because this wondrously awakened luminous nature is, from the beginning, no more nor less than the mind of the Tathāgata—equal and non-dual.
Yet, due to non-awakening, mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arose without cause.

Regarding the various characteristics such as the earth and so forth: if that is the case, then since the characteristics of mountains, rivers, and the like are non-awakening (*abodha*), whereas the wondrously luminous true nature (*tathatā*) is awakening (*bodhi*), it is said that awakening and non-awakening are distinct.

Yet, at present, these characteristics of mountains, rivers, and so forth are definitely existent, real, and permanent; however, the wondrously luminous true nature possesses both awakening and non-awakening.

It is not permanent; therefore, one suspects that permanence and impermanence are distinct. Thus, these various characteristics exist when there is no awakening, but do not exist when there is awakening.
How can I guarantee that what I have awakened to today will remain entirely non-existent tomorrow?
Furthermore, because the Tathāgata is now enlightened, he is free from these characteristics; yet I do not know when the Tathāgata [will pass away].
One does not realize that these conditioned habitual outflows will arise again at some point. Although this is a delusion common to ordinary people, they do not know that the true principle is thus.

Why? If on another day someone were to grasp at the clarity of awakening as being real and the various phenomena such as mountains and rivers as being false, yet has not reached such a state, how can they merely go on talking of "real" and "false"?
The mind has attained a state of evenness and stability. Therefore, following the formal answer, this passage is further supplemented to complete the preceding meaning.
Thus it is said. △ Second, the explanatory response.
The Buddha told Pūrṇa: "For example, it is like a person who has lost their way" (up to) "...enlightenment and nirvāṇa are also like this.

Next, he answers the explanation. The Buddha’s response consists of four analogies. The first two analogies explain the difficulties of delusion and awakening; the latter two analogies reveal that the Dharma is free from confusion.
Regarding the first analogy of one who is disoriented: from the words "The Buddha told... onwards, he first explains delusion, meaning that [the nature of reality] is originally non-existent.
There is delusion, yet there is no awakening. That we now speak of both delusion and awakening is precisely for the sake of those who are deluded; it is merely a way of speaking to the deluded.
If such a person has already awakened to the distinction between north and south, they will naturally no longer be deluded. This is also like realizing that, fundamentally, there is no delusion.
It is as if there were a deluded awakening. If such a person has already awakened to this awakening, they will naturally no longer be deluded;

this is called "releasing delusion. Next, regarding the metaphor of flowers in the sky: it is explained according to the previous resolution of difficulties. That is to say, space originally has no flowers; the flowers are merely a cataract of the eye.
If the eye is free from the cataract, the flowers likewise do not exist. Yet now, foolish people [cling] to the cessation of these flowers in the sky.
The ground awaits the flower to grow anew; whether such a person is foolish or wise can be known thereby.
It is like the nature that is fundamentally without delusion—delusion is simply confusion. Once one realizes this is delusion, one no longer gives rise to confusion.

Yet, when will these ignorant people ever again become confused regarding the wondrous, empty, luminous awareness? One can know that such a person is both mad and dull-witted. This is called "resolving difficulties."

Third, regarding the analogy of the gold ore: following the words of Pūrṇa, the Buddha first reveals the Dharma. Having seen that Pūrṇa had already grasped the meaning of the analogy, the Buddha said:
"This mad and deluded person is none other than you. Why is this? Previously, I stated that the fundamental awakening is inherently luminous;
yet you claim that fundamental awakening is not itself awakening, asserting that it must rely upon an object of cognition before it can be called awakening.
I say that awakening is not something that can be made manifest. You claim that the nature of awakening is not luminous, and that it must rely upon what is made manifest in order to be luminous;
this very point is your delusion. Because of this delusion, the mountains, rivers, and the great earth have arisen from it.
"The sentient beings of the world and their karmic fruits arise from this; such is my teaching. Yet you still do not understand.

Now you further claim that the Buddhas and Tathāgatas possess a wondrous enlightenment that is empty and luminous. When have they ever failed to be awakened? When would mountains, rivers, and the great earth ever emerge again?
Is this not the delusion and folly of your own mind? You simply fail to realize that the wondrously luminous true nature..."
It is like gold within its ore; once the gold is pure, how could it ever again become mixed with ore?

This is a metaphor for the fact that once delusion has been awakened to as the true nature, how could there be delusion again? This is called "revealing the Dharma. Regarding the fourth metaphor of ash and wood:
following the passage on "like wood," this clarifies the absence of delusion. If one awakens and is no longer deluded, they are like the forest trees.

Once it has been burned to ashes, how could it ever become wood again? By this analogy, once the Buddhas and Tathāgatas have awakened to Bodhi and reached the stage of Nirvāṇa, how could there ever be the re-arising of habitual outflows (*anuśaya*)? Such a principle is absolutely impossible; this is what is meant by being "without delusion.
2. The Response concerning the Differentiation of the Function of True Suchness According to Conditions, Answering the Doubt Regarding the Pervasiveness of the Great Nature.

The difficulty is divided into three parts: first, a brief explanation; second, a combined explanation; third, a re-explanation to resolve doubts and difficulties. Now, for the first, the brief explanation:
Pūrṇa, furthermore, as to what you asked [up to] "why do you again ask about those that are mutually incompatible?"
From the section following Pūrṇa, the initial doubt is restated. Previously, Pūrṇa doubted that the nature of earth is all-pervasive, asking how it could accommodate water;
and that the nature of water is all-pervasive, in which case fire would not arise. He then asked how it can be said that the two natures of water and fire both pervade empty space.
Furthermore, space is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), whereas the great elements and so forth possess the nature of obstruction; they cannot coexist or interpenetrate.

How then can they both be omnipresent throughout the Dharma-realm? This is the doubt held by Pūrṇa. Having previously raised this question, the Buddha now restates his doubt in order to provide an answer.
From the passage beginning with "Pūrṇa" onwards, two points are presented as metaphors, using the essence of space as the primary analogy.
It is not characterized by marks (*lakṣaṇa*), yet it does not reject the manifestation of those various marks.
This is just as the essence of the *tathāgatagarbha* is not characterized by marks, yet it likewise does not reject the emergence of that great nature (*mahā-dhātu*). Why is this?

Because that great nature follows karma, whereas the *tathāgatagarbha* is without action (*anabhisaṃskāra*). If the *tathāgatagarbha* were characterized by action, it would not admit that great nature. Why is this? Because that...
Because all characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), whereas space (*ākāśa*) is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
If space were conditioned, it too would not accommodate those characteristics. From this we know that space is unconditioned; therefore, it can perfectly reflect all characteristics.

Furthermore, because the nature of the treasury (*garbhadhātu*) is non-active (*anabhisaṃskāra*), it can perfectly integrate the great nature. Why is this so? [The following section consists of] three parts.
To explain the characteristics of this analogy: Question: Since all characteristics are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), how can they be called "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*)? Answer:
Because space is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), in contrast to it, the seven characteristics such as light and darkness are revealed to be conditioned.

Because the *ālaya*-nature is non-active (*akṛtaka*), in relation to the seven characteristics such as the great elements (*mahābhūta*), it is revealed to be active (*kṛtaka*). However, although the great elements...

This is conditioned activity (*saṃskṛta*). Because it cannot ultimately transcend the nature of the treasury (*tathāgatagarbha*), although all marks (*lakṣaṇa*) are conditioned, they cannot ultimately transcend space (*ākāśa*).
Regarding the phrase "What do you think? and so forth, there are four interrogative inquiries concerning the characteristics of the metaphors. As for "different regions": [text continues].
Their characteristics are not identical. As for empty space, it has the characteristic of non-existence. Now I ask:
regarding the characteristics of these various directions, do they arise spontaneously from the sun and so forth, or do they exist within empty space?

Just as the nature of the storehouse (ālaya) is not the nature of the great elements, and the nature of the great elements is not the nature of the storehouse, one does not know whether the nature of the storehouse gives rise to the nature of the great elements, nor does one know whether the nature of the great elements arises [spontaneously].
If they are produced, then the nature of the storehouse (ālaya) and the nature of the great [elements] must necessarily have distinct divisions.
Furthermore, those suns and so forth must also necessarily belong to the vast space. If, as stated below, the five analogies clarify the characteristics of what is produced:
if these various characteristics were produced by the sun and so forth, then, throughout the worlds of the ten directions, the solar radiance would not be situated within the void.
Furthermore, one sees the full sun. If it were merely the luminosity of space, why would its brilliance not be seen amidst clouds and mist at midnight?
Looking at this, one cannot say it is the sun, nor can one say it is space; one cannot say it is not the sun, nor can one say it is not space.
Yet, it is not different from space and the sun. This is the identity of the true and the false.
This is the critical juncture where one must see clearly; only then is it so. The same applies to the seven natures, beginning with the Great Nature (*mahātva*).
It is not correct to say that the *tathāgatagarbha* nature is the Great Nature, nor is it correct to say that the *tathāgatagarbha* nature is not the Great Nature.

Yet, it is also not something separate from the *tathāgatagarbha* nature. This is the critical juncture between nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*); one must see this with perfect clarity. Regarding the observation of characteristics...

[The preceding section] was omitted. Regarding the sixth point, the convergence of phenomena and meaning: generally speaking, when this matter is viewed with the eye of wisdom (*prajñā-cakṣus*), there is nothing mundane that is not true;
when viewed with the fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*), there is nothing true that is not mundane. Why is this? It is because of the perspective of the secular world.
When observing those various marks, they appear as if they truly exist; yet when observed through a vision that transcends the mundane mind, those marks are seen to be entirely illusory.
Once it is realized that they are illusory, how can one point them out? Since there is nothing to be pointed out, how can one debate whether they are empty or whether they are the sun?
If one says they are empty or that they are the sun, is this not like seeking flowers in the sky or hoping for knots in empty space?
Is it empty of fruit? Now, it is the same when speaking of the seven characteristics, such as "greatness" and so forth.
If one observes those seven characteristics with the fleshly eye, they appear as if they exist; yet if one observes those seven characteristics with the wisdom-eye, it is clear they are not real.
Since it is clear they are not real, what is there to point out? Since there is nothing to point out, how can there be...?

If one examines whether these characteristics are subject to extinction or not subject to extinction—if one says that the Way consists of these characteristics being extinguished or not being extinguished—is this not merely seeking the fruit of empty blossoms by waiting for them to form? In sum, when observing characteristics, they are fundamentally false and cannot be pointed out;
when observing nature, it is fundamentally true, being solely the wondrous, enlightened clarity. If one observes with the Dharma-eye:
This wondrously enlightened and luminous mind was originally neither water nor fire; it is the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha.

Since it is the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha, how can one ask whether it can accommodate or not? If one observes with the eye of the Way, this wondrously luminous true nature is precisely neither water nor fire;
it is fundamentally the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha. Since it is the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha, why ask?
"Is it contained? Is it not contained? △ Next, the combined explanation:
"The true, wondrous, enlightened clarity is also like this... (up to) ...if both are illuminated, then both appear."
Below the phrase "The true, wondrous, enlightened clarity," the first section cites scriptural meaning to demonstrate the correspondence.

For emptiness is without marks (*animitta*), and true enlightenment is likewise without marks. Because true enlightenment is without marks, one falsely establishes that which is illuminated, calling it "enlightened clarity.
Because emptiness is without marks, when the sun shines, it is bright; this is called "the clarity of emptiness. Yet how could emptiness say, "I am"?
It is clear, my friend. It is because false discrimination arises within your mind that emptiness appears as such.
If the characteristics of light, darkness, and so forth were each to manifest their own illumination, then each would appear individually.

Furthermore, if one person were to thus manifest illumination, and many people were likewise to each manifest such illumination, then they would all appear together. The nature of true awakening is also like this, due to its wondrous...
Upon the luminous essence, one falsely establishes that which is illuminated; thus, one clearly distinguishes the various characteristics of water, fire, wind, and so forth.
When these arise as delusions upon the essential nature, they each manifest individually.

Now, if one person gives rise to such delusions, and many people likewise give rise to delusions, then they manifest simultaneously. How could these manifested delusive appearances have any other source?
Ah! This is because True Suchness does not abide in its own nature, but follows conditions to grasp at delusion and thus come into being.
As previously stated: "If one place holds a mirror, another place produces fire; if one grasps throughout the Dharma-realm, it arises filling the entire world.
Since it arises pervading the world, how could it have a fixed location? In sum, all of this is merely the manifestation of phenomena according to karma.
What is meant by "appearing together"? From Pūrṇa [to] "one east and one west, with no prior fixed point.
What is meant by "appearing together below"? These two layers of analogies illustrate their falsity. Furthermore, what is the principle of appearing together?

It is like the reflection of the sun appearing in water; though the reflection is originally one, it appears differently according to two people walking east and west. Yet, as for these distinct reflections, how could the sun itself be divided?
However, the actions of the two individuals are each distinct; therefore, the sun appears simultaneously with both.
From this, we know that the division lies in the observer, not in the sun. Now, observe that the seven delusions are originally devoid of self-nature.

It is simply due to the power of delusion that the objects of observation differ accordingly, thereby forming the appearances of the seven delusions. How could these appearances of the seven delusions—

Does the nature of the storehouse (ālaya) possess divisions? It is only because of the forced awakening of the wondrous clarity that it establishes an object; thus, the seven delusions appear together with it.
From this one knows that division exists within the power of delusion, while it does not exist within the nature of the storehouse—this is clearly evident.
One should not raise the objection that "this sun is one [yet appears as many], which is a circular falsehood with no basis for reliance.
One should not raise such an objection below. Third, the characteristics of the phenomenon are distinguished. Now, the sun in the heavens is but one, yet the reflections in the water are not two.
This is truly because two people walk in opposite directions, east and west; therefore, the reflections appear accordingly for each.
Although reflections appear individually, the original object does not move; therefore, one should not raise the objection:
"Since this sun is one, how can it travel in different directions? Furthermore, while the essence of the storehouse-consciousness is one, its wondrously luminous function is non-dual.

This is simply because deluded awareness suddenly arises, and thus the seven kinds of delusion follow it and manifest individually. Although these delusions appear individually, the fundamental nature remains unmoving. Therefore...
One should not raise the objection: "This nature is pure and primordial; how could mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise from it?
Furthermore, for example, the sun has no intention to leave its reflection, yet the reflection does not exist apart from the sun. Ultimately, the manifestation of the reflection is illusory.

Yet what is observed varies according to the individual. Due to the provisional shadow, they manifest together through mutual succession. Although the shadows appear together, the substance of the sun is fundamentally one; therefore, one should not raise the objection:

"Since there are two suns for each person, how can only one appear? Furthermore, it is like this: the fundamental nature of awareness is inherently luminous, yet delusion creates the notion of 'luminous awareness.
Awareness itself is not that which is illuminated; rather, because of luminosity, an object is established. Once the object has been falsely established, [the subject arises...]

"Your 'delusion' is capable [of arising]. Thus, through the division into subject and object, they evolve into delusion in turn. Although delusion appears as both together, the nature of awakening is fundamentally one;
therefore, you should not raise the objection that the two natures of water and fire cannot overcome or destroy each other, nor that space and the great earth cannot coexist.
Why is this? For what is called 'luminous awareness' is already not the Truth; how much more so when one establishes the duality of subject and object?"
The reflection in the water is already not the sun; how much less can one calculate by following its shadow? As the shadow appears, all phenomena arise;
as subject and object are established, the seven elements come into being. These turn about and become empty; they turn about and become delusive.
One does not know what thing to take as a reliance, nor what thing to take as a basis. Therefore, the verse says: "By speaking of delusion, all truths are revealed; delusion and truth are the same."
The second is delusion. Since it is neither real nor unreal, how can there be that which sees and that which is seen? Generally speaking, even "the Real" is not [ultimately] so;
how much less so that which is "unreal"?
Pūrṇa, because you take form and emptiness [to be real], you give rise to the wondrously enlightened nature of True Suchness.
"Pūrṇa, you [should understand] from 'form is empty' downwards. The four [elements] differ in their application to the ultimate and conventional truths.
Form is the earth element; emptiness is the space element. Furthermore, form is not limited solely to the earth element;

all water, fire, wind, and so forth, as well as light and darkness—whatever possesses characteristics that can be conceptualized or described by shape—all fall within the category of the limit of form. Therefore, [the text] raises..."
Form is emptiness; this reveals the vastness and comprehensiveness of dharmas. Generally speaking, if one raises form, it obstructs emptiness;
if one raises emptiness, it obstructs form. Therefore, they are said to "mutually exclude" one another. Furthermore, when raising emptiness, one cannot speak of form;

when raising form, one cannot speak of emptiness. Therefore, they are said to "mutually usurp" one another. Moreover, the nature of awakening is inherently luminous, yet delusion creates the notion of "luminous awakening."
When cognitive clarity arises, the nature of awakening is obscured. Awakening is not that which is made clear; rather, it establishes an object through the act of making clear.

Once the object of clarity is established, true clarity is obscured. Therefore, this is called "mutual inclining. Since the subject that awakens is not the object awakened, and the subject that clarifies is not the object clarified, this is called "mutual usurping.
Within your own nature, such processes of arising and ceasing, mutual inclining, and mutual usurping occur continuously.
It merges with the *tathāgatagarbha*. Yet, the Tathāgata, in accordance with conditions, appears as form and emptiness, mutually inclining and mutually displacing one another;
arising and ceasing, it pervades the *dharmadhātu*. The *dharmadhātu* refers to the ten *dharmadhātus*. As it is with one *dharmadhātu*, so it is with the ten *dharmadhātus*.
As it is with the primary retribution of sentient beings, so it is with the environmental retribution of insentient things. Therefore, as soon as you—

When the wind of perceived objects moves, ignorance arises; like the brightness of the sun and the darkness of clouds, various phenomena cause the ground of sentient beings' minds to become bewildered and distressed.
They turn their backs on the pure awakened mind and unite with the turbid nature of worldly toil.
This is what is meant by the conventional truth employed for the appearances of the world. The Buddha’s intention is not so; in my presence, I do not see even a single thing.
When dharmas arise, one does not perceive the extinction of even a single dharma. It is simply that non-arising and non-extinction accord with the Tathāgatagarbha;
and since the Tathāgatagarbha is solely wondrous enlightened clarity, it perfectly illumines the Dharma-realm.

Even while illuminating the Dharma-realm, one perceives neither the characteristic of arising nor the characteristic of extinction. Since there is no arising or extinction, one sees the entire essence as its functioning. Therefore, it is said:
One is immeasurable; because the whole is identical to the essence, it is said that the immeasurable is one.

As for "the small containing the large," a mirror one chi in length manifests layers upon layers of radiance. As for "the large manifesting the small," layers upon layers of radiance appear within a mirror one chi in length.
This is the sovereign freedom between the broad and the narrow, and the mutual containment of the many and the one. Furthermore:

Just as one sees the worlds of the ten directions upon a single blade of grass—where that [grass] does not come here, nor does this [world] go there—it is said that the immovable site of enlightenment pervades the worlds of the ten directions.
This is precisely the perfection of the primary and its attendants, endowed with all virtues.
To see the space of the ten directions, one need only look at a single blade of grass; this does not go there, nor does that come here. Therefore.
It is said: "The body contains the inexhaustible voids of the ten directions; this is the simultaneous, complete, and corresponding state.
Furthermore, "as lands appear upon the tip of a hair, the primary and secondary realms are clearly and brilliantly manifested; this is the realm of Indra’s net.
"Turning the Dharma within a single mote of dust, correct vision encompasses boundless virtues; this is the generation of understanding by relying on phenomena to manifest the Dharma."
This is precisely the wondrous function of the inconceivable. If one follows the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, there are ten profound gateways;
here, five or six are cited, while the remainder are all subsumed within them. One should carefully discern this, for it can be understood through the mind.

Nevertheless, this wondrous function is fundamentally neither supernatural power (*abhijñā*) nor the nature of things (*dharmatā*); it is entirely the extinguishing of the turbid delusions of worldly toil and the manifestation of... [the enlightened state].

The awakening of untainted wisdom (anāsrava-jñāna) provides sustenance for both essence and function; its concealment and manifestation are non-dual. This is what is called the wondrous function of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
Thus, the Tathāgatagarbha is fundamentally the wondrous, perfect, and complete mind—neither identical nor different, neither the same nor not the same.
Regarding the passage "The Tathāgatagarbha, below," which clarifies the three truths:

according to the ultimate reality, within this Tathāgatagarbha—the essence of the perfectly luminous mind—there is no nature of the seven great elements such as space; there is no nature of the sense organs, objects, or consciousnesses such as the eye;
there is no nature of the causes and conditions of illumination, non-illumination, exhaustion, origination, or cessation; and there is no suffering or its accumulation.
The nature of the Four Noble Truths of Cessation and the Path is without wisdom and without attainment;

it is likewise without the nature of the Six Perfections, and even without the nature of the three titles of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, and the Samyaksaṃbuddha. Furthermore, there is no nature of the four virtues of Nirvāṇa.
All that has been discussed above—from the Three Categories and Seven Elements to Suffering and its Accumulation—constitutes the characteristics of the mundane world. From Cessation and the Path...
Furthermore, the wisdom of contemplating dependent origination and so forth are characteristics of the supramundane.

These characteristics of both the mundane and the supramundane do not exist at all within the wondrous, perfect mind. Because they are both negated—this "negation" is precisely the true essence of the *tathāgatagarbha*.
The teachings call this the "Ultimate Truth" (*paramārtha-satya*). Thus, one should know that the Ultimate Truth does not establish even a single dharma; yet, nevertheless...
Not a single dharma is discarded. Why is this? This wondrous, perfect, and luminous mind—how could it ever be separate from worldly appearances as a distinct dharma?
Because there is no separate dharma, it is simply the Tathāgatagarbha, the fundamentally luminous and wondrous mind.

According to conditions, one establishes the nature of the seven great elements, such as space; one establishes the nature of the true [nature] and so forth—the faculties, objects, and consciousnesses;

one establishes the nature of the causes and conditions of ignorance and its exhaustion, and of their cessation and reversal; one establishes the nature of the Four Noble Truths: suffering, accumulation, cessation, and the path;
one establishes the nature of the six perfections involving wisdom and attainment; and even establishing the *tathatā* (suchness).
The nature of the three titles of the Tathāgata is exhausted, and the nature of the four virtues of nirvāṇa is established.
All that is above—whether mundane or supramundane—is the *tathāgatagarbha* nature. It is formed by gathering the True [Dharmadhātu]; thus, all things are identical with it.

To be "identical" means to correctly perceive the wondrous function of the *tathāgatagarbha* nature. The teaching calls this the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). When the conventional truth is perfected, it becomes one.
All dharmas. In the True Truth (*satyārtha*), all dharmas are extinguished; extinction means that both nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are detached.

This is the simultaneous negation of both "is" and "is not. Therefore, it is said: "Detached from 'is,' detached from 'is not'. That which is detached from "is" and detached from "is not" is the single, wondrous mind.

The teaching calls this "double negation" (*ubhaya-pratiṣedha*). When perfected, both nature and characteristics are clarified; "is" and "is not" are both affirmed. Therefore, it is said: "Is, and yet is not; is, and yet is not. Is, and yet is not.

That which is not "identical" is solely this wondrous clarity. The teaching calls it "shining forth both. If one speaks of shining forth both, then the simultaneous negation of both cannot be attained;

if one speaks of the simultaneous negation of both, then the simultaneous shining forth of both cannot be attained. One must simply forget both negation and illumination so that names and words do not arise;
only then does one exhaust the great essence and great function of the *tathāgatagarbha*. The teaching calls this the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*). This...

These three truths are like the worldly letter *I*, neither vertical nor horizontal, neither unified nor separate—just like the three eyes on the crown of the Heavenly King Maheśvara, which are not the eyes of ordinary beings.
Reaching this stage cannot be conveyed by the path of language, nor can it be communicated through silent stillness; this is the ultimate limit of the Way, difficult to seek out.
It is commonly seen that "vijñāna" (consciousness) is used as a public proclamation. *Tathāgata*—translated in the Qin language as "Tathāgata";
*Arhat*—translated in the Qin language as "Worthy of Offerings" (*Ārha*); *Samyaksaṃbuddha*—translated in the Qin language as "Perfectly All-Knowing."
"How is it that sentient beings within the three realms of existence (down to) cherish the Lesser Vehicle and consider a little attainment sufficient?

"How is it that those in the world below... These six points constitute the reprimand for their errors. "The three realms of existence" refers collectively to all sentient beings in the mundane world.
"Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas" refers collectively to the two vehicles of the supramundane. The above [sections] concern the mundane.
If one is supramundane yet does not understand the nature of the Tathāgata’s ultimate illumination and ultimate awakening, but falsely establishes a mind that seeks to illuminate and awaken,
then one may either stagnate in emptiness or cling to existence. Erroneously regarding *nirvāṇa* as something to be produced and language as something to be debated,
one attempts to exhaust principle and fully realize one's nature through these means, and seeks to fathom the Tathāgata by such measures.
Furthermore, how could one possibly succeed? Why is this? Because one takes the mind that knows as the ultimate.
One fails to realize that this principle cannot be known by wisdom (*jñāna*) nor cognized by consciousness (*vijñāna*).
How can one attempt to reach the realm of Great Enlightenment with a mind that merely knows? Is this not, indeed, a mistaken application of the mind? It is like a lute or a zither—

The *konghou* lute requires skillful fingers before its exquisite tones can be produced. If one lacks skillful fingers, even if the instrument possesses sublime sounds, they can never be brought forth.
It is just so with Pūrṇa and all sentient beings: each possesses the precious, awakened true mind, which is no different from that of the Tathāgata in its perfect fullness.
It is like the *qin*, *se*, and *konghou* lutes; it is simply that [sentient beings] lack skillful fingers.

Therefore, wondrous sounds cannot be produced. Why is this? It is because you take form and emptiness to oppose and supplant one another within the Tathāgata-garbha, and thus the Tathāgata-garbha follows along with form and emptiness, pervading the entire Dharma-realm. The Tathāgata is not so.
I unite my wondrous clarity—neither extinguished nor born—with the Tathāgata-garbha; and the Tathāgata-garbha is solely...
The wondrous enlightenment and clarity universally illumine the Dharma-realm; this is like using a wondrous finger to produce a sublime sound.

As soon as I press the finger once, the Sea-Seal (Sāgara-mudrā) immediately radiates light. You, however, do not possess this wondrous finger; as soon as you raise your mind, worldly afflictions (*kleśa*) first arise.
This is due to nothing other than your attachment to the provisional vehicles and your failure to diligently seek the path of enlightenment. Even if...
To have something attained is nothing more than a minor matter; how can it not be lamentable? △ Third, resolving doubts and difficulties.
Pūrṇa said: "I and the Tathāgata... [until] ...self-obscuring our wondrous clarity and undergoing this drowning."
First, the false cause is explained individually. Previously, Pūrṇa doubted when the Tathāgata had last been deluded; now he doubts for what reason sentient beings possess delusion.
Previously, he doubted whether awakening and non-awakening were different; now he doubts whether the Buddha and sentient beings are not the same. Why is this?
They share the same precious awakening, which is non-dual and perfect. In the Buddha, all delusions are completely extinguished, leaving only the sublime.

It is true and eternal. Sentient beings themselves obscure their wondrous clarity and thus undergo this drowning in samsara. If that were so, then sentient beings and Buddhas would be eternally separate, and truth and delusion would be utterly distinct.
This Pūrṇa does not know that the original nature of sentient beings and Buddhas is equal, nor that delusion is fundamentally without cause.
It is simply because sentient beings are inverted, deluded about themselves, and pursue external objects, whereas the Buddhas awaken to this and turn away from the dust of the world.
This is a combined realization. Although delusion and awakening depend upon the person, in the ultimate sense, they do not concern the fundamental reality.
The Buddha told Pūrṇa: "Although you have removed your doubts... (up to)... this person’s mind is deranged, and there is no other cause."
Second, citing a specific incident to resolve doubts: *Yajñadatta* (演若達多) is translated here as "Sacrificial Bestowal" (*Cishou*).

*Chimei* (魑魅) refers to the monsters of mountains and marshes. The "original head" is a metaphor for the nature of awakening; the "mirror-head" is a metaphor for that which is awakened to; and "madness" is a metaphor for the subject who awakens.
Yajñadatta was deluded, thinking that the mirror-head was false yet could see his eyebrows and eyes, while the original head was himself, yet he failed to see it. From this, [his madness] arose.
"Taking him for a *chi-mei* (a mountain-demon), he ran out of the city. This is a factual occurrence within the city; have you not heard of it?
Furthermore, what is the cause of this man’s madness? Pūrṇa replied, "This man’s mind is deranged, and there is no other reason.
Why? Because his original head has not been lost. Since his original head has not been lost, he is not troubled [by demons]."
This concerns the matter of the head. Since the mirror has no inherent nature, it does not interfere with the matter of the head.
Not interfering with the head and not interfering with the mirror, one is nonetheless deluded by one's own false perceptions;
this is why one goes mad. Thus, it is clear that madness resides in the mind and is unrelated to anything else.

The Buddha said: "Wondrous enlightenment is bright and perfect; fundamentally it is round, bright, and wondrous" (up to) "...even though the Buddhas may manifest it, one still cannot turn back from it.

This third section clarifies delusion through phenomena. For instance, if wondrous enlightenment is bright and perfect, and fundamentally round, bright, and wondrous, when has there ever been delusion?
How could there ever have been a cause? It is because you fail to realize this that you forcibly establish the duality of subject and object;
this is like blaming one's own head for not seeing while claiming that the mirror can see it, and thus going mad. From this, deluded awareness arises.

Since delusion has no inherent substance, it does not pertain to the fundamental nature of awareness (*xing-jue*). Since the "object" must necessarily depend on the "subject," it does not pertain to the perceived object itself.
Since it involves neither the nature of awareness (*xing-jue*) nor that which is perceived (*suo-jue*), it is merely the forceful awareness itself becoming deluded;

therefore, it is designated as "delusion" (*wang*). Thus, it is certain that delusion resides in the "capable" (the subject), and has no concern with anything else. Now, regarding what you have asked:
for what reason do all sentient beings possess delusion? If delusion had a cause, how could it be called "delusion"?

Yes. It is just as the nature of awakening is not something that can be made an object of illumination; yet, based on the act of illuminating, an object is established. Once the object has been falsely established, your false subjectivity arises.
Thus they revolve and depend upon one another in a cycle that knows no end—what is called "one person spreading a falsehood, which ten thousand people pass on as truth.
From this, delusion accumulates upon delusion as you pass through kalpas as numerous as motes of dust. Why is this? Because the Buddha now reveals it in this way.
I have thus elucidated this for you, yet you still do not awaken; you even ask why sentient beings possess delusion.
How much less could one realize it spontaneously without someone explaining it? Therefore, accumulating delusion upon delusion, they drift and wander without returning—how pitiable they are!
Thus, the cause of delusion is itself delusion; how much more so that which is without cause, which is fundamentally non-existent.
This fourth section uses an analogy to clarify the point: one must understand the delusion of sentient beings simply by observing the delusion of Yan-ruo.
Once one realizes that Yan-ruo’s delusion has no cause, one will know that the designation "sentient being" is likewise without basis. Why is this? Sentient beings...
This delusion arises from ignorance; yet, if there were ignorance, it would have no basis. Since it has no basis, how can one ask what its cause is?
Yan-ruo’s madness arose from the confusion of his mind; yet, if there were such mental confusion, it would have no cause.
Since it has no cause, how can one ask what he was confused about? Thus, since even this confusion does not arise, what could possibly exist?
It ceases. Thus, this delusion fundamentally has no substance; what could serve as its cause? Now you ask me, "What causes sentient beings to have delusion? I shall now enlighten you:
it is like a person during the waking state recounting events from a dream.
Though the mind may be sharp and lucid enough to remember the appearances within the dream, by what causal conditions could one actually obtain the objects within that dream? It is simply a dream.

All things are without substance; therefore, they cannot be grasped. Even if the Buddhas were to attain Bodhi, and their minds were indeed perfectly enlightened and luminous, able to exhaust the delusive afflictions within the causal stage—by what causes and conditions could they possibly explain the delusive causes within that causal stage?
It is because the substance of delusion is causeless that it cannot be explained.
As it was with that person in the city, Yajñadatta (Evil-Eye), [up to: "Why rely on toil and hardship for cultivation and realization?
Fifth, this points to the ultimate destination through the facts of the matter: it is just like the madness of Yajñadatta in the city; how could there be any causal conditions for it?
If there were causal conditions, then he would no longer be his original head. But now, it is not so; because he failed to see his own original head, he was driven to blame it.
Therefore, one who becomes deranged does so not because of the mirror itself; rather, it is not present within the mirror. Yet this is not the case here.
Because of attachment, delusion arises regarding what is visible in the mirror. However, this is neither a causal condition (*pratyaya*), nor is it not a causal condition.
Why is this? Because the original head is not lost even in madness; the original head is not lost even in the absence of madness.
Since the original head is not lost, it is neither to say that the head is non-existent nor is it to say that it is not non-existent.
Why is this? Because the nature of delusion is without cause. The deluded nature of sentient beings is also like this; it is not to say that it has a cause.
Nor is it so. To say it is causeless is also not correct. Why? Because the nature of delusion has no substance.
Since the nature of delusion has no substance, how can one say that it exists or does not exist? Now, I shall tell you the truth.
This wondrous, perfect, and true nature—if you do not follow after the discrimination between clarity and non-clarity, then the true mind will be realized immediately.
Once the mind has attained this realization, the karmic fruits of worldly sentient beings and the conditions for the threefold continuity [of body, speech, and mind] will cease.
It will naturally cease. If these three conditions are severed, then the nature of the three causes—killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct—will likewise not arise.

It is just like the case of the man in the city, Yan Rudata: if he does not follow after the discriminating mirror-image or the original head, nor dwell on seeing or not seeing, then the mechanism of madness will immediately come to rest. If the mechanism of madness comes to rest, then the true mind is established.

When the deluded mind ceases, the awakened mind manifests. Once the awakened mind has manifested, one naturally realizes that one's own supremely pure and luminous mind has, from the beginning, pervaded the entire dharma-realm.
Yet, how could this supremely pure and luminous mind have been obtained through the instruction of another?
How could it have been fabricated by oneself? As the ancient masters said: "It is fundamentally and originally possessed."
It is sufficient. It merely lacks one’s own self-acceptance. If one can accept it, what need is there for the arduous labor of cultivation and realization?
"Ken" refers to the meat between the bones; "keng" refers to the knots where the muscles and sinews join. As the *Zhuangzi* says:
"The butcher's blade has never touched the ken or keng," let alone a large joint. This means that such effort is unnecessary; this is the teaching method of the Sudden School, which is immediate.
One must realize it before one can attain it.
For example, it is like a person who [finds] within his own garment... until he finally awakens to the fact that the divine pearl was not obtained from without.
These six layers of metaphors illustrate the primordial state; the Way resides within one's own person. How could it be necessary to seek it elsewhere? Yet people do not perceive this. Toward...
They run about externally, submerged and lost in the current; though they suffer drowning, the Way is never lost.
It is like a pearl tied inside one's garment, not requiring external searching, yet people do not know it. They wander to other lands, running about begging for food;
though they are truly impoverished, the pearl has never been lost. Suddenly, a wise person points out the pearl to them.

Whatever one desires follows from the mind, leading to great wealth and abundance; the Way is likewise so. Suddenly, when a wise person points out the Way, one immediately recovers the original mind and attains great peace and joy.
Only then does one realize that this original nature was not obtained from another, and only then does one realize that the divine pearl was not obtained from without.
△ Third, because of delusion due to false thoughts, the Truth is obscured, yet the Truth is fundamentally free from falsehood. [This answers Ānanda.]

The delusions regarding the principle of dependent origination are difficult to categorize, yet they can be divided into five parts: first, stating doubts to pose a challenge; second, citing examples to clarify the Dharma;
third, examining what is erroneous and what is correct; fourth, rebuking those who study superficially; and fifth, exhorting them toward authentic practice. First, stating doubts to pose a challenge.
At that moment, Ānanda was among the great assembly... [he requested] that the World-Honored One would deign to show great compassion and dispel his confusion and distress.
Ānanda said, based solely on what the World-Honored One had spoken: "You owe me my life; I shall repay you for your debt.

For this cause and condition, throughout hundreds of thousands of kalpas, we shall always remain bound in entanglement. According to this, one obtains the karmic fruits of sentient beings in the world.
The continuity [of existence] remains; this too is a causal condition (*pratyaya*). Furthermore, it is said that because the three conditions are severed, the three causes do not arise.
Based on this, the continuity and cessation of the karmic fruits of sentient beings in the world are likewise causal conditions.

Furthermore, when the madness of the *Evayūpātta* (the "Seeker") within the mind naturally subsides, this subsiding is itself *bodhi*. Based on this, the subsiding of the mad nature is the awakened mind.
This, too, is a matter of causes and conditions. For instance, I, Ānanda, once encountered the calamity of the demon Ḍombī while on my almsround;
now, because I have received the guidance and salvation bestowed by the Buddha Tathāgata, my mind has attained awakening.
Based on this, it is evident that awakening is likewise attained through causes and conditions. Furthermore, it is not only I, a young śrāvaka, but also Maudgalyāyana within this assembly...

Furthermore, Śāriputra and Subhūti, upon hearing the Buddha’s causes and conditions from an old brahmin, gave rise to the aspiration for awakening and attained the state of being free from outflows (*anāsrava*).
Based on this, they too entered the holy teaching by means of causes and conditions. Now, you say that bodhi does not arise from causes and conditions;
if that were so, then the doctrine of spontaneity (*svayambhū*) taught by the non-Buddhist heretics of Kauśāmbī in Rājagṛha would be established.
Is this the ultimate truth? This is what is called the difficulty of delusion regarding the principle of dependent origination.

It is because Ānanda did not understand that dependent origination is unborn; he merely spoke of causes and conditions and spoke of spontaneity, leaving these obstacles within his breast. When will they ever be resolved?
They do not understand that the Tathāgata’s teachings are merely the whip and the shadow for sentient beings, intended solely for the purpose of taming them.
They are like a boat or raft for crossing the sea, intended solely for the purpose of reaching the shore.
Those who now cling to the raft and refuse to let go speak only of the ship and the raft; those whose minds have not yet been tamed speak only of the whip and the shadow.

This is precisely what is meant by Ānanda. Question: Regarding the "arising from conditions as non-arising" (*pratītyasamutpāda-anutpāda*) and the "delusion regarding the principle of arising from conditions," how are they to be distinguished?

Answer: One may recall an ancient master asking a monk, "What is that sound right before you? The monk replied, "The sound of raindrops. The master said, "Sentient beings are inverted; deluded, they pursue external objects while losing sight of themselves. The monk asked, "How about you, Master? The master replied: [The master remained silent. This is the definitive distinction. In the former case, the sound itself is the manifestation of non-arising;

in the latter, the sound is taken as an object, and one is lost in the delusion of chasing after phenomena. Thus, the former is the realization of the true nature of conditions, while the latter is the failure to recognize the self-nature within those very conditions. This is the point at which the two are determined.
Since one is no longer deluded regarding oneself, this is precisely non-arising; it is also precisely being deluded regarding principle. Please examine this with certainty.
△ Second, citing an event to clarify the Dharma.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "It is just as in the city... [up to] ...the path of effortless cultivation where both birth and extinction are exhausted.
From the words "The Buddha told" downwards, he restates the opponent's calculation. It is like the deluded nature of Yanruo;

if one were to eliminate causes and conditions, there would then be something "spontaneous" (svabhāva). This is your calculation, and it does not go beyond this. This is what is called reaching the ultimate limit of reasoning.

This is a general statement of their [the opponents'] thesis; it will be refuted gradually below. From the passage concerning Ānanda onwards, the refutation proceeds by means of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) to dismantle their notion of "spontaneity" (*svabhāva*).
