To say that the head is spontaneous implies that there is nothing which is not spontaneous. Yet this is not the case.
It is because of causes and conditions that one runs out in a state of madness and terror. If it were due to causes and conditions that one runs out in madness and terror, then...
It is not something that arises spontaneously. If it were spontaneous, it would contradict its own causal conditions.
To say that the head is spontaneous yet becomes deranged due to causes and conditions—if that were so, then by virtue of those very causes and conditions, the head itself would be lost.
Yet now, the original head is not lost; although one runs about in madness, there has never been any change. Since the head is neither lost nor changed—

This is easily understood; what need is there to rely on causes and conditions? From the outset, [the opponent] has descended from madness to enumerate his shifting arguments, claiming that because the head inherently possesses the nature of madness, that madness is also spontaneous (*svabhāva*), and its non-madness is likewise spontaneous.
Setting aside for a moment the claim that "madness is spontaneous," suppose we consider the time before one was mad: where did that nature of madness reside in potentiality?
As for the question, "Where does it reside? Is non-insanity also something natural?"—let us set that aside for now.
Suppose one were in the midst of being insane: where would that natural nature be hidden? If the state of insanity has no place to lurk, we know that insanity is not inherently present.
If the natural nature has no place to hide, we know that the head was originally without delusion. The head...
The head is fundamentally without delusion; its nature is fundamentally without confusion. For what reason today do you fear your head and run about in a frenzy?

If you awaken to this, it concludes by returning to the fundamental intent: if you realize that the head is fundamentally without delusion, then you will know that the nature is fundamentally and originally true.
If you penetrate that the nature is fundamentally without confusion, then you will know that running about in a frenzy is delusion. Thus, one recognizes the root of delusion.
Since there is no source [from which it arises], one knows that both "causes and conditions" and "spontaneity" are equally mere conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*).

Therefore, it is said that for the sentient beings of the world, their karma and its fruits—should these three conditions be severed, they are themselves the bodhicitta. However, if one perceives the arising of a bodhicitta, this is still the mind of birth and extinction;
it remains merely a cognition of birth and extinction. Thus it is said: "This is merely birth and extinction. This includes even...
The mind of cessation and the mind of arising are both unattainable. Reaching this point, there is no place for you to apply your mind, nor any place for you to settle.
Therefore it is said: "When the mind of cessation is exhausted along with [the mind of arising], it is the path of non-effort.
Viewed from this perspective, only when the minds of arising and cessation are exhausted does one see that the original state is thus. △ Third, examining the heterodox and the orthodox.
If there were such a thing as spontaneity (*svabhāva*), then [the passage] up to this point would be called the "Dharma free from conceptual proliferation.
Alternatively, one might see that because it is taught to be without arising or ceasing and not dependent on effort, they claim it is a spontaneous nature.
If this were so, a mind of spontaneity would arise. If one perceives that there is spontaneous arising and ceasing, and that the mind ceases, this is still...
Such is the perception of arising and ceasing. Therefore it is said, "This too is arising and ceasing. Even this mind of arising and ceasing cannot be apprehended.
Reaching this point, one does not even see arising; how much less can one see ceasing? Thus it is said that that which is without arising and ceasing is called "spontaneous" (*svabhāva*).
Viewed from this perspective, if something were truly spontaneous, it would necessarily be without arising and ceasing.

This refers to knowledge and vision. The word "just as" serves as an illustration by means of a comparison. For example, when various characteristics in the world are blended together to form a single entity, this is called the nature of combination (*saṃyoga-svabhāva*).
When one points to the intrinsic characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of a thing that is not a combination, it is called the original nature (*prakṛti-svabhāva*).
"Original nature" (*benran*) is precisely spontaneity (*ziran*); "harmony and integration" (*hehe*) is precisely causes and conditions (*yin yuan*). These are the characteristics of this world.
To say that there is a separate "original nature" within the essence of the fundamental nature (*xingti*) is not correct;

to say that there is a separate "harmony and integration" within the essence of awakening (*jue ti*) is not true integration. Why? Because harmony and integration and original nature both function upon the essence of the fundamental nature and awakening.
One does not cling. Therefore it is said: "Both union and separation are abandoned. Even this mind that abandons both union and separation cannot be apprehended.
Reaching this point, the path of words is cut off and the sphere of mental activity ceases. Therefore it is said: "Both union and separation are neither.
Viewed in this light, if one perceives the state of true non-effort, only then is it the Dharma free from conceptual proliferation. △ Four.
He rejects the studies of his followers, [stating that] Bodhi and Nirvana still lie far away... until the river of craving is dried up, so as to bring you liberation.
Although what has been said above is thus, it does not go beyond dispelling their attachments and rejecting their frivolous disputations. If this is Bodhi...
They say that Nirvana is still far off. Why? It is because while the place of teaching is indeed it, the place of practice is not yet it;
the place of understanding is indeed it, but the place of realization is not yet it. Therefore, it is called "far. Generally speaking, this matter is like being a great dead person;
one must truly reach this stage before it is attained. Otherwise, even if one were to memorize and uphold as many [teachings] as there are in the ten directions...

Even if you come to understand the pure and wondrous principles within the twelve divisions of the scriptures, they will merely become idle chatter regarding your own nature and will be of no benefit.
From the passage "As for you... onwards, he cites examples as proof:
whether you speak of causes and conditions or of spontaneity, is this not something you have clearly understood? The world calls you the foremost in erudition; why then [do you remain thus]?

"You were spared from the calamity of the Mātanga woman. Furthermore, as soon as I proclaimed this divine mantra once, the lustful fire of Matanga was instantly extinguished and the river of your craving was dried up. Is this not indeed a proof? △ Fifth, exhorting him to true cultivation.
Therefore, Ānanda, although you have passed through kalpas [until now], how can you still deceive yourself by remaining attached to seeing and hearing?
As previously stated, when the Mātangī heard the Buddha’s divine mantra, the fire of her lust was immediately extinguished, and she became a forest of diligence within the Dharma.
Yet, although you, Ānanda, understand the twelve divisions of the scriptures, you could not avoid being ensnared by the *sāviya* arts.
[This is] a summary. Judging from this, to recollect and maintain the Tathāgata’s secret and wondrous adornments throughout kalpas is not as good as practicing untainted karma for a single day.
"Untainted" refers precisely to the Great Samādhi of the Śūraṅgama.
For one who has truly seen their own mind naturally does not fall into false views, does not leak into birth and death, and remains far removed from the two extremes of worldly hatred and love.
Suffering. Hatred and attachment are the very root of birth and death; among the eight types of suffering, these two are the most severe.
To further provide scriptural evidence, we turn again to the case of Mātanga. How do we know that the merit of a single day’s practice can surpass the retention [of merit] accumulated over kalpas?
It is as with Mātanga, who for successive lifetimes was a courtesan—not merely for one life—and yet upon hearing a single incantation...
Merit. It eliminates their craving and desire. The one now called Bhikṣuṇī Xiàngxìng and Yaśodharā have both awakened to their past causes together.
What was referred to as "transcending the entanglements" refers to Ḍaṅga; what was referred to as "receiving a prediction of enlightenment" refers to Yaśodharā.
This is all to reproach Ānanda—a dignified man—who willingly succumbed to sounds and forms, yet still clung to sights and hearing, and conversely [failed to do so for others].
It is like the two women who, upon hearing the Dharma, attained realization with such swiftness; was this not a case of deceiving yourself?
Some say that because Sundarī was defiled, she advanced to the third fruit [of Arhatship], while Ānanda, despite his faith, remains ranked among those of initial capacity.

Others say that although Ānanda’s understanding was perfect, he manifested as one of small capacity; this was a matter of employing skillful means. As for Sundarī, her cause was real and thus her fruit is profound.
It is only the Great Mantra that is manifest; the rest are not so. If one claims that Dhanagā was defiled while Ānanda maintained faith, this is the view of worldly convention (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
If one claims that Ānanda was a provisional manifestation while Dhanagā’s causal basis was real, this is the view of self and other (*ātma-para*).
The reality is not like this. One simply does not realize that Dhanagā is a single dharma and the *Uṣṇīṣa-vijaya-dhāraṇī* is also a single dharma.
The matter rests with the person. If a person’s single thought is defiled, they are an ordinary being; if a single thought is pure, they are a sage.
It is but a single mind, yet there is a difference between its defilement and purity. However, this difference is a difference within phenomena (*dharma*), not a difference within the mind itself.

Therefore, this sutra uses it as a means of revelation and establishes it as a *pratītyasamutpāda* (dependent origination). Question: Since it is but a single mind, how can there be purity and [defilement]?
[The interlocutor] said: "It is like water: if rock honey is cast into it, it becomes sweet; if yellow gall (huanglian) is cast into it, it becomes bitter.

Thus, neither the gall nor the honey is the nature of the water, and the water is not the medium for the gall or the honey. Through the conjunction of causes and conditions, there naturally arises purity and impurity.
Yet, if one investigates each to its root, the nature of the gall is bitterness and the nature of the honey is sweetness. [The text concerning] the water...
The nature is bland. All phenomena each abide in their own fundamental position. Sentient beings do not realize this and falsely perceive sweetness and bitterness, purity and defilement.
In reality, they are one mind, fundamentally without difference. Now, this sutra reveals that the true mind is no different from the original water.
Any talk of "true" versus "false" is merely a skillful means to assist in manifestation according to the capacities of those to be taught.
How could this truly be so? △ Second, the main exposition of the gate of contemplation, divided into five parts: 1. Showing the initial arousal of the mind of enlightenment;

2. Showing entry through one gate; 3. Verifying the severing of permanence and annihilation; 4. Clarifying the method for untying the knots; 5. Clarifying that when the six are untied, the one perishes.
First, showing the initial arousal of the mind of enlightenment, divided into five parts: 1. Requesting instruction on contemplation; 2. General presentation of the two determinations.
I. General Explanation. II. Specific Explanation of the First Meaning. III. Specific Explanation of the Second Meaning. IV. Exhortation to Careful Discernment.
Now, for the first [section], the invitation to observe:
Ānanda and the great assembly, having heard the Buddha’s instruction, remained in the assembly with single-minded attention, awaiting the Tathāgata’s compassionate decree.

In the following passage, Ānanda describes the benefits he obtained through the Dharma. This was because his attachment to the person (*pudgala-grāha*) had not yet been destroyed and the notion of a self (*ātman*) still remained;

consequently, his body could not attain physical ease (*praśrabdhi*). Furthermore, his attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) had not yet been destroyed and the notion of phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*) still persisted.

For this reason, his mind could not attain pliancy (*praśrabdhi*). Now, however, with both person and phenomena being empty (*pudgala-dharma-ubhaya-śūnyatā*), both body and mind have attained pliancy.
Regarding the passage "Then he addressed the Buddha," Ānanda describes for himself the benefits gained from the Dharma.
The "Pure Jewel King" (*viśuddha-ratnarāja*) is the *vimala-maṇi* (stainless mani-jewel). This jewel is inherently pure; whatever one seeks, there is nothing it cannot provide.
"It is as you wish. However, because it is ultimately detached from all worldly forms and appearances, it is called a 'king.
It is like the *tathāgatagarbha*, which is inherently pure; it possesses functional activity that accords with one's every wish.
Yet, because it is ultimately detached from all worldly conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), it is metaphorically called a 'jewel. Today, what the Tathāgata has revealed to me allows me to attain..."
Is this not that mani-jewel? How could it so skillfully open my mind and deliver me from the sea of suffering? [The World-Honored One] descends to explain the Gate of Contemplation:
The worlds of the ten directions are born from this very mind; therefore, they are called the "Nurturing Tathāgatas.
The lands of the ten directions are the wondrous objects of this very mind; therefore, they are called the "Buddha-lands of the Wondrously Awakened King. For this reason...
If one knows that this mind is thus vast and great, how could it be acquired through study? If this Dharma is thus all-pervasive, how could it be grasped through recollection?
Therefore, much learning is condemned as being without merit, for it does not equal the practice of cultivation.
Yet, since this Dharma is neither permitted to be studied nor permitted to be recollected, how can one be taught to enter it? This is the Parable of the Ornate Mansion.

The nature of the Tathāgatagarbha is like a gateway; the metaphors represent the practice and realization of entry. Viewed in this light, Ānanda has for the time being awakened to the mind, but has not yet awakened to the Dharma;
he has awakened to the essence, but has not yet awakened to its function. He is like a traveler who has merely made a temporary halt.
It is truly not yet reaching the destination; this can be seen herein. △ Second, the general presentation of the two meanings of certainty.
At that time, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for those in the assembly... [down to] ...the two meanings of certainty regarding the initial aspiration for enlightenment.

"Deciding" (*jue*) means to discern and choose; "determining" (*ding*) means to settle upon what is certain. A beginner must first discern whether the mind of the causal stage and the awakening of the resultant stage are identical or different;
there is a certainty to be reached here. One must also discern which of the six sense-faculties are complete and which are incomplete;
there is a certainty to be reached here. Only after such discernment and determination are completed can one enter the Path. To decide...

Discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā*) is precisely contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). Concentration (*samādhi*) is precisely the Dharma. These two definitive meanings regarding the initial mind’s contemplation and the Dharma must be understood by the student.
III. Separate Explanation of the First Meaning, in two parts: 1. Examining the similarities and differences between cause and effect.
What are the two meanings determined by the initial mind? (Up to: Because, from beginning to end, there is neither destruction nor cessation.

First, the phrase "What are... below indicates the meaning: one carefully observes that the stage of the causal ground (*hetu-bhūmi*) is characterized by arising and ceasing, whereas the stage of the fruition (*phala-bhūmi*) is characterized by non-arising and non-ceasing.
Now, as one carefully enters the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana*), is this [state] subject to arising and ceasing, or is it free from arising and ceasing? One observes the cause...
Are the ground and the ground of fruition the same or different? Next, Ānanda, the text below distinguishes what is not [the case]:
"If one now seeks the dharma of non-arising and non-ceasing with a mind of arising and ceasing, there is no such possibility.

Why is this? This is the dharma of non-arising and non-ceasing which is the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*). To study it by means of a mind of arising and ceasing—how could that be possible? There is no such principle.
Third, the following provides an analogy to clarify the meanings of arising-and-ceasing and non-arising-non-ceasing.

Suppose space is a dharma that does not arise or cease, while the vessel-world (bhājana-loka) is a dharma that arises and ceases. This is because the vessel-world is a product of conditioned activity and thus possesses arising and ceasing;
it will ultimately decay and perish. Space, however, is a dharma that is unconditioned and neither arises nor ceases; it never comes to an end.

It perishes. Thus one knows that because the mind at the stage of the cause (*hetu-bhūmi*) possesses arising and ceasing, it must perish; whereas that which is without arising and ceasing at the stage of the fruit (*phala-bhūmi*) does not perish.
Within these two meanings, one must make a definitive resolution and observe them. Only when this definitive resolution is attained can one enter the Way.
△ Second, distinguishing between the true and the false, and the pure and the turbid.
"Then, the solid quality within your body constitutes earth... (up to) your five layers of turbidity are likewise thus.

First, he provides a general indication of the characteristics of turbidity with respect to your lower [body]. Speaking from the perspective of what is most immediate, nothing surpasses the human body.
Regarding the body, it does not go beyond the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). It is by these four great elements that the profound, perfect, and wondrous mind becomes entangled and obscured.

From the beginning to the end, these constitute the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*); this is the nature of the phenomena of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha-dharma*). How does the following passage explain the causes of these turbidities?
That which is called "turbidity" refers to the mind of arising and ceasing; it is like clear water and dust, one being clear and the other turbid, their natures not conforming to one another.
When arising and ceasing are combined with that which is non-arising and non-ceasing, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are thereby accomplished.
This is what is called "delusion. It is also like when worldly people take dust and soil and throw it into clear water;
the soil loses its obstructive nature, and the water loses its purity. This is what is called "turbidity. Therefore, it is said that your five layers of turbidity are likewise thus.
"Ānanda, you see that empty space pervades the worlds of the ten directions" (up to) "this fifth layer is called the turbidity of life.

Next, Ānanda, the following section separately explains the characteristics of the turbidities. First, it clarifies the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*), which is the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).
The Sanskrit term *kalpa* is translated here as "time-period. This refers to the most extremely brief duration of a single moment, which is called a *kalpa*. You...
When one raises the eyes and beholds space, there is space but no substance; there is seeing but no awareness. Because there is no awareness, one fails to comprehend;
because there is no substance, right and wrong cannot be distinguished. This is entirely the nature of dull obscurity, and is therefore called the *kalpa-kaṣāya* (the turbidity of the eon).

Second, to clarify the *dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya* (the turbidity of views), this refers to the *vedanā-skandha* (the aggregate of sensation). It is precisely that preceding moment of ignorance and dullness which flows into [the subsequent state].
Within the nature (*prakṛti*), the massed substance forms perception (*buddhi*); through mutual contact, cognition (*jñāna*) is formed. Because there is cognition, water and earth provide resistance;
because there is perception, wind and fire revolve around one another. Thus, the nature and its characteristics become intermingled; this is therefore called the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*).

Third is the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*), which is the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*). It transforms the essence of the preceding ignorance (*avidyā*) into the past and gives rise to the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*).
The mind of knowing and seeing constitutes the present. Recitation and study are the subjective characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), while the appearance of forms is the objective characteristic.

The interweaving of these subjective and objective characteristics is therefore called the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*). Fourth is the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*), which refers to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
It is precisely this single thought-moment of arising and ceasing that never stops; by means of present knowing and seeing, one clings to the six sense objects through the three periods of time.
The nature of karma causes the migration of lands; these lands are the delusory objects of sentient beings. The six sense-objects (ṣaḍviṣaya) are the conditions upon which karmic movement depends.

When the mind contemplates the six sense-objects, karma flows through the three periods of time. Because nature and characteristics combine provisionally, this is called the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*).

The fifth is the turbidity of life (*āyuṣkaṣāya*), which is precisely the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*). "Seeing and hearing" refers to the six faculties of experience (*ṣaḍāyatanāni*), while "various objects" refers to...

Regarding the characteristics of the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) and so forth: ordinary beings point to the nature of consciousness (*vijñānatva*). Because the nature of consciousness has no substantial body, it is said to be "without form" (*anākāra*).
Because the characteristics of the objects are each distinct, they are said to be "separated. Although the characteristics of the objects are separated, the substance of consciousness is identical;

therefore, it is said to be "without difference" (*nirviśeṣa*). To speak of its lack of difference implies that they are contrary within their function; yet to speak of their separation implies that they are [contrary] within their nature.
They recognize one another; because they lose the standard through similarities and differences, it is called the turbidity of lifespan.
Ānanda, you now wish to cause seeing, hearing, awareness, and cognition (up to) all to accord with the pure and wondrous virtue of Nirvāṇa.
Third: "Now, [I] distinguish the false based on the true. Seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are the mind of the causal ground;

permanence, bliss, self, and purity are the awakening of the resultant ground. The five aggregates are the root of birth and death; perfect stillness is the dharma that is neither born nor extinguished."
In this regard, the student must decisively discern that "this is the mind of the causal stage" and "this is the awakening of the fruition stage," reaching a definitive conclusion.
They must decisively discern that "this is the mind of arising and ceasing" and "this is the dharma of non-arising and non-ceasing," reaching a definitive conclusion.
If today you wish to accord with the Tathāgata’s permanence, bliss, self, and purity, you must rely upon the dharma of non-arising and non-extinction;
only then can you achieve such accord. If you wish to eliminate the root of the five aggregates and birth-and-death, you must rely upon the perfectly湛 (zhàn) nature;
only then can it be eliminated. This perfectly湛 nature is precisely the wondrous *śamatha*, which is what is called "stopping" (*zhi*). This *śamatha*...
He ceases all the delusions of sentient beings. If the deluded mind is extinguished, one naturally returns to original enlightenment.
Upon attaining this original luminous awareness, one finally perceives that one's own original nature is fundamentally without birth or extinction, and fundamentally without delusion.
This very state of being without birth or extinction and without falsehood is that which gives rise to the aspiration for the ground of practice;
it will lead to the future realization and verification of the ground of fruition. It is like clarifying turbid water to reveal what lies beneath:

just as when turbid water is placed in a still vessel, if it remains deep and motionless, the sand and silt will naturally settle and clear water will appear—this is called the initial subduing of adventitious afflictions. Depart.
When the mud is pure, the water is clear; when ignorance is forever severed, the natural nature of awakening is pure and the water of the mind manifests.

This is called being in accord with the wondrous virtue of Nirvana. This power of sublime *śamatha* is the foremost, definitive, and wondrous Dharma within the stage of the causal ground (*hetubhūmi*);
it is something that cannot be attained if even a small portion is lacking. △ Fourth, the specific explanation of the second meaning has three parts. First, instructing him...
Contemplating phenomena. As for the second meaning: because you all necessarily desire to reach emptiness, which is formless and without the binding or unbinding of fetters.

This is the initial statement of the meaning at the beginning. The preceding was the cultivation of *śamatha* (calm abiding); this is the cultivation of *vipaśyanā* (insight). "Thorough examination" refers to that which is cultivated.
Regarding this contemplation: who creates and who receives? It is precisely the dharmas that are being contemplated.
Furthermore, for one who contemplates dharmas, they must investigate who creates birth and death, and who receives afflictions; they must reach a definitive conclusion.
They must examine in detail from where delusion arises, and what the sense organs and their objects are; they must reach a definitive conclusion. Contemplating in this manner is like...
If you can achieve such careful and detailed discernment, then you will possess the capacity for progress on the path of learning.

Did I not say previously that one must observe the sequence of dharmas and observe the stages of dharmas? Master Sanping said, "First move with concentration; afterwards extract with wisdom. This is precisely what he meant.
Next, in the passage beginning with "Ānanda, when you practice," there is a selection of what is not [the way]. Furthermore, there are two kinds of methods for observing dharmas.
One does not enter the Way. There are two types: those with wisdom and those without wisdom. Those with wisdom surpass it; those without wisdom fall short.
A person of wisdom, though they may not observe or examine minutely, realizes that birth-and-death is itself nirvana and that afflictions are themselves bodhi.
He perceives this easily and enters directly into the state of ordinary reality. When faced with actual matters, he again abides [in that state].
Yet regarding birth and death, this is the thief of wisdom and discernment; it is what is called a transgression. Those without wisdom do not observe or examine closely;
they do not know what the fruit of birth and death truly is, nor from where the afflictions arise.
Others find it difficult to perceive, and they enter one-sidedly into a realm of dullness. When faced with actual matters, birth and death manifest before them; this is to be ignorant and lacking...
"Know that this is what is called 'falling short. These two types of people both fail to enter the Way. Why?
Because they do not even know the delusory roots and objects of the afflictions; how then could they attain the stage of the Tathāgata?
Ānanda, observe the following analogy to clarify this: it is like the untying of a knot. If you see what was knotted, then you will know what has been untied. If you do not see what was knotted..."
If you are bound, you will not know how to be liberated. Why is this? If your mind were like empty space, devoid of form or characteristics, there would be no need for liberation.
But now it is otherwise: the eyes are filled with birth and death; the eyes are filled with worldly toil, dust, and afflictions.
How can one fail to observe them? How can one fail to examine them closely? △ Second, distinguishing the marks of luminous virtue.
Thus, your present eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and so forth, cannot transcend the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*).
First, I shall clarify the faults inherent in these faculties below. The various characteristics of the eyes and other senses act as intermediaries for thieves;

they entice the six external sense-objects and the six internal consciousnesses to plunder the treasures of one's own home. These "treasures of the home" are precisely the wondrous, perfect, and luminous nature. Because of this wondrous...
The nature of perfect luminosity has been exiled into the world and bound within birth and death. Were it not for the six thieves acting as its intermediaries, how could this be?

For sentient beings constitute the primary retribution (*sambhogika-niṣyanda-vipāka*), while the world constitutes the secondary retribution (*āśraya-vipāka*); thus, the primary and secondary retributions are together a single entanglement.
Therefore, they are unable to transcend it.
Ānanda, what is meant by the "world of sentient beings" (down to) each having twelve hundred merits?

Second, "Ānanda, what is below" explains their names and numbers. Past, present, and future constitute the "ages" (loka). The four intermediate directions and the four cardinal directions [constitute the world].

The boundaries are defined by the upper and lower corners. There are ten positions within these boundaries, yet the flowing numbers are only three. Within the wondrously luminous nature, a single thought-moment without cause agitates and moves, becoming sentient beings.
Furthermore, by means of this one thought-moment, it flows into the three periods of time and the four directions. First, these layers form twelve;
next, they transform so that each of the three periods and four directions becomes thirty, flowing into the four directions and the two [periods] of the three times.
They are folded into one hundred and twenty. Next, they transform into three hundred each for the four directions and the three periods of time.
These flow into the three periods and four directions, forming three layers that total one thousand two hundred—what is known as "three times four and four times three, revolving to twelve."

This summarizes the numerical progression of the transformations from beginning to end, so that one may see how the functions of the six sense organs are thus. Furthermore, the meaning herein is this:
if we speak in terms of the weaving of delusion, when one is deluded, one is universally deluded; therefore, when a single thought moves falsely, all ten realms are simultaneously deluded.
Thus, when the three periods of time and the four directions ride upon this, there arise multiples—tenfold, hundredfold, thousandfold, and so on.

This is the calculation of their numbers. If one discusses them in terms of merit and virtue: awakening is universal awakening; therefore, when a single thought is wondrously luminous, the ten realms are all clearly illuminated.
Consequently, as one rides upon the three periods of time and the four directions, there are numbers of two-fold, ten-fold, hundred-fold, and thousand-fold.
Viewing it in its entirety, although delusion and enlightenment reside in the person, that which is employed resides in the Dharma.
Now, I do not discuss the individuals, but rather their dharmas; therefore, they are praised by way of their merits.
Ānanda, you should further determine the relative superiority and inferiority among them (up to) those who have perfected one thousand two hundred merits.
Third, Ānanda, the specific merits are shown below. A single phrase establishes the general heading, while the subsequent sections provide detailed explanations, beginning with the eye faculty.
Regarding "the front being entirely bright," this refers to both corners; each of the two corners consists of fifty [parts].
Combined, the two squares total two hundred; thus, one side consists of three hundred. Regarding the observation of two-thirds from the side:
each of the left and right sides obtains two hundred and fifty, totaling five hundred, which, together with the full brightness of three hundred, totals eight hundred.
Furthermore, regarding the fully dark rear square: the fully dark side is three hundred, plus fifty from each of the two corners.

Speaking in terms of three parts, three parts constitute its functional capacity (*guṇa*) and one part lacks its inherent virtue (*guṇa*). Therefore, it is said that the eye-faculty possesses only eight hundred [units];
as its virtues are incomplete, it is considered inferior. Second, regarding the ear-faculty: movement is the domain of the ear, while stillness is the essence of the hearing-nature (*śravaṇatā*).
Since the domain has limits, it can be pointed out as being near or far; however, since the essence has no boundaries, [it cannot be so defined].
Listening throughout the ten directions, we do not now take a limited realm as the basis for discussing the boundless nature;
therefore, it is said that the faculty of the ear is endowed with one thousand two hundred merits. This is what makes it superior. Third, regarding the faculty of the nose, its functions intersect.
This is the locus where the mind resides. In the nose faculty, there is only exhalation and inhalation. Exhalation grasps objects, while inhalation opens to fragrances;
however, it lacks the intermediate junction. Speaking in terms of three parts, one part is without merit, while two parts possess virtue.
Therefore, it is said that the nose faculty possesses only eight hundred merits and is incomplete in its qualities; this constitutes its inferiority. Fourth is the tongue faculty.
What is spoken of in the world is conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya); what is discussed regarding the supramundane is ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
The principle of ultimate truth is inexhaustible, whereas the words of conventional truth possess limitations. Now, we take the ultimate and not the conventional.

As for the five body-faculties, their functions consist of separation and union, as well as opposition and conformity. When separated, the faculty and the object are both distinct; hence they are called "one. When united, the faculty and the object are a single awareness; hence they are called "a pair. When analyzed into three parts, one part is without merit and two parts possess virtue;

therefore, it is said that the body-faculty possesses only eight hundred [merits], its virtues being incomplete, which constitutes its inferiority. This concludes the six faculties. Silence and receptivity are the ground where the nature resides.

The mental object (dharmāyatana) is the objective sphere of the mind-faculty (manas). One should know that the mental objects are boundless, and the nature-ground (prakṛti-bhūmi) is likewise boundless.
Now, rather than discussing those mental objects, we discuss this nature-ground;
therefore, it is said that the mind-faculty is endowed with one thousand two hundred merits. This constitutes its excellence.
The reasons why the merits of the six sense organs shown above are thus are as follows:
Some, upon hearing that the organs and so forth are illusory, seek the Way apart from the body and search for heaven outside of emptiness.

They do not realize that this nature is like the brilliant void, and that each of the organs, objects, and consciousnesses is the Samādhi of Radiating Light. It is simply a matter of not grasping or becoming attached to them; this is it.
Liberation. Question: If that is so, why were the five turbidities (*pañca kaṣāyāḥ*) mentioned in the previous section? Answer:

As for the mention of the five turbidities in the previous section, it is like a person who, upon seeing something described as a foul substance, immediately covers his nose, unwilling to even hear of it.
When the Tathāgata speaks of *śamatha*, he intends only for people to distance themselves from the faults and afflictions of the world and to awaken to their own original face.
Now, regarding the explanation of the merits of the six sense organs within this context:
it is like a person who, upon hearing that there is a fine object, immediately feels envy and desires to take possession of it. When the Tathāgata speaks of *samādhi*, he requires people—
One merely attains the wondrous gate of the single flavor and equality, and realizes the samādhi of one’s own *dharmatā*. Nevertheless, things themselves possess neither beauty nor ugliness;

it is people who project these onto them. Now, when we speak of the five turbidities and the merits of the six sense organs, how could there be two distinct entities within a single human body? Please reflect upon this. △ Fifth, exhorting him to deliberate and discern.
"Ānanda, you now wish to go against the current of the flow of birth and death... until those six organs of cognition are simultaneously purified.
From the initial "Ānanda," he exhorts him to deliberate and choose. Above, the merits of the six faculties have already been demonstrated; now he exhorts Ānanda to deliberate and choose.
The three branches of nose, tongue, and body apprehend their objects through contact (*saṃyukta*), while the two branches of eye and ear apprehend their objects at a distance (*viyukta*).

Regarding the objective realm (*viṣaya*): that which is profound is superior; that which is shallow is inferior. "Complete" refers to one thousand two hundred [dharmas]; "incomplete" refers to eight hundred.

The "flowing faculty" (*āsrava-indriya*) is precisely the nature of perfect stillness (*paripūrṇa-sthiti*). The beginningless cycle of birth and death for sentient beings is "flowing with the current"; practicing the Way is the reverse of this.

It flows against the current; hence it is called "contrary. The Buddha’s intention is that although the six sense faculties differ in their degree of excellence, shallowness, or depth, one must personally examine and choose among them;
thus he asks, "Who? If one can discern and awaken through such examination, then the difference between the perfect and the imperfect will be such that their merits cannot be compared.
The second section, beginning with "I now," grants permission to provide an elucidation.
Regarding these six natures of profound clarity—whether superior or inferior, whether complete or incomplete—their full measure and distinctions are all clearly manifest herein.
If you examine and discern them in detail, it is not necessary for you to perceive them all; even if you can enter through a single gateway, I shall bear witness so that you may advance.
[The text] then cites people who have attained the fruit as witnesses from the ten directions, meaning those from the ten directions such as...
Coming to practice within the eighteen realms, there is neither superiority nor inferiority; there is no "that" which is much and "this" which is little.
All is the realm of perfect penetration; it is simply the nature of the single mind. Xuansha said: "The worlds of the ten directions are not other things;
they are merely you. To whom else would I have them listen? To whom else would I have them hear? It is all, in the end, your own mind-king."

What is being done here is to fully realize the Immovable Wisdom (*acala-jñāna*). From the perspective of Xuansha’s intent, observing what the Tathāgatas of the ten directions have realized is precisely the same in its essential meaning.
The passage beginning with "Fourthly, as for you... distinguishes the Perfect [Teaching]. Ānanda possessed an inferior vessel and a small capacity;

he could not equal the Tathāgatas of the ten directions in bearing the burden of the Perfect, Sovereign Wisdom (*pariniṣpanna-svatantra-prajñā*) upon one shoulder. This wisdom can only be approached through a single gate.
"Enter deeply. If one enters deeply and attains realization, one will see that this principle is fundamentally without delusion.
Those six faculties of cognition are likewise fundamentally without delusion. What is superior and what is inferior? Why should there be more of one and less of another?
All are the realm of perfect penetration; it is simply the nature of the single mind. II. Showing the Deep Entry into One Gate. 1. Requesting [Instruction].
Furthermore, Ānanda said to the Buddha, "World-Honored One... [omitted] ...it can cause the six faculties to become pure simultaneously.
Ānanda harbored a doubt, thinking that while their essential nature is one, the six functions are divided; for instance, the eye presides over seeing and the ear presides over hearing.
The nose, tongue, body, and so forth each have their own specific domains. Why, then, do you speak of "entering deeply through a single gate"?

Furthermore, cognition is a single unity, yet the six apertures are each sealed off; just as the eye does not depend on sound and the ear does not depend on form, the nose, tongue, body, and others each have their own boundaries.
Why, then, do you speak of "simultaneous purification"? Moreover, if the sense organs and their objects were real, one could not even attain [liberation].
He said, "One? If the faculties and their objects are illusory, one cannot even speak of 'six. If that is so, I do not know which is 'one' and which is 'six.
Since neither 'one' nor 'six' can be established, how can you speak of flowing against the current to enter [the source]? Thus, he harbored doubts."

I respectfully submit this further request for benefit. Generally speaking, Ānanda, although your self-grasping (*ātma-grāha*) has been shattered, your grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) still entangles you;

therefore, you are unable to attain liberation. You do not realize that the six delusions have no substance and are merely provisionally established within the one mind. Since even the mind is but a provisional establishment, how could there be any substance to the delusions?
If the substance of the delusions does not exist, how could there be any objective phenomena (*dharma-rasa*)? Question: If this is indeed so...
"How can it be said that one enters deeply through a single gate and the six sense faculties are purified simultaneously?

He replied, "To speak of 'entering deeply through a single gate' is nothing more than a provisional teaching to lead you back to the source and restore you to the origin, serving as a starting point on the path.

To speak of the 'six faculties being purified simultaneously' is nothing more than a provisional teaching to have you return home and sit upon the ground, serving as a place of rest. How could these be ultimate dharmas?"
Yet how could there be only one or six? Have you not seen when a monk asked an ancient worthy, "What is the meaning of the Westward Journey?
The worthy replied, "Do you hear the sound of the Yan River water? The monk said, "I hear it. The worthy said, "Enter from here.
Is this not the principle of entering deeply through a single gate? Furthermore, Yangshan asked Muzhou, "The hundreds of thousands of myriad objects..."
"What about when they come at once? Muzhou said, "Green is not yellow; long is not short.
All dharmas each abide in their own place; it is no concern of mine. Is this not the principle of being pure all at once?
Nevertheless, these two men certainly do not stop here; you must continue to investigate thoroughly. II. Extensive Explanation.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "You have now attained [the understanding of] the limits and the enumeration of arising, abiding, change, and cessation.
The single phrase "that which is abandoned by vision" (*darśana-heya*) refers to the eighty-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*) of the three realms; these are the delusions of view.
The single phrase "that which is abandoned by cultivation" (*bhāvanā-heya*) refers to the eighty-one grades across the nine stages; these are the delusions of thought (*klesha*). Ānanda...
Since it was difficult for him to come here, he first severed the delusions of views and first shattered the grasping at a self; thus, he is one who has ascended to the first fruit (*srotāpanna*).

However, his attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) has not yet been forgotten, his delusions of thought (*bhāvanā-heya-kleśa*) have not yet been eliminated, and there still remain delusions of ignorance as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

What is now described as "accumulated empty habits over many lifetimes within the faculties" refers precisely to these delusions of the sands of the Ganges; "birth, abiding, change, and extinction" refers to [the delusions of] ignorance.
To clarify the delusions: if these two types of delusion are not eliminated, how can one discern the reasons for the "one" and the "six"?

If the "one" and the "six" are not discerned, the ground of the mind remains uncomprehended; how then can one advance on the Path? Therefore, within this section, the reasons for the "one" and the "six" are first distinguished, followed by the demonstration of the falsity of the root-knots.
"Now, you should first observe the six faculties present before you... (up to)... the faculty of reception is likewise so.
[The phrase] "Now, you... below serves as a double inquiry; that is to say, since you doubt whether they are one or six, then within your own body—
There must be one, and there must be six. Now I ask: are these six sense organs one, or are they six? Ānanda, I shall now refute the notion of "one.

If you say they are one, then the ear should be able to see forms, the eye should be able to hear sounds, the head should be able to walk, and the feet should be able to speak. You certainly do not accept this; therefore, know that they are not one.

This is one [point]. Below this, the six [positions] are refuted. If it were these six, then as in the case of hearing the Dharma with the ear, the body should not arise in reverence, nor should the mouth come to inquire about the meaning. You certainly do not hold such a view; thus, we know it is not these six.
Therefore, the following pair refutes this: these six faculties of cognition cannot be said to be one and not six, nor can they be said to be six and not one.
Why is this? Is it that your body possesses both a "one" and a "six"?
This is not logical. Ānanda, the conclusion follows: you should know that these faculties are neither one nor six.

Because from time immemorial the nature of awareness has been inverted, there is the perception of six; because from time immemorial it has fundamentally been subject to fluctuation and change, there is the perception of one.
Thus, know that the notions of "one" and "six" are entirely the accumulation of delusions from the beginningless past.
This is what is being established. Your two statements regarding the *srotāpanna* are a direct reprimand of Ānanda. The name *srotāpanna* means "one who has entered the stream.
Not entering into form, sound, fragrance, and so forth is precisely the "extinction of the six [objects]. To cling to the six sense organs as a single entity is to have not yet forgotten the "one.
Although Ānanda has attained the first fruit and does not receive the six sensory objects—this is called the extinction of the six—he still clings [to them].
Because of this view of dharmas, you have not yet forgotten even a single one. This is illustrated by the following analogy of the great void:
just as the great void is said to be "one" because it takes on different forms according to its vessels, does that great void actually possess distinctions such as unity or diversity?
Because the sense organs do not enter the six sense-objects, they are said to be "one"; yet how could that hidden nature (tathāgatagarbha) possess characteristics such as being one or six? Now, you—
As for those who maintain that there is one [entity] or six [entities], how does their position differ from that of the Great Void (*mahā-ākāśa*) becoming distinct or becoming one?

This is because, through the mutual conditioning of the two aspects of light and darkness, and so forth, the five sensory faculties (*pañca-prakṛta-indriya*) and the four sense objects (*catur-viṣaya*) flow outward and rush toward mental phenomena (*dharma*).

Third, the demonstration of the falsity of the faculties and their fetters. First, the characteristics of the six faculties are shown. Regarding the eye-faculty, from "light and darkness" (*āloka-tamas*) downward:

light and darkness are the phenomenal aspect (*nimitta*); the wondrously perfect nature (*prakṛti*) is the essence. When the nature and the phenomenon meet, they adhere to the profound stillness (*gambhīra-sthiti*) to form seeing.

This is precisely what was stated in the preceding text: "Awakening is not that which is illumined; because of illumination, an object is established. The essence of seeing (*darśana-śuddha*) is the capacity for awareness, which reflects forms.
This is that which is capable of seeing; it is precisely what was previously described in the text as "that which you have falsely established as the false capacity for arising.
Regarding the phrase "binding form to constitute the sense organ": this refers to the *paramārtha-indriya* (ultimate sense organ).

Although the ultimate sense organ is composed of the eight dharmas—both the primary elements (*bhūta*) and their derivatives (*bhautika*)—it is formless and invisible. Because it is invisible, it is designated as "pure" (*viśuddha*). This is due to...

That which is called the "essence of the eye" is the ephemeral sense-organ (*bu-chén gēn*). This ephemeral organ is likewise composed of the eight dharmas consisting of the primary elements and their derivatives.

However, it possesses form that can be seen; because it is visible, it is like a cluster of grapes. This refers to what was previously mentioned in the section on "the absence of identity or difference," namely, "that which blazes forth as difference.
As for the statement that the four objects of the ephemeral organ flow out and rush toward [their objects]...

Regarding form (*rūpa*): the peripheral sense organ (*bāhyendriya*) is that which is without sensation and without vision; the ultimate sense organ (*paramārthendriya*) is that which possesses sensation and vision.
For example, when forms such as blue or yellow reach the sense organ, that which possesses sensation and vision immediately retains them.
Because that which lacks awakening and vision does not remain, it is said to be "fleeing and galloping. Furthermore, that which is empty, false, and unreal is called "floating.
That which lacks seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing is called "dust" (*rajas*). The "creator" refers to the four great elements, such as earth and so forth; the "created" refers to...
This refers to the four subtle elements, such as form and so forth. These primary creators and their derived products do not possess separate substantial entities;
they are all produced by the single deluded mind. The following cases should be understood accordingly. Due to movement and stillness, the lower two ear-roots initiate hearing;

this is the locus of delusion. The essence of hearing is the deluded capacity. That which rolls up sound to form the root refers to the ultimate sense organ (*paramārtha-indriya*). The substance of the ear is like...
The "newly rolled leaf" refers to the *fu-ch'en-ken* (the physical sense organ). For the wondrous, perfect nature cannot hear by itself;

rather, it rolls up sound to form deluded hearing, and from that hearing, it forms deluded capacity. As this capacity and its object mutually permeate one another, the *fu-ch'en-ken* cannot contain or restrain [the consciousness];

instead, it flows outward and rushes toward sounds, thereby forming the sense organ. This is explained through the passage on "openness and obstruction," following which are the three sections concerning the nose.
The sense organs (*indriya*). Their true and false natures and characteristics are explained as before. All vital energies (*qi*) naturally ascend, yet the sense organs must descend to join them;
therefore, the nose is shaped like two hanging melons. This, too, is brought about by the nature of karma. From the state of tranquility, the four lower sense organs transform.
Their true and false natures and characteristics are explained as before. However, since taste arises from external objects, it must be extracted by means of squeezing; thus, the tongue—

Its form is like a crescent moon that has just been bent. "Bent" (yǎn) means lowered and receptive to tasting. This arises from the conjunction and separation of the five lower body-faculties (*kāya-indriya*).
The nature and characteristics of the true and the delusive are as explained previously. "Grasping" (*bó*) refers to seizing; "contact" (*chù*) refers to striking.
Just as a drum must be struck before it produces sound, so too the body must be touched before cognition arises. Therefore, the form of the body is like this. It arises from birth.

The extinction of the six [objects] below refers to the sense organ of the mind (*manas*). The nature and characteristics of the true and the false have been explained as before. Generally, "mind" (*manas*) is like a mental image;
it is like being in a dark chamber where nothing is seen, yet the mind must form an image of the object and cognize it in advance.
However, the reason one speaks not of "objects" but of "dharmas" is that birth and cessation have no substantial body, and what is grasped is but a phantom reflection.
Ānanda, these six faculties—from that awakened clarity (up to) the realization that there is neither extinction nor arising—thus find their secure resting place.
This clarifies the origin of the knots of the faculties. The preceding text stated: "The nature of awakening is necessarily luminous; delusion makes it the 'awakening of luminosity'. Now it says:
"From that awakened clarity, there is luminous luminosity-awakening. From this, one knows that the wondrous luminosity of fundamental awakening was originally and inherently complete.
Due to the nature of clear cognition, one falsely conceives of it as luminous awareness; from this false awareness arises, and fundamental awareness vanishes.

From this false clarity emerges, and true clarity is obscured. Thus, as for how the six sense faculties now emit light by adhering to stillness—is this not caused by that very nature of clear cognition?
Therefore, the conclusion is drawn: brightness and darkness are mere appearances; that which is perceived is delusion.
Why is this? If one were separated from the characteristics of external objects and so forth, there would be no essence of seeing.

This is because the essence of seeing merely takes the characteristics of objects as its provisional form (*rūpa*), rather than taking the actual substance of objects as its object; therefore, it is said that what is seen is false.
This applies universally to movement, stillness, openness, and obstruction—all are likewise so. In sum, they are all nothing but a single falsehood.
"You need only not follow after movement and stillness, union and separation... (up to)... all other five types of adhesions; they should be uprooted and you shall achieve perfect liberation.
This is the method of showing the five as entering into the one. 'Not following' means not pursuing.

By not pursuing the various conditioned marks such as movement and stillness, the essence of delusion naturally vanishes. Since the essence of delusion is gone, what need is there for anything that is not true? Therefore, I teach you not [to follow them]."
It must be so for all six sense organs. One need only take one organ and detach it from its stickiness; as it returns to the fundamental reality, all others will naturally achieve perfect liberation.
Question: What is meant by "perfect liberation"? Answer: It is like a dark room that has been shut up for a thousand years—a single lamp is sufficient to dispel it.
The six gates are firmly closed, yet a single aperture can pass through. This is because the mind has no dual essence and awakening is not twofold.
Once a single faculty is uprooted, the five attachments are completely liberated; what cause for doubt could there be?
Not arising from the objects before one’s senses (up to): "thereby the six faculties function for one another.
These six directly manifest their fundamental function; previously they were obstructed by external objects, and for that reason they could not communicate with each other.

Now, because they do not arise from external objects, this clarity does not follow the sense organs, yet there is the manifestation of activity; "directly" (*zhí*) is also used here as a metaphorical designation.

That is so. Furthermore, since they are called "provisional" (or "entrusted"), there is no impediment to their mutual functioning according to the faculties [of beings]. Question: What is meant by "mutual functioning"? Answer:
It is like rivers, streams, ditches, and canals; the nature of water is not divided among them. Or like hairpins, bracelets, bowls, and basins; how could the gold’s form be different?
For True Suchness is unchanging yet follows conditions; even in following conditions, it remains unchanging. How could one be deluded about this?
Ānanda, do you not know that—up until—the moment of mindfulness transforms into supreme awareness?
Seventh, taking humans as an illustration: Ānanda provides the preceding example; here, another person is cited.
Anuruddha—translated as "Free from Poverty"—was the son of King Droṇodana and the younger cousin of the Buddha. Because he was prone to excessive sleep, the Tathāgata rebuked him.

He then practiced the path with diligent effort for seven days and seven nights, whereby he lost both eyes. The Buddha instructed him to cultivate the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), after which he attained vision extending across half his head.

He perceived the three thousandfold world-system. The dragon Bāḍananda—translated here as "Worthy Joy"—constantly protects the kingdom of Magadha, causing rains to fall at the proper times; he is the same one subdued by Maudgalyāyana.
He is the deity of the Gaṅgā River, which flows from the Silver Elephant’s Mouth of Lake Anavatapta and flows eastward into the land of Eastern India; Zhuangzi calls him the Lord of the River (Hébó).
Kauṇḍinya (Gavāmpati), here translated as "Ox-Aspect," suffered from a chronic cough because oxen consume much food that causes such symptoms;
this was likewise the result of his past karma. Śūnyatā (Śunyata), the deity of space, possesses no material form, yet the Tathāgata temporarily enabled him to be seen within his radiance.
Mahākāśyapa, the Great Kāśyapa, had long since extinguished his mental faculties (*manas-indriya*) because he had attained the samādhi of permanence.
Vimalakīrti said: "Without arising from the samādhi of cessation, one manifests all manner of dignified postures. Furthermore, Yongjia said: "Vigilant clarity within stillness is it;
stillness within a state of non-recording is not. Stillness within vigilant clarity is it; vigilant clarity amidst discursive thoughts is not. Moreover, an ancient worthy said:
"Constantly knowing with perfect clarity—this cannot be expressed in words. This is precisely the perfectly clear and luminous awareness that does not depend upon mental conceptions.

This is the intended meaning. Ānanda, the passage below correctly demonstrates the appropriate capacity for the teaching. Like the six people mentioned above, [Ānanda] does not rely on the cognitions and views arising from external objects;
therefore, he is able to give rise to wondrous function. If, as is the case now, Ānanda’s various sense faculties were perfectly uprooted [of delusion], [he would likewise attain this].

It is also capable of internally illuminating and radiating light. If it can indeed internally illuminate and radiate light, then those superficial defilements will vanish like ice melting in boiling water;
this is also called "easy. If its wondrous function can indeed surge forth, then at the mere thought of it, it shall transform into supreme wisdom and insight; how could this be difficult?
Ānanda, it is like those worldly people whose visual perceptions are gathered at the eye... (up to) ...how could the awakened clarity fail to be perfect and wondrous?
Eighth, this is verified by means of phenomena: as for what worldly people see, it is all gathered at the eye. Suppose the eyes were closed;
not only would one be unable to discern external objects, but even one's own head and feet could not be distinguished. Why is this? Because of the six sense faculties.
This is because it is naturally dark. Suppose that person were to trace their body with their hand once;
although the other’s eyes are closed, without needing to deliberate, their mind becomes clear and they can distinguish between head and feet. Why? Because the faculty of cognition is identical.
Thus, by observing how the pointing finger reveals the false as the true, we may infer this: where there is seeing, there is light; where there is no seeing, there is darkness.
That which arises following the sense organs and their objects is precisely a false manifestation. Verifying it by this means, one sees that light cannot obscure it and darkness cannot darken it.
That which arises from its own intrinsic nature is precisely true awakening. Therefore it is said:

"Since the sense organs and their objects have already been eliminated, how could the clarity of awakening not be perfectly wondrous? 3. Examining Annihilation and Permanence. Part One: Extending the Argument.
Doubtful, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One... [omitted] ...I only pray that you will bestow great compassion and dispel my ignorance and hesitation.
Ānanda subsequently recounted what he had heard: that which is awakened to is what the Buddha has realized; therefore, it is called *bodhi*. It neither perishes nor arises.
This is the ultimate truth; therefore, it is called *nirvāṇa*. Being free from all falsehood and having a nature that never undergoes change, it is called *tathatā* (Suchness).
Being free from faults and transcending all non-virtue, it is called *buddhadhātu* (Buddha-nature). Being stainless and undefiled, it is called *amala-vijñāna* (the immaculate consciousness).

Since not a single dharma is established therein, it is called the *śūnya-tathāgatagarbha* (the empty womb of the Tathāgata). Universally reflecting all phenomena, it is called the *ādarśa-jñāna* (Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom). Although these names are seven, [they refer to one reality].
Its essence is one; it is entirely pure, firm, and solid—the eternally abiding, indestructible nature of the Vajra King. If one questions this further:
the preceding text states that by using stillness to revolve back against its own delusion, one extinguishes birth and death, subdues [delusion], and returns to original enlightenment.

Thus, one attains the fundamental, luminous enlightenment, which possesses a nature free from birth and death, serving as the mind for the causal stage. Only then does one perfectly fulfill the fruit.
This is the teaching shown by the World-Honored One regarding the cultivation and realization of the stages (*bhūmi*).

Ānanda, according to what the Tathāgata has taught, the awakening of the causal stage is the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing; the awakening of the resultant stage consists of the seven stages of awakening, such as *bodhi* and so forth.
Now, regarding the statement that it does not arise from the cognitions and views produced by external objects (*pūrva-rajas*), if one were to say it does not arise from external objects—
It may be so if one arises [from this state]. However, it is not possible if one claims to be separated from knowing and seeing. Why?

If this seeing and hearing are separated from brightness and darkness, motion and stillness, then there is no "mine" (我所). If one is separated from the essence of mindfulness, then there is no "self" (我心).
Thereupon, he engaged in subtle contemplation: if he advances toward the stage of fruition, there is no "self," so by what means could one discern awakening?
If he retreats to the causal stage, there is no "mine," so who is it that seeks the Way? Thus, he investigated through both advancing and retreating.
If one were to say, "I originally have no self and furthermore have nothing belonging to a self," this would result in total annihilation.

How could one take such ultimate annihilation as the cause for cultivation? If it were ultimate annihilation, yet the Tathāgata further speaks of the profound, quintessential, perfect, and eternal—then if one follows this perfection and eternity, the claim that "I have no mind" would instead become annihilation. This would be to disregard the Buddha’s words and establish something else.
In principle, this would further contradict truthful words; yet if one relies on the Buddha’s teaching, there is likewise no basis for such a logic.
In the end, it becomes mere frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*). Reflecting upon this now, how could it possibly be acceptable? △ Second, refuting their perversion.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "In your study of extensive learning, you must eliminate your doubts regarding all mundane affairs.
Although you have studied extensively and possess great erudition, you naturally know the cause of inversion within your mind;

yet, because true inversion manifests before you, you have truly not been able to recognize it. Why is this? It is as when one speaks of a cognitive perception that does not arise from external objects."
This is precisely a direct pointing to one's original source. Yet Ānanda failed to realize it; he mistakenly took it to be annihilation.
All dharmas are provisional names and lack substantial reality, yet Ānanda did not comprehend this and erroneously identified them as permanent.
Is this not his delusion? If you do not believe this, try using matters of the mundane world to dispel your doubts. △
Third, the examination of the three [points].
At that time, the Tathāgata commanded Rāhula [to investigate]... [until] he heard the truth and said, "There is none. Who knows there is none?
First, this was to manifest the perversion by way of the facts. The Buddha asked once and verified once; each had its own reason. "At that time" and below first rely on...
The faculties are used to verify the nature. For instance, when a bell is struck, there is hearing; when the ringing ceases, there is no hearing.
This is merely the presence and absence within the act of hearing; it does not concern the nature of hearing itself. Why is this? Because the nature is fundamentally autonomous.
Even if the nature were not autonomous, it could not be made to exist or cease to exist. The Tathāgata further commanded that, secondly, one should examine the objects.
Examining the faculty: When a bell is struck, there is sound; when the bell stops, there is no sound. This is the presence and absence of sound, not something pertaining to the auditory faculty.
Why is this? Because the fundamental source of the faculty is unmoving. Even if the faculty were to move, it would still be unable to hear whether there is sound or no sound.
From "The Buddha said to Ānanda" onwards, the third section examines the true by means of the false. Part two.
He examined him closely. Ānanda’s words were evasive and contradictory. How could this not be due to the nature of hearing and the faculty of hearing?
If there were truly no hearing, and the nature of hearing had already ceased, then your body would be like a withered tree;
who then would know whether sounds exist or not? To know existence and non-existence is the nature of hearing; that which is either absent or present is the auditory object.

The object of sound has arising and ceasing, whereas the nature of hearing has no arising or ceasing. Even if the nature of hearing were subject to arising and ceasing, how could it constitute your own existence or non-existence? This is certainly not the case.
Therefore, Ānanda, regarding sound within hearing—from its being obstructed to its being open—it is taught that hearing has no inherent nature.
Second, this refutes delusion to reveal the eternal. In general, it is sound within hearing that possesses arising and ceasing; it is not the nature of hearing that has arising and ceasing.
Now, Ānanda does not know that the nature of hearing is unmoving, and instead is deluded by taking sound to be hearing. Regarding this—
When there is sound, it is said that there is; when there is no sound, it is said that there is not. What is so strange about the nature of hearing becoming dull and obscured?

Ānanda does not realize that the true nature is sovereign, yet he is deluded by taking what is permanent to be intermittent. Thus, when hearing exists he says it exists, and when hearing is absent he says it is absent;
is this not the arising of a self-inflicted inversion? Therefore I say: the knowledge and vision that arise do not depend on external objects.
This is precisely the fundamental permanence; it is not something apart from movement and stillness, or penetration and obstruction. Thus, one might claim it has no nature.
For example, consider a person in deep sleep, lying soundly upon their bed and pillow—how could this nature be extinguished for you?
Third, the explanation is established by means of metaphors. Deep sleep is a metaphor for delusion; it is a state of being shrouded in darkness that causes one to lose awareness of the body.
The sound of pounding is the true object; hearing the sound of pounding is the true nature. The sound of a bell is a distinct object; the wood and stone are distinct consciousnesses.
Separate consciousnesses lack intrinsic nature; separate objects lack substantiality. Since they lack substantiality and lack intrinsic nature, how could they not be illusory?

The metaphor of a dream correctly illustrates the existence or non-existence of auditory objects: suddenly awakening, one realizes that both mind and objects are equally empty. This applies to stillness and agitation, penetration and obstruction, and so forth.
The six delusions are all empty; though life ends and the form dissolves, the One Reality remains undiminished.
It is like Ānanda being in a dream, mistaking sound for hearing. Therefore, the retribution of response is not fixed, yet true awakening experiences hearing.
Mistaking the constant for the intermittent, one becomes confused from beginning to end, unable to hear or awaken for oneself—no different at all from that sleeping person.
Because all sentient beings, from time immemorial [until] why they do not achieve unsurpassed enlightenment—these four points conclude the return to the source.
Sentient beings have existed since the beginningless past merely following after sounds; therefore, when sound arises, they arise.
When sound ceases, it is extinguished. Therefore, one wanders through the flow of every thought. Sentient beings invariably follow only what is habitual;

thus, hearing "existence," they say there is existence, and hearing "non-existence," they say there is non-existence. Consequently, birth after birth is defiled. Now, if one wishes to weary of and leave behind these defilements, one must sever birth and extinction.
If one desires to cast off this wandering cycle, one must maintain the true permanence. Should the light of permanence manifest before you, [the mind will be liberated].
Then, birth-and-death, the faculties, objects, and the consciousness-mind will all dissolve and fall away simultaneously. Why is this?
It is because when there are objects before one's eyes, clarity is obscured; once these obstructions are removed, the breast naturally becomes open and expansive.
This is truly because the mind-ground has dust that causes lack of clarity; if defilements are dispelled, the Dharma-eye will immediately become clear and bright.
Indeed! Once the mind-ground is illuminated and the Dharma-eye is opened, how could one fail to achieve unsurpassed perfect enlightenment?

"Conceptualization, characteristics, consciousness, and emotion" refers to the sense organs (*indriya*), objects (*viṣaya*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), and mental afflictions (*kleśa*). For emotion is itself the organ, and characteristics are the object;
when organ and object combine, consciousness arises. These three—organ, object, and consciousness—defile the mind-ground, which is what is meant by "impurity."
The Correct Vision of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra, Scroll Four;

The Correct Vision of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra of the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa, the Tathāgata’s Secret Cause for Cultivation and Realization, the Definitive Meaning of the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas, Scroll Five.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Jishi, residing at the Ancient Xingfu Chan Monastery in Ludong.

From the beginning of the first fascicle to the third fascicle, he expounds upon the two gates of mind and views; this is the refutation of the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *saṃyojana-kleśa*).
Next, from the beginning of the fourth fascicle to the end of the present fascicle, he expounds upon all objective phenomena (*dharmārambaṇa*); this is the refutation of objective phenomena.
The sand and the delusion are confounded. Reaching this point, he requests the method for untying the knots; his intention lies in destroying the innate delusions of ignorance (*avidyā*).
For it is said that if these innate delusions are severed, True Suchness (*tathatā*) will be fully revealed; when the ten directions are awakened together, what would remain obscure?

However, these three delusions do not arise arbitrarily or without cause; they have their origins. Did I not say previously: "The nature of awakening is inherently luminous, yet it falsely manifests as the awareness of luminosity.
Since awakening itself is not an object of illumination, one establishes an 'object' based on that luminosity. Once the object has been falsely established, your false subjectivity arises.
Now, for there to be subject and object within the essence of awakening—is this not the delusion of views and thoughts? And within the essence of the nature...

There is false clarity and false awakening; are these not the delusions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges? Furthermore, within the essence of True Suchness (tathatā), there is that which is neither clarity nor awakening;
this state of being neither clarity nor awakening—is it not the delusion of ignorance (avidyā)?

Nevertheless, these three delusions are collectively termed "ignorance" because they are dharmas that obstruct the Path. Therefore, that which is to be destroyed proceeds from the shallow to the deep, and from the coarse...
It is exceedingly subtle. Does not the Sūtra say: "Principle must be awakened to suddenly; through awakening, all is simultaneously extinguished. Phenomena must be eliminated gradually;
they are exhausted through successive stages. Is it not so? Is it not so? △ Fourth, showing the method for untying the knots.
First, the description of delusion.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One" (up to) "...awaiting the unsurpassed revelation of the Tathāgata.

This first section describes the expression of doubt and the request for the Dharma. It refers back to what was previously said: "The one who observes the world and unties the knots does not see that which is knotted. Why is this?
"How do you know? This is a restatement of the second point from the preceding discourse. Ānanda spoke for himself: "I am indeed like this. Why?
At times it is bright, at times it is dark; at times I attain understanding, at times I do not.
Is this not the delusion of ignorance? Even now, I seem afflicted by a tertian fever, with alternating chills and fevers, arising again and again."
First, there is the inversion: one wishes to sever what cannot be severed and wishes to dispel what cannot be dispelled, not knowing how the body and mind can be made so.
How does this differ from one who does not know how to untie a knot? For if one does not know where the knot is tied, how can one know how to untie it?
"Is this not what is meant by 'not-self'? Thereupon, he earnestly entreated the World-Honored One, saying: "Please teach me the method for untying the knots.
Ultimately, how are they knotted? How are they untied? △ Second, showing the characteristics.
At that time, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for Ānanda (and so forth, until) this great assembly attained what they had never experienced before.
Regarding the phrase "at that time... first [the Buddha] touched their heads": when a superior loves an inferior, they touch the head; when an inferior respects a superior, they grasp the feet.
The present act of stroking the crown of the head signifies the meaning of "gathering and receiving" (*saṃgraha*). It further symbolizes that, upon encountering the essence, there is no distinction.
Generally, within one's own body, everything can be seen except for the crown of one's own head;

therefore, he strokes the crown so that [the disciple] may personally realize the crown that is beyond seeing, thereby gathering and receiving them. Immediately thereafter, the various Buddhas below emitted light. Ten.
The preceding single phrase is the general [principle], while the six kinds [of phenomena] below are the particulars. As for what is called "particulars":
suppose a single sentient being possesses the characteristics of the sixfold faculties, objects, and consciousnesses;

likewise, every sentient being throughout the entire Buddha-world also possesses the characteristics of the sixfold faculties, objects, and consciousnesses. Such beings as numerous as atoms, and such worlds as numerous as atoms, are not separate entities.
This is the single characteristic of universal awakening. Why is this? When viewed with the fleshly eye, there is nothing true that is not mundane;
