when viewed with the Dharma-eye, there is nothing mundane that is not true. By this, one knows that all the characteristics of the faculties, objects, and consciousnesses of sentient beings within the micro-dust worlds are precisely the realm in which the Tathāgata dwells. All phenomena characterized by movement and transformation are entirely these [realms].
Regarding the Buddha’s Samādhi of Emitting Light: as for the light he emits, each ray does not emerge from the crown of the head (*uṣṇīṣa*). Why is this?

Because the realm of the Buddhas is not comprised of the characteristics of sense organs, objects, or consciousness; it is because they abide in the profoundly deep, and because there is nothing to be seen.
Now, since there is nothing to be seen and they abide in that which is profoundly deep, how could this not be the awakening of the crown? Therefore...
It is said that each has a precious light issuing from their crown, which again comes to the Jeta Grove to drench the crown of the Tathāgata’s head;

this signifies that they share the same vision. To share the same vision of the Jeta Grove is to see it as the realm of all Buddhas; to share the same vision of the great assembly is to see it as the *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas.
Thus, since they share this vision, how could there be any delusion caused by ignorance? How could there be any [defilement of the] faculties?
Is it bound by dust? Where there is no binding, there is no liberation; where there is no delusion, there is nothing to be severed.
This is the samādhi of the single characteristic and the single principle. All who gaze upon it cannot fail to give rise to the thought of its rarity. △ Third, all Buddhas speak in unison.
Thereupon Ānanda and the great assembly [realized that] it is none other than your own six faculties. Question:
The root of the bonds of birth and death pointed out by the Tathāgatas of the ten directions is nothing but your six faculties; there is no other thing.
That "quiescent, wondrous, and eternal" is none other than your own six sense faculties; what does this mean? It is said:
For example, it is like a person who receives an object entrusted to them by another, yet out of greed, they conceal it and treat it as their own private property.
Or again, it is like a high-ranking official who accepts excessive bribes, and because his misconduct is discovered, he is subsequently executed or disgraced. Its...
The arising of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing at the gates of the six faculties—is this not the taking of a deposit?
The arising of delusion and the creation of karma—is this not the guilt of receiving a bribe? Thus, both receiving and not receiving rest with you.
To receive is to have birth and death, and to have karmic retribution; it is for this very reason that one's original nature is obscured. Not to receive is purity.
[The Master] said: "To serve as an upright official, to abide in peace and bliss, and to attain the wondrous permanence—all these arise from this very source.

Therefore it is said: 'It is only your six sense faculties; they are not other things. Question: "If that is so, then as for the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, what do they mean by 'microscopic particles' (*rajas*)?

What is their abode? Answer: "There is a profound meaning behind this. Generally, the finest of particles is called a 'microscopic particle. When subtlety reaches its limit, it becomes so minute as to be invisible."

Only when sunlight leaks through a window can it be seen; likewise, the delusion of ignorance is so subtle and minute that it cannot be perceived, yet only the Sages who have ascended to the stages (bhūmi) can perceive it.
Are the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, as numerous as motes of dust, not like the sun shining through that window?
Why is this? Because since beginningless time, sentient beings have remained ignorant of every single mote of dust and every single thought.
How many atoms are there? And how many thoughts are there? Yet, because his wisdom is turbid, he is unable to perceive them.

Today, Ānanda has received the Buddha’s instruction; he has already severed the delusions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-āsrava* and *bhāvanā-āsrava*), and has already shattered the delusions as numerous as motes of dust (*rajas*).
Nevertheless, when looking at himself, it is as if he were still suffering from a quotidian malaria. From this perspective, his fear of birth and death is most urgent.

As for the shedding of tears, it is truly pitiable. Therefore, as soon as the Buddha touched their heads, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions simultaneously emitted light and spoke with one voice in instruction—was this not like the sun shining through a window?
If such is the case even with the sun through a window, how much more so with the Great Illumination in the midst of heaven? Its subtlety, being as minute as a mote of dust, is beyond words.
...Indeed. △ Fourth, the Repeated Request.

Although Ānanda had heard such a Dharma-sound [until] "these are likewise the six sense-faculties and nothing else," Ānanda’s holy mind was profoundly versatile and his understanding of the principles was brilliant;
how could he truly have been ignorant? It was merely that he wished to personally...
I submit this to the World-Honored One. In the past, the Wise One (Zhiyi) attained awakening upon reading the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*;

he personally beheld the assembly on Vulture Peak as if it were still present, perfectly intact and undispersed. The Wise One lived during the Chen and Sui dynasties, more than one thousand nine hundred years after the Buddha’s passing.
The claim that he personally saw [the Buddha] is not to be trusted; yet, in truth, the matter is not as it appears.
If one has truly severed the discriminating mind and reached the stage of self-acceptance, then what is said regarding the personal vision of Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa is also not false.
Now, Ānanda personally saw countless Tathāgatas emitting light and personally saw countless Tathāgatas giving instruction; when compared with this—

The wise have said that time and its conditions are equal. Nevertheless, if one were to say that its light has a visible form that can be pointed out, or that its preaching has an audible sound that can be heard, this would be no different from seeing a ghost before one's own skull. Why is this?
"This is the realm of the Tathāgata," [the Buddha] secretly indicated to Ānanda. How could it be possible to conjecture or describe it through sounds, forms, or appearances?
For this reason, I humbly entreat the World-Honored One to explain and clarify this matter. V. The Buddha’s Explanation (in two parts):
1. Directly pointing out the source of the root-knots.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "The faculties and their objects share the same source" (up to) "how could anything else be admitted within this?

From the words "The Buddha told" onwards, he first presents both the true and the deluded side by side. Because within the wondrous perfection one falsely establishes the "subject that perceives," there is the appearance of the faculties;
because within the wondrous mind one falsely establishes the "object perceived," there is the appearance of the objects. Thus, as for the faculties and the objects...

Although they are divided, their nature is one; therefore, they are said to share the same source. If one discriminates and clings within the faculties and objects, there is the appearance of bondage.
If one realizes non-arising within the faculties and objects, there is the appearance of liberation. Thus, although bondage and liberation are distinguished, their essence is one;
therefore, they are said to be non-dual. Furthermore, neither the single faculty nor the single object arises [independently].

Nor does it arise [independently]. Consciousness arises through the convergence of the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*). Although the characteristics of consciousness arise, its nature is fundamentally void; thus, it is like a flower in the sky.

[The passage] beginning with "Ānanda" below next explains the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) for both. The various sense faculties belong to the external, while the mental faculty (*manas*) belongs to the internal.
Whatever the mind knows is entirely drawn in by external objects. The characteristics of the various sense faculties are all, in fact, the mental faculty.
False conditions and the characteristics of false conditions are provisional appearances. The cognition that is drawn into them is false cognition.

Both this false cognition and these provisional appearances are empty in essence; yet, when there is something seen, it is because they lack inherent nature, being like the metaphor of two reeds leaning against one another.
The nature of the reed is empty; therefore, it is used as a metaphor. Thus, below, three points specifically clarify bondage and liberation:

knowing belongs to the mind (*manas*), and seeing belongs to the eye (*cakṣus*). This means that the mind itself should know, and the eye itself should see; one cannot establish "knowing" on top of what is already known.
If one perceives an established perception upon the perceived, that is false perception. If one knows an established knowledge upon the known, that is false knowledge.
This false knowledge and false perception are the very root of the ignorance of arising and ceasing; this is what is called "bondage.
Indeed, when the mind does not harbor knowing and the eye does not retain seeing—when the eye does not retain seeing—that is true seeing.
When the mind does not cognize existence, this is true knowledge. True knowledge is non-knowing; true seeing is non-seeing.

This non-seeing and non-knowing is precisely nirvana—what is called liberation. These categories of bondage and liberation, as well as nirvana and ignorance, are established through mutual relativity and opposition;
they are not real. Why? Because this very state is untainted, truly pure, and stainless.
Within the wondrously luminous essence, how could there be room for any other thing? △ Second, a verse reiterating the preceding meaning.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
The verse consists of nine lines. The first four lines versify the text of the preceding three sections. The next line versifies the response that resolves the inquiry.

The third section, spanning one and a half lines, specifically versifies the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*). The fourth section, consisting of one line and three phrases, directly demonstrates the essential function of the school's tenet.
The final three phrases conclude by establishing the teaching. Generally speaking, this is the style of verses in the Western [Indian] tradition, wherein there are instances of direct versification.
The section concerning *geya* (verses) now contains both [verse and prose]; this will be understood from the text itself.
"The true nature of conditioned phenomena is empty because they arise dependently, like illusions" (up to: "...upon realization, one is liberated."
The line beginning with "True nature" (*zhenxing*) is the first section of the prose commentary on the verse. The preceding text states: "Roots and objects share the same source;
bondage and liberation are non-dual. Here, roots and objects constitute bondage, while true nature constitutes liberation. If one contrasts true nature with roots and objects:
To perceive the true nature (*dharmatā*) is itself conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). Why? Because the true nature is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);

even if it were to arise from conditions, it would in reality be identical to a magical illusion. Now, let us establish a formal inference (*pramāṇa*): The thesis (*pakṣa*) is that the true nature is a category of existence;

the reason (*hetu*) is "because it arises from conditions"; the concordant example (*sapakṣadṛṣṭānta*) is "like a magical illusion. If one contrasts the unconditioned with the conditioned, this [inference] is thereby established.
The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is likewise not real. Why? Because the unconditioned is without characteristics (*animitta*), yet it possesses arising and ceasing;

thus, it is identical to a flower in the sky (*khapuṣpa*). Now, the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is established as follows: The subject (*pakṣa*) is the unconditioned; the thesis (*pratijñā*) is that it is not real;

the reason (*hetu*) is "because it has arising and ceasing"; and the concordant example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is like a flower in the sky. The line and a half beginning with "The words are false" comments upon the second section of the prose commentary.
The preceding text states: "Cognition arises from objects; appearances exist because of the sense organs. Cognition and vision that arise due to external objects are false;
cognition and vision that do not arise due to external objects are true. Yet, since the true is manifested by means of the false, even the true is not truly true.
Why? Because the true does not exist as such through dependence; now, since it is manifested by means of the false, it is clear that it is not the true. Since the true...

It is not real. How could there be any characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) that can be perceived? If there were a characteristic that could be perceived, it would be a false perception; if there were a reality that could be known, it would be a false cognition.

Both are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) and are truly like bundles of reeds leaning against one another. Now, I establish the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) as follows: "Reality" is a positive term, yet its thesis (*pakṣa*) is that it is not real.
The reason (*hetu*) is: "because it is manifested through falsehood. The concordant example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is like bundles of reeds. [End of section on] Binding and Liberation.
One line and a half. This is a verse commentary on the third section of the prose. The preceding text states: "To establish knowledge within knowledge-and-vision is the very root of ignorance;

to have no vision within knowledge-and-vision is itself nirvana. Here, "knowledge" refers to the knowledge that clings to the existence of delusion, and "vision" refers to the vision that adheres to the reality of the True.
This is precisely ignorance. [Knowledge] above does not exist... the knowledge that clings to the existence of delusion. Vision... [text fragment].
If one does not cling to the view that perceives the truth, this itself is nirvāṇa.

Nevertheless, if one dogmatically clings to the notion that nirvāṇa is an existent entity, it immediately becomes a fallacy. Why? Because nirvāṇa is emptiness (*śūnyatā*), while ignorance (*avidyā*) is existence.

Since one is empty and the other is existent, neither departs from their respective causes; how, then, could this not constitute a fallacy? Furthermore, it is like a single moment of deluded obscuration.
Lack of awakening is itself bondage. If one realizes that the nature of delusion has no substance, this is liberation.
Nevertheless, if one insists that liberation is a substantial existence, this also constitutes a fallacy. Why? Because confusion and obscurity constitute bondage.
To clarify: this is liberation. One is bound and one is liberated; yet neither is apart from that which they depend upon. How, then, could it not be established as non-existent?

From this perspective, within the single true Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), it is said that not only are the fetters of ignorance empty, but even liberation and nirvāṇa are unattainable. Why is this? Because this is the untainted, truly pure, and wondrous [reality].
The essence of clarity admits no other thing to adhere to it.

The sequence for unraveling the knots follows a progression of six; when the first is unraveled, even the root perishes. By selecting the perfect penetration (*pariśuddha-āyatana*) and entering the stream, one achieves true awakening.
The following verse explains the untying of the knots, answering the previous question regarding their binding and release. In the preceding text, Ānanda had requested:
"Today, what constitutes the knots of body and mind, and from what does 'release' derive its name? Now, in this verse, the Buddha teaches: "To untie the knots, one must follow a specific sequence.
As for what is meant by "sequence," it begins first with *śamatha*, which brings to rest the objects of deluded perception. This is because...
Deluded conditions are bondage. Next, by means of samādhi, one contemplates the emptiness of all dharmas; this emptiness of dharmas is liberation.
Once the six sense faculties are liberated, even "one" does not exist. Why is this? If one clings to a single mind as being liberation, [it is not true liberation].
This is *nirvāṇa*. This, however, is a dharma that obstructs the Path; it is therefore unacceptable.

If one can truly cause all that is attained to vanish, and subsequently select a single faculty (*indriya*) to cultivate its perfect penetration (*pariṣphuṭa-prativedha*), then once perfect penetration is achieved, this is the very season for entering the Path.
Furthermore, what is called "entering the stream" refers to the "middle entry into the stream" within the first stage (*prathamā-bhūmi*) mentioned in the subsequent text.
This refers to the "perfectly wondrous blossoming. This single verse answers the previous question by Ānanda regarding the binding and untying of knots.
The explanation of its meaning will follow later; it shall be seen in the text itself.
"The *ādāna-vijñāna* is a subtle consciousness whose habitual tendencies form a violent torrent... [until] ...non-illusory things become illusory phenomena.
This one and a half lines beginning with *ādāna* describe the habitual tendencies of the *ālayavijñāna*. *Ādāna* means "grasping" or "maintaining," referring to the eighth consciousness;

it is so called because it can grasp and maintain the seeds and the physical body, preventing them from perishing. Within this context, the characteristics of this consciousness are profound and subtle.
Because it is perfumed by beginningless ignorance, it is like a rapid current of water: the flow is so swift that it cannot be seen, yet this does not mean there is no flow.
If a practitioner were to hold that this consciousness is not empty, then even if they were to practice for three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, their efforts would be in vain.
However, the Buddha never spoke of it [as such] because there is a reason. If he had said that this consciousness is real, people would...
They grasp it as a self and as permanent. If one were to say that this consciousness is not real, people would then grasp it as being subject to destruction or annihilation.
Because of these two faults, [the Buddha] did not previously expound upon it. Now, the Great Sage cites this verse primarily so that Ānanda may understand this:
the two lines concerning "one's own mind" specifically exclude those two faults, meaning that this consciousness is not something separate. All phenomena...

The Dharma is such that only the sixth consciousness fails to understand it, falsely discriminating external reflections and grasping at the eighth consciousness as its own mind manifesting in various transformations.
Although these various consciousnesses appear, each is unreal, like a magical illusion;
they were originally non-existent and suddenly become existent, and are therefore called "illusory. Now, it is pointed out that the original true mind is not illusory.
The characteristics of the sense organs, objects, and consciousnesses are illusory phenomena. Yet, since they are called "illusory," how could they possibly be real?
Therefore it is said: "The self-mind grasps the self-mind; that which is not illusory becomes an illusory phenomenon."
Now, examining this based on consciousness (*vijñāna*), the three preceding sections of the prose exposition represent the function of transforming consciousness into wisdom (*jñāna*).
How is this known? By observing the text of the first section, it says "the nature of the faculties, objects, and consciousness";
this distinguishes the first five consciousnesses from the sixth consciousness, because the sixth is characterized by discernment and cognition. Because...

The first five [consciousnesses] are so called because they grasp objects. If one can see through them and realize that the nature of the sense organs (*indriya*), objects (*viṣaya*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) is like flowers in the sky, then this is precisely the transformation of the sixth consciousness into the Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*) and the transformation of the first five into the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*).
Next, examining the second section of the text, the statement "Cognition arises from objects; appearances exist because of the sense organs" serves as a distinction.

This is the seventh consciousness (*manas-vijñāna*). Because this consciousness is the cognizing mind, it takes the eighth consciousness as the "self" aspect (*ātma-lakṣaṇa*), and it takes the sixth consciousness’s discernment as the "knowing" aspect.

If one can see through to the bottom that this cognizing aspect and the root of knowing are like two bundles of reeds leaning against each other, then one has transformed the seventh consciousness into the *pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna* (the wisdom of wondrous observation). Furthermore, the seventh...
Examining the third section of the text: the phrase "establishing cognition upon knowledge and vision" serves to distinguish the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).
Because this consciousness contains and maintains the seeds (*bīja*), it contains the sixth consciousness as the "known" (*jñeya*) and contains the first five consciousnesses as the "seen" (*dṛśya*).
Furthermore, "establishing cognition" means that it takes the seeds directly produced from the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) as its cause.
If you can see through this, then this consciousness being empty is precisely the transformation of the eighth consciousness into the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*).

This function of transforming consciousness into wisdom is perfectly clear; yet the reason it is not explicitly stated in the text is that the Buddha’s intention was to cut off Ānanda’s heels, compelling him to achieve liberation and transformation for himself. This is the Buddha’s subtle application and hidden mechanism.
This is the Dharma. Those who study the teachings must know it.
"Not grasping, there is nothing that is not illusion, and thus even non-arising [does not exist]" (up to) "a snap of the fingers transcends the stage of No-More-Learning.

One need not take up the following line or three phrases; this verse directly reveals the function of the Essence (Zong). It continues from the preceding by stating that, fundamentally, there are no illusory dharmas.
Because one grasps at objects through conceptual discrimination, illusory phenomena arise. If one does not grasp at objects through discrimination, then illusions would not arise of their own accord.
Since illusions do not arise, even if illusory phenomena were to appear before one, from what could they be established?
When illusions have no basis for establishment, this is the absence of illusion. The absence of illusion is the absence of defilement; the absence of defilement is true purity. There is no...
Illusion is itself the outflow-free (anāsrava). This essence of the outflow-free, truly pure, wondrously luminous, is able to open the Buddha-nature (buddhadhātu).
Once the Buddha-nature is opened, it is the lotus flower appearing in the world. Furthermore, from the "not taking" [section] below, its essence is revealed;

from the "Vajra" [section] below, its function is revealed. "Vajra" signifies ultimate hardness; "Jewel" signifies ultimate luminosity. It is by means of this awakening, which is both ultimately hard and ultimately luminous, [that one realizes it].
They give rise to the contemplation of illusion and do not enter into various meditative absorptions; they do not manifest formal deportment nor traverse sequential stages.
In the mere twinkling of an eye, they transcend the stage of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). For this stage of no-more-learning is the fruit-position of those belonging to the three vehicles.
Those of the three vehicles must practice for three great *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas before they can realize this stage;
now, it does not require such effort—it is resolved directly and immediately.
This Abhidharma is the single gateway to Nirvana for the Bhagavāns of the ten directions.
These three phrases at the end of the passage conclude by attributing [the teaching] to the Dharma. "Abhidharma" means the peerless Dharma (*anuttara-dharma*).
The Bhagavān possesses six qualities: namely, sovereignty (*vaśitā*), brilliance (*tejas*), physical excellence (*darśanīyatā*), renown (*yaśas*), auspiciousness (*śrī*), and nobility (*māhātmya*).
The Buddhas of the ten directions possess these six meanings; therefore, they are called Bhagavān. The Buddhas of the ten directions all attain this incomparable Dharma, and thus reach Nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, "road" (mārga) signifies the path for reaching the goal, while "gate" (dvāra) signifies the meaning of entry through realization.
In the "Entry into the Dharma Realm" chapter of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, when Sudhana arrives at the gate of the pavilion, Maitreya snaps his fingers.
The Master said, "Enter. This is precisely that meaning. △ Section 56: One Extinction, One Petition.
Thereupon, Ānanda and the great assembly [requested]... bestowing the sound of the Dharma to wash away their deep-seated defilements.
Thus, one celebrates what has been heard. A single phrase from the narrative of the scripture that causes the mind and eyes to open and become clear is the key to penetrating the entire sutra.
Previously, Ānanda had already broken through the delusions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-āsrava* and *kleśa-āsrava*) regarding the two gates of the mind and seeing;

he had already awakened to the essence of wondrous stillness. Yet, this was not yet "opening and clarifying. Furthermore, within the faculties, objects, and consciousnesses, he had already washed away...
The dust-like delusions have been purified, and one has already verified the attainment of the true and eternal; yet, this is still not yet full enlightenment.
Only now, with the manifestation of the Buddhas of the ten directions, are all innate ignorance and delusions eradicated from within one’s perception and cognition.
Only then does the Bodhi-mind become clear and the Dharma-eye open. Therefore, it is stated: "The mind and eyes were opened and enlightened," an event praised as unprecedented. This...
This is truly unprecedented; that it has now been attained—how could one not be filled with joy? Ānanda then proceeds to state his doubts.
Ānanda had previously requested, saying, "What is this 'knot' regarding today's body and mind, and from what is it called 'untying'?
In response, the Buddha said in verse: "The untying of the knots follows a sequence; when the six are untied, even the one perishes. Its...
My mind is already exhausted; that you now request this again is because it must be brought forth by the World-Honored One.
For only when heard with the ears and witnessed with the eyes can a matter be verified as real. As an ancient worthy said: "To realize through conditions is swift in attaining resonance;
to resolve within the essence is slow in gaining mastery. This is precisely what is meant. △ Second, showing the formation of the seal.
Immediately, the Tathāgata [upon the lion throne]... sequentially answered the Buddha; this is called the "conclusion" (kṣepa).
From "immediately" (*tatkṣaṇam*) onwards, one verifies the grasping at the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*). *Nivāsana* is the undergarment. *Saṃghāṭī* is the outer robe.
It is also the *saṃghāṭī*. "Kāpala" means "time-portion" (*kāla-bhāga*); it refers to the Yāma Heaven.
This cloth was offered by that heaven, and thus it is called the "Kāpala cloth. It has had its own origin. Ānanda gave rise to a view based upon this cloth.
Based on the knots, delusions arise; thus, the confusion regarding the faculties and their objects has a long history. The Buddha, however, was not like this.
He regulated his inner state and withdrew his external focus, thereby manifesting the mark of mastery. When he gathered up the cloth from the table, he manifested the function of mastery.
By tying one knot, there arose the name "one knot"; by tying six successive knots, there arose the appearance of "six knots. The cloth—
It was held in the Buddha’s hand, yet the Buddha did not recognize it as a knot; it was tied upon the headcloth, yet Ānanda recognized it as such.
That Ānanda recognized it as its being a knot, while the Buddha did not recognize it as such, illustrates the nature of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

As the Sūtra says: "When I press my finger, the Ocean-Seal manifests its radiance; when you briefly raise your mind, the afflictions arise first. Observe how Ānanda perceived the knot as arising from the headcloth.
[This is] false. It falls into the attachment to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
The Buddha told Ānanda: "When I first tied the cloth (up to) the second and third [knots], they were not called knots."
The second section, from "The Buddha said" onwards, examines the grasping of parikalpita-svabhāva (imagined nature). When I first tied the cloth, you named it a "knot.
That there was one cloth and one knot is a matter that may well correspond to reality. However, if you were to falsely calculate a second or third knot, what basis would you have for such a claim?
Would this not result in a successive chain of delusions? Furthermore, the cloth consisted of only a single strip, yet by tying it, six knots were formed. By means of...
When one contemplates these six, right and wrong are clearly distinct; yet you further engage in contention, entangling yourselves in a hundred knots—how can this ever come to an end?
Will it not result in nothing but endless wandering into emptiness? As the Sūtra says: "The nature of awareness is inherently luminous, yet delusion creates the notion of 'luminous awareness.

Awareness itself is not that which is illuminated; rather, because of luminosity, an object of illumination is established. Once the object is falsely established, your false subjectivity arises. Within that which is devoid of both sameness and difference..."
When they burn fiercely, they become distinct. Consider Ānanda’s discarded cloth as he grasps its knots: it falls into the category of the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature).
The Buddha told Ānanda: "This precious flower-cloth... how could one cause these six knots to be called in a disordered manner?"
The Three Buddhas said: "Examine the similarities and differences. The similarity lies in the cloth; the difference lies in the knots.
Because the knots differ, there are six; because the cloth is the same, it is one. To take the six and make them one is truly impossible; to take the one and make it six is ultimately not real.
If one insists that it must be either one or six, where does one arrive? Right and wrong arise from delusion and accumulate further delusion."

As the Sūtra says: "That which differs from what is differentiated establishes sameness based on difference. From the manifestation of both sameness and difference, one further establishes neither sameness nor difference.
This is precisely how we observe that Ānanda’s clinging to the six [senses] and his clinging to the one [mind] evolve into delusion.
The Buddha said: "In this way, these six knots are different [yet] ultimately identical; from within ultimate identity, ultimate difference arises.

From the words "fourthly, according to the Buddha's speech" onwards, the Dharma and the analogy are revealed together. If one looks back to their origin, they were originally but a single cloth; if one follows their manifestations, they clearly form six knots.
Once the one and the six are distinguished, it is ultimately difficult to merge them into one; therefore, it is said: "to cause them to be intermingled."
Chaos can never be established. Furthermore, if one looks to its origin, it is fundamentally the One Reality; yet if one follows its causal conditions, it clearly manifests as the six delusions.
Since the "one" and the "six" are distinct, they can never be identical. Therefore, it is said that within ultimate identity, ultimate difference arises.
As the Sutra says: "When stirred, it becomes the world; when still, it becomes empty space. Empty space represents identity, while the world represents...
They are different. Yet there is neither identity nor difference in that which is truly conditioned. As the verse says: "Originally one refined spirit is divided into six harmonious combinations.
This is precisely what is meant when observing Ānanda grasping his cloth and grasping its knots; it is the accumulation of delusion upon delusion. △ Third, showing the method of liberation.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "If you find this [binding] so distasteful... (omitted)... it cannot even be called 'one' or 'six';

how then could it be established? From "The Buddha told" onwards is an inquiry. Previously, the characteristics of the binding were already demonstrated; now, the method for its release will be taught.
On the headcloth, there is originally no knot; where there is no knot, there is not even the name "one" or "six.

That there is neither knot nor name upon the substance of the headcloth constitutes its being "formed as one. If there were a knot on the headcloth, then with that knot there would naturally be the appearance of "one" and "six.
That there is a knot and an appearance upon the substance of the headcloth constitutes its being "not formed as one. Now, I ask:
"You must surely find it unsatisfactory that there is a knot on the headcloth; yet, if there were no knots at all, would the headcloth itself be established?
This is a probing question, intended to lead Ānanda to realize for himself that 'the six are resolved and the one perishes.'"
The Buddha said: "The dissolution of the six and the disappearance of the one is likewise thus" (up to) "...are all merely the deluded toil of inverted, flower-like appearances.
Second, [this is] the application of the principle to the facts. Ānanda, if you were to completely resolve this, then there would be no appearance of "one" and "six," nor of "this" and "that.
The Buddha said: "What I call the 'dissolution of the six and the disappearance of the one' is also like this. For the mind is the sovereign."
The essence is the totality of phenomena; knowledge and vision are the faculty; the arousal of delusion is the object; and the wearying of vision is consciousness.
These characteristics of the faculty, object, and consciousness in their state of madness exist upon the substance of awakened clarity like mad flowers;
they arise neither from external causes nor from internal causes, but are entirely due to the exhaustion of the eyes. Furthermore, it is not only this. Internally...
The body with its sense organs and the external physical world constitute the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*).
The realm of Buddhas and nirvana constitute the world of enlightened beings (*buddha-loka*). Mountains, rivers, and the great earth constitute the physical world (*bhājana-loka*).

These various appearances of the three worlds arising in disorder are, upon the essence of profound clarity, like the illusory flowers seen by one with cataracts; they are neither caused by something external nor do they arise from themselves.
The cause is simply that the eyes are fatigued; it is just like the knots on the same cloth. It is neither a different cause nor a self-cause;
it is entirely brought about by what has been constructed. If all the knots were untied, there would be no "one" or "six" to speak of.
If the faculties and their objects were untied, there likewise would be no "one" or "six" to speak of.
Ānanda said: "This toil is the same as the knot" [up to] "if you wish to remove the knot, you must act upon the heart of the knot.
These three points distinguish between partiality and completeness. First, regarding the inability to untie it when pulling from the left:

this refers to the ordinary person’s attachment to existence (*bhava*). Existence is a one-sided extreme; for existence is the dharma of birth and death, yet those who study the Path now mostly grasp with the mind.
The mind uses fire to extinguish fire; this is the mind of arising and ceasing. How could a mind of arising and ceasing ever be liberated?
Next, regarding the inability to untie the right-hand knot: this refers to those of the Two Vehicles who are attached to emptiness. Emptiness is a one-sided view;

because emptiness is a dharma of annihilation, they are unable to subdue their minds. For the most part, they have extinguished their will and suppressed their wisdom, sinking into emptiness and remaining stagnant.
"Ji! This is the nature of death. How can the nature of death be untied?

As for the fact that the three [ends] could not untie it, each pulling from the left and right, this refers to the various non-Buddhists who cling to permanence, cling to annihilation, cling to neither existence nor non-existence, or cling to both existence and non-existence.
There are four phrases; these are also partial views. For not following one's own mind but wandering outward is entirely the dharma of external paths (*tīrthika*).

Nowadays, those who do not skillfully employ their minds may identify with the "host" (the self), or identify with the sounds and forms before them, or say that letting go is natural, or say that the Way is everywhere. These are all confused hairs of knowledge.
"I see it. As for knowing and seeing the variegated hairs, how could you possibly understand them? Now I ask Ānanda: suppose you employ skillful means, how would you come to understand them?
There is no other way than this: it is precisely that one must awaken to one's own mind. If one awakens to one's own mind, that itself is understanding."
"Ānanda, I say that the Buddha-dharma arises from causes and conditions" (up to) "the whiteness of the crane and the blackness of the crow all have their fundamental origins.
The four Buddhas demonstrate the perfect penetration. Ānanda, [the passage] below first discriminates causes and conditions.

Since Ānanda previously clung to the idea that things arise from causes and conditions, the Buddha once rebuked him. Now, when the Tathāgata himself says that the Buddha-dharma arises from causes and conditions, is this not also...?
Is this not the fault of contradicting [the conventional] characteristics? I say: it is not so. The causes and conditions grasped by the world are merely coarse manifestations of conjunction;
they are phenomena subject to arising and ceasing, and thus are rejected. What I now speak of as causes and conditions is the realm of the equality of Original Enlightenment (benjue).
This, too, must rely upon causes and conditions to be awakened to. Upon awakening, this is termed Initial Enlightenment (shijue). Therefore, it is said that one "knows" them.
The fundamental cause arises from the object-condition (*ālambana*). Thus, following this, the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) are explained in turn.
Previously, when Ānanda clung to the sense-base of the knowable, the Buddha rebuked him; now the Tathāgata himself declares that he knows the number of drops in every single drop of rain.
Is this not a fault of contradicting what has been established? I say: it is not so. That which the world clings to as "the known" is a dharma that constitutes an affliction obstructing the Path;
therefore, it is rejected. Now, when I speak of the "known" within the Buddha-dharma, it is the realm of the perfect penetration of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
There is no dharma that is not understood, and no thing that is not awakened to. Because it is awakening, that which is dwelt in is profoundly deep; this is called "perfect."
It is pervasive. Therefore it is said: "Even a single drop of rain beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, its number of drops is known.
Regarding the various phenomena appearing before one, all their fundamental causes are fully understood. These two meanings differ: the former negates their non-arising and thus rejects them;
the latter awakens the faculty of enlightenment and thus opens them. Otherwise, Ānanda would remain stuck in attachment and lack penetration, becoming merely a single [obstructed] being.
If you strictly prohibit yourself from dwelling [in this state], you will leave yourself no way to enter the Way. Little do you realize that this is a realm of self-knowledge;
it can only be entered through the presence of the right conditions. Once entered, naturally every object and every situation is the Way itself.
This is also one method for untying the knots.
Therefore, Ānanda, follow what is in your own mind [until] all delusions have been extinguished; what need is there to wait for anything that is not real?
Having already explained the two matters of causes and conditions and that which is known, the Buddha now exhorts Ānanda to untie the five knots himself.
This is self-explained. "Explanation" refers to how each of the six sense organs grasps its respective object to produce consciousness; this consciousness is precisely the "knot.
In reality, even the six sense organs cannot grasp objects; it is the self-mind that grasps them.

Yet, even the self-mind cannot grasp the substantial form of external phenomena, but only grasps the provisional form of external phenomena, just like the substance of a dream. If one awakens to the self-mind...
Consciousness has no basis from which to arise. If consciousness itself does not arise, how can objects be established? Therefore, I urge Ānanda to simply awaken to his own mind;
there is nothing else to do, and one will immediately attain liberation. It is like a fine horse that is startled by the reflection of another but not by its own reflection;
this is the proof for realizing one's own mind.
"Ānanda, I now ask you... [up to] "...attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) from samādhi.
Regarding the sequential explanation of the Dharma according to the Six Teachings, the section beginning with "Ānanda" clarifies the method of understanding.
Previously, he exhorted him to understand for himself so that he might see his own mind; now he asks Ānanda how he understands it. "And now these six knots appear before you. If you wish..."
Unraveling the Tangle: I do not know whether it is possible to remove [the knots] all at once, rather than following a gradual sequence.
I am uncertain, sir, as to whether one does not untie them at the center of the knot, but instead resolves them all together in a single untying.

This is just like a student who does not skillfully apply the mind, who fails to examine the underlying principles, who does not know the origin of the Dharma, and who does not understand where the aim of the Way lies. I have humbly gained a small amount [of understanding].

Such a similar view conflates [the teaching] with principle; one recognizes a mere field of emptiness as being correct, or carries around something that is neither a name nor a thing and simply rests there.
This not only leads oneself astray, but also misleads others. If it is like this, how can one possibly understand?

The words of the Buddha clarify the sequence and the correspondence to the Dharma; in general, although this matter— (Note: The provided text fragment ends mid-sentence. The translation reflects the partial nature of the source.)
There is no sequence, yet there is certainly a sequence. Although it is not clearly manifest, in reality there is indeed clarity. Why?
If these root-knots are not severed, the study of the Way will be in vain. Therefore, one must first resolve all ignorance and karmic consciousness within the root and its objects.
Once this karmic consciousness is resolved, it is called "emptiness of persons. Since emptiness...
[The stage of] Illumination (*āloka*): There still remains a dharma; therefore, one must next eliminate the afflictions of the beginningless dwelling-place (*anādikālikā-vāsabhūmi-kleśa*).
When these afflictions are severed, it is called the emptiness of dharmas (*dharma-śūnyatā*). Although both person and dharmas are empty, there still remains an "emptiness" [itself].

Only when even this "emptiness of both" does not arise does one exhaust the contemplative wisdom of *samādhi* and attain the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). This is called the sequential order.
This is the explanation.
From the beginning of the fourth fascicle up to this point constitutes the text on *samāpatti*.

Regarding the method of contemplation in *samādhi*, one contemplates the three types of inverted characteristics of the karmic fruits of worldly sentient beings; all of these are the luminosity of awakening, which is extremely clear and pure.

[It is] understood. [One sees that] these are all manifestations following after delusion. Furthermore, one observes that the delusions of the five turbidities and the functions of the six senses are entirely the workings of one's own mind.
Moreover, one observes that the characteristics of the five faculties and the causes of their binding and fettering are likewise not external things;
they are all the misdeeds committed by the faculties, objects, and cognitions. It is like a painter who paints the various forms of the world.
Or one may see paintings of tigers, wolves, and lions that strike fear and terror into the heart;
or, as in a dream, one sees the heavens, the earth, the sun, the moon, and various men and women; or one dreams of gathering with enemies, or of being driven, coerced, bound, beaten, or killed.
Such experiences vanish one by one upon waking, and only then does the mind become peaceful and joyful, recognizing that they were merely paintings and that the fear was groundless.
They are unarisen. The karmic fruits of the sentient beings in this world, as well as the characteristics of the faculties, objects, and their binding attachments, are likewise so.
Now, by the power of the wisdom of samādhi-observation, one illuminates them all as being like dreams or paintings; not a single dharma accords with the mind.
Only then does the mind become peaceful and joyful, and fear no longer arises. This is precisely the news of having arrived home.

△ Section Three: The Text on the Samādhis, Part Six. 1. Requesting Instruction on the Perfect Penetration; 2. General Inquiry to the Various Sages; 3. Each Presenting Their Own Path of Realization; 4.
The Edict Entrusting Mañjuśrī to Select the Perfect; 5. Reciting Verses to Distinguish and Evaluate; 6. Hearing the Dharma and Attaining Benefit.
In the preceding stage of *śamatha*, one destroys the afflictions of views and thoughts and thereby attains the wisdom of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).

In the subsequent stage of *samāpatti*, one severs the innate afflictions of ignorance and thereby attains the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). Only when both the emptiness of persons and the emptiness of phenomena are realized does one become a pure vessel.
One may advance into *dhyāna*. In Sanskrit, *dhyāna* means "quiescent contemplation" (*jìjìng sīwéi*); it refers to the silent realization of the mind’s penetration.
To enter this gate, one must transcend the functioning of mind, intellect, and consciousness (*citta-manas-vijñāna*) and sever the paths of both the mundane and the sagely.
Only when a single thought-moment achieves resonance can one be said to have entered. Nevertheless, for those at the stage of a beginner, it is unavoidable to rely upon [external aids].
With a single faculty and a single object—whether taking up a single matter or focusing on a single sense-base—one investigates the path of the mind until reaching the ultimate goal.
When one suddenly collapses and breaks through completely, that is the very moment of resonance. The twenty-five sages below are precisely this:
what is called the "original root of perfect penetration," whereby one borrows a path to enter the Great Dharma-realm.

Only upon reaching the stage of *dhyāna* is it appropriate to allow the mind to rest. [At this point] Ānanda and the great assembly requested instruction on the Perfect Penetration (*yuan-tong*), withdrawing into their inner chambers to conceal their private inquiries in hopes that the Buddha would grant them secret transmission.
Ānanda then presented his understanding and requested the Dharma. He said: "The body is the aggregate of the various faculties, and the mind is the sovereign of all phenomena.

Since I have previously attained the liberation of the faculties and the removal of knots, such that both person and phenomena are non-existent, my body and mind have become luminously clear and are now fit to advance upon the Path.
Thereupon, he requested the method of Perfect Penetration (*pariśuddha-vyūha*) to achieve the ultimate model of practice. Thus spoke the World-Honored One.
The following describes my private aspiration. If we speak in terms of accumulated delusion: to be perpetually tossed by the rising and falling of every thought is called "drifting and wandering";
to be lost and lingering within the five realms of existence is called "solitary and exposed. If we speak in terms of the awakened nature:

when one's nature is identical to the Buddha-nature, one is born together with the Buddhas; when one's awakening is identical to the Buddha’s awakening, one is already included among the Buddha’s kin.
If we speak in terms of the fundamental and the initial, fundamental awakening and non-awakening are like a nursing infant who has lost its mother’s milk;

now attaining initial awakening is like suddenly encountering a compassionate mother. Ānanda thought to himself: "If one attains the Way at this juncture, what difference would there be between awakening and non-awakening?
If it is identical to the fundamental enlightenment, then there would be no distinction between having heard [the teaching] and not yet having heard it. As it is said:
Originally, people of old did not change their former conduct; this was Ānanda’s private vow, his intention being to attain realization.
He only entreated that the Buddha would secretly bestow his grace. Ānanda looked to the Buddha for favor: "If you would grant me the secret majesty, it need not depend on words and speech.
I shall then withdraw and conceal my subtle mechanism, so that no thoughts arise in the mind. No thoughts arose.
Contemplation does not reside in verbal expression; it lies solely in the secret transmission of perfect penetration.
Judging by this, Ānanda’s narration is complete both in principle and in practice, manifesting that which lies beyond words. Truly, this is not his former self;
he is now settled and at ease, truly in the state where spiritual work is continuous and subtle. △ Second, the general inquiry of the various sages.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the entire assembly (up to the point where he asks): "By what skillful means does one enter samādhi?
Regarding the general category of dhyāna and abhijñā, there are two intentions behind the Tathāgata’s statement that "he has never uttered a single word.

First, it is in response to Ānanda’s request: "Grant me the secret and majestic phrases. "Secret" refers to the concealment of the matter; "majestic" refers to the solemnity of the Dharma. As for the Dharma...
Only after being solemn does one perceive the reality of the situation; only when matters are kept secret does one know the truth of the intention.
Therefore, there is no teaching. Second, herein there is originally no place for teaching; even if there were teaching, it would teach that others do not cling [to it].
This is because this is the inconceivable realm, which even the faculty of thought cannot fathom. Therefore, there is no teaching. *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Fascicle One.
This entire section is expounded by the precious nets of the Cloud Terrace (*Yun-tai*) and by various bodhisattvas. The Buddha himself spoke only two chapters:
"The Incalculable" (*asaṃkhyeya*) and "The Radiance of the Minor Marks" (*anuvyañjana-prabhā*). Question: If that is so, what is it that the twenty-five sages have taught? Answer:
That which was presented by the twenty-five sages is entirely the Dharma of skillful means (*upāya-dharma*). As for "skillful means" (*fangbian*):...

One simply takes up a single faculty and a single object, or selects a single phenomenon, or focuses on a single sense-base, employing the practices of cessation and contemplation, concentration and wisdom, and so forth;
this is called the "path. By means of this path, one can enter [the state], though it is not said that the path itself is *dhyāna*.
Only after having entered is it the stage of *dhyāna*. Therefore, he asked the various sages, "Who among you has attained perfect penetration? From which direction did you enter?"
He then entered samādhi. Furthermore, samādhi is called "contemplative wisdom" (vipaśyanā-jñāna). By means of this contemplative wisdom, one attains perfect penetration;
thus, one realizes the state of dhyāna. For this reason, the patterns of practice cultivated by the twenty-five sages are borrowed to assist Ānanda’s capacity for entering the Way.
△ Third, each presents their door of realization. First, the sense-object of sound.
The five bhikṣus, including Kauṇḍinya, immediately rose from their seats... [up to] "...as I have realized, sound is supreme.
When the Buddha first left the kingdom, King Śuddhodana commanded three members of his clan: first, Aśvaka; second, Bhadrika;
third, Mahānāman Koliya. There were also two cousins: first, Kauṇḍinya; second, Daśabala-Kāśyapa. Thus there were five.
[The Buddha] saved their lives. Afterwards, they each departed. After the Buddha had attained the Way, he went to the Deer Park and turned the Wheel of Dharma for them three times.
He asked them, "Do you understand? Candra replied, "I have understood; I have known. Therefore, he was named Ājñāta [Kauṇḍinya].

This is called "understanding" (*jie*). To understand that sound is a sensory object (*viṣaya*), is adventitious, and is a phenomenon subject to arising and ceasing—this is the skillful means for a beginner.
To generate understanding by taking the principle of the Four Noble Truths as an object is the "lesser" [approach].

Now, it is not so. One realizes that sound itself is eternal and that hearing itself is wondrous. Why? Because one awakens to the non-dual awakening. By virtue of this non-dual awakening, one attains [realization].
The wondrous sound is secretly perfect and complete. As Vimalakīrti said: "Arising and ceasing constitute duality. Since phenomena are fundamentally unarisen, they are now without cessation.
To attain this patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) is to enter the gate of non-duality.

From this, we know that to perceive a distinction between arising-and-ceasing and non-arising-non-ceasing is itself a dualistic view. If one does not realize that the nature of sound is originally empty, how could there be any arising or ceasing?
△ Second, the object-field of form (*rūpa*).
Upānanda rose from his seat... [up to] "...as I have realized, form is the supreme cause.
Upānanda means "the nature of the object-field" (*dharmatā*); it is also called "near-little" (*upa-niṣada*), referring to the subtlest aspect of the object-field.
It is rare nowadays. When Śāṭha first contemplates the impurity of the body—seeing it as pus and blood, or as mucus and saliva—he asks, "What is there to be attached to?

Next, he contemplates the body as white bones; seeing only white bones, he no longer perceives the mark of a self (*ātman*). He further contemplates these as minute particles and as the nature of emptiness (*śūnyatā*);
this is the expedient teaching for those with a beginner's mind. Upon reaching the state of emptiness, even that is non-existent.
Why is this? Because one conceives of emptiness as something created by oneself, emptiness is likewise non-existent.

When both emptiness and form are non-existent, they constitute the single true nature, and only then does one become an Arhat (one beyond training). Now, however, it is not so: form itself is wondrous, and the body itself is eternal.
Why? Because one awakens to the awakening that is non-dual. By virtue of this non-dual awakening, one attains the subtle, wonderful, secret, and perfect [state]; this is the truth.
He is one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). △ Third, the sense-object of fragrance.
The youth Gandhahastin immediately rose from his seat... (up to) "...as I have realized, the severity of fragrance is supreme.
It arises from awakening; because he does not give rise to dualistic views, he is called a 'youth. By means of the three faculties of nose, tongue, and body, they combine..."
Because one takes the object within, one first upholds the Buddha’s teaching by contemplating conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).

Since conditioned phenomena are characterized by arising and ceasing, one immediately perceives arising and ceasing as non-arising and non-ceasing; this is the skillful means of the initial mind. Departing from the Buddha to seek stillness is itself unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);
the fragrance coming to enter the nose is itself conditioned. Now, one contemplates that it is neither wood, nor space, nor smoke, nor...
Fire. As for fragrance, it has no place of origin. Since fragrance has no arising, what does the mind differentiate? Since the mind does not exist, one attains the outflow-free (anāsrava).
Nevertheless, there were still sensory objects (rajas) present, and one had not yet attained direct manifestation of the essence.
Now, the scent of these objects suddenly vanishes; the wondrous fragrance is subtle and perfect. This is true "beyond-learning" (aśaikṣa). △ Fourth, the sense-object of taste.
The two Dharma Princes, Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata... (up to) "As I have realized, the cause of taste is supreme.
Born from the Buddha’s mouth, transformed by birth from the Dharma, they are worthy to succeed the Buddha; therefore, they are called Dharma Princes.
The Dharma can deliver oneself and can also deliver others. Delivering oneself is Bhaiṣajyarāja; delivering others is Bhaiṣajyasamudgata. This is because medicine can..."
It is so named because it cures the illnesses of sentient beings. Following its fundamental flavors, there are five; following its minor expansions, there are five hundred;
following its major expansions, there are one hundred and eight thousand. This is the general outline of these numerical categories.
Serving the Tathāgata, one comes to fully understand the nature of flavor, for it is awareness that is able to know flavor. This is the initial mind.
This is a skillful means (*upāya*). One contemplates that phenomena are neither empty nor existent, and neither separate from nor identical to [their conditions].

Why is this? Because their nature is non-arising (*anutpāda*). However, speaking in terms of body and mind, these refer to the characteristics of the sense organs (*indriya*), objects (*viṣaya*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).
When one investigates these three locations, one finds no arising. Since there is no arising, subject and object are immediately severed. From this, one attains awakening and realizes:

Being of one flavor, pure, and equal, they are thus named Dharma-Prince (Dharmarāja-putra). Furthermore, because they are able to awaken themselves and awaken others through the clarity of their awakening, they ascend in rank to the stage of Bodhisattva. △ Five: The Sense-object of Touch.
Bhadrapāla, together with his companions... [up to] "...as I have realized, contact is the supreme cause.
Bhadrapāla—here translated as "Worthy Protector" (Xiangu)—is that which lies beyond form and is called "majesty" (wei); it is that which lies beyond sound and is called "resonance" (yin).
This represents the realm of initial awakening, wherein the view of self has not yet been established and consciousness has not yet arisen; thus, names and words do not apply.

At the time of his birth, he was called the Buddha Vairocana-rāja (Vibhūṣaṇa-rāja). According to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, twenty-two thousand koṭis of Buddhas named Vairocana-rāja appeared in succession.
During the period of the True Dharma (*saddharma*) of the first of these Buddhas, this Bhadrapāla was possessed of overweening pride;
he slandered the Dharma and fell into hell. Once his retribution was exhausted, he emerged and encountered the era of a later Vairocana-rāja, whereupon he left the household life. Following...
For example, when entering the bath, one encounters this water; through this cause, one realizes that the nature of touch is ultimately ungraspable.

Thereupon, right faith arises. This is the expedient means for the initial mind. Because one contemplates that sensory objects have no self-nature, what use is there in washing away dust? Even touch is but a phantom arising.

Furthermore, how could one wash away [the defilements]? The two emptinesses of nature and characteristics are such that there is nothing within them. Yet, although this awakening to nature has not been forgotten, the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) remains vividly present.
It was only until today, when I left the household life following the Buddha, that my deluded views were extinguished, and I finally attained the stage of No-More-Learning (aśaikṣa).
Now it is not so. It is precisely this contact that is eternal; it is precisely this cause that is wondrous. Why? Because there is no duality in awakening.
By virtue of this non-dual awakening, one attains the manifestation of wondrous contact and dwells as a son of the Buddha.

Furthermore, the sixteen noble youths were originally the retinue of those who, while still within the causal stage, gave rise to pride and false views. Now that the root has already attained awakening, the branches...

They were at peace and did not undergo further transformation. Therefore, they equally realized the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) and likewise joined this assembly. △ Sixth, the dust of dharmas (*dharmaraja*):
From "Mahākāśyapa and the Purple Golden Light" up to "As I have realized, the cause of dharmas is supreme."
Mahākāśyapa—this translates as "Great Kauruṣya" or "Drinking Light. Ziguang Jinini was the wife of the Venerable One while he was still a householder;

the full details of their causal connection are found in other biographies. Having heard the Dharma from Candrasūryapradīpa Buddha and practiced it as a student, this was precisely the arising of right faith through the awakening of clarity.
When the darkness of the Dharma continued, he sustained that clarity; after the Buddha had departed...
Furthermore, the act of painting an image is precisely the entrusting of a superior mind to accomplish the substance of the Dharma.

When husband and wife simultaneously give rise to the aspiration and together manifest a gathering of light, this is precisely being protected by the correct cause and thereby escaping the bonds of affliction.
The above has described the expedient means for the initial aspiration. Now, observing that while the six sense-objects undergo change and decay, empty space remains unchanging; for this reason:

By cultivating the dharma of emptiness, one extinguishes all mental activity. When the nature of the mind is extinguished, it is empty; thus, passing through hundreds of thousands of kalpas is like the snapping of a finger.
That which possesses arising and ceasing is the domain of the mind; that which is unchanging and unmoving is the permanence of the nature of emptiness.
Emptiness is unmoving, and the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is likewise unmoving. Therefore, hundreds of thousands of kalpas are as easy as a finger-snap;
yet now it is not so. This very dharma is wondrous; this very clarity is eternal. Why? Because awakening is non-dual awakening.
By virtue of non-dual awakening, one attains the opening and clarification of the wondrous nature and accomplishes the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*). △ Seven Eyes.
The Faculty.
Aniruddha then rose from his seat... [until] ...revolving the vision and tracing its source; this is the foremost.
Aniruddha—also called Anuruddha, which means "Free from Poverty," or "As One Wishes"—is indeed pure.

He was the son of King Droṇodana, the second son of King Śuklodana, the cousin of the World-Honored One, the elder brother of Ānanda, and the uncle of Rāhula; he was no ordinary man. The Duke of Zhou sighed and said:
"I am the son of King Wen, the younger brother of King Wu, and the uncle of King Cheng; in all under heaven, I am no lowly man. So it was with Nanda.
Is this not what is meant? Nanda followed the Buddha in his studies; because he was so prone to drowsiness, the Tathāgata rebuked him severely.

Consequently, Nanda was so stirred that he did not sleep for seven days, whereby he lost both his eyes. When the World-Honored One showed him the Vajra-samādhi, it was because he had received illumination within the mind, without relying on external things.
In general, one should focus the conditions of attention upon a single point, exerting effort so that the mind is free from distraction.
After a long time, the essence becomes naturally refined and true, penetratingly illuminating all things. One observes the ten directions as clearly as seeing fruit in the palm of one's hand.
What is called "fruit in the palm" is likewise the verification of revolving the vision to follow the Origin. Furthermore, a sutra says:

"When Nalakalīra practiced dhyāna, he attained the power of the four great elements and derived matter (bhautika-rūpa) such that he could see the three thousandfold world system with only half his head. Now it is said: "One observes the ten directions; the essence is refined and true, penetratingly illuminating."
As for "illumination," it refers to the difference in what is seen by the divine eye at earlier and later stages. △ Eighth, the faculty of the nose:
Cūḍapanthaka immediately rose from his seat... (until)... reversing his breath and following the void; this is the foremost.
Cūḍapanthaka (translated as "Successor of the Path") was, in a past life, a great Dharma master with five hundred disciples. He was stingy and unwilling to teach others.
Consequently, he was reborn dull-witted; yet, due to his past roots of goodness, he encountered the Buddha and went forth into the monastic life.

Although he and his five hundred companions were all given the same stanza, he could not recite it after ninety days. The Buddha then taught him the practice of counting the breath (*ānāpānasmṛti*) to cure him.
Regarding that distraction: at first one practices counting the breaths; later, one reverses the breath and follows it into emptiness.

Upon reaching the point where not even a single kṣaṇa allows for the mind’s activity, one then forgets all conditions and perceives the true mark, thereby accomplishing the path of no-more-learning. △ Nine: The Tongue Faculty.
Gavāmpati immediately rose from his seat... [up to] "...returning to the flavor and revolving within the faculty of cognition;
this is the foremost. Gavāmpati means "the Cow-Chewer" (*gavāṃ-pati*). The origin of this name is as stated in the text: whenever a cow eats, it invariably engages in the act of rumination.
The Venerable One was afflicted by this illness, and many people laughed at him. The Buddha showed him the Dharma-gate of the single flavor (ekarasa-viśuddhi).
As for what is called "the single flavor," he taught that one should chew it within the mind, not chew it as a taste; when one chews the taste, there is no cause [for it].

When chewing, the mind finds no flavor. If there is no flavor, what illness can there be? If there is no cause, what aversion can there be? This not only cures illness, but can also lead one into the Way.

Regarding the observation of flavor, it appears again below as an observation of practice (*guanxing*). It is not that the substance is the sense organ (*gen*); it is not that the object is the flavor itself.
This means that the cognition which perceives flavor does not exist within the object, nor does it exist within the substance; it exists in between.
There is also no object of focus. Investigate in this manner, and you will naturally enter the state of non-thought.
This is like the present-day Zen practitioner who looks within without sending thoughts outward, and does not allow external objects to enter.

If one awakens to birthlessness, then one’s original nature becomes lively and active, just like a bird escaping from its cage. This practice depends entirely upon returning to the flavor and revolving back to the knowing. Thus it is said:
Thus he attained the path of no-more-learning. △ Tenth: The Faculty of the Body.
Piliṅgaputra immediately rose from his seat... [until] "...to leave the body through pure awakening; this is the foremost."
Piliṅgavatsa—this means "remnant habit. In his past life as a Brahmin, he had many remnants of arrogance. Once, while crossing the Ganges, he shouted, "Hey, little slave-girl!
Stop the current! The deity of the Ganges split the river into two channels for him. When the deity went to report this to the Buddha, the Buddha ordered him to offer an apology.
Piliṅgavatsa immediately joined his palms and said, "Little slave-girl, do not be angry. The great assembly laughed at him. He offered his apology, yet continued to insult her.

The Buddha said: "This is due to past habituation; in truth, there is no conceit. As for 'that which cannot be enjoyed,' it refers to the impermanence of the world and the impure sufferings of birth and death.
While on his almsround, he contemplated the Dharma-gates and was unaware of the thorn [in his foot].
This is because one perceives pain through non-perception; it is the realm of body and self. The character 'know' (知) at the beginning refers to that which is perceived."
The lower [level of] "knowing the word" refers to the capacity for awakening. Upon the mind that is originally pure, there has never been the duality of subject and object.
If there were the marks of subject and object, it would be two separate awakenings. Investigate in this manner until you reach the state of non-thought;

suddenly, body and mind become empty, and you recover original awakening (*mūla-bodhi*). Since there is no longer any bodily form to be reckoned with, one becomes one who has nothing further to learn (*aśaikṣa*).
△ 11. Regarding the faculty of mind:
Subhūti immediately rose from his seat... [omitted] ...to return to the Dharma and find it in non-existence; this is the foremost.
Subhūti is here called "Born of Emptiness" (*Śūnyatā-ja*) and also "Well-Appeared" (*Sujāta*). While still in his mother’s womb, he already understood emptiness and quiescence.
This is the domain of the mind. Knowing that the primary retribution (the individual self) is empty, one knows that the secondary retribution (the environment) is also empty;
thus, one perceives the emptiness of the ten directions. Knowing that one's own nature is empty, one knows that the nature of others is also empty;
thus, one causes sentient beings to realize and attain the nature of emptiness. Why is this so? Because all phenomena are merely manifestations of one’s own mind. Nevertheless.
If one knows the nature of emptiness yet has not severed it, while the marks of bondage remain clearly present, this is not yet the perfect principle.
Now, awakening to the fact that the nature of awareness is fundamentally empty—what need is there to "know" it? The ten directions are equally awakened; how can one speak of self and other?

From this, one illuminates true awakening and enters suddenly into the precious, luminous ocean of emptiness. Thus, even as all phenomena enter into non-existence, that non-existence itself is exhausted.
This is the turning of the Dharma back to non-being; it is the realization of the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*). △ 12. Eye-consciousness.
Śāriputra immediately rose from his seat... [until] ...his light and supreme knowledge and vision are foremost.
Śāriputra—this is translated as "Body-Son" (*Śarīraputra*), derived from his mother’s name. *Śā* indicates the father; *Li* indicates the mother.
Because both parents are manifested together, he is called Śāriputra. *Putra* means "son. As stated in the preceding text:

"Due to the mutual conditioning of the two aspects of light and darkness, within the wondrously perfect [nature], the clarity of stillness becomes attached, giving rise to vision. The essence of vision reflects forms, and by binding with forms, the sense organ is formed. The sense organ...
Originally, it was designated as the "pure four great elements," hence the name for the substance of the eye. It is like a cluster of grapes;
the "floating root" refers to the four sensory objects (*viṣaya*) rushing forth and flowing toward forms—this clarifies the substance of the eye. The present text says:

"Throughout kalpas past, my mind and vision have been pure, and thus I have taken birth as many times as the sands of the Ganges, manifesting various transformations of both the mundane and supramundane worlds. One.
"Upon seeing, one universally attains unobstructedness" refers to the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*). "The mind's vision is pure" refers to the sense organ (*indriya*).
"Various transformations" refers to the consciousness (*vijñāna*). Below, in the section on "On the Road," I shall describe the attainment of the benefit of the Dharma.
Another sutra states that while on the road, he saw Aśvajit (also known as Mañjuśrī). His deportment was dignified and orderly.
Because [the Buddha] asked him about his teacher’s doctrine, Aśvajit replied: "All phenomena arise from conditions; all phenomena cease due to conditions.

My teacher, the Great Śramaṇa, always speaks thus. Upon hearing this once, [the Buddha] attained realization; this refers to the understanding of the Noble Dharma of the Four Truths. Now, it is said that on the road...
Encountering the exposition of causes and conditions by the brothers Kāśyapa, those who awaken to the boundlessness of the mind understand the Dharma of the Three Truths and Nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, being born from the Buddha’s own mouth and transformed through the Dharma, this is the manifestation of enlightenment through the provisional sense organs.
Rely on wisdom, not on consciousness; therefore it is said that the mind’s vision emits light, and when the light reaches its limit, one attains knowledge and vision.
This awakening to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision is identical to that in the *Lotus Sūtra*. △ Thirteen: Ear-consciousness.
Samantabhadra Bodhisattva then rose from his seat... [up to] ...this mastery of discernment is foremost.

The three faculties of nose, tongue, and body apprehend their objects through contact; they know when there is contact and do not know when there is no contact. The eyes and ears apprehend their objects without contact;
yet the eye is clear in front but not behind, as if lacking half its capacity. The nature of the ear alone is without obstruction.
If drums are struck simultaneously in the ten directions, they are heard at once in all ten places. This hearing occurs within the mind;
while sound has arising and ceasing, the mind has neither arising nor ceasing, because the nature of awakening is equal and impartial.

When it is now said that one is a Dharma Prince to the Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, it is because the ear-consciousness arises from awakening; thus, one is called a "son. This is the teaching of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions.

Among his disciples, this faculty alone is supreme. All that arises from the resolve for enlightenment is termed the "conduct of Samantabhadra. This is because the conduct pervades the entire Dharma-realm, hence it is called "Universal" (Samanta);

and because its stage borders upon the ultimate sages, it is called "Worthy" (Bhadra). Since all of this is fundamentally the mind arising in reliance upon awakening, it is named the "Conduct of Samantabhadra.

The preceding section clarified the characteristics of the mastery of the auditory consciousness. From the passage beginning with "From the World-Honored One" onwards, it clarifies the self-... of the auditory consciousness.
To employ it is the function of the mind; "hearing" refers to the ear-consciousness. The knowledge and views of sentient beings do not transcend their own minds.
The mind does not deviate from the nature of awakening; only awakening can know, and only awakening can see. When deluded, one is a sentient being;
when awakened, this is the functioning of awakening. Therefore it is said: "to discern all the knowledge and views possessed by sentient beings. This discernment is itself unimpeded wisdom.

This is the function of sovereign mastery. As for the phrase "beyond the worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in other directions," this refers to the essence of the awakened nature (*prakṛti-bodha*), which is not a matter pertaining to the boundaries of mind, intellect, or consciousness (*citta-mano-vijñāna*); therefore, it is described as being "beyond the realms.

When there is a sentient being who clarifies and brings forth the practice of Samantabhadra, this is precisely to perceive the equality of one's own mind and to perceive the manifestation of phenomena from within one's own mind.
Wherever the body may be, even if there are obstructions such that it cannot be seen clearly, this does not impair its fundamental enlightened awareness (*prakṛti-bodha*). Why is this?

Because through this practice, one will ultimately attain benefit; therefore, I say that I personally bestow the empowerment of touching the crown of the head upon such a person in the midst of darkness.
Roughly speaking, the realm of mental hearing is precisely this inconceivable wonder; it is not like other sense organs which involve contact with objects to grasp their characteristics.
△ Fourteen. Regarding the nose-consciousness:
Sundarananda immediately rose from his seat... [up to] "...being perfectly enlightened and extinguishing the outflows, he is foremost.
Sundarananda; this is translated as "Glorious Joy. "Glorious" (Sundara) is the name of his wife, and "Joy" (Nanda) is his own name. This serves to distinguish him from others.
"Nanda the Ox" refers to him together with his wife. Previously, based on the *indriya* (faculties), their number was taught;

now, based on the *vijñāna* (consciousness), the contemplation of the breath as white is taught. Contemplation means the mind is fixed upon one point. The mind is like fire, consciousness is like fuel, and the breath is like smoke.
When the fire is stilled, the fuel does not burn and the smoke naturally disperses. When the mind is stilled, consciousness does not function.
Thus, the breath naturally disperses. Consequently, one perceives the inhalation and exhalation within the nostrils as if they were smoke.
