The aggregate of consciousness transmigrates through kalpas, treating the true nature as if encountering an enemy thief. It is not so for the Bodhisattva: when sounds cease and hearing becomes perfect, there is nothing internally upon which to depend;
when the power of compassion arises universally, there is harmony with Heaven manifested externally. Therefore, even when passing through perilous paths, [the Bodhisattva remains unshaken].
Thieves cannot plunder them. Furthermore, the five ghosts represent the fierce manifestations of the five desires (*pañca-kāma*).
Yakṣas are translated here as "the valiant and strong"; rākṣasas as "the terrifying"; kumbhāṇḍas as "hypnotizing and bewitching ghosts";
piśācas as "ghosts that devour vital energy"; and pūtanas as "ghosts of feverish disease. The methods above are for transcending the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

Ninth: "The perfuming of hearing leaves the sense-objects behind, so that one is not plundered by forms" (extending to): "All those with *icchantika* tendencies are forever freed from the darkness of ignorance.

Sentient beings have greed as their established nature and are plundered by forms; the Bodhisattva, however, does not follow after sounds when hearing, but hears the nature of what should be heard, and thus succeeds in remaining far removed from greed and being unmoved by forms. Sentient beings have anger and resentment as their established nature and are [plundered] by hatred...
They are carried away by [the afflictions]. Bodhisattvas have pure sounds that leave no dust; since their faculties and objects are one, there is neither subject nor object.

They remain far removed from the anger of sentient beings whose natures have become dull and obscured, who are carried away by the darkness of ignorance. For Bodhisattvas, auditory consciousness is dissolved and forgotten;

their awakened clarity turns back into stillness. Thus, they attain a body and mind within the Dharma-realm that are bright, radiant, and utterly transparent, remaining far removed from the darkness of ignorance.

*Ātyantika*. This is translated as "the mind devoid of goodness. Its nature is an obstruction, which is precisely delusion (*moha*). The above constitutes the method for transcending the afflictions such as the three poisons.
Twelfth: "Fusing the Form" (furthermore, hearing of the Immovable Bodhimanda... up to ... women with physical marks who are loved and respected by the multitude).
"Melting away form and returning to hearing" is precisely the absence of attachment to a self (*anātman*). If there is no attachment to a self, what could it not respond to?
Even in responding, there is no partiality; thus, one does not destroy worldly phenomena while making offerings to as many Buddhas as there are atoms.

Furthermore, he gives birth to a daughter with auspicious marks to correspond to his own mind. Moreover, "male" is a designation for the Way of Qian (Heaven) that takes charge of affairs, while "female" refers to the Way of Kun (Earth) that responds with flexibility.

Fourteenth: Within this trichiliocosm (up to), by my cultivation, I have attained true and perfect penetration.
One Mount Sumeru and one sun and moon constitute one world; likewise, ten billion Mount Sumers and ten billion suns and moons [constitute a great trichiliocosm].
A hundred billion worlds collectively constitute one great trichiliocosm. There are three thousand such great trichiliocosms.
That this is a realm manifested by the mind is a delusion. In contrast to delusion, awakening is revealed; awakening, in turn, remedies delusion.
Therefore, they are called Dharma-Prince sons. Within this great trichiliocosm, there are as many Dharma-Prince sons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River;
yet the Dharma-gates they preach are equal to those of Avalokiteśvara alone, and their merit is identical. Moreover, one need only hold the single name of Avalokiteśvara.

The merit of [bestowing] those many names upon others is likewise equal. This is because the Dharma-gate realized by Avalokiteśvara does not require the passage of kalpas as numerous as motes of dust;

it does not stir the consciousness. Wherever it is heard, there is immediate awakening; because of this awakening, there is immediate response. In the place of response, there is no trace; in the place of function, there is no partiality.
In every mote of dust and every buddha-field, there is nothing that is not encompassed, nothing that is not universally pervasive, and nothing that is not profoundly deep.
There is nothing that is not mastered. For this reason, the Dharma-gate of Avalokiteśvara is called the most supreme.
The above constitutes the Dharma of the Bodhisattva’s vocal teaching.
This is called the fourteenth: the power of bestowing fearlessness, which provides all beings with merit.

"World-Honored One, I have further attained this perfect penetration (up to) the four inconceivable, unconditioned, and wondrous virtues."

This indicates the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa-citta*). As for why these immeasurable minds are called "inconceivable," it precisely reveals the wondrous power of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*);

its functioning is such that there is no deliberate mind. It is precisely because its functioning is without deliberate mind that, above, it attains identity with the compassionate power of the Buddhas of the ten directions, and below, it attains identity with the sorrowful longing of sentient beings in the six realms. Those who behold this—
Rejoice! May those who seek find fulfillment. If there were anything within the scope of thought or deliberation, it would constitute an obstruction;
how then could one attain sovereign mastery to respond extensively to all? This is the general heading; what follows is the detailed explanation.
First, by virtue of my initial attainment of the wondrous and sublime mind of hearing [the Dharma], I have attained great mastery in rescuing and protecting sentient beings.
The head is the totality of the body; the arms are the function of the body; and the eyes are the illumination of the body.
Furthermore, the head is wondrous response; the arms are wondrous power; and the eyes are wondrous contemplation. Expanded, these comprise the eighty-four thousand dharmas.

The Gate. Briefly stated, it consists of the two dharmas of wisdom (*prajñā*) and meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Initially, the Bodhisattva hears without following the sound; he hears with a mind that should hear.
If one were to say that this mind is still characterized by traces, even now, though there is a hearing-mind, he does not dwell in or cling to it;
therefore, it is called "sublime" (*miao*). Furthermore, this sublimity cannot be expressed in words, hence it is called "sublime-sublime. This sublimity also exists within sentient beings, but...
Because they are separated by seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, they sink into birth and death. It is not so for the Bodhisattva;
there is only the single, pure jewel-like awakening, which responds universally to all without division. It manifests bodies and preaches the Dharma everywhere without becoming confused.
For this reason, it is called "wondrous. This is precisely the Bodhisattva’s immeasurable mind of compassion that rescues and protects sentient beings.
This is the Dharma.
Second, by means of what I have heard and contemplated, one is liberated from the six sense objects (up to the point where it says) "all are named as me, the Bestower of Fearlessness.
Regarding "manifesting each individual form," this means not being restricted to a single realm; whenever there are signs, [the forms] manifest. Regarding "reciting each individual mantra,"...

This means that one does not restrict oneself to a single matter, but rather provides relief whenever affliction arises. Therefore, its form and its mantras pervade the ten directions and as many lands as there are motes of dust.
It is called the "Bestower of Fearlessness" because, through the two wisdoms of hearing and reflection, it transcends the six sense objects;
it is purely the wondrous function of the true mind. Just as sound passes through a wall without any obstruction, it is likewise free from all impediments. Because it is without impediment—
Therefore, the suffering of sentient beings is the suffering of the Bodhisattva; the sorrow of sentient beings is the sorrow of the Bodhisattva.
In brief, sentient beings take suffering and affliction as their catalyst, while Bodhisattvas take compassion and pity as their dharma.
Sentient beings take fear as their catalyst, while Bodhisattvas take fearlessness as their dharma. Generally speaking, sentient beings and Bodhisattvas...
Together they share a single life. Having shared this life, how could one not feel profound compassion and provide extensive salvation?
This is precisely the Bodhisattva’s immeasurable heart of compassion, the method for uprooting and rescuing sentient beings.
Third, by virtue of my cultivation of the fundamental, wondrous, and perfect penetration (up to: "I have discarded my body and precious treasures to seek your compassion").

What preceded was first the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*); this wisdom takes the wondrous existence as its dharma. Next was the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*); this wisdom takes the wondrous mind as its dharma.
Now, what follows is the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*); this wisdom takes the wondrous emptiness as its dharma. Thus one cultivates.
This is the wondrous samādhi of emptiness. To attain this wondrous, perfect penetration—the pure fundamental root—is itself the wisdom of emptiness.
One who travels through the world with this wisdom of emptiness is such that sentient beings have not seen them for kalpas on end; even if they were to see them, [they would not recognize them].
Spontaneously rejoicing, one abandons all stinginess and parsimony to seek compassion;
this is the bodhisattva’s immeasurable mind of joy, the dharma that benefits all beings.
Fourth, I have attained the Buddha-mind and realized the ultimate (up to: seeking great nirvana and attaining great nirvana).

The three types of wisdom mentioned above are as follows: the first liberates one from the sense faculties; the second liberates one from the sense objects; and the third liberates one from consciousness.
As each of these—the faculties, objects, and consciousnesses—is individually detached, this arising and ceasing is extinguished, and quiescent extinction manifests before one.
Therefore, it is said: "I have attained the Buddha-mind and realized the ultimate. The Buddha-mind is the fundamental Dharma; the ultimate is fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).
By means of this fundamental wisdom and this fundamental Dharma, one brings forth the treasures of one's own house to make offerings to the ten [directions].
From the Buddhas above down to the sentient beings of the six realms, whatever they may seek, all shall have their wishes fulfilled.
This is the Bodhisattva’s immeasurable mind of relinquishment, the dharma that benefits all. Thus concludes the four immeasurable minds.
Each and every one emerges from the operation of no-mind; therefore, it is called "inconceivable.
These four inconceivables are brought forth to realize the wondrous function of the fundamental wisdom of our own original Dharma. They are not within the realm of mind, intellect, or consciousness;
they are truly and authentically produced through the practice of subtle and refined cultivation—how could they possibly be achieved by mere casual means?
"The Buddha asked about the perfect penetration, and I [responded] from the gateway of the ear... therefore the name Avalokiteśvara pervades the worlds of the ten directions.

This concludes the response to the question. "Perfectly illuminating samādhi" concludes the phrase "nirvāṇa is manifest before one. "Mastery over the conditioned mind" [concludes the preceding section].

This concludes the section on the three types of wisdom derived from hearing, reflection, and cultivation. Furthermore, "perfect illumination" (yuanzhao) is precisely "quiescent illumination" (jizhao).
Being quiescent while constantly illuminating is the *ekavyūha-samādhi* (one-practice samādhi); being illuminating while constantly quiescent is the *eka-lakṣaṇa-samādhi* (one-mark samādhi).

This *ekavyūha* and *eka-lakṣaṇa* samādhi is precisely the gateway to the perfect penetration of the *dharmadhātu*, and it is the realm of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Now, regarding these three...
It cannot be attained through ignorance; one must rely upon the method of the three kinds of wisdom (*trividya*) to be able to reach it.
For the three kinds of wisdom are the path; by means of this path, one arrives at *bodhi* and arrives at the stage of *samādhi*. As the verse says:
"If you wish to attain *samādhi*, you must truly enter through hearing"—this is the proof. Question: Regarding the twenty-four sages...

[Question: "One attains it. How does this compare in quality to what Avalokiteśvara has attained? [Answer: "In truth, there is no difference in quality; it is simply that their application of mind differs.

For example, as for what the twenty-four sages have attained, it requires reaching the point where discrimination is exhausted. Is discrimination not, after all, a matter pertaining to the edge of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*)?
With Avalokiteśvara, it is not so: he does not involve himself in discursive thought, nor does he move along the paths of the mind. He directly touches [the source]."
The place is itself realization; the place of realization is itself understanding. It is for this reason that they differ.
Furthermore, that which is attained by the twenty-four sages can only benefit themselves and is incapable of responding to the capacities of others.

That which is attained by Avalokiteśvara truly enables one to enter both the holy and the mundane, the true and the conventional, to rescue those burning or drowning in water and fire, and to relieve the thirst and deprivation of sentient beings—even within butcher shops and wine taverns.

Whether it be the lands of Buddhas or the palaces of Māras, among the various species and their manifold sounds, one may cast oneself into them without anything being contrary to one's wishes and without lacking mastery. Yet, when compared to the other faculties, this is not the case;

for the nature of those other faculties is subject to obstruction, being either conscious or unconscious, and either complete or incomplete. Only the nature of the ear-faculty is without obstruction, neither... [omitted].

He does not abide; there is neither perception nor non-perception. Simply by not grasping at the dharmas of the aggregates, nor at a self within the aggregates, he naturally enters the mindless samādhi and attains the state of perfect penetration. For this reason, the single gateway of Avalokiteśvara is the most swift;
it is truly no exaggeration to call him the "Bestower of Fearlessness" in this Sahā world.
At that time, the World-Honored One was upon the lion throne (until) the Brahma-songs and hymns were spontaneously performed.

the Tathāgatas, as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions, likewise emitted light from their five limbs. Those who attained the intermingling of these intersecting lights were all sealed by Avalokiteśvara.

The realization of this Dharma is unerring. Furthermore, it reveals that this Dharma is neither ordinary nor sagely; it is the non-dual equality of the three vehicles and five natures, and of sentient and insentient beings.
Question: If you say that sentient beings share the same awakening, that may be so. But why do forests, trees, ponds, and marshes also proclaim the sound of the Dharma?
Answer: Do you see these forests, trees, ponds, and marshes? If you see them, [then you know they are no different from sentient beings].
I have finished preaching the Dharma for you. If you do not perceive it, you yourself do not even know it; how then can you claim to discern it? Furthermore, this is not so:
every thing has a true essence—whence speak of self and other? Every instance is the Way—why rely on intimacy or distance?
If you turn the light back to reflect within, you will immediately be identical to what was originally attained. Why then do you doubt that things do not proclaim the sound of the Dharma? This is so.

Those of lower capacity receive benefit according to their faculties; indeed, the twenty-four sages each differ in the depth of their realization, and their partial or complete attainments are not uniform.
Thus, whatever they have attained remains within its original state. Consequently, they see mountains and rivers as merely mountains and rivers, and see empty space as merely empty space;
even to the point that this realm is not seen as that realm, and this nature does not merge with that nature.
Therefore, there are distinctions of high and low. Now, by entering the single gate of Avalokiteśvara, one attains the dissolution of the faculties and their objects.
Thereupon, one universally obtains the Vajra Samādhi and awakens to the single nature of equality. Consequently, one no longer perceives mountains, rivers, or the great earth;
one sees only the lands of the ten directions as merging into a single realm. This "single realm" is the One Dharma; it is the Single Awakening. Having awakened to this—
The Dharma is awakening. How could one not rejoice in what has been encountered and give rise to praise? "Fanbai" (Brahma-chanting) is translated here as "praise.

The Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī, having received the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, spoke these verses in response to the Buddha.
There are sixty lines in total. The first five lines eulogize the source of both the real and the delusory. The next twenty-four lines eulogize the inferiority of the dharmas of various sages.
The following three lines eulogize the superiority of Avalokiteśvara’s path. The final three and a half lines eulogize the various faculties.
1. One verse of five lines distinguishes [the teaching] from others; 2. one verse of three lines distinguishes the fundamental root; 3. two verses of six lines directly reprimand the recipient; 4.
seven verses of ten lines and one line announce and instruct Ānanda; 5. three verses of three lines conclude with exhortations for practice and study.
The nine lines of the five-character verse are selected to clarify the underlying intent; they are explained in the section on "Encountering Meaning.
From "The nature of the ocean of awakening is clear and perfect; its perfect clarity makes awakening fundamentally subtle" (up to) "the difference between slow and fast is beyond comparison."

These five verses concern the source of both the true and the deluded. Mañjuśrī, having received this command and being about to select [the appropriate verse], first set forth the Great Meaning to explain it.
This Great Meaning refers to the ocean of wondrous enlightened clarity, which is originally tranquil and profound, and originally numinous and subtle.

Because it is wondrous, there is no dharma that it does not encompass; because it is profound stillness, there is no object that it does not illumine. Though it illumines, it is without mind; though it encompasses, it leaves no trace.
Because it leaves no trace, it is called "wondrous"; because it is without mind, it is called "profound stillness.

Therefore it is said: "The nature of the ocean of awakening is limpid and perfect; this perfect and limpid awakening is fundamentally wondrous. This is the principle of True Suchness (Tathatā) being unchanging while following conditions, and being sovereign.
This is as stated in the preceding text: "The nature of awakening is wondrously luminous; fundamental awakening is luminously wondrous. Alas, sentient beings do not understand this.

They engage with objects and give rise to the mind. The object is that which is perceived (*viṣaya*). Once the perceived is established, illumination is lost. When the mind arises, the nature is obscured.
When the nature is obscured, one wanders through delusion and confusion. When illumination is lost, the whole being is unawakened. Because of this delusion and confusion...
Awakening, it thus becomes empty space. Depending upon space, there are worlds. Therefore it is said: "The fundamental clarity shines and gives rise to the objective realm;

once the objective realm is established, the nature of the shining light perishes. Through deluded ignorance, empty space arises; depending on space, there are worlds. Furthermore, these flow and shift through the three periods of time.

The flow does not go beyond the objective realm (*viṣaya*). When the objective realm confines thought and thought becomes clear, it forms a land. When emptiness is inert and lacks awareness, that very awareness is delusion.

Because one uses deluded awareness to know delusion, there are sentient beings. Thus it is said: "When thought becomes clear, a land is formed; when there is knowing and awareness, there are sentient beings.
This is the characteristic of True Suchness (*tathatā*) which, while remaining unchanging, follows conditions to undergo arising and ceasing. This refers to the preceding passage.

It is said: "The nature of awareness is inherently luminous, yet delusion manifests as the perception of luminosity. Awareness itself is not that which is illuminated; rather, because of this luminosity, an object is established.
Once the object has been falsely established, your false subjectivity arises. Thus, in general, the worlds, lands, and sentient beings all depend upon emptiness and existence.
Emptiness arises within the midst of awareness, resembling a bubble on the water. When the bubble vanishes, it is non-existent, yet the nature of emptiness likewise [remains].
There is none; how much less could there be sentient beings of the three realms of existence within space? It is clearly known that these lack intrinsic nature. Therefore it is said:

"Empty birth arises within the Great Awakening, like a single bubble emerging from the sea. When the bubble ceases, the space was originally non-existent; how much more so the various realms of the three existences."

The "three realms of existence" (*tridhātu*) refers collectively to the three worlds. If one observes them with the physical eye, these sentient beings of the three realms appear to be truly existent.
However, if one observes them with the wisdom-eye, these sentient beings of the three realms are in reality identical to a single awakening;
once awakened, there is nothing else remaining. Therefore, in investigating this Way, one must seek that which is one.
Sublime awakening. Through awakening, one realizes that all phenomena belong to a single family. Yet, there are many gateways to this awakening.
It is like people arriving at the capital city of Chang'an: some come from the south, some from the north, and some from the east or west;
they do not advance by only a single route. Those who study this Way are likewise so. For although it is indeed a dharma-gate of a single characteristic and a single principle, nevertheless—
One may take up a single dharma, or address a specific matter, or employ a single opportunity or circumstance;

yet, one does not limit oneself to a single path, but rather takes reaching the goal as the ultimate aim. Thus it is said: "The nature of returning to the source is non-dual, though there are many gates of skillful means.
Although there are differences between the sudden and the gradual, from the perspective of the Buddha-ground, each and every thing is equal.

Both the inverse and the direct are permissible. In the inverse, cognition does not arise from external objects (*viṣaya*). In the direct, it is manifested by relying on the faculties (*indriya*), such that one understands everything wherever contact occurs.
There is nowhere this is not correct; hence it is said: "The nature of the Sage is all-pervading; both the direct and the inverse are skillful means.
If one is at the stage of a beginner, there will be differences in speed; as for the slow, these are the practices cultivated by the twenty-four sages.

It is so. That which is swift refers to the single gateway of Avalokiteśvara. Although there are differences in speed and slowness, when considered as a whole, they are all nothing other than skillful means.
Therefore it is said: "When the beginner enters samādhi, their progress may be slow or fast, differing in kind."
"The perception of form is bound by dust; though one may understand it with extreme clarity, it cannot penetrate through. How, then, can one attain perfect penetration?
These six lines of verse distinguish the dharmas of the six sense objects. First, the selection of Śāṭa, who attained awakening by contemplating the object of form:
although he took the object of form as his meditation and achieved an extremely refined understanding, it still could not penetrate through. Why? Because the nature of form is...
Darkness. The essence of awakening is luminosity; luminosity and darkness do not intermingle. If they do not intermingle, how could awakening be perfect? How could the Dharma be pervasive?

Next, let us examine Dharmapāla’s realization through the observation of the sense-object of sound. He took sound as his object of contemplation, yet sound has limitations and cannot universally encompass all things.
Why is this? The ocean of meaning is boundless, beyond the reach of names and words. Words and meanings...

Since it is not all-pervasive, how could awakening be perfect? How could the Dharma be universally penetrating? Third, regarding Xiangyan’s discernment: he attained enlightenment by contemplating the sensory object of fragrance.

Because he used fragrance as his object of contemplation, his awakening was not constant. Why is this? Fragrance is perceived when the sense organ and the object meet; when they separate, it is no longer perceived.
Since their meeting and separation are unequal, how could the awakening be perfect? How could the Dharma be... [universally penetrating]?
Regarding the fourth, [the Buddha] distinguishes Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata from those who awaken by contemplating the sense-object of taste.
Those who take the sense-object of taste as their contemplation do not achieve constancy; why? Because taste exists only when being tasted and does not exist when not being tasted.

Since its nature is not constant, how could awakening be perfect, and how could the Dharma be universally penetrating? Regarding the fifth, [the Buddha] distinguishes Bhadrapāla from those who contemplate the sense-object of touch.
As for those who attained awakening by taking the sense-object of touch as their object of contemplation: its nature is not fixed. Why? Because when there is contact, it is clear;
when there is no contact, it is not clear. Since its nature is not constant, how can awareness be perfected? How can the Dharma be fully penetrated? This sixth [case] distinguishes Kāśyapa.

As for those who attained awakening by contemplating the sense-object of mental phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), they take mental phenomena as their object of contemplation; yet subject and object are not all-pervasive. Why?
Although one may extinguish all outflows (āsrava), one still guards against internal dust. Internal dust is emptiness, and emptiness is also an object.
Where there is a subject and an object, how can awakening be perfect? How can the Dharma be fully penetrated?
"Although the seeing-nature is brilliantly clear, it is bright before but not behind" (up to) "how can one attain perfect penetration?
These five lines of verse distinguish the methods of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).

First, as for Nālada, who attained awakening to perfect penetration by turning back his sight and following its source because he had lost his eyesight—now [the text] distinguishes him by saying: "If one takes the sense base of the eye and the turning back of sight as one's contemplation..."
The nature [of the perception] is not uniform. Why? Because what is seen in front is entirely bright, while what is behind is entirely dark; even in the four intermediate directions, half is missing.
Since there is both light and darkness, how could awareness be complete, and how could its nature be pervasive? The meaning of "missing" is explained in the preceding text.
Regarding the principle of entering into grasping and turning the light back to reflect: "revolving the seeing to follow the source" is precisely this act of returning the reflection.

Second, regarding Pāṇṭaka: because he was dull-witted, he practiced the contemplation of counting the breaths; yet, by instead following the breath back into emptiness, he attained awakening to perfect penetration.

Now, [the text] distinguishes this, saying: "If one takes the breath through the nose and follows it into emptiness as the contemplation, it will be fragmented and fail to achieve completion. Why is this?"
The inhalation and exhalation of the breath each proceed in their own direction without the two gases mingling; even in the middle [of the process], there is no mingling.

If this is so, how can awareness be considered perfect, and how can its nature be considered pervasive? This mingling occurs precisely within the process of inhalation and exhalation, yet it has no interaction with the true nature.
Third, Gavāmpati suffered from the ailment of "ox-chewing"; he attained realization of perfect penetration by returning the flavors and revolving the faculty of cognition. Now...
The selection states: "If one takes the tongue-faculty (*jihvā-āyatana*) as the basis for awakening and realization to constitute 'contemplation,' this too is not a universal principle.

Why? The tongue-faculty does not arise without cause; it necessarily exists because of flavors. When flavors cease, cognition ceases. How then could awakening be perfect, and how could its nature be pervasive?
As for the four *Vatsas*, who, having had their feet wounded by poison, attained the realization of perfect penetration by withdrawing their mindfulness from the body—now...
The Commentary states: If one takes the entry of the body into sensation as contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), this too is not true. Why?

Because the body is the subject that perceives (*neng jue*) and contact is the object perceived (*suo jue*). When there is a distinction between subject and object, it is difficult for them to merge in silent union (*ming hui*).

Since they do not merge in silent union, how can awareness be perfected? How can its nature be pervasive? "Distinction" (*ya liang*) refers to limits and measures. Five, Shanji, by means of the mind...
Regarding those who attain perfect penetration by returning to non-existence through the unimpeded revolving of dharmas, the present selection states:

"Consciousness and vision are a mixture of the three harmonies; I refute the claim that they are not characteristics" (up to) "how can one attain perfect penetration?
These six lines of verse distinguish the dharmas of the six consciousnesses. First, Śāriputra: "That which is realized through the mind and vision emits light;

Phenomena arise only through the conjunction of three factors. To abandon these three is to fall into the characteristic of non-existence;

that which lacks characteristics is non-being, while that which possesses characteristics is the objective realm. If one investigates their origin, there is initially no fixed point of reference. How, then, can one attain perfect penetration?
Regarding the second point, that Samantabhadra Bodhisattva attained awakening through the sovereign discernment of the mind’s hearing as its fundamental cause:
"mind-hearing" refers to the ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*). That one hears not with the ears but with the mind is because the mind is the totality of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Therefore it is said that "the mind-hearing penetrates the ten directions. However, one must rely on the power of great causes to be able to enter this state.
Great causes include such things as the practice of the Dharmadhātu Contemplation and the arousal of the great vow; yet these are still too lofty.
This is not suitable for a beginner; therefore, it is excluded, as it is difficult to attain perfect penetration through it.

Third, regarding Sūndarananda, who attained awakening after long-term practice of observing the white breath at the tip of the nose: observing "white" refers to the olfactory consciousness (*ghrāṇavijñāna*).
While observing the white at the tip of the nose may serve as a provisional means to collect the mind, one cannot enter the Way by relying on this alone.
It is acceptable. Why? Because the true mind has no abiding place; if there were abiding, it would not be the true mind, but would instead become a mental factor (*caitta*).
How, then, could one attain perfect penetration? As for the fourth, Pūrṇa, who attained awakening by eliminating all outflows through unimpeded eloquence:

Now, having received Mañjuśrī’s instructions, his mental traces have become perfectly clear, and he has realized the Dharma-gate of attaining Buddhahood.
By practicing in reliance upon this, one will be free from delusion. Next, the passage beginning with "Furthermore, I have constantly heard" formally sets forth his vows.
For it is heard that the fundamental purpose of studying the Way is to deliver sentient beings; delivering sentient beings is precisely the vow to deliver boundless sentient beings.

While for the Tathāgata self-awakening is already perfected and he is able to awaken others, it is not so for a Bodhisattva. Rather, [the Bodhisattva thinks]: "It would be better for me to remain undelivered myself than..."
He entered *nirvāṇa*. Having previously vowed to deliver sentient beings, Ānanda looked up to the Tathāgata and realized he could not fulfill that vow;
thus, he also vowed to learn from the Bodhisattvas by generating the bodhicitta. He asked: "Sentient beings are infinite; how can they ever be delivered? [The Buddha] replied:

"The Bodhisattva contemplates his own mind as being like a mirror, and views sentient beings as being like reflections. Although reflections appear within the mirror, the mirror itself is inherently without arising. To realize this is..."

Non-arising is itself deliverance. Thus one knows that one delivers oneself through oneself, and awakens and perfects oneself through oneself. Such is the extent of the Bodhisattva’s deliverance of sentient beings.
Thereafter, the World-Honored One descended to prevent wrongdoing and request the Dharma; he collected his mind and entered meditative concentration.
This is precisely the vow to sever afflictions that are inexhaustible. The teaching of false teachers is itself affliction.
To gradually distance oneself from the Buddha is non-awakening (*abodhi*). Because of non-awakening, various afflictions arise; this is the work of Māra.
Ānanda, you say you wish to practice cultivation, yet if your illumination does not reach [the source], thoughts will arise through non-awakening, making it difficult [to succeed].
To restrain the mind is itself affliction (*kleśa*). Furthermore, in the final age, when false teachers flourish, it will be difficult to enter meditative absorption (*samādhi*);
this is the work of Māra. Now, how can one cause afflictions to be severed so as to advance toward Bodhi?

How can one ensure that no works of Māra arise so as to establish oneself securely in the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*)? This Ānanda has formulated the Four Great Vows to practice and enter the Way, yet he harbors apprehension.

"I feared that my strength was insufficient; therefore, I made this request. △ Second, the granting of permission to proclaim [the teaching], in three parts: First, praising the excellence [of the request].
At that time, the World-Honored One, amidst the great assembly... (until) Ānanda and the great assembly responded, "So be it," and respectfully received the instruction.
"Zànshàn" (Praise for Excellence) means to grant approval to his request. It signifies that Ānanda has well grasped the Buddha’s intention and skillfully upheld the teachings of the Dharma.
Indeed, the Buddha’s intention was not to leave these as mere empty words, but rather to require others to practice them.

Since the path of cultivation is inevitably beset by many demonic obstacles, it is necessary to rely upon established regulations. This is truly beneficial for those present and provides a remote salvation for the final age; therefore, [the request] was granted.
The Buddha granted his request, exclaiming "Excellent! twice. △ Second, the general heading:
The Buddha addressed Ānanda: "You have often heard me... (up to)... this is what is called the three trainings in the absence of outflows."
This is a general indication of the three definitive meanings. *Vinaya* is also called *vini*, which translates as "extinction" (*miè*).
Its direct translation is "discipline" (*lǜ*). "Discipline" means "dharma. This is the common designation for the precepts of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.

Among these three definitive meanings, the precepts are primary; furthermore, concentration and wisdom arise from the precepts. Therefore, *vinaya* is mentioned here. However, regarding these three...
The Dharma is called the Threefold Training in the Outflows-Free (anāsrava-śikṣā). The Buddha has often proclaimed that Ānanda must practice by restraining the mind and relying upon this training.
This is the method of skillful means for the initial attainment of the Way by all Tathāgatas of the ten directions;

it is something absolutely indispensable. Therefore, it is named the "Three Definitive Meanings. △ Third, the detailed explanation is divided into three parts: first, the training in ethical discipline (śīla-śikṣā); second...
The training in concentration, the training in wisdom, and the training in ethical discipline. First, regarding the precept against sexual misconduct:
Ānanda, how does one restrain the mind? That which I call "ethical discipline" (śīla)—[this continues] until: the first definitive, pure, and clear instruction.
First, Ānanda, I shall distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox. The root of birth and death is lust; it stands at the head [of all afflictions].
If one’s mind were free from lust, birth and death would naturally have no means by which to continue. Therefore, the precept against lust is considered orthodox.

Conversely, if the lustful mind is not eliminated, then even if one possesses great wisdom and meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one will inevitably fall into the path of Māra. Therefore, failing to observe this precept is considered heterodox.

This is heterodox. To discuss those who follow this heterodoxy: they practice dhyāna while harboring lust, and because there are degrees of depth and shallowness in their practice, their retributions vary as superior, middling, or inferior.
Each of them likewise claims to have realized the unsurpassed Way; yet though they have achieved that state, they do not realize it is actually heterodox.
After my parinirvāṇa, I shall clarify these benefits and harms so that, because of this heterodoxy, they may not continue to wander in delusion.
Alas! In later generations, there have even been those who falsely claim to be masters of knowledge (*jñānin*), thereby confusing the Buddha-dharma and seducing sentient beings.
They cause them to lose the true path and fall into the pit of craving and false views (*dṛṣṭi*); the harm and benefit involved here are no small matter.

You have clarified the instructions and admonitions below, so that these matters of benefit and harm may be properly addressed. Therefore, for those practicing *samādhi* according to my teaching, [it is essential to be] profound...
That which one must guard against is this: one must certainly bring about the total eradication of its nascent thoughts; therefore, it is spoken of in terms of the mind.
This is the definitive teaching of the Buddha, the foremost pure and clear instruction.
Therefore, Ānanda, if one does not sever lust (and so forth)—if it is not spoken thus, it is the teaching of Pāpīyān.
For this reason, the following provides a further analogy regarding gain and loss: from precepts arises concentration; from concentration arises wisdom; and wisdom is the Dharma-body.
The Dharma-body is pure and must be attained within meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*); how could it be sought with a body of lust? Even if one were to [seek it] through lust...
To seek meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) with a body of lust is like boiling sand in the hope of producing rice;

even if it continues for hundreds of thousands of kalpas, it remains nothing more than hot sand. To seek meditative concentration with a lustful body means that even if one attains subtle insights, they are merely the root of lust.
Not only will one fail to attain the Way, but one will inevitably transmigrate through the three miserable realms (*trāya*). This is so.

This constitutes what is lost. Therefore, I exhort those who truly cultivate meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) to surely seek wondrous awakening, so that the mechanism of lust is suddenly severed and both body and mind are simultaneously cut off, such that even the nature of this "cutting off" is non-existent. Only through such purity can one hope for Bodhi;
this is what is gained. As I have just paired these two points above, it means that by relying on the aforementioned instructions of the Buddha, one immediately—
This is the correct teaching. That which does not rely on the Buddha’s instruction above is false teaching. Furthermore, "Pāpīyan" is a corruption;
the correct term is *Pāpīya*, which means "extremely evil. This is the designation for the most extreme among evils, referring to the Māra King.
△ Second, the precept against killing.
From "Ānanda, furthermore, the sentient beings of the six realms in all worlds" (up to) "the second decisive, pure, and clear instruction.
Below this, Ānanda distinguishes between the heterodox and the orthodox. Regarding the karmic bonds of birth and death, the mind of killing is the most severe. Even if that mind...
If one does not kill, birth and death will naturally cease to continue. Therefore, abstaining from killing is considered correct.

Conversely, if the intent to kill is not eliminated, then even if one possesses great wisdom and meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one will inevitably fall into the path of demons. Thus, failing to observe this precept is considered erroneous.

Viewing it from the perspective of those who are heterodox: they practice meditation while harboring the intent to kill, which varies in depth and shallowness; thus, their retributions range from superior, middling, to inferior.
Each of them likewise claims to be practicing the unsurpassed path; though they may achieve their respective goals, they do not realize that these are actually heterodox.
After my parinirvāṇa, I shall clarify these benefits and harms so that, because of such heterodoxy, they may no longer proliferate and spread in all directions hereafter.

In this world, there are those who falsely assume the title of "spiritual friend" (kalyāṇamitra), openly consuming meat, defiling the Buddha-dharma, and seducing sentient beings to become part of the hordes of ghosts and spirits;
the harm and benefit involved here are no small matter. Below, Ānanda specifically demonstrates what is permitted and what is prohibited.
The five kinds of pure meat are those that are not seen, not heard, and not suspected [to have been killed for oneself], as well as meat from animals that died naturally, and meat left over by birds.
Because these five do not involve the severing of the life-faculty, they are called "pure. The Buddha established these during times of famine;

in lands that were either humid and damp or composed of sand and stone where grasses and vegetables would not grow, these five types of pure meat were produced through his supernormal powers. The Buddha...
Within the Hīnayāna schools, meat-eating was provisionally permitted; this is what is meant by "allowance" (*anujñā*). Conversely, it was prohibited;
this is what is meant by "restraint" (*pratiṣedha*). Now, this sutra clarifies the definitive teaching on the Buddha-nature of the One Vehicle.

How can one who eats meat be called a son of the Śākya (a *śākyaputrīya*) and yet claim to have realized the definitive doctrine? [The following] shows the faults of eating meat for you all. This is indeed the teaching of the Śākya...

A "son" here refers to one who studies the Way. If a student of the Way eats meat, even if they have attained an awakening that resembles the stage of *samādhi*, they are nothing more than a *rākṣasa*.
A *rākṣasa*—which in this context means "violent and evil"—mutually kills and devours one another;
as sheep die to become humans and humans die to become sheep, their cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*) has not yet ceased. How could such a person escape from the three [realms]?
This is a matter of vital importance regarding the faults of eating meat. You have clarified the instructions in your teaching below;
observe that the fault of eating meat is truly the source of both benefit and harm. Therefore, for those practicing *samādhi* according to my teachings, this is something they must strictly avoid.
The precept must ultimately lead to the cessation of killing. This is the Buddha’s definitive resolution.
This is the fixed dharma; it is the second pure and clear instruction.
Therefore, Ānanda, if one does not cease killing [and so forth], and if it is not spoken thus, then it is the speech of Pāpīyān.

Therefore, the following section uses a heavy analogy to illustrate gain and loss. Since the Buddha-nature of the One Vehicle naturally possesses a mind of compassion and forbearance, one must realize this mind of compassion and forbearance;
it can only be attained within meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*). How could it be sought through a murderous intent?
To seek meditative concentration with a murderous intent is like covering one's own ears while shouting loudly, hoping that others will not hear. This is because...
The more one conceals it, the more it is revealed. To seek compassion and patience with a murderous mind is like increasing one's endurance while simultaneously increasing one's disorder.
To clarify this, the text below cites an analogy: even a pure bhikṣu does not consider it sufficient merely to refrain from killing living beings;
he would not even bear to trample upon living grass, let alone consume the flesh and blood of sentient beings. This is the comparison.

To speak by way of analogy: the silks and fabrics of the East, the furs and woolens of the West, as well as items such as milk and curd—if one does not wear or consume them, one has truly attained liberation and escaped the three realms. Why is this so?
If one consumes the physical parts of sentient beings, one naturally becomes an object of their [retributive] perception. It is like eating the hundred grains of this world:
one naturally cannot escape the earth. If even consuming food is thus, how much more so for those who swallow and kill one another without falling into ruin?
This is what is lost. Therefore, I exhort those who truly practice meditative concentration (dhyāna) that they must necessarily possess loving-kindness (maitrī).
With a mind of forbearance, one must ensure that both body and mind remain untainted by clothing and untainted by food.
Only through such purity can one hope for Bodhi and truly attain liberation. This is what is gained. As I have concluded below, the meaning is as previously stated.
△ Third, the precept against stealing.
Ānanda, furthermore, regarding the sentient beings of the six realms within the world... [up to] the third definitive instruction on pure clarity.
Below, Ānanda distinguishes between the heterodox and the orthodox. In the cycle of birth and death, the mind of theft is most severe.
If one’s mind does not steal, birth and death will naturally not continue. Therefore, the precept against stealing is the orthodox path. If one steals...

If the mind is not eliminated, even one with extensive wisdom and meditative concentration will inevitably fall into a heterodox path; therefore, the failure to observe the precepts is considered heterodoxy.

Regarding those who follow such heterodoxy: if they cultivate meditation while harboring a thieving mind, there are varying degrees of shallowness and depth, and thus their retributions range from superior to middling to inferior.
Each of them likewise claims to have achieved the Unsurpassed Way; yet, though they achieve that way, they do not realize that it is—
This is heterodox. In the section on my own parinirvāṇa, I clarify the benefits and harms. Because of such heterodoxy, people deceive one another in secret;

in later generations, there are even those who falsely pose as spiritual teachers (*kalyāṇamitra*), luring sentient beings into the ranks of demons and heretics, causing them to lose their minds and ruin their families.
These harms and benefits are by no means trivial. In the section of my teaching concerning the specific demonstration of benefits and harms, how can this be made clear?
This is its benefit. Buddhist bhikṣus wander from place to place to beg for food. "Wandering from place to place" means following the Dharma established by the Buddha.
"Begging for food" means seeking alms to sustain the fourfold assembly, thereby accomplishing the dharma of non-attachment.
"Not cooking food for oneself" demonstrates a mind free from worldly concerns. "Traveling through the three realms" demonstrates that there is nothing to [cling to].
This is a lingering attachment. These rules for the purity of *śīla* (moral discipline) are beneficial to the world; therefore, they are called "beneficial" (*hita*).
Furthermore, how can one clarify their harmful consequences? The Buddha ordained that *bhikṣus* should practice the Path with purity, yet now it is not so.
Internally harboring deceit, they externally manifest dignified deportment while surreptitiously donning the Tathāgata’s Dharma robes to deceive the donors and faithful.
Wealth and property are contrary to the true category [of the Dharma]. You yourself practice deception and create all manner of karma, yet you claim it all to be the Buddha-Dharma;
this harms the transformation of others and ruins social customs, and is detrimental to sentient beings—therefore, it is called "harmful.

If, after my passing, we distinguish between the true and the false through specific verification, those who previously concealed their wickedness and deceit out of private motives, claiming to be "good spiritual friends" (kalyāṇamitra), shall again...
Because they steal the mind [of the Buddha], they falsely assume my robes to trade in the name of the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, because they do not believe in their own minds, they treat other renunciants who possess the precepts and follow the path of the Hīnayāna as if they were merely people of the final age. It is thus.
"How shall one distinguish between the true and the false? The Buddha said, "It is not so. After my parinirvāṇa, there will be bhikṣus who resolutely cultivate samādhi;
they may burn their own bodies with a single incense stick or a single lamp, or even burn a finger-joint.
I say that such a person has at once repaid all karmic debts from beginningless time and is forever liberated from all outflows (āsravas). Why is this? Because a person..."
To secretly harbor deceit and fraud out of self-interest is the mark of the conception of a self (*ātman*).

Now, being able to offer one's own body as a lamp to make an offering to the Tathāgata is the absence of the mark of a self. Because people possess a thieving mind, they act as parasites who trade upon the Tathāgata.
This is the conceptualization of a person (*pudgala-nimitta*). Now, being able to burn even a single finger joint as an offering before an image is to be without the conceptualization of a person.

That one does not believe in one's own mind, but instead regards others who possess the precepts as practitioners of the Small Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), is the conceptualization of a sentient being (*sattva-nimitta*).
Now, being able to burn a single incense stick upon one’s body to verify the self-mind and achieve self-awakening is...
There is no mark of a sentient being. Such a person is thus devoid of these three marks; are they not indeed a true bhikṣu?
This is what constitutes reality. If it is not so, I say that even if such a person practices until they reach the field of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), they are not a true practitioner.
This is merely a provisional teaching. Why? Because you cannot forget the self, the three marks remain vividly present; how can the retribution for past deeds ever end?

When the Buddha in the past rebuked a bhikṣu for eating horse barley, he now experiences it himself—is this not surely the fruition of past karma? As long as the notions of self and other have not been extinguished, how does this differ from that?
You have already instructed those below to clarify the admonitions; yet if one observes that the former thieving mind has not been eliminated, this is precisely...
This is the source of profit and loss; therefore, those who cultivate samādhi in my teaching must strictly observe this as a warning.
They must certainly sever the taking of what is not given. This is the third clear instruction of purity, a definitive teaching of the Buddha.
Therefore, Ānanda, if one does not sever theft [and so forth]... if it is not spoken thus, it is the speech of Pāpīyān.

For this reason, the following provides a further analogy regarding gain and loss. Now, that which is without self, without person, and without sentient beings is precisely the untainted, wondrously pure, and luminous mind.
To perceive this untainted, wondrously pure, and luminous mind must necessarily be attained within meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
How could one seek it with a thieving mind? Even if one were to obtain it by means of a thieving mind, it would be like pouring water into a leaking cup;
even after hundreds of thousands of kalpas, it would never be filled. If one seeks wondrous purity with a leaking mind, even if a wondrous awakening occurs, it cannot be sustained.
This is what is lost. If the bhikṣus fall below this, they commit a transgression.
Regarding the benefits achieved: that which is called "not storing even a fraction of what remains from one's robes and alms-bowl" is the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*).

That which is called "giving the remnants of one's begged food to hungry sentient beings" is the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*). That which is called "joining one’s palms and paying homage to the assembly in a great gathering" is the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
That which is called "regarding those who strike or revile one as being the same as those who offer praise" is the perfection of... [vīrya-pāramitā].
The perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*). To renounce both body and mind and share them with sentient beings is the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*).
Not to mislead beginners with teachings of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*) is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*).

These six perfections above, when contrasted with the three previous faults, are transformed into three benefits. Why is this? The former [faults] were merely feigning the robes of a Buddha to deceive and trade upon the Tathāgata.

Now, though he does not store even a fraction [of provisions], he is further able to beg and give to other assemblies. Previously, this was not the practice of one possessing full precepts for the sake of the Small Vehicle path;
now, though he joins his palms and bows to the assembly, he is further able to strike and revile others while treating it as equal to praise.

Previously, he was hidden away in deceit, falsely claiming to be a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). Now, having surrendered both body and mind, he is further able to reveal the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) to beginners.
A bhikṣu who thus forgets his own person for the sake of others truly attains *samādhi*. This is what has been attained.
As before, the concluding intent of my [commentary] below is as previously stated. △ Fourth, the precept against false speech.
Ānanda, thus [the teaching for] the sentient beings of the six realms in this world... [up to] the fourth definitive, pure, and clear instruction.
Ānanda, below this, [the text] distinguishes between the heterodox and the orthodox. If one commits killing, stealing, or sexual misconduct, these are still worldly karmas;
though they are grave, they are still forgivable. However, if it is false speech, it not only deludes and misleads oneself, but also deludes and misleads immeasurable multitudes.
[This] gives rise to [the severing of] roots of goodness forever; one must not fail to observe the precepts. Therefore, we now set forth that false speech has four faults:
first, one cannot attain samādhi while practicing dhyāna; second, the mind-ground does not become pure; third, one falls under the influence of the demons of craving and views;
fourth, one loses the lineage of the Tathāgata. This is what is meant by the detailed explanation below: it refers to falsely claiming to have attained what one has not actually attained. Truly...

Having not yet attained realization, to falsely claim "I have realized" is for this mind to harbor a calculation of self; this is the mark of the self (*ātman*). Therefore, one practices meditation but does not enter samādhi.
Furthermore, to falsely claim "I have attained my realization," being the most honored and supreme in the world, the foremost in the world, is for this mind to harbor attachment;
this is the mark of the person (*pudgala*). Therefore, the ground of the mind cannot attain purity. Moreover...

To falsely claim to others, "I have attained the fruit of a Srotāpanna, the fruit of a Sakṛdāgāmin, up to the ten stages, or the stage of a Bodhisattva prior to the stages"—this is the demon of views (*dṛṣṭi-māra*).
Furthermore, to seek people's prostrations and repentance, coveting their offerings—this is the demon of craving (*tṛṣṇā-māra*).
Such a mind that harbors desires is the mark of a sentient being (*sattva-nimitta*); therefore, one falls into the demons of craving and views. This person...
Thus, those who falsely claim attainment, speak falsely, and delusively exalt themselves as supreme and foremost give rise to great *asmimāna* (the conceit "I am").
This is one form of madness; such a person is like a *kṣatriya* who has killed a Buddha. It is comparable to cutting down a *tāla* tree with a blade: there is no possibility of its ever reviving.
Therefore, one loses the lineage of the Tathāgata. False speech has these four losses, which forever extinguish the roots of goodness and cause one to sink into the three miserable realms;
this is what constitutes "perversity" (*icchantika*). This term means "one who severs the roots of goodness," a transgression equivalent to a *pārājika* offense.

The passage "After my parinirvāṇa" clarifies his dispatching of emanations. The section beginning with "He instructs the various bodhisattvas" indicates the fundamental [nature], while the section beginning with "Or he manifests as... indicates the traces [of his activity].
Regarding what is called the "fundamental" (ben): the fundamental has fixed affiliations. First, it belongs to Mahāyāna bodhisattvas; second, to the arhats of the two vehicles.
These two can be manifested through transformation (nirmāṇa), whereas others cannot. Regarding what is called the "trace" (ji): the trace has no fixed affiliations.

Whether they be śramaṇas, laypeople, kings, officials, or even those who are deceitful thieves, butchers, or merchants—whenever there is an occasion for a karmic response, there is no one to whom he does not manifest his body.
This is what is meant by "gathering through common purpose" (*samānārthatā*) among the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*).

Thus, one knows that all Great Beings who are true emanation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) bear secret mandates. Having received such a secret mandate, how could they allow it to be exposed or publicized, thereby causing delusion and confusion?

World-Honored One. Except for such instances as the final testament left to disciples to signify that the life of wisdom is not severed, he likewise did not say, "I am a bodhisattva" or "I am an arhat," lest he reveal the Buddha’s secret causes. What are these two phrases?
This refers back to those previously mentioned who, having not attained realization, claim to have attained it; they delude sentient beings and are decidedly and utterly heterodox.
By contrast, those who secretly assist and provide covert support are considered orthodox. The following section clarifies the instructions and admonitions:
since the harm of false speech is of great consequence, I teach that those practicing *samādhi* must strictly observe the precept against lying and eliminate all falsehood.
This is the definitive Dharma of the Buddha; it is the fourth pure and clear instruction.
Therefore, Ānanda, if [one] does not sever this... if it is not spoken thus, then it is the speech of Pāpīyan.

Therefore, the following section uses a metaphor to illustrate gain and loss. That the Tathāgatas of the ten directions share one and the same path is precisely what constitutes the direct mind (*ṛjukacitta*).
To realize this direct mind, one must necessarily attain it within meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*); how could it be sought through deception or falsehood?
If one seeks meditative concentration through deception and falsehood, it is like carving human excrement into the shape of sandalwood; it only serves to increase its foul stench.
In the end, there will be no fragrance. To seek *samādhi* through deception and falsehood results only in emptiness and delusion; ultimately, no benefit will be gained.
In my teaching, I urge the elimination of the deluded mind even during the four modes of deportment—walking, standing, sitting, and lying down—which are the ordinary activities of daily life.
If even these ordinary activities should not be false or artificial, how much more so when claiming the fruits of the four stages (*catur-phala*) or the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*)?

This is the dharma of the superior person (*uttamapudgala*). If one were to falsely claim the dharmas of the superior person, such as the four fruits or the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), it would be like a destitute man falsely styling himself an emperor;
his crime would surely lead to execution and annihilation. If one deceives and falsely usurps the position of the Dharma King, the retribution will not stop at mere execution and annihilation;
one will fall into the bottomless abyss. Why is this? Because the ground is not true, the response...

The result will naturally be circuitous. For now, let us not discuss its causes and effects; rather, if one seeks the fruit of bodhi based solely upon a crooked and circuitous mind, can it ever be attained?
It would be like a person trying to bite their own navel—it will certainly not succeed.
Therefore, those below are exhorted to practice a straightforward mind; thus, those who cultivate samādhi should simply eliminate the delusions of beginningless time.
If there are no false or evil thoughts, then there are no demonic activities. At all times, let [the mind] rest in a state of ease;

wherever it encounters anything, it is immediately employed, and as soon as it is employed, it is finished. This is precisely the straightforward mind. The Patriarch said: "It is only valued for its emptiness and leisure, yet it does not obscure its functioning.
This is the accomplishment of the Bodhisattva’s unsurpassed awakening. As for the phrase "As I... below, the concluding intent is as previously stated.
