△ Fifth, a summary of the general meaning. Question: Has Ānanda’s body and mind still not yet been purified upon reaching this point? Or is it that his realization has not yet reached its ultimate depth?
Answer: There are two reasons for this. First, what Ānanda has realized belongs to the gate of understanding (*jiewén*), not the gate of practice (*xíngmén*).
Because it is the gateway, awakening to the principle of equality is the *dharmakāya* in its primordial state, as it lacks the adornment of merit.
Second, Ānanda transmits and maintains the substance of the teaching because he must thoroughly exhaust the source of the Dharma.

For example, although Ānanda was born at the same time as the Buddha and inherited the Buddha’s sacred power to reveal, awaken, and lead others, had there been no such model for future generations, how could those who study and practice be instructed?

From what point does one enter the Way? Therefore, following the exposition on perfect penetration (*yuantong*), the three trainings of the outflows-free (*anāsrava*) are presented once more to complete the essence of the teaching.
How could this be because Ānanda’s body and mind were not yet pure, or his realization not yet thorough?

This is not so. Nowadays, when people have achieved even a slight degree of awakening, they immediately cast aside the precepts and openly consume alcohol and meat, indulge in sexual desire, and claim that nothing hinders them.
This is actually the dharma of celestial demons and external paths, not the Buddha-dharma.
They do not realize that after awakening, one must observe the precepts with even greater rigor—not only to encourage oneself, but also to inspire others. What is more...
This refers to purifying Buddha-lands in every place and bringing sentient beings to maturity.
Therefore, before the concentration and wisdom were explained, the four grave prohibitions were first presented as a model for later students entering the Path.
First, the exhortation to uphold the precepts.
"Ānanda, regarding your question on 'gathering the mind' up to 'how do all demonic activities arise':
Ānanda, the following section exhorts the maintenance of the precepts. Your phrase 'gathering the mind' restates the previous request by Ānanda, saying:
'Desiring to gather the mind and enter samādhi, how may one establish the site of practice (bodhimaṇḍa) so as to remain far removed from all demonic activities?'"
One attains an irreversible resolve regarding the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*). The Buddha answered me that within my *vinaya*, he proclaimed the practice of the three definitive principles:
namely, to take the gathering of the mind as the precept (*śīla*); from the precept arises concentration (*samādhi*), and from concentration issues forth wisdom (*prajñā*).
Thus, one knows that concentration and wisdom arise from the precepts. Therefore, he first taught the four grave prohibitions (*catur-uttara-saṃvara*) as the foundation. This is the root.

Since [the root] does not arise, the branches and leaves naturally do not exist. "Branches and leaves" refers to the other precepts. Among the three actions of the body and four of the speech, the coarse ones are cited as being weighty;
among form, sound, smell, taste, and touch, the subtle ones are cited as being minor. These constitute the characteristics of the other precepts.
In short, whether light or heavy, great or small, there shall be no transgression; naturally, the mind-ground will become pure and one will enter samādhi.
△ Second, the exhortation to uphold the mantra:
"If there are past habitual tendencies that cannot be extinguished... (up to) "...the heart-mantra spoken while seated upon the precious lotus flower."

Having extensively demonstrated the methods of precepts above to restrain present karma, [the text] now exhorts the recitation of mantras out of concern that heavy obstacles from past habits might prevent one from entering the Path;
therefore, it recommends the recitation of the *Pañcarakṣā* mantra. In Sanskrit, it is called *Svasty-astu-pañcarakṣā*;
here, it is translated as "White Parasol" (*Bai Sangai*), a name derived from the functional power of this divine spell. Why?
Know this: the parasol is the emblem of the majesty of kings, lords, and nobles; it is the banner of the valor and strength of great generals.
By means of this, one subdues them, and petty people naturally withdraw and hide; the demonic armies naturally submit and are brought under control.
This divine mantra was spoken by the Buddha of the Unconditioned Mind; it is the Dharma of the Unseen Uṣṇīṣa. By reciting this, one’s past habitual tendencies [are purified].

They will naturally be extinguished, and the obstacles of retribution will naturally not arise. Furthermore, the mantra is the name of a king of ghosts and is also a designation for a secret injunction.
When reciting this mantra, one attains the secret of the body, the secret of the speech, and the secret of the mind.
The whole is concentration itself. Apart from this, I do not believe there is any separate dharma of concentration.
△ Third, citing examples as proof:
Furthermore, when you were in a former life with Mātaṅgī... [up to] ...what difficulty could there be in raising [a sail] with a following wind?
Furthermore, you have cited the case of Āṅgulimāla as proof: his attachment to Aṅgulī was a result of past habituation, and his birth as a bandit was a karmic obstacle.
Yet, upon hearing a single divine mantra, his past obstacles were eliminated, he attained the stage of No-More-Learning (aśaikṣa), and realized the fruit of the path—how easy this was!
How much more so for a Śrāvaka who has severed their habits; if they rely on this [mantra] for recitation and maintenance, it is like scattering dust in a favorable wind. Thus one enters [the path].
What difficulty is there in the Way? △ Fourth, showing the method of practice:
"If there are those in the final age who wish to sit at the site of enlightenment... [until]... they shall emit a light of great compassion to come and anoint their crowns."
If there are those who display the methods of practice below, their observance of precepts and cultivation of concentration are not merely empty matters;
they must necessarily possess the method to grasp its true essence. What is meant by "method"? It is like a straight form casting a straight shadow: when the teacher is stern, the Way is honored.
Therefore, prior to undertaking the rite, one selects a pure and great śramaṇa as a teacher. If there is no teacher, that which is studied will surely [fail].
It is not accomplished. Why? Before the time of King Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja, it was permissible to be without a teacher;
after the time of King Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja, it is not permissible to be without a teacher. Observing this, one must take the Dharma of a teacher as the standard.

Once the teacher has attained that Dharma, he then dwells in seclusion and recites the mantra one hundred and eight times. "Dwelling in seclusion" means the subduing of body and mind. [He] recites one hundred...
The "eight cycles" refer to the extinguishing of the one hundred and eight afflictions (*kleśa*). Once the afflictions have been extinguished, body and mind are restored to purity;

thus, one becomes a worthy vessel. For this reason, the site of practice (*bodhimaṇḍa*) is used as a symbol. However, the site of practice is not for the sake of aesthetic beauty, nor is it intended to please the ear.

It is surely so that one may take the objective realm as a condition to arouse the aspiration for enlightenment (*cittotpāda*), and take that aspiration as a condition to seek awakening. Therefore, I request your presence.
To abide in the empowerment conferred by the Tathāgatas of the ten directions is precisely the meaning of the mutual resonance between the path and its response.
△ Fifth, explaining the resonance and response:
"Ānanda, such pure bhikṣus in the final age... [until]... he will stroke their heads in consolation, causing them to attain awakening."
Below, concerning Ānanda: this clarifies the response of resonance. Upholding the Buddha’s pure precepts constitutes the study of morality (*śīla*).

Formulating the bodhisattva vow within the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) constitutes the study of concentration (*samādhi*). Practicing the path through the six periods of the day without sleep constitutes the study of wisdom (*prajñā*).
These three studies may be practiced and maintained by all four assemblies; their fruit is the attainment of the stage where the mind and its essence are darkly unified.
"I myself manifest my body to stroke [your] head. What is meant by "stroking the head"? To study the Way, one must attain wondrous enlightenment.
If one attains wondrous enlightenment, that is precisely the Buddha stroking one's head. Why? Because awakening is non-dual with awakening. What is meant by "manifesting the body"?
Once one possesses wondrous awakening, it is essential to see through to one's own self. To see one's own self is precisely for the Buddha to manifest his body.
Why? Because the essence is not a dual essence. Furthermore, as for the Tathāgatas of the ten directions who previously emitted light to perform the consecration:
This is precisely initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*). Because initial awakening arises from conditions, it is said that the Tathāgatas of the ten directions confer empowerment (*abhiṣeka*).
When the Buddha now manifests his own body to touch the crown of one's head, this is because fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*) has nothing upon which to depend;
therefore, it is said that "I myself manifest my own body."

The preceding discussion on the characteristics of the precepts, which included exhortations to practice divine mantras and the request for the Buddha’s empowerment, was intended for this very purpose.
Now, the delusions and karma of sentient beings vary in depth, and their retributions vary in severity.

For those whose afflictions are shallow, the delusions of views, thoughts, and ignorance arise when the six sense organs encounter their objects; these are the entanglements that bind one within the realms of existence, as previously described.
This refers to karma. Present karma is light and easy to escape from; it is simply by upholding the precepts that the mind naturally comes to rest.

As for the "deep" [karma], this refers to the dust-like and river-sand-like afflictions of ignorance contained within the eight consciousnesses, which are entangled beyond the realms—namely, what is called the obstacle of retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*).
The obstacle of retribution is heavy and difficult to escape; it must rely on the power of the Buddha and the power of divine mantras to be permeated and only then exhausted. Upon reaching...

Regarding that which is most extremely subtle and profound: it is the innate ignorance (*sahaja-avidyā*) that clings to the very essence of awakened clarity, enveloped within the realm beyond [the senses].
This is what is known as the fundamental afflictive obstruction (*kleśa-āvaraṇa*). This fundamental delusion is further subtle and difficult to eliminate;

throughout the stages of progressive cultivation, one severs one grade of ignorance and realizes one portion of *tathatā* (suchness), continuing in this manner until the stage of Sublime Enlightenment (*suvi-bodhi*) on the Vajra Path.

When the state is entirely True Suchness (tathatā), ignorance finally comes to an end. Therefore, the three untainted trainings (trīṇi śikṣāṇi) are taught to correctly eliminate the three obstructions and the three delusions;
this constitutes the primary expedient means, the three kinds of definitive dharmas. Regarding the training in ethical discipline (śīla-śikṣā), it has been fully detailed above;

as for the training in concentration (samādhi-śikṣā) and wisdom (prajñā-śikṣā), they shall now be explained in detail. II. The Training in Concentration (Samādhi-śikṣā). This section has two parts: 1. The Proclamation.
The Ritual of the Mandala. Second, the proclamation of the divine mantras. First, the presentation of the ritual of the mandala, which has four parts:

first, receiving the clarification of the mandala ritual; second, the formal presentation of the mandala ritual; third, the presentation of the practice; fourth, clarifying gain and loss. First, receiving the clarification of the mandala ritual.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One... [omitted] ...this accords with the pure regulations of the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
Following the previous instruction on the training in the precepts (*śīla-śikṣā*), he now exhorted the establishment of boundaries (*sīmā*) and the construction of a *bodhimaṇḍa*.
Now, a *bodhimaṇḍa* is the place where the practitioner treads; a boundary is the objective sphere upon which the practitioner focuses. As for these spheres, there are ten."
Yet their underlying principle is one. Now I ask: how can the one encompass the ten? How can the ten encompass the one?
If the one encompasses the ten, that is the Samādhi of One Characteristic; if the ten encompass the one, that is the Samādhi of One Practice.
Ānanda has already awakened to the Dharma-gate of attaining Buddhahood and already knows how to cultivate it.
Having realized the path of no-more-learning, [I ask] only for the sake of providing a skillful means for practice in the final age. By what dharma should this be done?
Therefore, I seek clarification from the World-Honored One. II. Correctly Demonstrating the Ritual of the Altar. 1. Smearing the Ground.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "If people in the final age [up to] grind the earth into mud to smear upon the site, the site and its surface represent the Dharma.
For now, I shall rely on the interpretations found in various traditions; I shall not discuss them further. I will simply take the meaning of the title of this sutra to explain it.
Essentially, the mind is originally without form (*lakṣaṇa*); form must manifest through color. Now, taking the white ox of the Snowy Mountains, [I shall] blend..."
As for sandalwood, is it not of a single color? Is it not of a single characteristic?

To take a single color as its characteristic—wherein the characteristic is non-characteristic and non-characteristic is the characteristic—this is what is called "mystery. Indeed, phenomena have no inherent cause;
a cause must be manifested through awakening. Now, taking the grass from a cow’s mouth to spread upon the ground—is this not a single cause? Is it one?
Is it awakening? To take a single cause as awakening—awakening that which is not awakening, and taking non-awakening as awakening—this is what is meant by "cause.
Speaking from this perspective, to take the signless as a sign, and for that sign to be signless, is therefore called "suchness" (tathatā).
Taking what is not a cause as a cause, and because that cause is itself no-cause, it is called "coming.

Those who merely come but cannot accord with suchness (tathatā), and cannot come in accordance with suchness, are ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). Those who can come while in accordance with suchness, and can accord with suchness while coming, are Buddhas.
Therefore, this is used for the secret cause, cultivation, and realization of the Tathāgata. Generally speaking, this cause is too sublime for a beginner.
Among those who have divided [the land], there is certainly no one capable of performing [the ritual]. Although there is no one capable of performing it, one must nevertheless study by means of this;
therefore, one takes the dung of the white ox from the Snowy Mountains to smear upon the ground. As for those who are incapable of doing even that:
One should keep [the vessel] five chi above the ground and mix it with the ten fragrances; this may also be understood as the practice of walking.
What is meant by "five chi above the ground"? It is the removal of the five turbidities. What is meant by "mixing with the ten fragrances"? It is the ten pāramitās.
Furthermore, taking the yellow earth signifies self-awakening; applying it to the site of the field signifies awakening others. By means of oneself...
Awakening oneself and awakening others—being able to practice these ten deeds is precisely what constitutes the myriad practices (*sahasra-caryā*) of this Bodhisattva.
Therefore, yellow earth is specifically selected and mixed with the ten fragrances to smear upon the ground. △ Second, showing the shape of the altar.
A square and round altar, sixteen feet in circumference, is made with eight corners (up to: flowers and leaves are placed in the water as available).

Since the ground was previously smeared [with cow dung], it is now further prepared as an altar. The altar must be constructed by raising the earth, just as a practitioner, through the merit of the Buddha, gives rise to a mind of faith and joy;
they have faith and joy in the inconceivable [powers] of the Tathāgata. They believe...
Because one delights in the adornment of the myriad practices of all bodhisattvas, the maṇḍala is used to symbolize this.
That it is sixteen feet square and octagonal is because the stage of awakening resembles a circle, while the stage of faith resembles a square;

furthermore, as in the *Lotus Sūtra*, there are two sides on each of the eight directions, thus forming sixteen feet. This is the shape and measurement of this maṇḍala. Once the shape and measurement are established, the stage of faith is already [perfected].
It is proclaimed: one should seek the wondrous Dharma. This wondrous Dharma is not separate from the attainment of Bodhi by the Tathāgatas of the ten directions;
it is the primary expedient method of wondrous *śamatha*, *samāpatti*, and *dhyāna*. Therefore, it is symbolized by four materials—gold, silver, copper, and wood.
Gold and silver possess the significance of firmness and clarity, symbolizing the methods of wondrous stilling (*śamatha*) and wondrous contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
Furthermore, copper possesses the significance of universal penetration, representing the dharma of the perfect penetration of *dhyāna*.
Wood possesses the significance of the beginning and end of flowers and fruit, representing the dharma of the initial skillful means.

The bowl is a vessel that accords with measure, representing the various capacities and the various measures possessed by those of the Three Vehicles. As for its containing the dew from the eighth month:
The eighth month is the midpoint of heaven and earth and the rectitude of yin and yang. One nourishes [the mind] with the water of meditative concentration and wisdom to cool the heart.
As for placing flowers and leaves therein, it is like the lotus, which carries the meaning of both budding and blooming;
thus, floating flowers and leaves upon the water precisely symbolize that within one's nature there is the flower of awakening as a latent cause.
△ Third, the demonstration of the method of offering.
Take eight circular mirrors and place each in its respective direction... (until) to present them to the Buddhas and the great Bodhisattvas.
Sentient beings do not awaken; therefore, they are universally deluded. When Bodhisattvas practice, they ought to realize this through awakening; therefore, they are suspended.
The mirrors at the eight corners symbolize his wisdom and awakening. Furthermore, flowers manifest color, while incense clarifies touch;
these represent the delusions of sentient beings. Now it is not so: he does not allow them to see the fire, for he has brought his mind to rest and no longer clings to objects.
Cow’s milk, fried cakes, sugar, ghee, and honey represent the cravings of sentient beings; now it is not so.
Nevertheless, by individually honoring each of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, one returns from delusion to the truth. The above demonstrates the method of *śamatha*.
Furthermore, as each of the six sense organs encounters its respective object, each is accompanied by wisdom; thus, the eight directions multiplied by the [four] numbers result in sixteen.

This is because the mirror represents wisdom (*jñāna*) and the flowers represent awakening (*bodhi*). These sixteen in the eight directions likewise symbolize the pervasiveness of wisdom and awakening.
This is the image of *che* (pervasion).
Whenever at mealtime or even in the middle of the night, [the ritual implements] are spread out by the side of the door, arranged on both the left and right.
Now, to draw analogies from distant objects and from one's own person—this is an excellent illustration. Thus, at the time of eating...
The blending represents the True Dharma (*saddharma*). Washing the charcoal with water represents non-attachment. Casting ghee into the blazing fire represents the absence of relish.
Since there is neither relish nor attachment, what else could this be but the True Dharma? This is what is called an excellent analogy.
Furthermore, by observing the body through the Dharma, the sense faculties (*indriya*) do not arise of themselves. By observing objects (*viṣaya*) through the Dharma, the realms are without arising.
Non-arising and non-birth—what are they if not right contemplation? This is what is meant by "taking what is near from one's own body.
Furthermore, banners and flowers are suspended everywhere within the altar, and images are displayed upon the four walls;

this is what is meant by "taking what is distant from external objects. If one takes what is distant from external objects, then those objects are not merely themselves; there is nothing that is not the holy and the true. If...
Beholding the holy truth, there is nothing that is not the single awakening. Since it is one and the same awakening, what further matter could there be?
This is what is called an excellent analogy. The above has set forth the dharma of samāpatti; as for the separate placement of the small fire-hearth, [it follows].
This is to manifest the natural state (*dharmatā*) of phenomena. Furthermore, the phrase "all the images of the Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions" serves as the general heading.
Below this, one should list the specific names individually, as in the text, facing forward.
Furthermore, take eight mirrors and suspend them inverted in the void [until] their forms and shadows interpenetrate one another in successive layers.
As for taking the eight mirrors previously to surround the flower-bowl, this represents the dharmas of śamatha-vipaśyanā and samādhi-prajñā. How is this clarified?
Because there is a bowl within the flowers, and leaves within the bowl; now, the eight mirrors are taken to face the inner bowl.
This signifies the dharma of perfect penetration and non-obstruction. How is this clarified? Because the light of the mirrors within and without mutually reflects and encompasses one another.
Furthermore, the flower-bowl represents the capacities of sentient beings, while the circular mirror represents the wisdom of all Buddhas.

There is no capacity of a sentient being that does not manifest through the wisdom of the Buddhas, and there is no wisdom of the Buddhas that does not [manifest through] the capacity of sentient beings.
This is concluded. Therefore, it is illustrated by means of mirrors suspended inside and out. Furthermore, this manifests the inexhaustible nature of the multilayered (chong-chong) interpenetration.
For example, if one mirror contains one flower-bowl, then eight mirrors each likewise contain one flower-bowl.
Not only do the eight mirrors each contain a flower-bowl, but within each single mirror there are eight mirrors, each containing one flower-bowl. Within that single mirror, there are eight...
Each mirror also encompasses eight mirrors, each with a single flower-bowl. As it is for one mirror, so it is for the eight mirrors in a succession that is inexhaustible;

as it is for the inner mirrors, so it is for the outer mirrors—what is called a succession that is inexhaustible, and an inexhaustibility that is successive. This is the inconceivable realm, free from obstruction.

This is the natural law of wisdom (*prajñā*). When one fully grasps the principle through a specific instance and fully realizes the function through its essence, the practitioner who understands this immediately realizes the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*).
The above has set forth the method of *dhyāna*; therefore, the mirror in which one rests is taken up so that its surfaces face one another.
During the first seven days, one should perform prostrations with utmost sincerity until the body and mind become as clear and pure as lapis lazuli.

Each of the three periods of seven days has its own specific purpose. During the first seven days, one prostrates to the Buddha and recites mantras. Prostrating to the Buddha shows reverence for that which abides [the Buddha-nature];
reciting mantras obstructs the manifestation of karmic actions. This represents the method of the training in morality (*śīla-śikṣā*), severing present obstacles.
During the second seven-day period, one should single-mindedly make vows. Being single-minded means being free from distracting conditions; making vows means having a fixed direction.

This represents the dharma of the training in concentration (*samādhi*), which severs the obstacle of karmic retribution. During the third seven-day period, one should exclusively and single-mindedly maintain the divine mantra.
If one proceeds single-mindedly, one may ascend through the stages; if one maintains [the practice] with exclusive devotion, the response of the enlightened ones will be swift.
This represents the method for the study of wisdom (*prajñā-śikṣā*), which severs the hindrance of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*). This serves as a general indication of the initial preparatory method;

therefore, it is demonstrated by means of prostrating to the Buddha, making vows, and reciting mantras. The above, together with the preceding four sections, constitutes the ritual procedure for entering the maṇḍala. This indicates...
For future generations, I cause practitioners to cultivate according to the Dharma so that their body and mind will surely become as pure as lapis lazuli;
only then can Bodhi be hoped for, and demonic activities will not arise. △ Fourth, clarifying gain and loss.
Ānanda, if this bhikṣu’s original preceptor (up to: you ask how the site of enlightenment was established, it was thus:

the ritual for the altar necessarily requires ten people, which symbolizes that those awakened in the ten directions are one and the same. Furthermore, as for appointing a single person as the teacher:
This indicates that wisdom and awakening serve as the standard. Furthermore, ten people take one person as their benchmark, and one person takes ten people as their target.
If one misses the target, then even with a masterful craftsman, there is no way to apply his technique.
If one misses the benchmark, then even with skillful learning, there is no way to manifest one's wisdom. Therefore, if there is even one who is not pure—
"Purity. Such a site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) is often not accomplished. Question: "If one person is impure, there are nine others;
why is it that so many do not achieve success? Answer: "This is a dharma of mutual pervasion and mutual inclusion.
If it is lost in one place, it is likewise lost in all other places. It is comparable to a mirror and a bowl: if one mirror is missing, the other bowls are also lost. Therefore..."
It is said: "If such a site for the Way (bodhimaṇḍa) does not lead to much accomplishment, this constitutes what is lost.

If, however, the master obtains the necessary resources and the resources obtain the Dharma without any deficiency, then the holy fruit may naturally be expected; there will be progress and benefit in the study of the Way.
This constitutes what is gained."
*Srotāpanna* means "entering the stream," which refers to entering the stream of the sages.

What is meant here by "entering the stream" is not entering the stream of the minor sages of the *Āgama* [teachings], but rather participating in the stream of the Great Sages of the Vaipulya [Mahāyāna] teachings.
One who enters the stream of the Great Sages of the Vaipulya will certainly know for themselves that they shall attain Buddhahood. 2. Proclaiming the Spiritual Powers.
Fifth: Requesting the Teaching.
Ānanda prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and addressed the Buddha, saying: [omitted] "...I await the hearing of the Tathāgata’s secret verses.
Previously, Ānanda was encountered by Ḍombī, who employed the malevolent arts of Brahmā; he was mistakenly led into a chamber of lust. The Buddha then commanded him...
"Mañjuśrī, by secretly reciting divine mantras, he was protected in secret and thus attained liberation. However, he had not yet personally heard the explicit teaching.
Thereupon, he again entreated the World-Honored One (as detailed in the text). △ Second, the Buddha manifests supernatural transformations.
At that time, the World-Honored One emitted light from his *uṣṇīṣa* (fleshly protuberance), and the Tathāgata Ruciraketu proclaimed this divine mantra.
As for the *uṣṇīṣa*, it is the Buddha’s mark of the invisible crown of the head. That sentient beings are able to see it is merely due to their cognitive consciousness (*vijñāna*).
The Buddha is devoid of such consciousness; therefore, there is nothing to be seen. Because he sees by means of non-seeing, [the mark] is thus relied upon.
The *uṣṇīṣa*. The *uṣṇīṣa* is precisely seeing. This seeing is non-seeing; is this not the light of the mind? Therefore it is said:
"From within the *uṣṇīṣa*, a hundred jewel-lights surge forth. When there is light in the ground of the mind, there is form.
Where there is form, there is perception. Therefore it is said: "Within the light, a thousand-petaled jeweled lotus surges forth, and from it, a manifested Tathāgata appears."
Sitting amidst jeweled flowers—these thousand-petaled jeweled flowers—are they not the marks of non-mind? There is an emanated Tathāgata—is this not the awakening of non-mind?
Since awakening is termed "emanation," such emanation is unobstructed. Since emanation is unobstructed, it does not hinder further emanations.
That these emanations manifest the light of a hundred jewels and ten *gaṅgā* rivers of sands is the wondrous function of the mind.
To manifest the form of Vajrapāṇi, the Secret Lord, and to manifest the majestic power of one who upholds a mountain and wields a vajra—this is the wondrous power of the mind.
Possessing such power and possessing such function, there must surely be that which is called its cause.
Are those divine mantras not the secret sounds emanated by the inconceivable power of this mind? Because the great assembly cannot fathom or deliberate upon them, they give rise to [doubt].
I revere and love you. △ Third, the actual recitation of the divine mantra:
*Namo satvatha sugatāya* (through to) *hūṃ huṃ dhu ruṃ phaṭ svāhā*. Regarding the five reasons why ancient translators did not translate the words of this mantra:
first, they are the secret language of the Buddhas; only a Buddha and a Buddha [can fully understand them].
It can be known [only by the Buddha], for no one else is able to know it. Second, it is a *dhāraṇī*, because it contains manifold meanings within a single term.
Third, it is the name of a king of ghosts, invoked so that he may provide protection. Fourth, it is a seal of the Buddhas, as it is transmitted from Buddha to Buddha.
Fifth, it is inconceivable, as it is not within the realm of the mind or consciousness. Because these five reasons exist, it is not translated. The rest...
It is said that it is most excellent not to translate it; even if one were to translate it, there would be nothing to say. Why?
This is the Buddha’s intentional terminology (*saṃdhāyabhāṣita*), an inconceivable (*acintya*) dharma. Since it is called the Buddha’s intentional terminology, it is not something known by others;
how, then, could it be translated? Since it is called inconceivable, it cannot be fathomed by the conscious mind (*manovijñāna*); furthermore, how could it be translated? Therefore, it is said:

It is indeed very good not to translate [the term]. Nevertheless, it is not that the Buddha’s words are cryptic; rather, sentient beings fail to understand him in every encounter and thus claim that the Buddha’s words are cryptic.
Furthermore, the Buddha is not one who lacks thought; the Buddha is one of profound intellect and deep talent, a king among literary masters—how could he be said to lack thought?
It is simply that what sentient beings think about consists of the phenomena of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), and they are unable to transcend these five aggregates.

"Thought" means that the Buddha is beyond thought. In general, the Buddha employs the Dharma that transcends worldly emotions to deliver sentient beings from the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) of the world, causing them to leave all suffering behind and attain liberation.
Through his words of truth, the Buddha delivers sentient beings from what they know, enabling them to realize non-arising (*anutpāda*) and witness nirvāṇa.
For this reason, the Buddha causes people to recite this mantra. If a person recites this mantra...
The entire body is the Great Samādhi of the Śūraṅgama. How is this known?
If the mind conceives thoughts without clinging to mental consciousness, this is the secret of the mind. If the mouth recites without being bound by speech, this is the secret of the mouth.
To act through the body without giving rise to the view of a self-body is itself the secret of the body. Each of the three wheels is a secret and inconceivable;

is this not what is meant by the Great Samādhi of Śūraṅgama? Thus we know that when the Buddha causes people to recite this mantra, he is precisely demonstrating to them the method for practicing samādhi. This must be understood.
Furthermore, this heart-mantra is identical to the mind of quiescent extinction realized by Avalokiteśvara. Avalokiteśvara said:

"When birth and death have ceased, the state of quiescent extinction manifests before one. Suddenly transcending both the mundane and supramundane worlds, one attains universal clarity throughout the ten directions and achieves two kinds of excellence.
The first is that it harmonizes upward with the fundamentally wondrous enlightened mind of all Buddhas of the ten directions, becoming one with the Tathāgatas."

First, one shares the same power of compassion. Second, one merges downward with all sentient beings of the six realms throughout the ten directions, sharing the same sorrow and longing as all those beings.
Now, if you uphold and recite this divine mantra and attain this secret dharma-gate, it is identical to the mind of quiescent extinction (*nirvāṇa*).
Having attained the mind of quiescent extinction, two kinds of benefit arise: first, one gives birth to all Buddhas; [the second is that] one gives birth to all sentient beings.
Benefit. Second, there is the benefit for sentient beings. Because these two benefits exist, one is exhorted to practice this divine mantra.
△ Fourth, the narration of the two kinds of benefits of the divine mantra, in four parts. First, describing the benefit of Perfect Enlightenment.
Ānanda, it is impossible for [the Buddha’s] crown-light mass (to) distance itself from all demonic activities; such a thing cannot exist.
These eleven kinds [of mantras] provide benefit to all Buddhas. *Siddhārthapratāra* is the general designation for the meaning of the mantra;
its interpretation is as seen above. As for what is called the "mantra-heart" (*dhāraṇī-hṛdaya*), it does not mean that the mantra possesses this...
It is the mind; it is the mantra held by the practitioner, which is the mantra of the mind.
Yet this mantra-mind does not arise dependent upon the sense organs or their objects, nor does it fall into the two extremes of emptiness or existence.

Simply by single-mindedly upholding this divine mantra, one attains the mind of quiescent extinction; it is the mind of the Great Samādhi of the Śūraṅgama. All Buddhas of the ten directions [rely] upon this...
He was born; by this he attained unexcelled enlightenment; by this he subdued Māra and turned the wheel of the Dharma; he rescued the multitude from suffering and delivered them from all calamities.

He is just as he is today, compassionately rescuing Ānanda and gathering in those with whom he has a karmic affinity, even until his final entry into Great Nirvāṇa, where he entrusts the Buddha-dharma and leaves behind his final instructions for the future. Throughout the beginning and end of his entire career, there is nothing that is not [for this purpose].
This is the essence of the mantra-heart. Thus one knows that this mind is inexhaustible; this mantra is also inexhaustible;

kalpas as numerous as motes of dust are inexhaustible, and the verses and phrases expounded therein are likewise inexhaustible. Furthermore, following the explanation of this mantra, [the text] demonstrates the faults of not upholding it.
Moreover, since this mantra is named the "Crown of the Tathāgata," and the Tathāgata has already transcended saṃsāra, [it is beyond all limits].

Even those who have realized the path of nirvana are still able to receive, uphold, and never forget [this mantra], let alone those in training who have not yet crossed over saṃsāra or reached the stage of a Tathāgata—how could they hope to realize the fruit without encountering demonic obstacles if they do not uphold this mantra?
This would surely be a failure. Question: What is meant by "receiving and upholding"? Answer: It means to take the mind and seal it with the mantra. Take...

The mantra-seal and the mind are what is meant by "receiving and upholding. Why is this? Because there are practitioners today who either cling to the mind as being empty and practice with an empty mind;
this is the teaching of Māra. Even if one were to apply this mind to the ordinary affairs of daily life, could it still remain empty?
If it cannot remain empty, then those who falsely claim to practice with an empty mind are not [practicing correctly].
Is this the teaching of Māra? Furthermore, some cling to the mind as being existent, practicing with the belief that the mind exists; this too is the teaching of Māra.
Even if this mind were to persist until the time of death, the time of fainting, or the time of deep sleep, would it still be found?
If there are those who, failing to attain [realization], falsely practice with a mind of grasping, is this not the teaching of Māra?
Observing this, the Buddha taught people to uphold this divine mantra in order to sever such demonic influence.

Furthermore, at the very moment of correct recitation, whether one speaks of attainment or speaks of emptiness, neither is applicable; at such a time, even the Buddha cannot perceive it, so how could Māra possibly invade it?
Why is this so? Because the mind enters into perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). To recite this divine mantra with a mind of perfect enlightenment is what is called "the mantra of the mind.
