If it can be written down, one should write it; carry it not merely on one's own person. Whatever can be carried, one should carry it.
Although this may not be recited, one still receives its benefits. Therefore, the fact that poison cannot cause harm is precisely the body receiving these benefits.
Ānanda, I shall now further reveal two additional benefits. Regarding the section beginning with "If, after my parinirvāṇa": this describes the benefits received through oral transmission.

If one is able to uphold and recite [this teaching] orally, or teach others to recite it, one will be freed from five kinds of fears—namely, those of water, fire, various forms of anger and venom, malevolent spirits and demons, and evil discursive thoughts.
Not only will these not cause harm, but they will all acknowledge one’s profound kindness, and one’s speech will become sweet.
"Exposure" refers to receiving benefit through the mouth. "Ānanda, you should know" and so forth describes receiving benefit through the mind.
Whether the mind is distracted or not settled in concentration, as long as one remembers with the mind and maintains it with the mouth, one will obtain the attendance of all spirits.

If this is so even when distracted, how much more so when the mind is focused and determined? Naturally, Bodhisattvas will bestow their grace, and the essence of the mind will give rise to consciousness. Moreover—
That once consciousness has been awakened and one never forgets for kalpas thereafter is precisely the mind receiving benefit.
The above constitutes the three benefits of being encouraged to uphold [the teaching]. II. Describing the Extensive Benefits.
From the first kalpa until the final body, even those who do not observe the precepts of fasting and discipline will naturally come to observe them.

From the first kalpa downward, one is not born in evil realms; the *yakṣas* and others belong to the realm of ghosts (*preta-gati*), while those with physical forms and so forth belong to other realms.
What is called the "first kalpa" refers to the initial stage when one first undertakes the mantra practice. As for the "final body":
This refers to the time when one attains the fruit through the recitation of mantras.
That from the initial cause until the attainment of the fruit, one does not fall into evil states throughout every successive birth, is due to the superior power of the mantra.

Furthermore, that through reading, reciting, copying, and making offerings [to this mantra], one is not born in places of suffering, also demonstrates the noble majesty of the mantra’s power. Below these various assemblies, the Buddha—

It bestows the benefit of merit. Suppose this person lacks personal merit; nevertheless, by virtue of the merit from upholding the mantra, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions are born together with them.
This is the blessing bestowed by the Buddhas. Furthermore, the analogy of being "born together" is like the *aśvattha* tree:
its seeds must always grow in threes, sharing a single stem. The cultivation through the practice of upholding the mantra is likewise similar to this fruit; it is not divided.
It is dispersed. Therefore, it descends to accomplish the benefit of wondrous conduct. The phrase "therefore"承接 (inherits) the meaning of the preceding text;
it refers back to the aforementioned point concerning wearing and holding [the mantra]. Because one wears and holds the divine mantra, one will not fall into evil realms in birth after birth.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that the Tathāgatas of the ten directions bestow [merit] upon one who does not personally perform meritorious deeds—this leads some to mistakenly claim that [the mantra] is effective through mere holding alone.
Regarding divine mantras: if one does not cultivate sublime conduct, it is because sublime conduct takes the six perfections as its primary basis.

Now, by briefly citing two or three of these to complete the set, one sees that sublime conduct is fundamentally complete. Furthermore, "breaking the precepts" and "lack of diligence" refer to the two groups of the ordained;
"impurity" and "not observing the fast-precepts" refer to the two groups of the laity. This has already been established.

To broaden the benefit for the multitude: by reciting mantras, one is born in a blissful realm; furthermore, the Buddha bestows blessings upon them, and they simultaneously accomplish sublime conduct.
This is precisely what is meant by broadly demonstrating the benefit for the multitude. △ Third, the elimination of their karmic offenses.
"Ānanda, when these sons of good family uphold this mantra... (until) before long they shall all attain the realization of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Ānanda, [the passage] below provides a general indication of heavy and light karmas. [The passage] beginning with 'Even if' separately opens up the category of light karmas.

Drinking alcohol, eating pungent foods, and wearing impure things are prohibitive offenses (*pratikṣepaṇa-śikṣāpada*); they are prohibited so that such acts do not arise. If one commits these, it constitutes intentional [transgression]."

[This is] a transgression. If one does not repent, one shall fall [into hell]. If one commits the lower [offenses], such as sexual misconduct, killing, stealing, and lying, these are specifically categorized as grave karmas.

These are natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*). If one violates these, they constitute extreme evil and do not admit of repentance; they are what are called "abandoned offenses" (*tyājya-āpatti*).
The above refers to present karma. "Ānanda, if there are sentient beings... and so forth refers to past karma. The Buddha’s intention regarding the mind is as follows:
If there is even the slightest doubt in one's mind, then it will not be in resonance with the essence of the mantra.

Therefore, it is said that for a practitioner, even if they have violated prohibitions—whether minor or major, whether from present actions or past karma—before holding the mantra, once they now hold the mantra, it is as if hot water douses snow, and everything is instantly extinguished. For the essence of the mantra is like...
The nature of the karma of *tāṇḍya* is like snow; delusion cannot withstand the Real, and therefore it dissolves and perishes. △ Fourth, according to their wishes:
Furthermore, Ānanda, if there are women... (up to) ...the lowliest strata of the borderlands, let alone those of mixed forms.
A mantra is a prayer of aspiration. Whatever a person seeks, if they maintain this divine mantra, there is no wish that is not fulfilled.
Whether it be for male or female progeny, physical life, vitality, or rebirth in a central land—all these are what people desire;

yet by merely reciting the divine mantra, there is nothing one does not obtain. Thus one perceives the greatness of the mantra’s power. △ Third, describing the benefits for the vessel-world (the physical environment).
Ānanda, whether it be kingdoms, prefectures, counties, or villages, [up to] no evil portents or calamities shall ever be able to enter.
The above described the benefit for the Perfectly Awakened One and for sentient beings; now we clarify the benefit for the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*).
The receptacle world is the environmental support (*niśraya-vipāka*) for sentient beings; this environmental support must be traced back to good and evil karma. If it is good, then the human mind...

If [the conduct] is neutral, it is responded to with blessings. If it is evil, the human mind becomes perilous, and this is responded to with calamities. There are seven kinds of disasters and nine kinds of untimely deaths.

These calamities and misfortunes may affect the common lot of many beings, or they may occur within a single country, a single province, a single district, a single village, or even upon a single family or a single individual.
One should simply, with a single-minded heart, offer worship to the divine mantra. First.

All calamities and misfortunes shall be entirely extinguished. First, "Ānanda, if in any land... and below clarifies that if there is trouble within a family or a nation, one is exempted from it by being exhorted to uphold this divine mantra.
Second, "Ānanda, in every place... and below indicates that regardless of the location—whether family or nation—if the mantra is present, there will be peace.
Third, "Ānanda, in this Sahā world... and below extensively explains [the benefits] within the common lot of sentient beings.
When one observes calamities and anomalies, it is difficult to resolve the situation unless one encourages the establishment of ritual boundaries (*sīmā*) and the recitation of mantras.

Furthermore, that which descends from heaven is called a "calamity" (*zāi*), while that which comes from without is called a "portent" (*xiáng*). A "portent" is so named because one must examine the source from which it originates. A *caitya* is a place where offerings may be made;

furthermore, that which contains *śarīra* (relics) is called a "stūpa," while that which lacks *śarīra* is called a *caitya*. *Dhvaja* is translated as "banner" (*dǒng*). △ Fourth, the summary of the above.
[The Buddha] said:
"For this reason, if the Tathāgatas were to proclaim this mantra [and it were ineffective], then the Tathāgatas of the ten directions would be speaking falsehoods.
The phrase "for this reason" below summarizes the preceding passage concerning the benefits for the three worlds. "Body and mind are at ease" refers to meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

It is sustained by power. "Attaining great peace and stability" means being free from the disturbances of Māra. Since there are no disturbances from Māra, one is further able to maintain meditative concentration;
thus, being free from calamities and adversities, one enters *samādhi*. For this divine mantra is a secret dharma.
If one does not reach the stage of *samādhi*, it would not accord with the Buddha’s intent.

From "You and those below" onward, this is a summary of the preceding text concerning the construction of the altar and the recitation of mantras. That the precept master one receives from is a pure monk is because the precepts cause the mind to be gathered.
That no doubt or regret arises regarding this mantra-heart is because concentration gives rise to wisdom. Thus, from the precepts, concentration is born.
Wisdom arises from meditative concentration. Therefore, one attains mental penetration throughout the ten directions, becoming unimpeded. This is because the Tathāgata speaks words of truth;
if he did not attain such mental penetration throughout the ten directions, it would be a false speech. △ Fifth, the oath to protect by spirits and deities.
1. The oath to protect by various deities.
Having spoken these words, immeasurable [beings] within the assembly attained the realization of Bodhi, such that they would forever be free from demonic interference.
Brahmā is the lord of the First Dhyāna; Śakra is the lord of the Desire Realm. *Yakṣa* is translated here as "valiant and strong";
*rākṣasa* is translated as "terrifying"; *piśāca* is translated as "stench-demon" (foul hungry ghost); *kumbhāṇḍa* is translated as...
This is the *yātudhāna* spirit; the *piśāca* is said to be the spirit that devours vital essence (*ojas*).

The *pināyakas* are the two messengers with the heads of pigs and the trunks of elephants. Furthermore, a celestial deity is called a *deva*, an earth deity is called a *kṣiti-devī*, and a human deity is called a *bhūta*.
The spirits and deities mentioned above each have their respective symbolic representations. Vajra symbolizes the majestic power of destroying evil. Brahma... [text fragment ends]
This commentary explains how the virtuous host maintains its excellence; the king of ghosts provides secret assistance, while the sun and moon act as aids through their brilliant illumination.
Wind and rain sweep away ignorance, thunder and lightning shake off the delusions of the sands, and the stars govern what is seen.
The Circuit Inspector reflected: "The Mountain God presides over the earth; Hai’ruo presides over the waters; the spirits and essences of the myriad things are the deities of fire and wind;
those who travel through space are the deities of wind. Whether they are formless or possess form—whatever has characteristics does not transcend the realm of desire.
These various signs of the three realms and the forms of the four great elements are none other than the mixed vapors of the good and evil karma of sentient beings."
This refers to the retributive obstacles of various afflictions. Now, if one enters the samādhi of *samaya*, all those deities will protect me;
how could one say that external objects can repel [the power of the mantra]?

Thus we know that turning away from the heterodox to return to the orthodox, and destroying evil to accomplish good, is none other than the merit of divine mantras. △ Second, the Vow of Vajragarbha to Protect.
At that time, eighty-four thousand nayutas (up to) constantly caused this person’s actions to be fulfilled according to their wishes.
*Nayuta* means ten billion; *koṭi* means one hundred million. As for the term "eighty-four thousand": [it refers to the number of kalpas].
If sentient beings possess eighty-four thousand afflictions in a single thought-moment, then by means of every successive thought-moment, their afflictions would be incalculable.
Now, taking even one *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* (Ganges-sand) as a unit, they are already incalculable;
if one were to take ten trillion *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka*, the number of their afflictions would be beyond words. For now, let us take just one.

Ten multiplied by ten makes one hundred; thus, there is the designation of "ten billion. Later, upon reaching the stage of generating the bodhicitta and practicing to advance to the rank of the Vajra Path, all their defilements and afflictions (*kleśa*) are transformed into ten billion kings of the Vajragarbha, as numerous as the sands of ten million *koṭis* of Ganges Rivers.
This is precisely the efficacious power of the Great Samādhi of the Śūraṅgama. Yet, having long since attained Bodhi, they do not [manifest it].

"Nirvāṇa" here refers to the intense resolve to protect the Dharma; it is for this reason that he retains afflictions to moisten his rebirth. Below, the World-Honored One formally sets forth his vow to protect [the teachings].
As for Maheśvara, he is the deity of the sixth heaven of the desire realm. This heaven is named Paranirmita-vaśavartin, meaning "Mastery over the Creations of Others.
It signifies that the deities of this heaven do not delight in their own creations, but rather rely upon the works created by others to achieve their own pleasure. That is to say...
Regarding the Māra King: some say there is a separate heaven within the Six Heavens of Desire called the Māra Heaven, which is also subsumed under Maheśvara.
As for the statement that the jeweled vajra shattered his head, this refers to the power of the vajra-like meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
The Māra King lacks a heart free from desire. To use a heart devoid of desire to resist the Great Vajra Samādhi—how could he avoid having his head shattered?
This is the vow of Vajragarbha to protect those who uphold the mantra; it also demonstrates the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
*Yojana* is translated here as "limit" or "measure," which corresponds to what is now called a *chuan-shè* (a relay station). The distant one is eighty [yojanas].

The distances are sixty *li* for the middle [level] and forty *li* for the nearest. This is because the mountains and rivers differ between the center and the periphery, and thus the travel distances are unequal.
From the time of Ānanda’s request for the method of establishing the altar until now, this constitutes the Dharma of the Study of Concentration (*samādhi*).
How is this clarified? Sentient beings have consistently relished delusion within the realm of desire, sinking and wallowing in the three realms.
Now, by revealing the methods of the altar, one assists their superior resolve and awakens their cognitive capacity.

Sentient beings have consistently relished following after worldly knowledge and views, rushing to and fro through the five paths. Now, by revealing the divine mantras, one gathers back their scattered minds and opens their [faculties].
This is dhyāna-concentration. Concentration does not fall into the extreme of emptiness; therefore, the method for constructing the altar manifests its essential substance.

The objective realm does not cling to the extreme of existence; therefore, the recitation of divine mantras elucidates its secret function. When secret, the mind does not leak; when substantial, the essence is not void.
One must ensure that the divine light coalesces within and virtuous countenances manifest without. Practicing in this manner, [liberation] occurs spontaneously.
One attains the stage of *samādhi*. As the subsequent text states: "When the mind maintains the prohibitive precepts (*śīla*), the entire body becomes light and pure;
when the mind maintains mantras and mudrās, one’s gaze becomes majestic and resolute—this is the verification. The above clarifies the completion of the training in concentration (*samādhi-śikṣā*).

Below, the stages of virtue (*guṇa-sthāna*) are clarified. "Stages of virtue" is a term for personal practice and realization; therefore, where there is such virtue, there must necessarily be such a stage.

This is not like the teachings of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), which lack any sequential stages and involve swallowing dates whole. Here, one must certainly proceed step by step. As stated previously:

"Sever one grade of ignorance and realize one portion of *tathatā* (suchness), continuing until the stage of *samyak-saṃbodhi* (perfect enlightenment), where only pure awakening remains and all traces of dust are eliminated;
this is what constitutes attainment. This shall be clarified in the following text. △ III. The Study of Wisdom (*prajñā-śikṣā*)
Three. First, the clarification of the two inversions; second, the clarification of the three gradual stages; third, the clarification of the distinctions between the stages and positions.
Regarding the first, the clarification of the two inversions: first, the formal petition.
Ānanda immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and stood gazing up at him with fixed eyes, awaiting the Buddha’s compassionate voice.

Recalling the previous instruction—that the mind is gathered through the precepts, that concentration arises from the precepts, and that wisdom is developed through concentration—Ānanda then requested the ritual for the altar and the proclamation of the divine mantra.
Thereupon, he realized the benefit of true cultivation and recognized the nature of the outflows and hindrances.

This is truly loathsome. By hollowing out the heart and transforming one’s thoughts, one will enter the Way without doubt. Now you have requested an explanation of the characteristics of the stages and causal positions of the Grounds (*bhūmi*).
A "position" (*wei*) refers to that which is trodden upon to accomplish practice. Beginning from the point of initial awakening, it is called the Ground of Dry Wisdom (*gāndhy-bhūmi*);

this serves as the fundamental basis for cultivation. Progressing through the stages of Faith (*śraddhā*), Abiding (*sthiti*), Practice (*caryā*), and Direction (*mukha*), along with the four preparatory practices (*prayoga*), these constitute forty stages in total.
The four minds are called "practice" (*xing*). From the first stage (*bhūmi*) to the tenth stage is called "awakening," which is termed "stages. A stage is the ground upon which one treads.
Progressing through the ten stages to the ultimate position is called "Equal Awakening" (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). These constitute the fifty-five positions.

This is the wondrous path to Bodhi; however, as it has not yet reached the destination, it is called a "path. Once one reaches the stage of Wondrous Enlightenment (Samyak-saṃbodhi), it is termed Nirvāṇa.
Having arrived at the home of Nirvāṇa, all that was to be done comes to rest, and both practice and the stages of the path are concealed.
This is what is meant by "entering the Tathāgata’s ocean of wondrous adornment," "perfecting Bodhi," and "returning to non-attainment. This meaning is set forth below. A.

Fearing that you might not understand the names, meanings, stages, causes, and effects of the *caryābhūmi*, I have thus asked these questions. △ Second, the granting of permission to preach, which has three parts.
First, the praise of his goodness:
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Ānanda, saying... [until] "...with palms joined and hearts emptied, he silently received the instruction."
The Buddha’s granting of his consent and praising what was well-said has two meanings.
First, Ānanda’s request on behalf of the great assembly and sentient beings of the final age represents the universal mind of those who study the Way.

Second, [the request] for the sake of those cultivating samādhi and seeking the Mahāyāna represents the profound mind of those who transmit the Buddha’s life-force of wisdom. These are the two meanings.

Therefore, the Buddha praised his goodness and granted his request. Furthermore, the two characters for "carving out the heart" (*kuxin*) precisely reveal the point where Ānanda forgot his own person for the sake of the Dharma—the place where his spiritual practice was continuous and subtle. II. Clarifying the Fundamental Source.
The Buddha said, "Ānanda, you should know that the wondrous nature [up to] Great Nirvāṇa are the two designations for the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).

As the Buddha was about to reveal the Dharma of the study of wisdom (*prajñā-śikṣā*), he first brought forth the fundamental principle (*mūla*) to explain it. Now, this fundamental principle has two meanings."
The Buddha said: "First, I shall directly point to their original source.
In this original state, there is no characteristic of sentient beings, no characteristic of worlds, nor is there the name 'Tathāgata,' nor the name 'bodhi,' nor the name 'nirvāṇa.'"
Why is this? These names and characteristics exist upon the essence of enlightened clarity; they are entirely empty as one whole.

This is because their fundamental nature is emptiness, for one perceives that one’s own true substance is no different [from it]. This is what is called the "Original. Because of delusion... [the text continues below].
Next, the origin of the true and the false is further clarified. It is because the clarity of awakening reaches its ultimate limit that non-awakening occurs;

a single thought of deluded movement flows into the three periods of time, thereby giving rise to the appearance of worlds. Because of delusion there is birth, and because of birth there is extinction.
Therefore, the existence of the mark of sentient beings is what is called delusion. Now, wishing to transform that non-awakening by relying upon fundamental awakening, there is the name "bodhi.
Now, wishing to transform that arising and ceasing by relying upon the absence of arising and ceasing—

Therefore, there is the designation "Nirvana. This is what is called "the Real. Thus one knows that the two characters "name" (nāma) and "form" (rūpa) are both the cause of the mundane world and the fruit of the supramundane. To investigate and discuss these causes and effects thoroughly:
Within the wondrously perfect nature, all is entirely real. This is because all phenomena are real, and one perceives that the essence of one's own wisdom has no dependence;

this is what is meant by the "Principle" (zong). This fundamental Principle is the precious mirror of the study of wisdom (*prajñā*), the excellent method for realizing the cause and attaining the fruit, reaching the ultimate stage. Students must not fail to understand this; therefore—
First, this is raised here. △ Third, the general presentation of the two inversions and the four [inversions]. First, the general presentation:
"Ānanda, you now wish to cultivate the true *samādhi*... (until) this is the Tathāgata’s true *samādhi*."
This is a general indication of the two types of inversion. Inversion arises from non-awakening (*abodhi*); non-awakening results from pursuing the delusive.
To pursue the delusive while neglecting the Real is what is called inversion. Now, if you wish to practice cultivation, you must first recognize this inversion.
When inverted views no longer arise, one may then enter the stage of the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, the three kinds of coarse characteristics of the karmic fruits of worldly sentient beings explained in the first four fascicles are spoken of in terms of the manifest forms currently before us.
Now, the explanation of the two inversions (viparyāsa) together with the twelve classes of beings is discussed in terms of their causal characteristics (*hetu-lakṣaṇa*).

Generally speaking, the characteristic of arising (*bhava-lakṣaṇa*) originates from the world, while the causal characteristic arises from sentient beings. What is called "inversion" specifically refers to this causal characteristic.
As the nineteenth patriarch told Jayata: "Karma arises from delusion (*moha*); delusion exists because of consciousness (*vijñāna*). Consciousness...
"Based on non-awakening; non-awakening is based on the mind, which is fundamentally pure, without arising and without ceasing.
This also clarifies the causal conditions from which [non-awakening] arises. A student must first recognize this; to recognize it is to have found the gateway.
△ Second, the analysis of the delusions of sentient beings.
Ānanda, what is meant by the "delusions of sentient beings"? [This continues] until: "For this reason, there are the delusions of sentient beings."
"Ānanda, descend. This clarifies the cause of inversion. "Nature" (xing) is the fundamental substance; "mind" (xin) is the substance of thought;

"luminous perfection" (mingyuan) is the substance of awakening. Although there are three meanings, their substance is one. That is to say, when a person possesses a mind of thought, it must necessarily arise from nature.
Furthermore, that which arises from nature is necessarily the awakening of luminous perfection; it does not exist within sensory objects. Therefore, it is said: "arising from..."
The nature of the mind is luminous. Because the nature of the mind is luminously perfect, why is it that people cannot grasp this luminous perfection and instead receive illusory dust?
"Dust" refers to the empty shadows of things. Since one receives these empty shadows and yet possesses a conceptualizing mind, this is delusion.
Generally speaking, the arising of the nature of delusion must also proceed from the luminous nature; thus, the luminous nature gives rise to delusion.
Therefore, deluded vision arises. Thus it is said that the nature [of things] is manifested through clarity, yet this nature gives rise to deluded vision.

Upon thorough investigation, this deluded vision is ultimately devoid of inherent nature, for the objects do not reach [the senses]. It is precisely because the objects do not reach them that deluded vision arises.
This is precisely what is called "delusorily existing. Therefore it is said: "From ultimate non-existence, one establishes ultimate existence.
As for "existence," it is the delusory capacity of the nature (*prakṛti*). Capacity must have an object; that which is the object is but a hollow reflection.
Thus it is said: "This existence has an object. However, this hollow reflection is not the cause of the nature. The nature does not arise from being caused by it, yet it gives rise to delusion.
This nature, conversely, becomes the cause of this delusion. Therefore it is said: "It is not the cause of causes. Furthermore, a hollow reflection cannot serve as the locus where nature dwells;
yet nature itself can dwell within the hollow reflection. Although the hollow reflection has a dwelling place, it ultimately lacks a root;
although nature can dwell by itself, it likewise must lack a foundation. Therefore it is said: "The characteristics of the dweller and the place of dwelling are entirely non-existent."
Fundamentally, empty reflections have no root, and the nature of phenomena has no basis; both are non-abiding.

To establish worlds and sentient beings based on that which is non-abiding—is this not the same as a single inversion? Furthermore, "abiding" refers implicitly to the world, while "the characteristic of abiding" refers implicitly to sentient beings.
The above constitutes a single presentation followed by a double conclusion: the world arises from sentient beings.
"It is because it arises from inverted causes. The section beginning with "Deluded regarding the fundamental" below clarifies the characteristics of inversion.

The first part, "losing the fundamental and undergoing immersion," means that by being deluded regarding the perfectly luminous awakening and pursuing a false and illusory nature, one falls into inversion. Why is this so?
Delusion has no fundamental substance and does not have anything upon which it relies. If it had something upon which to rely, it would then have a place of abiding.
If delusion had a substantial essence, it would possess the characteristic of arising, and thus it would not be delusion.

Next, as for those who loathe delusion and long for the Real, they seek to restore the true nature of True Suchness by means of illusory and false phenomena; this is a further inverted view. Why is this? Because True Suchness...
The true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Yet one seeks it through delusion; even if one were to attain it, it would no longer be the truly real nature of *tathatā*.
Third, as for "pursuing the non-true with that which is non-true": this is precisely a dharma that is not the true [mark], yet one delusively claims it to be the reality of *tathatā*.
Thus, one sees a succession of inverted views. Why is this? *Tathatā* is unborn, yet one delusively claims it has birth. If this is so, then it constitutes...
It is not born. True Suchness (tathatā) does not abide; to falsely claim that it abides is itself non-abiding.
True Suchness is free from mental conceptualization; yet to seek it with a mind is to produce what is non-mind.
True Suchness is detached from all marks (lakṣaṇa); thus there is no dharma. Yet to seek it by clinging to marks is to produce what is non-dharma.

This is the nature of phenomena (*dharma*). Through successive stages, they descend and form inverted misconceptions (*viparyāsa*). From these successive inversions, delusions are successively produced;
as the production of delusions does not cease, karma is perfumed according to the degree of gravity or lightness and strength or weakness of those inversions, thereby forming sentient beings.
For this reason, when karmas of a similar kind interact, love is produced; when karmas of a dissimilar kind interact, hatred is produced. It is by means of this that...
Hatred and love give rise to partiality; thus, they cause one another to arise and perish. Within the three periods of time, they revolve without end.
This is what constitutes the perversion of sentient beings. △ Third, the analysis of the perversion of the world.
Ānanda, what is meant by the "inversion of the world"? [This continues] until: "exhausting the twelve transformations, they become a single cycle of return.

Below this, Ānanda, the cause of inversion is clarified. The past, future, and present constitute the "world" (*loka*); the zenith, nadir, and the four cardinal directions constitute the "realm" (*dhātu*).
If the mind does not give rise to delusion, then there will be no reckoning of the three periods of time. If the faculties do not grasp at sense-objects, then there will be no...

This is the distinction between the realms and their states. When the mind is free from deluded thoughts and the sense faculties do not engage with sensory objects, it becomes one with the Dharma of True Suchness;

this is precisely what is meant by "original nature. Yet, at present, this is not the case. This is because one fails to maintain the original nature, instead pursuing delusions and giving rise to the mind.
Deluded by the realm of dust, the true mind thereby sinks away and fragmented delusions arise; this is precisely what constitutes perversion.
If one investigates its origination, those sensory objects have no inherent nature and cannot serve as a causal basis.

It is simply because people pursue objects for themselves that distinctions are formed, resulting in the divisions of realms and positions. Therefore, it is said: "Not the cause, yet the cause of causes. If...
Examining its causal origin, that delusion has no substance and cannot serve as a locus for abiding.

It is simply because people themselves grasp at it that they falsely give rise to the notion of a "dwelling place," and thus there arises the calculation of the three periods of time. Therefore it is said: "There is no dwelling, yet one dwells therein.

When one engages with the world through spatial directions, transformations are categorized accordingly; when one engages with spatial directions through the world, the flux of change never ceases. [The three periods and the four...]
Together, these form twelve. This is precisely the cause for the inversion of the world. Therefore, the following clarifies the characteristics of inversion.

Generally, "world" (*loka*) refers to the characteristic of movement, while "realm" (*dhātu*) refers to fixed positions. There are three types of moving characteristics, and only four fixed positions; these are sound, fragrance, taste, and touch.
This is because visible form (*rūpa*) is a substantial entity and mental objects (*dharma*) are empty entities; these two have no fixed position.
These are subsumed within the various sense objects (*viṣaya*), for all categories such as the body and so forth are fully present therein.

For example, when a false object arises and moves, there must necessarily be sound that reaches [the senses]. Thus, the ear is directed toward it; the eye is turned toward it; the nose is drawn toward it;
the mouth speaks because of it; the body moves because of it; and the mind is delighted because of it—and it is further delighted by this delight.

It does not stop there; the mind becomes deranged following it, and the body dances along with it, even manifesting such symptoms as twitching of the eyes and heat in the ears—these are called the six types of deluded thoughts that arise all at once.
Moreover, it is not only sound that acts in this way; one must know that fragrance, flavor, and touch are likewise so.
This is how it is with favorable conditions, and unfavorable conditions are just the same—it is merely a single false thought.

The flow extends through the three periods of time and the four directions; each exhaustively undergoes twelve transformations to form one cycle of return (*xuánfù*). This cycle of return is precisely what is meant by "revolving" (*lúnzhuǎn*).
Furthermore, it is like a single thought of ignorance where the wind of delusion moves: the fire of the mind must surely flare up, and the saliva of the mouth must surely flow.
Such things as the entire body feeling uneasy are responses to the internal division of the four great elements within the phase of karma.
Such things as wind sweeping like surging seas, trees uprooted, and mountains collapsing are responses to the external division of the four great elements within the nature of karma.
Yet these internal and external divisions are nothing other than the total transformation of a single deluded thought; this is the world.
This is the characteristic of perversion. △ Fourth, the detailed explanation of the twelve classes of beings has three parts. First, the general heading:
"Because they ride this wheel-turning characteristic of perversion" (extending to) "...neither-perception-nor-non-perception."
If one discusses the inversion of the world, it arises from sentient beings; because they are deluded regarding their own fundamentally perfect luminosity, this gives rise to false conceptualization.
Now, in analyzing sentient beings, we see that they arise from the world; because they produce one another through mutual conditioning, karma is thereby formed.
Thus it is said: "Riding upon this wheel of inverted characteristics. Below, the twelve classes of living beings are enumerated. That is to say:
This clarifies their inverted views. How do we know this is so? Suppose a sound comes to the ear;

when it is heard, one hears it within awareness, and in that awareness there is nothing else. Now, however, it is not so. Being deluded regarding fundamental perfect luminosity, they give rise to perverse defilement.
Consequently, some grasp at sounds with攀缘 (pān-yuán—clinging/conditioning) and become attached to them, falling into conceptualization.

The aggregates [of grasping] bring about birth as an egg-born being. Or, if one gives rise to cognition and views based on sound and falls into the state of conceptual existence, it brings about birth as a womb-born being.
Furthermore, if one lingers in deluded attachment toward sound and falls into the state of clinging to rebirth, it brings about birth as a moisture-born being.
Furthermore, some, out of weariness with sounds, rejoice in the new; thus they fall into false attribution and are reborn among the classes of beings subject to transformation.
Others, regarding sounds, calculate them as existent or non-existent, each forming four propositions and falling into wrong views, thereby establishing eight inversions.
These sentient beings take perception (*saṃjñā*) and the like as their cause, and the egg-born, womb-born, and so forth as their fruit.

Thus, within a single sound, such emotional attachments and conceptual reckonings arise; likewise, with respect to other objects—odors, tastes, and tangibles—emotional attachments and conceptual reckonings do not fail to arise.
Flowing through the three times and the four directions, each exhausts the twelve transformations to form a single cycle. This is what constitutes sentient beings.
The characteristics of the distinctions among karmic fruits are none other than inverted; they truly constitute suffering. △ Second, the detailed enumeration:
First, the moving species.
Ānanda, from the world of causes and conditions, through false transmigration... (up to) fish, birds, tortoises, and snakes, their various kinds fill the world.
Regarding "by way of cause": this refers back to the preceding text. The preceding text states: "From ultimate non-existence, one achieves ultimate existence," and further states:
"This is that which possesses existence; it is not a cause for a cause. This is the cause by which inversion arises.
Now, observing that false conceptualization is not the [primary] cause, yet it cannot help but be stirred by the winds of objects—these winds of objects are what constitute the cause.
Indeed, existence arises from causes; that which exists must depend on conditions to come into being. When the vital energies (*qi*) attain union, this constitutes "existence.
From these causes, the species of oviparous creatures are able to be born. Yet, their varieties are not of a single kind.
One should not assume they are identical. When we now speak of "eighty-four thousand," it is merely a conventional enumeration based on the fullness of their karma.
Because their karma is complete, some fly when riding the winds, while others sink when riding the vapors; thus, these species differ.
Although these species differ, the deluded and inverted perceptions of them are one and the same. For this reason, among the fish and birds of the world...
Turtles and snakes fill the space without end. *Kalala*—translated here as "congealed mucus"—is the stage when the embryo and egg have not yet differentiated.
△ Second, the category of desire-beings.
From "due to the world’s defiled saṃsāra" (up to) "humans, beasts, nāgas, and seers, their kinds filling it.

Regarding "defiled": this refers to the non-uniformity of greed (*rāga*). The nature of greed itself is not the cause; rather, it is the agitation caused by the fire of desire that constitutes the cause.

This is because the "conditioned existence" (*bhava*) exists as the underlying cause. Where there is existence, there must necessarily be dependence upon something else—namely, the water of craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
Nourishing and uniting them constitutes that which is "possessed. By means of these causes, the fetal constituents are able to arise.
However, their types are not of a single kind, nor are their dispositions uniform. It is now said that there are eighty-four thousand [such types].

However, this merely refers to the completion of the full measure of one's karma. Because the karma is complete, if one contains the nature of the five constants, one is born into the vertical category;
if one contains the nature of deviance and perversity, one is born into the horizontal category. Thus, these lineages differ.
Although the lineages differ, their defilement and perversion are one and the same. Consequently, the world is filled with humans, animals, dragons, and immortals.
It does not end there. Passing beyond *pú-tán*—here translated as "blister"—is the stage where the embryo or egg first begins to divide. △ Third, the categories of beings:
due to attachment to the world of causes, [beings] revolve in saṃsāra (up to) crawling insects and wriggling creatures, their species filling every space.

"Grasping" (執) means to hold fast; "clinging" (著) means to take up and adhere to. This refers to the fact that whenever one sees an object, one takes it up, clings to it, and holds onto it without letting go.
One does not realize that this grasping and clinging fundamentally have no cause; yet, helplessly, craving flows forth toward objects, and this craving is precisely the cause.
For the cause exists because there is "existence" (有), and existence necessarily arises through dependence, just like a bubble on a stream.
The warmth and heat are all capable of mutual resonance; this constitutes "that which exists. "Flipping and turning" means revolving or circulating.
Because one does not abandon craving and thirst, one thus revolves and proceeds toward rebirth. *Bhisa* is translated here as "tender flesh."
This class does not enter a womb; therefore, there is no preceding stage. They are born as soon as they encounter a moist and warm environment, and thus have no fixed place of belonging.
△ Fourth, the apparitional class.
From "due to the world’s transformation and saṃsāra" up to "transforming and shedding their bodies to fly, filling the air. "Transformation" (bian) refers to transition;
"change" (yi) refers to the alteration of what is constant. This means that while the nature of the mind is constant, it undergoes transition according to its objects.
In one moment it is here, in another it is there; this is the body that undergoes transformation. This transformation is fundamentally not caused by external factors.
It is unavoidable that they rely on what is unreal; this reliance is precisely the cause. For that which serves as the cause exists, and existence necessarily arises through dependence.
Just as the nature of earth perceives touch and thereby achieves conjunction—this is what is meant by "existence."

"New and old" refers to the principle of discarding one and taking up another. This is because beings born by transformation (*upapāduka*) depart from their former physical substance and respond to a new reception;

this is called "departing and responding. *Kalala* (here translated as "hard flesh") undergoes transformation and shedding, such as when a worm becomes a butterfly, it transforms its mode of movement from crawling to flying;
or when a sparrow becomes a clam, it sheds its state of flight for that of submergence—these are examples of such categories.
...and so forth. △ Five: The Categories of Obstructions.
Due to the world of causes, beings remain obstructed and transmigrate (up to) the spirits of portents and omens; their kinds fill the space.
To grasp form as being existent is for existence itself to become an obstruction of the mind-ground; this constitutes an obstruction. Because of this obscuration, [one's desires...]
Seeking to clarify this point: it is said that one eventually moves the essence of radiant beings to manifest as celestial phenomena in the world, such as the stars, the sun, and the moon;
or as the markings on grasses and the spirit-tortoise, and all other entities possessing refined vitality and spiritual intelligence.

These are all capable of producing calamities or auspiciousness, misfortune or fortune, in response to the good or bad fortune of human beings. Furthermore, *kalala* (the embryonic stage) is not restricted to the category of solid flesh. There is...
"Sentient" and "insentient" are general designations according to their characteristics. △ Six: Categories of Delusion.
From the world of causes dissolving and revolving (until) empty, scattered, and submerged, these categories fill and obstruct.
To grasp at form as being empty, and for that emptiness to dissolve all existence (*bhava*) so that it returns to non-existence—this is delusion (*moha*).

Because of this delusion, the knots of darkness become obscured as the aggregates (*skandha*). This is like the "non-thought" (*asaṃjñin*) of the non-Buddhists, the ignorance and obscuration of sentient beings, and the dull emptiness of the formless realms (*ārūpya-dhātu*), and so forth.
Those who experience such categories as the dissipation and sinking of emptiness have their spirit and vitality exhausted.
If directed upward, it becomes empty and dispersed; if exhausted downward, it becomes dissolved and submerged.
It all ultimately returns to the field of voidness and loss. △ Seven: Analogies of Shadows.
"Due to the causes of the world’s *wangxiang* (ethereal-phantasmal) saṃsāra... down to spirits, ghosts, and numinous essences, their kinds fill [the world].
*Wang* means non-existence; *xiang* means existence. If one calls them existent, they are faint and invisible; if one calls them non-existent, they are manifest and can be verified.
Hence they are called *wangxiang*. These are the ignorant masses who lack knowledge... [The text continues with the description of external objects.]

Relying upon [external] influences, one internally focuses solely on faith and recollection. Is it not a case of inverted delusion that one possesses the inherently existent nature of perfect enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) yet falls into the realms of emptiness, spirits, and ghosts? △ Eight: The Class of Delusion.
Due to the causes of the world’s ignorance and dullness in saṃsāra (up to) earth, wood, stone, and metal, these types fill the realm.

That their nature is obscured is called "ignorance" (*mūḍha*); that the mind has no function is called "dullness" (*jaḍa*). This refers to those who hope for longevity while entrusting their thoughts to non-existence;
like Zhuangzi’s description of the body as withered wood and the mind as extinguished ashes, they belong to the class of the deluded, stubborn, and useless.
...Also. △ Nine: The Class of Falsities.
From "The world of causes revolves through mutual dependence" (up to) "using shrimp as eyes; their kind fills the world. Regarding "mutual dependence":
it is like a shadow depending on a form, and the *wangliang* (a shadowy phantom) further depending on the shadow. Furthermore, it is not [the case that] they are not themselves...
There is form. Seeing form as having form, one is immediately defiled. Being oneself without marks, seeing marks as having marks, they are immediately produced.
This is what is called relying upon one another in a reciprocal manner; it is a reciprocal falsity. △ Ten: Categories of Nature.
Due to the mutual attraction of the world's phenomena, beings revolve in saṃsāra (until) they give rise to curses and incantations, and their kind fills [the world].
"Mutual attraction" refers to the talismans, water-mantras, and secret instructions forged by sorcerers, as well as the carving of human figures and so forth;

following any one of these matters, they take it as a method of refinement. They refine their nature to accomplish curses and prayers, capable of summoning immortals and spirits, and capable of enlisting them to labor.
They employ ghosts and spirits, using various heterodox arts to deceive the world and harm others.

They do not realize that these so-called external entities truly do not exist and cannot be summoned. Even if they were to achieve some success, it would still be produced solely by their own deluded, deceptive, and inverted karmic forces. 11. Deceptive Beings.
From "due to the world’s conjunction with delusion and cyclic existence" (up to) "different natures forming one another, their kinds filling all space":
by joining delusion with delusion, this is to deceive and mislead. Because of this deception and misleading, each thing becomes empty and each thing becomes distinct.
This is because, within the causal ground, they only know to use deception and misleading to dupe the world, yet do not realize they are using deception and misleading to dupe themselves.
Consequently, successive generations have inherited these errors, and the true nature of the mind has been lost. The *pulu* is the slender-waisted wasp, also known as the *die’ong*.
It takes a silkworm as its offspring; after seven days of incantation, it becomes a wasp. This is a case of sheer fabrication and deception.
△ Twelve Categories of Killers.
Due to the cycle of enmity and harm in the world... (until) they all meet their end by being devoured, such beings fill the realm.
In the world, parents regard the birth of a child as an act of grace; yet when a child devours its parents, it is regarded as an act of enmity. Thus, enmity and grace are mutually entangled.
Consequently, they come to kill one another; how strange this is! Furthermore, some conceive of those with perception as sentient beings and those without perception as insentient things.
Since the insentient and the sentient are opposites, they come to harm one another; is this not a perversion? △ Third, the conclusion.
These are called the twelve kinds of sentient beings.

Among the twelve classes of beings listed above, the first consists of the actualities of emotional and conceptual thought; the subsequent ones consist of the transformations of emotional and conceptual thought.

First, regarding the reality of emotion (*qing*) and perception (*xiang*): just as form (*rūpa*) is the characteristic of the four great elements and the aggregate of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), so too emotion is not defiled except by form, perception does not move except by form, moisture does not flow except by form, and transformation does not shift except by form.
Thus we know that form is the root of the five aggregates and the reality of emotion and perception. Yet, the five aggregates possess arising.
All [of these] are complete. As for their classification by category now, it is because they each take birth according to where their respective tendencies predominate.
Next, regarding the transformations of emotion and perception: some are originally formless yet conceive perceptions of form, such as those spirits of auspicious and inauspicious portents;
others are originally possessed of form yet conceive perceptions of formlessness, such as those that vanish into emptiness or dissipate away.
Furthermore, that which is originally without perception (asaṃjñā) yet forms perceptions of existence—such as the class of spirits, ghosts, and numinous beings—is one example.
That which is originally with perception yet forms perceptions of non-existence—such as the class of earth, wood, metal, and stone—is another.
The above are the manifestations transformed by perception. Moreover, that which is originally not of form yet constitutes a form-manifestation is like the *śiśumāra* (water-jelly).
These are examples. Originally they were not formless, yet they manifest the appearance of being formless; this refers to things such as spells and curses.
Originally they were not with perception, yet they manifest the appearance of having perception; this refers to things such as the *pulu* (a type of insect).

Originally they were not without perception, yet they manifest the appearance of being without perception; this refers to things such as the *tuxiao* (an owl). All of the above are appearances transformed by the mind.
These manifested appearances and the delusions of the five aggregates are nothing other than that which is created by a single false and inverted state.
A practitioner must first recognize that such things are fundamentally non-existent; because one was originally deluded regarding this, one undergoes immersion in suffering.
If one now investigates and penetrates each of them one by one, one will no longer be turned by them.
