Summarizing the preceding inverted causes:
"Ānanda, among each and every class of such sentient beings... [up to] they are fully possessed of such false and delusive discursive thoughts."
This concludes the preceding section and introduces what follows. Regarding the statement that each [sense-faculty] possesses [its objects] individually:

for example, when the eye perceives and becomes deluded by a form, then sounds, odors, and other phenomena act as auxiliary causes to bring it about. Likewise, when the ear perceives and becomes deluded by a sound, then odors, tastes, forms, and so forth likewise act as auxiliary causes to bring it about.
In this manner, these twelve inversions are present in every category and pervade every category; such is the nature of karma.
As for the seeds of consciousness, how could they merely number eighty-four thousand? They are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River.
When one contemplates these seeds of affliction, as many as the sands of the Ganges, within the wondrously bright, true, and pure mind, it is just like pressing on the eyes and seeing flowers;
they have no separate nature at all, but are simply the delusions of one's own mind. △ Second, the headings and enumeration.
"You are now cultivating and realizing the Buddha’s samādhi... (up to) third, 'progressing while contradicting one's manifest karma.

The vessel is a metaphor for the wondrous, perfect, and luminous mind; the poison and honey are metaphors for perversion; the hot water and so forth are metaphors for precept, concentration, and wisdom—the fundamental causes.
'The original causes' refers to the aforementioned twelve perversions. Within the wondrously luminous mind, these perversions exist just as they do within the vessel."
Within this [world] there is this poison-honey. If the vessel is not pure, it cannot hold the nectar of immortality;
if the mind is not pure, one cannot enter samādhi. The establishment of these three gradual stages is precisely the method for preparing the pure vessel.

The method for cleaning a vessel must involve two or three washings before it becomes pure. The method of spiritual cultivation must involve gradual progression and increasing depth before realization is attained.
These three kinds of gradual progression are the methods for washing away the defilements of the mind; they must not be neglected.
△ Third, the specific explanation of the three [gradual stages] has three parts. First, the specific explanation of the auxiliary causes.
What are the auxiliary causes (upakāra-hetu) [leading] to the first stage of progressive advancement?
Regarding the sequence of practice: as for auxiliary causes, when sentient beings possess karma, they possess bodies; they require food to nourish them.

If this nourishment is not obtained through the correct method, it may even lead to the destruction of the body; this, moreover, is a fault of eating. Therefore, one must discern between the wholesome and the unwholesome regarding food.
The wholesome benefits me; the unwholesome is the opposite. Ānanda, thus below this world, four types of sustenance (āhāra) are enumerated as the basis for existence:

first, edible food (kavaḍīkāra-āhāra), which refers to the taking of physical morsels in the desire realm as food, because it provides nourishment through the three [objects] of fragrance, flavor, and tangibility.
Second, contact-sustenance (sparśa-āhāra), which is the contact of the sixth mental consciousness with its corresponding object, giving rise to joy and pleasure.
Therefore: (3) The nutriment of volition (*manosaṃcetanāhāra*) corresponds to the seventh [consciousness], as it functions together with desire and the aspiration for objects is predominant.

(4) The nutriment of consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*) corresponds to the eighth, because by means of the power of the assistance provided by the first three nutriments, it sustains the sense faculties (*indriya*) and the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), thereby attaining nourishment and growth.

Furthermore, among humans there is the nutriment of physical food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*); among ghosts and spirits, the nutriment of contact (*sparśāhāra*); among the heavens of the dhyāna realms, the nutriment of volition; and among the four formless heavens...
The consciousness-food (*vijñānāhāra*). Although these four types differ according to the three realms, there is none that does not subsist through nutriment.
Therefore, the four nutriments are designated as auxiliary causes. "Ānanda, all sentient beings," and so forth, correctly distinguishes between harm and benefit:
eating sweets leads to life, which is benefit; eating poison leads to death, which is harm. Furthermore, the "five pungent roots" (*pañca-garaka*) refer to garlic (*laśuna*).
*Gecong*, *Cicong*, *Lancong*, and *Xingqu*—these are the five pungent vegetables (*pañca-gandhaka*). Their nature is malevolent and their odor is rank; therefore, they are considered "poisons.
Because poison harms the body, one must abstain from them. Following these five kinds of pungents, the faults of pungency are shown:

lust and anger are the foremost of the three poisons and the leaders of all evils. Thus, for a person who eats pungent things, [the heavens... *(Note: The source text appears to be a fragment. The final sentence is incomplete, but the translation reflects the available portion.)*
The immortals abandon them; furthermore, when their merit is exhausted, they dwell with ghosts. Even those who excel in dhyāna ultimately become part of Māra’s faction.

Once their power of the heterodox has declined, they fall back into ruin. This is their fault. Below, the passage beginning with "Ānanda cultivated bodhi" concludes by establishing the precepts to be observed.
Thus we know that pungent and turbid things are truly causes that assist evil. If these causes of evil are eliminated, right view will arise, and the samādhi of spontaneity will manifest before one;
this is called the foremost method for the progressive cultivation of practice. △ Second, the specific explanation of the correct nature.
What is the second stage of progressive cultivation within the state of correctness?

How does the following section generally exhort the observance of the precepts? Killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct are natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*); consuming alcohol and meat are prohibited transgressions (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*).
With these two forms of non-restraint, there is no possibility of escaping the three realms. Why is this?
If the lustful mind is not eliminated, then birth and death will not cease; if the murderous mind is not eliminated, then enmity will have no end.

Indeed, practitioners of the Way do not even consume the fruits of the earth, fearing they might stir violent vapors, let alone eat the flesh of sentient beings. They do not even allow the sound of hairpins or bracelets to be heard, fearing...

To involve oneself in what is subject to reproach and suspicion is already improper; how much more so to engage in such deeds? Furthermore, the poisonous snake is a metaphor for sexual misconduct, and the vengeful enemy is a metaphor for killing.
Regarding the method of "excavating the heart," one must contemplate in this manner before one can discern the direction of benefit and harm.

First, the sequence of the precepts for the Śrāvakas is clarified: for a bhikṣu, committing sexual misconduct, killing, stealing, or lying constitutes the four pārājika offenses; for a bhikṣuṇī, these are doubled. Therefore—

There are eight *pārājika* offenses; in the Sanskrit language, *pārājika*, which here is translated as "abandoning offenses. This means that if one commits these, one is permanently cast outside the boundaries of the Buddha-dharma;
hence they are called "abandoning. When it says "the four abandonings and eight abandonings of the śrāvakas," this refers to the precepts of the Hīnayāna.
When it says "the pure discipline of the bodhisattva," this refers to the precepts of the Mahāyāna. Furthermore, "maintaining the body in immobility" refers to...

The coarse is when the body does not move; the subtle is when the mind does not stir. One must first observe the Śrāvaka precepts so that the body remains unmoving, and subsequently observe the Bodhisattva precepts so that the mind does not stir.
First, one restrains the coarse manifestations of afflictions (*kleśa*); later, one restrains the subtle aspects of deportment (*īryāpatha*).
To cultivate the mind in this manner is not to skip over stages. Below the section "Accomplishment of the Prohibitive Precepts," the receiving of the precepts is described.
Furthermore: by not engaging in sexual misconduct, one is free from entanglements; by not killing, one is free from debt; by not stealing, one is free from lingering karmic obligations.
Thus, the prohibitive precepts are perfected. As for the statement that "no divine eye is required," it means that the physical eye is itself the divine eye.
For when killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct are not practiced, the mind-ground naturally becomes unobstructed, and the six sense faculties naturally become clear and penetrating.
As it is said, "observing and seeing the worlds of the ten directions" refers to the supernormal power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣur-abhijñā*).

As it is said, "beholding the Buddha and hearing the Dharma" refers to the supernormal power of the divine ear (*divyaśrotra-abhijñā*). As it is said, "attaining great supernormal powers" refers to the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others (*paracitta-jñāna-abhijñā*).
As it is said regarding wandering through the worlds of the ten directions, this is the supernormal power of the divine foot (ṛddhividhi-jñāna).

As it is said regarding the purity of past lives, this is the supernormal power of recollecting past existences (pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna). As it is said regarding attaining freedom from peril, this is the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣaya-jñāna).

Furthermore, if one knows the events of hundreds of thousands of births, this is the clear knowledge of past lives (pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-vidyā). To see all sentient beings giving rise to wholesome [roots] is [the clear knowledge of death and rebirth].

Discerning the Path and the Non-path is the Clarity of the Divine Eye (*divyacakṣur-abhijñā*). Severing the afflictions of view and thought (*dṛṣṭi- and bhāvanā-heya-kleśa*) within the three realms so as to no longer undergo birth and death is the Clarity of the Exhaustion of Outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*).

These three clarities and six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) are all accomplished through the observance of the prohibitive precepts (*śīla*), whereby one attains the purity of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya-viśuddhi*).
Therefore, even with the physical bodies of present parents, one realizes such a stage; this is called the first [stage].
Second, the method for the progressive cultivation of practice. △ Third, the detailed explanation of manifest karma.
What is manifest karma? [It extends] to the third stage of the gradual sequence of progressive cultivation of practice.

"What is meant by 'below'? This clarifies the virtue of *prajñā*. "Present karma" refers precisely to the present activities of seeing, hearing, and so forth, which arise from the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*).
However, the arising of present karma must necessarily be constructed by the mind. If the mind does not take [objects] as its conditions, then the functions of the six faculties do not proceed.
If the six functions do not proceed, then the faculties have nothing with which to couple. When the faculties have nothing with which to couple, they are [united] with the Real.
The constant nature is one. If the mind does not take objects as its conditions, it then revolves back to its own source. Why is this?

Because by having long since lost the root and undergone immersion in delusion, one was unable to maintain oneness; now, by abandoning the false and returning to the true, one attains the reversal of the flow and the merging with the nature.
Furthermore, what is meant by "the mind is free from lustful desire" and "does not flow excessively toward external objects" refers precisely to the cessation of present karmic activity.
The following passage from the *Daśadig* [Sūtra] provides an analogy to clarify this point: the bright moon represents the mind, and lapis lazuli represents the sense faculties.
This illustrates that when present karmic activity does not arise, the mind is naturally pure; and since the mind is pure, the sense faculties are likewise pure. This is the correct [explanation].
When the retribution is pure, the environment upon which it depends is also pure. When one land is pure, even the lands of the ten directions are likewise pure.
Therefore, it is said that the lands of the ten directions are brilliantly pure, like a bright moon suspended within lapis lazuli.
This is called the wisdom-virtue of *prajñā*. The following section on "body and mind" clarifies liberation (*vimukti*).
Virtue. By means of this very wisdom-virtue, one contemplates the worlds of the ten directions;
whether oneself or others, there is no distinct dharma whatsoever, but only the single, wondrous, perfect true mind, equal and non-dual.
Because it is equal and non-dual, all Tathāgatas are my own mind, and my own mind is the Tathāgata. Yet, one does not discriminate between my own mind and the Tathāgata.
The mind. Why is this? Because all dharmas are entirely unattainable. At this very moment, it is precisely where I relinquish body and life;
therefore, it is said that body and mind are blissful, wondrously perfect and equal, attaining great peace and stability—this is called the virtue of liberation.
From "All Tathāgatas" onwards clarifies the virtue of the Dharma-body, which is the secret, perfect principle. Pure.
It is wondrous wisdom (*prajñā*). It is called "wondrous" because this wisdom cannot be cognized; it is called "subtle" because its principle is all-pervasive.
When the practitioner realizes the field of the equal true reality (*bhūtatathatā*), the secret, perfect, pure, and wondrous Dharma-body of all Tathāgatas spontaneously manifests therein.
Therefore, it is said that the secret, perfect, pure, and wondrous [nature] of all Tathāgatas is fully revealed.
Among these, this is called the virtue of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). This refers to the conclusion of the preceding three virtues. As Avalokiteśvara said:

"When birth and cessation have both ceased, quiescent extinction (*śānti*) manifests before one. This refers to the patience and wisdom of quiescent extinction (*śāntikṣāntijñāna*). At the time when this patience and wisdom manifest, [the Dharma-body is realized].

The three types of wisdom all subside. Why is this? It is because the three types of wisdom constitute understanding (*parijñā*), while patience (*kṣānti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*) constitute practice (*pratipatti*).

When practice arises, understanding ceases; therefore, the three types of wisdom all subside. Now, it is said that when knowledge merges with principle, it cannot be known by knowledge nor cognized by consciousness.
When this patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) manifests before one, at the very moment this patience manifests, the three...

The three virtues are all concealed. Why is this? It is because the three virtues constitute understanding (*jñāna*), while the patience with the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*) constitutes practice (*caryā*).

Furthermore, it is through practice that understanding is brought to cessation. Therefore, the three virtues are all concealed. From this point onward, one employs only the wisdom of patience (*kṣāntijñāna*) to traverse the fifty-five stages.
Whatever practice is undertaken does not depart from the patience with the Dharma as its foundation; this is called the third stage of progressive cultivation.
This is the Dharma. Question:

Since the characteristics of the precepts (*śīla*) have already been explained in detail previously, why is it that in this current exposition of the three gradual stages (*tri-ānupūrvi-dharma*), the precepts are shown once again?

Answer: The previous explanation of the characteristics of the precepts was according to the sequential order of the teachings; because the precepts ought to come first, they were treated there. Now, however, [the precepts are presented]...
"Gradual" refers to the sequence of stages within the treatise. Since the precepts constitute the preceding stage for the practitioner, a question is asked:
"How can the precepts constitute a stage? It is said: "This is because we are now demonstrating the Perfect and Sudden Teaching of the Mahāyāna, which differs from the Hīnayāna.

The Hīnayāna adheres solely to phenomenal characteristics and does not clarify the fundamental principle; however, that which is to be observed as a precept in the Mahāyāna must first clarify the principle. Furthermore, the Mahāyāna...

The aspect of non-arising is the characteristic of understanding, which is the principle being elucidated. One must necessarily embrace the precepts to establish practice before one can truly perceive this reality;
therefore, the precepts are placed in the preceding stage. Question: What kind of practice must be initiated to perceive the principle of the Mahāyāna? Answer:
As it is said, "auxiliary causes" refer to external conditions, while "right nature" refers to internal obstacles. As it is said...
What is described as "present karma" refers to the manifestations arising from the faculties and their objects. These are the habit-energies (vāsanā) perfumed by beginningless false delusions;
they consist precisely of ignorance, the dust-like afflictions, the views, and the thoughts of outflows.

Now, by means of the three gradual stages of practice, one sweeps away the internal and external obstructive conditions, as well as the present karma arising from the faculties and their objects, and thereby perceives that the person in question is originally non-existent.
It arises. Yet, if one sees that from the beginning there is no arising, this is precisely the principle of the Mahāyāna.
Based on this principle of non-arising in the Mahāyāna, fifty-two stages are established according to their respective meanings;

when the four stages prior to the [ten] bhūmis are added to the initial stage of Dry Wisdom (śuṣka-prajñā-bhūmi), there are fifty-seven stages in total, at which point the ultimate is fully realized. The meaning of this will be seen in the following text. △
The ten stages of the Threefold Knowledge (trividyā): First is the Stage of Dry Wisdom (śuklavipaśyanā-bhūmi).
Ānanda, when this son of good family’s craving for sensual desire has dried up... [up to] ...having wisdom that is dry, it is called the Stage of Dry Wisdom.
The Patriarch said, "A mind like a wall can enter the Way. Furthermore, an ancient worthy said, "It is not that dust does not intrude;
it is simply that I have no mind. To say "no mind" does not mean the absence of a mind altogether; it merely means the absence of a worldly mind.
When worldly thoughts have perished, it is called "dryness" (qian); when the grasping mind is empty and luminous, it is called "wisdom" (hui). Thus one sees.

Attaining one's own original enlightenment is called the "ground" (*bhūmi*). Furthermore, although the initial awakening of wisdom is perfectly polished throughout the ten directions, it lacks the capacity for active application;
this is wisdom that exists in a state of dryness. Therefore, it is called the "Ground of Dry Wisdom" (*śuklavidarśanā-bhūmi*).

This follows upon the meaning of the third gradual stage mentioned previously. Previously it was said, "the mind is free from greed and lust"; now it is said, "desire and love are dried up. As for the previous...
It is said that [the mind] does not flow excessively outward toward the six sense objects. Now it is said that this present physical remnant shall no longer continue to be reborn.

Observing it from this perspective, it is clearly different from one's previous efforts. If those who first set out on the path of cultivation do not understand this principle, how can they skip over the stages?
Teachers who are unacquainted with this merely pair together names and characteristics; thus, they fail the Buddha.
The essential meaning [of this] is further in great contradiction to the textual sense; therefore, it is not accepted. △ Second, the Stage of Faith.
First, the Mind of Faith:
when the habitual tendencies of desire have begun to dry up but one has not yet attained the pure truth of the Middle Way of the Tathāgata, it is called the Abode of the Mind of Faith.
The two phrases concerning "the habituation of desire" refer back to the preceding stage. That stage possesses only the virtue of cessation (*prahāṇa-guṇa*) but lacks active function;

therefore, it has not yet connected with the Dharma-stream of the Tathāgata. It is like a practitioner who, for the first time, applies effort and attains the severance of the past and future limits of body and mind.
This is a barren concentration that lacks utility; it is devoid of the water of principle.
Because it causes [the Dharma] to flourish and develop, this section below exhorts the practitioner: "Upon reaching such a state, one employs this stage to enter the flow from the center of the mind.
Here, "center" (*zhong*) refers to the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*). The Middle Way is that which is free from all dharmas of dualistic opposition, such as existence and non-existence.
"Flow" (*liu*) refers to the direct mind (*ṛju-citta*). The direct mind spontaneously turns toward all dharmas. As for what is said:
"Perfectly wondrous and fully blossomed": "perfectly wondrous" refers to awakening (*bodhi*); "fully blossomed" refers to wisdom (*prajñā*).
This means that by means of the straightforward mind of the Middle Way, one must correspond with the awakening of wisdom; only when one attains the authentic ground of insight is it truly "wondrous."
Therefore it is said: "Reiterating the True Wondrousness. "True Wondrousness" refers to the true mind.

It is like originally attaining the authentic ground of realization and decisively believing and knowing that this mind is wondrous and a permanently abiding dharma; hence it is called "Wondrous Faith in the Permanently Abiding.
If one believes that this mind is permanently abiding, then there will be no deluded thoughts or inversions to serve as cognitive obstacles (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). Hence it is called "One."
All deluded thoughts are extinguished without remainder. Furthermore, when the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are severed, deluded thoughts do not arise.
When one does not fall into the two extremes, the Middle Way becomes pure and true. Thus, by means of the wisdom of the Middle Way, one believes in this true mind;
this is called the "Abiding in Faith" (*śraddhā-vihāra*). 2. The Mind of Mindfulness (*smṛti-citta*).

Truly believing and clearly understanding that all is perfectly interfused (*yuan-tong*)—up to the point where one attains non-forgetfulness—is called the "abiding of the mind in mindfulness" (*nianxin-zhu*).

"Clearly understanding" (*ming-liao*) means the sense of being accurate and correct. Because the preceding afflictions have been extinguished and there remains only the single true mind, one perceives with accuracy and clarity that there is nothing else;
everything is, in its entirety, the perfectly interfused Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Therefore, regarding the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*)...

Third, they cannot act as obstacles. Furthermore, the discarding of one body and receiving another constitutes birth-and-death by segmentation (*paricchinna-saṃsāra*), while all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) constitute birth-and-death through transformation (*pariṇāma-saṃsāra*).
Now, when observing these with the wisdom of the Middle Way, they are seen solely as the realm of True Suchness (*tathatā-viṣaya*).
Therefore, events spanning incalculable eons can all be remembered; there is no distinction between long and short durations, for everything manifests within a single thought-moment.
Therefore, it is called the "mind dwelling in mindfulness. △ Third is the mind of diligence:
"Wondrous, perfect, pure, and true; from true essence, transformation is initiated" (up to) "advancing toward true purity is called the mind of diligence."

For the wondrously perfect wisdom is without admixture; hence it is called "pure" (*chún*). The wondrously perfect mind is without delusion; hence it is called "true" (*zhēn*). "True" is precisely clarity; "pure" is precisely refinement. When transformation is initiated by this refined and pure mind, the beginningless habitual tendencies are all transformed into purity. When one advances toward realization with this true and luminous mind, the functions of its refined brilliance—whether in stillness or movement—are such that they cannot be obstructed. Thus, the essence of the mind is inherently pure and true. Because it is pure, it is not defiled; because it is true, it is not false. Because it is not false, it is unchanging; because it is not defiled, it is eternally bright. This is what is meant by the "wondrously perfect mind. It is the source of all dharmas, the root of all phenomena. It is the ultimate reality of the Buddhas and the fundamental nature of sentient beings. It is the pivot of the three realms and the foundation of the six paths. It is the treasury of the ten thousand virtues and the sovereign of the myriad practices. It is the gate of liberation for all Bodhisattvas and the path traversed by all sages. It is the mirror of the Tathāgatas and the eye of the Buddhas. It is the root of the Dharma-body and the source of the Nirmanakaya. It is the essence of the *dharmadhātu* and the substance of the *tathatā*. It is the mother of all Buddhas and the father of all sentient beings. It is the master of the three bodies and the lord of the four wisdoms. It is the sovereign of the ten directions and the king of the three times. It is the treasure of the three jewels and the foundation of the four truths. It is the light of the sun and moon and the wind of the great earth. It is the water of the ocean and the fire of the sun. It is the air of space and the earth of the world. It is the sound of the drum and the fragrance of the incense. It is the flavor of the ambrosia and the touch of the lotus. It is the color of the gold and the form of the mountain. It is the principle of the Middle Way and the function of the Great Vehicle. It is the gate of the *samādhi* and the treasury of the *dhāraṇī*. It is the power of the *vidyā* and the seal of the *mudrā*. It is the mantra of the Buddha and the mudrā of the Dharma. It is the compassion of the Sangha and the merit of the field. It is the vow of the Bodhisattva and the practice of the Śrāvaka. It is the wisdom of the Pratyekabuddha and the faith of the ordinary person. It is the seed of the noble and the sprout of the holy. It is the earth of the world, sustaining all without bias. It is the sound of the drum, rousing the slumbering. It is the fragrance of the incense, spreading through the distant and the near. It is the flavor of the ambrosia, nourishing the starving. It is the touch of the lotus, quenching the heat. It is the color of the gold, beautifying the physical form. It is the form of the mountain, making the mind firm. It is the principle of the Middle Way, departing from extremes. It is the function of the Great Vehicle, ferrying all to the other shore. It is the gate of *samādhi*, penetrating the deep. It is the treasury of *dhāraṇī*, retaining the extensive. It is the power of *vidyā*, overcoming obstacles. It is the seal of *mudrā*, concentrating the spirit. It is the mantra of the Buddha, the voice of the Dharma. It is the mudrā of the Dharma, the gesture of the Sangha. It is the compassion of the Sangha, the benevolence of the world. It is the merit of the field, the virtue of the Path. It is the vow of the Bodhisattva, the conduct of the Śrāvaka. It is the wisdom of the Pratyekabuddha, the faith of the ordinary person. It is the seed of the noble, the bud of the saint. It is the fruit of the Path, the blossom of the Dharma. It is the light of the sun and moon, shining upon the dark. It is the wind of the great earth, dispersing the web of confusion. It is the water of the ocean, rinsing the grime of suffering. It is the fire of the sun, incinerating the brushwood of action. It is the air of space, filling all without limit. It is the earth of the world, bearing all without discrimination. It is the sound of the drum, stirring the dormant. It is the fragrance of the incense, reaching both the remote and the proximate. It is the flavor of the ambrosia, fulfilling those who hunger. It is the touch of the lotus, removing the fever. It is the color of the gold, adorning the person. It is the form of the mountain, steadying the heart. It is the principle of the Middle Way, free from the two extremes. It is the function of the Great Vehicle, delivering all beings. It is the gate of *samādhi*, entering the profound mystery. It is the treasury of *dhāraṇī*, maintaining the vast teachings. It is the power of *vidyā*, vanquishing the maras. It is the seal of *mudrā*, unifying the mental faculties. It is the mantra of the Buddha, the utterance of the Dharma. It is the mudrā of the Dharma, the sign of the Sangha. It is the compassion of the Sangha, the grace of the world. It is the merit of the field, the excellence of the Path. It is the vow of the Bodhisattva, the discipline of the Śrāvaka. It is the wisdom of the Pratyekabuddha, the devotion of the ordinary person. It is the seed of the noble, the shoot of the sage. It is the fruit of the Path, the bloom of the Dharma. It is the light of the sun and moon, illuminating the gloom. It is the wind of the great earth, tearing asunder the mesh of delusion. It is the water of the ocean, purging the filth of afflictions. It is the fire of the sun, reducing the thicket of karma to ashes. It is the air of space, pervading everywhere without blockage. It is the earth of the world, supporting all without favoritism. It is the sound of the drum, awakening the sleepers. It is the fragrance of the incense, diffusing through the far and the near. It is the flavor of the ambrosia, satisfying the famished. It is the touch of the lotus, cooling the inflamed. It is the color of the gold, embellishing the body. It is the form of the mountain, making the mind stable. It is the principle of the Middle Way, transcending
It is not by advancing that one attains clarity; rather, through the vigor of clear wisdom, one accomplishes these pure practices, and thus it is called the mind of vigor.
△ Fourth is the mind of wisdom:
when the essence of the mind manifests before one, being purely characterized by wisdom, it is named the dwelling of the mind of wisdom.
By means of the first three stages, one first severs the obstacle of the manifest: because the faculties and objects do not encounter one another, and deluded thoughts are extinguished.
Next, one severs the obstacle of retribution: because the five aggregates, twelve bases, and eighteen elements can no longer act as obstructions.

Third, one severs the obstacle of afflictions: because beginningless habitual tendencies merge into a single, pervasive spiritual clarity. Now that these three obstacles have been eliminated, it is purely wisdom. Therefore—
This is called the Abiding of the Mind of Wisdom (hui-xin-zhu).

△ Fifth, the Abiding of the Mind of Samādhi (ding-xin): To maintain the clarity of wisdom so that it is pervasive, tranquil, profound, and eternally concentrated is called the Abiding of the Mind of Samādhi.
By means of wisdom, clarity is sustained; this clarity is able to uphold samādhi. "Pervasive" refers to the function of wisdom, while "eternally concentrated" refers to the essence of samādhi.
Furthermore, because concentration is maintained by means of clarity, it is called "the mind dwelling in concentration. △ Sixth, the Mind of Non-retrogression:
When concentration gives rise to illumination and the luminous nature penetrates deeply such that there is only progress and no regression, it is called the "Mind of Non-retrogression."

The former was wisdom born of concentration; now it is insight born of concentration. This insight is clarity (*vidyā*). By means of this clear insight, one penetrates deeply to illuminate the principle;
because there is progress and no regression, it is called the "Mind of Non-retrogression. △ Seventh, the Mind that Protects the Dharma.

The mind advances with composure, maintaining its state without loss; the interfusion of the vital energy (*dhātu*) of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions is called the "mind that protects the Dharma.
In the preceding initial stage, one perceived the principle alone, yet the three obstacles were not severed and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) were not eliminated.

Therefore, one had not yet attained connection with the flow of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-water, and the ground of the mind was not at peace. Now, however, the mind advances toward the wondrous principle. The three...
Obstacles have been severed and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) have been eliminated; furthermore, one attains the dual support of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).

Therefore, one enters into communion with the portion of the Tathāgata’s essence, and the mind-ground becomes tranquil. Because this concentration and wisdom maintain [the state] without loss, it is called the "mind that protects the Dharma.
△ Eighth, the Mind of Dedication (*pariṇāmanā-citta*).
The clarity of awakening maintains itself through its wondrous power (up to) the mutual penetration of layers upon layers, which is called the mind of dedication (*pariṇāmanā-citta*).
"Dedication" means turning the mind toward the Buddha. Because one has hitherto been single-mindedly attached to the self, one has treated the Buddha and oneself as two separate entities.
Now, by means of the power of concentration and wisdom, one provides sustenance to the vital energy of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions.
Through the transition of stages, one realizes that this mind is the Buddha and the Buddha is this mind; thus, mind and Buddha are merged into one. Therefore, it is said:
"Awakened clarity maintains [itself]. Furthermore, what is called "maintaining" refers precisely to the non-duality of stillness and illumination.
Stillness itself is illumination; thus it is said that one turns toward the Buddha’s compassionate light. Illumination itself is stillness; thus it is said that one dwells securely facing the Buddha.
Since stillness and illumination are non-dual, they can manifest and enter into one another, like two mirrors reflecting each other so that wondrous images appear in infinite layers.
Therefore, it is called the mind of dedication (*pariṇāmanā-citta*). △ Ninth, the mind of ethical discipline (*śīla-citta*):
The light of the mind secretly turns back to protect [the Buddha], remaining constantly concentrated until one attains non-forgetfulness; this is called abiding in the mind of ethical discipline.

Because one first beheld one’s own mind previously, one had not yet attained the *dharmatā*. Later, by connecting with the portion of the Tathāgata’s power, one has already attained the *dharmatā*, yet the view of a Buddha still persists.
Next, by turning back the compassionate light of the Buddha, the view of a Buddha dissolves, and there is a silent, solitary illumination.
Therefore it is said: "Previously one dwelt facing the Buddha; now the light of the mind turns inward in secret, and thus the illumination..."

It cannot be established. Reaching this point, both the view of Buddha and the view of phenomena are forgotten; causal nature and resultant nature are utterly severed. Pure awareness alone is perfected;
therefore it is said that one attains the Buddha’s eternal stillness and supreme, wondrous purity. This is precisely the field of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
This is extremely difficult to attain. As it is said: "Before withered trees and craggy cliffs, mistaken paths abound; one must be most careful.
Therefore, it is called the Abiding of the Mind in Precepts. △ Tenth, the Mind of Vows.
Abiding in the mastery of precepts, one is able to travel throughout the ten directions; wherever one goes, it accords with one's vows—this is called the dwelling of the vow-mind.
Furthermore, having reached the field of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and attained the mind of precepts, there is no longer any hindrance.

When there is no hindrance, then when a Hu comes, a Hu appears; when a Han comes, a Han appears. At the gateway of sound and form, one is sovereign over both the adverse and the favorable throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
The realm arises according to one's vows; therefore, it is called the dwelling of the vow-mind. Question:
Since the mind has no place of dwelling, why is the stage of the ten faiths also called a "dwelling"? Answer: "Dwelling" refers to the state where the mind’s intention does not shift.

It is like a student who, having not yet seen what is essential, must see it; having not yet realized what is essential, must realize it—once they have seen and realized it, [the intention is fulfilled].

It is finished. The essential point lies in corresponding with the place of awakening and establishing one's footing in the place of seeing. As the ancient masters said: "To attain this matter is like leaning against Mount Tai;
how could it possibly be a mere empty abstraction? This is precisely the teaching-gate of the Sudden School:

once awakened, one awakens forever; once seen, one sees forever. It is not like the Gradual Teaching, where one must first hear the Buddha’s words before believing, or see the Buddha’s physical marks before seeing [the truth].

Only then can one truly believe that, having nothing of one's own to attain, one relies upon the gradual stages of others. This is precisely what it means to see for oneself and to accept for oneself.

Where there is acceptance, there is faith; where there is faith, there is abiding. Therefore, within the Ten Faiths, abiding is defined in terms of the place of dwelling, while within the subsequent Ten Abidings, abiding is defined in terms of the place of faith.
Generally speaking, although faith and abiding are distinguished, their meaning is one and the same; they do not differ except in the degree of clarity and illumination.
This concludes the contemplation of principle. △ Third, the stages of abiding. First, the Abiding of Resolving the Mind.
Ānanda, this good man... [up to] ...perfectly accomplishing the one mind is called the Abiding of Resolving the Mind.
"Expedient means" (*upāya*) is precisely wisdom (*prajñā*). "The essence of mind" (*citta-sāra*) is precisely the wondrous.

This means that the aforementioned ten minds are all developed through wondrous wisdom, such that one perceives the wondrousness of the essence of mind; it does not mean that these ten minds truly exist as separate entities.

Rather, the single mind is the reality, while the ten functions are the wondrous. Because the true mind is revealed through these ten functions, it is called "perfectly accomplished" (*pariniṣpanna*). By virtue of this reality—
The mind possesses these ten functions; therefore, it is called "interpenetration. This is the sovereign function wherein the one and the many mutually accommodate one another.

When a practitioner perceives this principle, they abide therein; hence, it is named the Stage of Initial Resolve (Prathamacittotpādavihāra). 2. The Stage of Cultivating the Ground (Caryāpratipattiviṣayavihāra).
The illumination within the mind is like pure lapis lazuli (up to: treading upon this to establish the ground is called the Dwelling of Cultivating the Ground (*kṣitigata-vihāra*).

This means that one has previously perceived this mind and this principle; from this, the wondrous function is illuminated, which is metaphorically likened to lapis lazuli in which refined gold appears within.
Refined gold is a metaphor for the principle, and lapis lazuli is a metaphor for the mind. The illumination of this principle within the mind is precisely based upon [this].
Because one governs the mind according to this principle, it is called the Stage of Governing the Ground (*bhūmi-vyavasthāna*). △ Third, the Stage of Cultivation (*caryā-pratipatti-vyavasthāna*):
When both the mind-ground and its cognitive engagement become clearly manifest, and one traverses the ten directions without obstruction, it is called the Stage of Cultivation.
To govern the mind through principle, the ground of the mind engages with cognition; to govern conduct through wisdom, both become clearly understood.

For while cognition has its limits, the application of wisdom is inexhaustible. Thus, one who traverses the ten directions without obstruction or hindrance has attained the function of all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñatā*). Furthermore, the "ten directions" refers to the ten realms (*daśadhātu*). [The four] noble...

The four elements and the six realms of ordinary beings—when the practitioner fully realizes that this mind neither increases when in the state of a sage nor decreases when among ordinary beings, it is equal in every thought-moment and does not give rise to the mark of cognition. To maintain this is what constitutes cultivation;
therefore, it is called the "Abode of Cultivation. △ Fourth, the Abode of Noble Birth.
When one’s practice becomes identical to that of the Buddha and one receives the Buddha’s portion of spiritual influence, this is called the Stage of Birth in the Noble Lineage of the Tathāgata.

As the ancient masters said: "It is better to be a teacher of the mind than to have the mind as one's teacher. This is because what was previously attained remains in its former state and lacks the power of self-mastery;

such a person is still one who takes the mind as their teacher. Now, as one's practice is identical to the Buddha's and one receives the Buddha’s portion of spiritual influence, [one has transcended this].
There is a stage of self-power, wherein one acts as a master of one's own mind. It is like the intermediate state being (*antarābhava*) who seeks out its own parents.

When the practitioner attains this knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), they penetrate the fruit of Buddhahood through their own power; this is called the Stage of Noble Birth (*janmaja-vihāra*).
△ Fifth, the Stage of Fulfillment of Skillful Means (*upāyasaṃpad-vihāra*).
Having already entered the womb of the Way and personally received the lineage of the Awakened One (up to) being named the Stage of the Perfection of Expedient Means:
Now, since one has already received the Buddha’s vital energy and been born into the womb of the Way, one shall naturally possess all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*) as a scion of the Buddha.
This all-encompassing wisdom consists precisely of the two wisdoms of the provisional and the real. One's own practice is the real; transforming others is the provisional.
This is expedient means (*upāya*). When a practitioner attains this skillful means, it is likened to a person whose physical features are complete and without deficiency.
For this principle is fundamentally inherent from the outset; therefore, it is called the "Abiding in the Fulfillment of Expedient Means. 6. The Abiding in the Right Mind (*samyak-citta-vihāra*).
Their physical appearance is like that of a Buddha and their mental characteristics are likewise;
this is called the "Abode of the Right Mind. What was previously described regarding the signs of the womb is a metaphor for the skillful means (*upāya*).

The practitioner who attains these skillful means transcends the stage of ordinary beings and transcends the stages of the two vehicles, being born into the womb of the Buddha. Once born into the Buddha-womb, one naturally comes to resemble the Buddha's form.
Regarding the Buddha, it is said that his "appearance is like that of the Buddha. Now, if his outward appearance is like the Buddha’s, how could his inner mind not be so?
Therefore, it is said that "the characteristics of the mind are also the same. Furthermore, if the outward appearance is like the Buddha’s, one must manifest a countenance of compassion and patience;

if the inner mind is like the Buddha’s, one must possess the wisdom of compassionate vows. Because the internal and external are as one, it is called the Stage of Abiding in the Right Mind (*samyak-citta-vihāra*). △
Seventh is the stage of non-retrogression (*avivarta-sthāna*). When body and mind are unified and daily growth occurs, it is called the stage of non-retrogression.

Regarding the skillful means (*upāya*) of the initial resolve, there is both self-cultivation and the transformation of others. In transforming others, one externally manifests compassionate conduct; in self-cultivation, one internally...

The mind is filled with fulfillment. This self-benefit and benefit for others results in such signs. Now, one’s practice follows the turning of the Buddha’s wheel, and transformation is accomplished in tandem with it.
Therefore, the internal and external are harmoniously integrated, and body and mind are as one. By maintaining this, there is progress and no regression;
hence, it is called the Stage of Non-regression (*avinivartanīya-vihāra*). 8. The Stage of Youthful Truth (*kumārabhūta-vihāra*).
The simultaneous perfection of the ten bodies and their spiritual characteristics is called the Stage of Youthful Truth (*kumārabhūmi*).

As for the "ten bodies," they are: the Body of Enlightenment (*bodhi-kāya*), the Body of Vow (*praṇidhāna-kāya*), the Transformation Body (*nirmāṇa-kāya*), the Body of Sustaining Power (*baladhāraṇa-kāya*), the Ornamented Body (*vyūha-kāya*), the Body of Majestic Power (*anubhāva-kāya*), the Mind-born Body (*manomaya-kāya*), the Body of Merit (*puṇya-kāya*), the Dharma Body (*dharma-kāya*), and the Wisdom Body (*jñāna-kāya*). Furthermore, by "spiritual characteristics" (*liṅga*) is meant:
The ten aforementioned types are the spiritual manifestations within the Dharmakāya. Furthermore, regarding the term "child" (tóng): all those under fifteen years of age are called children;

here, however, it refers to one who has attained physical form. Although the practitioner who cultivates these skillful means has not yet reached the level of a Buddha, [they are nonetheless so designated].
Yet, in a single thought-moment, one is able to fully possess the ten kinds of sovereign and wondrous responses, just as the features within a womb are fully formed.
Therefore, it is called the Stage of Youthful Truth (*kumārabhūmi*). △ Ninth: The Stage of the Dharma Prince (*dharmarājaputra-bhūmi*).
The stage of being formed and having emerged from the womb is called the "Abode of the Prince," because one is now a true child of the Buddha.

Regarding "being formed and having emerged from the womb": previously, because one was enveloped by ignorance (*avidyā*) and the vital breath (*prāṇa*) was not yet sufficient, one was likened to not yet having emerged from the womb.
Now, however, ignorance has been exhausted and the body of wisdom (*jñānakāya*) is fully matured; this is likened to being formed and having emerged from the womb. This is "true" [birth].

Those who are sons of the Buddha possess the full complement of virtuous marks and have attained the perfection of partial awakening; they are worthy to serve as the lineage of the sages and to perpetuate the Triple Gem.
Therefore, this stage is called the "Abode of the Dharma Prince."
From the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*) up to the stage of Cultivation (*prayoga-vihāra*), it is the inclusion of the fruit within the cause;

this is because, like the first appearance of the new moon, one perceives the whole body [of the Buddha-nature]. Because one has attained a semblance of awakening, one believes that this very mind is the Buddha.

However, because the ground of beginningless ignorance (*anādikālikā-avidyā-āśraya-bhūmi*) has not yet been severed, from the stage of Noble Birth (*janma-kula-vihāra*) onwards, it is the inclusion of the cause within the fruit, just as at the beginning...
Because the moon of the seventh and eighth nights gradually becomes full, one awakens through the attainment of partial realization and dwells within the Buddha-body, nurturing the holy embryo.
Thus, reaching the present ninth dwelling, one emerges from the womb of the aggregates (*skandha-garbha*) and attains the dwelling of a Dharma Prince (*dharmarāja-putra*).
This is like the moon of the sixteenth night, which is without deficiency; it is because the perfect essence of reality (*tattva*) is free from all obstructions. Furthermore, as previously stated:
The nature of wisdom is perfectly luminous, adorning the realms of the ten directions; this is the meaning of "perfect fusion" (*yuanrong*).

Yet, perfect fusion does not obstruct sequential progression (*xingbu*). Consequently, from the essence arises function: in each stage one realizes the principle and in each stage one eliminates hindrances, until ultimate enlightenment is reached and ignorance is finally exhausted;
this is the meaning of "sequential progression. Furthermore, sequential progression does not obstruct perfect fusion. Therefore, by means of this...

Subsuming function into essence, every stage is the Truth; every stage may be ascended until one reaches Wondrous Enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi*), thereby thoroughly exhausting the source of all phenomena.

However, as the various sūtras differ according to the sequence of their teachings, one need not force them into artificial alignment or synthesis, lest the fundamental intent of the original scriptures be compromised.
△ Ten: The Stage of Consecration (*abhiṣeka-vihāra*).

"Manifesting the completion of the person, like a great king of a country" (up to) "the stage of consecration (*abhiṣeka-vihāra*), which is named 'consecration,' because it manifests the completion of the person.
The single phrase "manifesting the completion of the person" is the general statement; the following section, "like a great king of a country," provides the detailed explanation of its fulfillment.

"Manifesting" (*biao*) means to extol their virtuous deeds and to reveal their inherent nature. As the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "This is truly my son, and I am truly his father. This is the meaning of the present text.
It is said: "When that Kṣatriya king’s crown prince has grown to maturity and the rites of consecration are set forth, this signifies his inherent nature.
Furthermore, I now possess abundant gold, silver, and rare treasures, filling my treasuries; as for their quantity therein—"
"You must fully understand all that ought to be received and given. Now, the text says: "It is like a great king of a nation who entrusts all state affairs to his crown prince;
this is to extol his virtuous achievements. Furthermore, regarding the presentation of the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
"The crown prince born of a Wheel-Turning Sage King has a mother who is the principal queen, and his physical marks are complete."

Seated upon a precious white elephant throne of exquisite gold, with a great lattice-canopy spread above and various musical instruments playing, he takes the waters of the four great oceans and places them within a golden vase.
The king holds this vase and pours it over the crown of the prince’s head; at that moment, he is said to have received the royal office.
It is the same when a Bodhisattva receives his office: because the waters of the wisdom of all Buddhas are poured over his crown.
He is named the Bodhisattva who has received the office of Great Wisdom. This constitutes the array of the consecration; therefore, it is called the Stage of Consecration (*abhiṣeka-vihāra*).
△ Fourth, the stages of practice (*caryā-vasthā*): first, the Practice of Joy (*pramuditā-caryā*).
Ānanda, once these good men have become sons of the Buddha (up to the point where they are said to be) "in accord with the ten directions," it is called the Practice of Joy.

"Practice" (*xing*) refers to function (*yòng*). It carries the meaning of functional application. This is because, although the essence has been attained through what preceded, its function has not yet been attained.

Therefore, the phase of being in the womb is used as a metaphor for nurturing. Now that the nurturing is complete, one is able to give rise to the wondrous function of True Suchness (Tathatā), and thus there is joy.
Because what was previously attained consisted of only a single faculty and a single wisdom, the immeasurable wisdom had not yet been acquired;

therefore, the stage of childhood is used as a metaphor for training and growth. Now that the training and growth are fully accomplished, one is endowed with the immeasurable, wondrous [wisdom] of the Tathāgatas.
One rejoices because of virtue. Due to what was previously attained, there was a separation between the noble and the ordinary, and one was not equal to a Buddha;
since one had not yet attained compliance with the ten directions, the analogy of a crown prince who has not yet received the office of consecration was used.

Now that the office of consecration has been received, one attains compliance with the ten directions and thus rejoices; therefore, it is called the "Joyful Practice. △ Second, the "Beneficial Practice."
Being well able to benefit and profit all sentient beings is called "Beneficial Conduct" (Upakāra-caryā).
Furthermore, since there are immeasurable sublime virtues, they immediately constitute immeasurable sublime functions.
Thus, to accord with the ten directions is "benefit" (rā), and for all to receive transformation is "profit" (ya); hence it is named "Beneficial Conduct. △ Third, Non-Anger (A-krodha).
The practice of freedom from resentment: to awaken oneself and awaken others without encountering opposition is called the practice of freedom from anger and resentment.
If there is a self, there is an other; if there is awakening, there is non-awakening. Therefore, opposition is frequent. Since it is frequent...
To resist and reject is to have contention and attachment; it is to harbor anger and resentment. Now, it is not so.
One is enlightened by oneself, and one enlightens others—this is enlightenment. Enlightenment is one; there is no self and no other, no enlightenment and no non-enlightenment.
In this single path of purity, there is no resistance or rejection. Since there is no resistance or rejection, there is no contention or attachment, nor is there any anger or resentment.
Therefore, it is called the practice free from anger and resentment. △ Fourth is the inexhaustible practice.

Its various manifestations arise throughout the limits of the future, being equal across the three periods of time and pervasive throughout the ten directions; this is called the inexhaustible practice.
"Arising according to species" refers to horizontal pervasiveness. "Reaching the limits of the future" refers to vertical exhaustion.

By means of this vertical exhaustion of the three periods of time and horizontal pervasion of the ten directions, one transforms beings according to their types; that one is able to penetrate them all is because one thoroughly understands them as empty and quiescent.
Through the wisdom of emptiness and quiescence, manifesting bodies that accord with each type constitutes inexhaustibility. Therefore...
This is called the practice of inexhaustibility. △ Fifth is the practice of being free from delusion and confusion.
To attain non-erroneousness regarding all the various dharma-gates that are unified as one is called the practice of being free from delusion and confusion.
The Bodhisattva manifests various bodies and necessarily preaches various dharmas. Though the dharmas are manifold, their principle is without divergence.
Since the principle is without divergence, these manifestations are non-manifestations. Since manifestations are non-manifestations, how could there be any bodily marks to which one might cling?
Since the principle is without divergence, how could there be any mental marks to be calculated? For the marks of the mind and the marks of the body are one and the same.
It is entirely empty; therefore, it is said that "all things are identical. To be identical means to return together to the state of non-thought (*amanyana*).

Since thought is itself non-thought, how could there be deluded or chaotic conceptions? Hence, it is called the practice of being free from delusion and confusion. △ Sixth, the Practice of Good Manifestation.
Thus, within the identical, a multitude of differences manifests; each distinct characteristic is perceived individually, yet they are all equally termed "well-manifested" (*suvyakta*).

Previously, the immeasurable was treated as one, and thus it was said that "all are identical. Now, the one is treated as the immeasurable, and thus it is said that "differences manifest within the identical.
These differences are different in terms of phenomena (*dharma*), but not different in terms of principle (*tattva*); therefore, it is said that "each is perceived individually."
"Identical. Identical means identical with principle (*li*), not identical with phenomena (*shi*). Therefore it is said: "Within identity, a multitude of differences is manifested.
For manifestation as a body is a phenomenal characteristic and thus constitutes difference; manifestation as teaching is a characteristic of principle and thus constitutes identity.

Because the characteristics of principle are inexhaustible, the characteristics of phenomena are likewise inexhaustible. Although phenomena and principle are inexhaustible, they are ultimately not separate from one another.
It is manifested by fundamental wisdom; therefore, it is called the practice of "Good Manifestation. △ Seventh, the Practice of Non-Attachment:
Thus, extending even to the empty space of the ten directions, [to be] without mutual obstruction is called the Practice of Non-Attachment.
The phrase "thus" (evam) refers back to the preceding meaning. In that preceding meaning, it was explained that within the totality of all things being identical, diversity manifests;
hence, it is said "thus. However, this merely describes diversity manifesting within unity; it does not yet describe diversity manifesting within diversity.

Now, it is taught that the ten directions manifest within every single object, and every single object manifests the ten directions; this is precisely diversity manifesting within diversity. Therefore, it is said:

Furthermore, the manifestation of the present objects of the ten directions within [the mind] is the manifestation of the small within the great; the manifestation of those objects throughout the ten directions is the manifestation of the great within the small.
Although the small and the great differ, the essence of wisdom is sovereign; therefore, it is called the Practice of Non-Attachment.
△ 8. The Practice of Reverence.
All various manifestations that appear before one are called the "Practice of Reverence" (*gurukāra-caryā*) within the first *pāramitā*.
Thus far, whether identical or different, small or great, physical or verbal, principle or phenomenon—of all such varieties...
The manifestation of these seeds is all accomplished through the unimpeded wisdom of *prajñā*. As for *pāramitā*, it is translated as "reaching the other shore.
This means that this unimpeded wisdom is the foremost method for reaching the other shore.
Since it is extremely difficult to attain such a stage, it is called the "practice of reverence. △ Ninth, the practice of wholesome dharmas.
Such perfect interfusion can accomplish the norms of the Buddhas of the ten directions; this is called the practice of wholesome dharmas.
Question: How can one perceive this perfect interfusion? Answer: It is like the light of pearls in Indra’s net, which mutually pervades and mutually encompasses one another.

This unimpeded wisdom is also characterized by mutual pervasion and mutual inclusion; a single stage universally encompasses all stages, and each of those stages likewise universally encompasses all others.
Therefore, it is called "perfectly interfused" (*yuánróng*). By means of this perfectly interfused dharma-gate, every single Buddha and Tathāgata follows this as the rule for their practice;
because it is the most excellent of wholesome dharmas, it is named the "Practice of Wholesome Dharmas. △ Ten Truths.
Practice. Each and every one is pure, untainted, the single true, unconditioned nature that is inherently so; therefore, it is called "True Practice.

This term collectively encompasses all the aforementioned stages. There is no distinction between these stages; they are solely the inherent virtue and function of the self-nature of True Suchness (Tathatā).
How is this clarified? Because its essence is precisely *tathatā* (suchness), it is called "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*).

Because its function is precisely the self-nature (*svabhāva*), it is called "original. Since the former are all functions of the self-nature, they are seen as identical throughout the ten directions.
Since all that precedes is the manifestation of True Suchness (tathatā), one perceives the wondrous within a single atom. That which is wondrous is not the atom;

that which is identical is not the realm. It is, in its entirety, the singular, perfectly interfused characteristic of the Great Dharma-realm. At every step it is reality; at every point it is the Way.
Therefore, it is called "True Practice. Question:
Since this is the single, true, and perfectly interfused Dharma-realm, why are there further distinctions of stages and characteristics? Answer: It is like the following analogy:
True Suchness is the eye; its self-nature is light. When the cataract is removed, the nature is naturally luminous, and the eye is naturally pure.
However, the cataracts are not removed instantaneously; they must be removed gradually. Therefore, the distinctions between the stages [of practice] are taught.

Clarity is not attained gradually; it must be attained instantaneously. Therefore, the "perfect interfusion without obstruction" is taught. This perfect interfusion without obstruction is spoken of in reference to one with pure vision.
The distinctions between the stages are spoken of in reference to those at the initial stage of skillful means. Question: If that is so, regarding the eye...
"Are these two distinct? He replied: "Because fools engage in false conceptualization, they perceive duality; because the wise have thorough realization, they perceive non-duality.
Therefore, the wise eliminate the affliction but do not eliminate the phenomenon; the foolish eliminate the phenomenon but do not eliminate the affliction.
This is precisely the difference between what the wise and the foolish employ. 5. The Stage of Dedication (Pariṇāmanā).
"Ānanda, these good men... (up to)... pure, clean, and refined, far removed from all lingering afflictions.

The passage "Ānanda" and below serves as a general conclusion to the meaning of the preceding stages. The phrase "perfected in supernormal powers" concludes the ten practices (*caryā*), for these practices are supernormal powers.
The phrase "accomplishing the work of Buddhahood" concludes the ten abidings (*vihāra*), for these abidings bring the task to completion. "Pure" [refers to the purity of the ten faiths].

The phrase "the refined and true single phrase" concludes the Ten Faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*), for faith is the true mind (*tathatā-citta*). The phrase "far removed from all lingering afflictions" concludes the Stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-jñāna-bhūmi*);

because the remaining physical substance is manifest before one, it will no longer continue to take birth. Furthermore, Dry Wisdom is wisdom (*jñāna*), while the Ten Faiths are virtue (*guṇa*), the Ten Abidings (*daśa-vihāra*) are principle (*li*), and the Ten Practices (*daśa-caryā*) are conduct (*caryā*).
These—principle, wisdom, conduct, and virtue—are all present concurrently in every stage; they are not exclusive [to any one].
The stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*) consists of solitary insight without the nourishing development of practice;
it possesses wisdom alone, while the remaining stages—Faith, Abiding, and Practice—are each fulfilled and accomplished one by one. This is beyond the reach of conceptual deliberation.
Yet, if one observes with the correct eye, these practices and so forth still belong to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and are not the truly ultimate *tathatā*. How is this made clear? It is because...
The true mind is without marks; to have faith is to deviate from it. True principle is formless; to have a dwelling place is to miss it.
True practice is non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*); that which is conditioned is illusion. True wisdom is without knowing; that which knows is delusion.

Since the ground of the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) does not admit even a speck of dust, how could it tolerate so many designations? Therefore, know that the clarity of "practice" and so forth belongs to the conditioned and is not [the ultimate].
This is the true principle of True Suchness (*tathatā*). Indeed, within the gateway of the myriad practices (*sādhana*), one must not abandon a single dharma;

it is like an oar in midstream—until the shore is reached, it simply cannot be dispensed with. Thus, one knows that these practices for investigating the truth, severing delusions, exhausting the principles, and perfecting one's nature are absolutely indispensable.
Therefore, after the practices are fulfilled, one should give rise to the mind of dedication (*pariṇāmanā-citta*) and dedicate [the merit].

The minds of the preceding stages were directed toward the path to *nirvāṇa*. Why is this? Because the preceding factors such as faith (*śraddhā*) and so forth were "proceeding forward," whereas the present mind of dedication (*pariṇāmanā-citta*) is "returning back.
It turns from the ultimate toward the conventional, and turns from wisdom (*prajñā*) toward compassion (*karuṇā*).

This is entirely the refinement of this mind until it reaches the stage of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-avasthā*). 1. Saving and Protecting All Sentient Beings and Causing Them to Depart from the Multitudes [of Suffering].
The dedication of the mark of birth:
one should deliver sentient beings while extinguishing all marks of the perfections (up to the dedication of being detached from the mark of sentient beings).

Originally, when a bodhisattva practices, their primary task is to deliver sentient beings; however, if they perceive that there are sentient beings to be delivered, [they have not yet attained true dedication].
To instead treat it as the "characterized" (*lakṣya*) is untenable; therefore, it is said that one should deliver sentient beings while extinguishing the notion of "delivering.
Furthermore, if one perceives a "birthless" state as something to be delivered, this clearly becomes the "characterizer" (*lakṣaṇa*), which is likewise untenable;

therefore, it is said that one should turn the unconditioned mind toward the path to Nirvāṇa. "Path" (*mārga*) refers to the Way; "Nir" (*nir*) means birthless, and "vāṇa" (*vāṇa*) means non-extinction. This is the general explanation.

This is the path of neither arising nor ceasing. Because there is fundamentally no arising, it is said that there is no nirvana; because there is fundamentally no ceasing, it is said that one rescues and protects sentient beings. This is non-arising; therefore, it is said that [the Bodhisattva] protects and delivers sentient beings. The Bodhisattva thus delivers beings and thus protects sentient beings, yet does not perceive the mark of a sentient being; therefore, it is said that they are detached from the mark of a sentient being.

Generally, in the preceding ten practices, there was an exposition of phenomena and principles, and an exposition of the sense-fields (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*), which remained largely stuck on the side of substantiality and could not be integrated into a single whole.
In this dedication, principle and phenomenon are one; the ultimate and the conventional are one; wisdom and compassion are one; essence and function are one.
All are profoundly unified within a single principle, forged into a seamless whole; thus it is called "dedication.
The general meaning is simply to turn that one end toward this side for practice. Only when practice reaches the point of total perfection does it truly fulfill the intent of dedication.
The following sections are modeled after this. △ Second, the Dedication of Non-Destruction (*akṣaya-pariṇāmanā*).
To destroy that which is destructible and to remain far removed from all forms of detachment is called the Dedication of Non-Destruction.
That which is "destructible" refers to the objects of perception (*ālambana-viṣaya*). That which is "to be detached from" refers to the perceiving mind (*ālambaka-citta*).

Furthermore, if one discusses the mind that acts as the perceiver—whether it be described in terms of various principles, wisdom, the profound, or the subtle—all such things belong to the perceiver and are thus subject to abandonment.

If one discusses the objects that are perceived—whether they be various manifested sensory realms or lands, appearing as identical or different—all such things belong to the perceived and are thus subject to destruction. From this, one should know that all conditioned activities...
All phenomena are subject to destruction, whereas the Way of True Permanence is indestructible.
By this reasoning, all thoughts and mental deliberations are things that can be abandoned, whereas the nature of True Suchness (Tathatā) is beyond abandonment.
That which is destroyed cannot be destroyed; that which is detached from cannot be detached from. This is true indestructibility. Therefore, it is called the "dedication of non-destruction.
△ Third, the dedication equal to all Buddhas.
The fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*) is serene and its realization is equal to the realization of the Buddhas;
this is called the dedication that is equal to all Buddhas. What was previously described as the indestructible nature is precisely one's own fundamental awakening.

This fundamental awakening is serene and devoid of destruction or non-destruction, separation or non-separation, because it is, in its entirety, a single awakening. When there is awakening, one is directed toward the Buddha. Since they are identical...
Regarding the Buddha, there is neither saint nor ordinary person, neither self nor other; it is identical with all, primordially equal.
Therefore, it is called the "Dedication Equal to All Buddhas. △ Fourth, the Dedication Reaching All Places.
The phrase "the essence of purity and truth illuminates, such that the ground is like the Buddha-ground" refers to the dedication known as "reaching all places.

Here, "essence of purity and truth" refers to wisdom (*jñāna*), and "Buddha-ground" refers to principle (*tattva*). Since the former has already become identical to the Buddha, it follows that the Buddha’s wisdom is luminous.
Since the Buddha’s wisdom is already luminous, whatever he perceives is nothing other than this principle. Having perceived this principle, there is nowhere he goes that is not correct;
therefore, it is called the "Dedication Reaching All Places. △ Fifth is the Dedication of the Inexhaustible Treasury of Merit.
The mutual interpenetration of worlds and Tathāgatas, attaining non-obstruction, is called the Dedication of the Treasury of Inexhaustible Merit.
Because the preceding refinement of the true essence has brought forth illumination, body and land reflect one another.

Thus, sometimes the world manifests as the body of a Tathāgata, and sometimes the body of a Tathāgata manifests within the world; each does not borrow from the other, yet this constitutes their mutual interpenetration.
At times, the body of the land manifests as the body of the Tathāgata; at other times, the body of the Tathāgata manifests as the body of the land.

Each does not obstruct the other; this is non-obstruction. Non-obstruction is wisdom (*jñāna*); interpenetration is principle (*li*). When wisdom and principle are one, their wondrous function is inexhaustible;
therefore, it is called the Dedication to the Treasury of Inexhaustible Merit. 6. Accordance with Equality.
The dedication of roots of goodness.
Within the stages that are identical to the Buddha-ground, each [stage] is called the "dedication of roots of goodness in accordance with equality.
The Buddha-ground is the cause, and Nirvana is the fruit. The Buddha-ground is precisely the aforementioned manifestation of the refined and true, through which one perceives and attains this.

Principle (*li*). That is, based on this principle, one manifests it as practice (*xing*). Practice is able to lead toward the fruit (*guo*). Thus, by means of the myriad practices, one forms the cause;
by means of the myriad practices, one completes the fruit. The fruit does not transcend the cause, and the cause does not deviate from the fruit.
Therefore, it is called the "dedication of roots of goodness in accordance with equality. △ Seven: Accordance with the Equal Contemplation of All Sentient Beings.

Dedication. Since the true roots have been established, [the dedication] for the sake of sentient beings throughout the ten directions is called the "dedication of conforming to the equal contemplation of all sentient beings.
"True roots" refers to the attainment of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). By virtue of having previously realized the principle of equality, [all things] are of the very nature [of reality].
The accomplishment of virtue. Thereupon, one contemplates the sentient beings of the ten directions with equanimity; they are not separate entities, for all are my own fundamental nature.

Since I have attained this, I shall likewise bring sentient beings to fulfillment. Therefore, it is called the dedication of "contemplating all sentient beings with equanimity in accordance [with reality].
△ Eighth, the Dedication of the Aspect of True Suchness (Tathatā).
This is the dedication of all phenomena, which are free from all marks, up to the mark of *tathatā*.
Because one contemplates that all sentient beings are one’s own fundamental nature, it is said that "all phenomena are [the self].
Since they are all one’s own fundamental nature, they are not [separate] sentient beings; therefore, it is said to be "free from all marks. Nevertheless, if by means of equality...
Contemplate its nature. One does not cling even to the teaching, nor does one cling to being free from the teaching. Why? Because all things are suchness (*tathatā*).
Therefore, it is called the dedication of the mark of true suchness. △ Ninth: The Dedication of Liberation Without Bondage.
Truly attaining suchness, which is unimpeded throughout the ten directions, is called the dedication of liberation from bondage.
For where there is self, there is other; where there is a Buddha, there are sentient beings. Being bound by all phenomena, one perceives the ten directions as obstructed and limited.
Now, having attained that all things are suchness—neither Buddha nor sentient being, neither self nor other—one is liberated.
Originally liberated, one therefore perceives the ten directions without obstruction. Being unobstructed, there is no attachment; being without attachment, there is no bondage.
To be without bondage and without attachment is itself liberation. Therefore, it is called the Dedication of Unbound Liberation. 10.
The Dedication of the Infinite Realms of the Ten Dharma-Realms.
When the inherent virtues are perfectly fulfilled and the measure of the *dharmadhātu* is extinguished, it is called the "Dedication of the Immeasurable *Dharmadhātu*.
In the first stage (*bhūmi*), one perceives compassion within practice, for compassion is able to rescue and protect sentient beings.

In the second stage, one perceives wisdom within compassion, for wisdom is able to destroy [afflictions] and bring about detachment. In the third stage, one perceives principle within wisdom, for principle pervades all phenomena. In the fourth...
Fourth, seeing phenomena within principle, because phenomena pervade principle. Upon reaching the fifth stage, one enters the gateway of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
First, inexhaustible function is the principle Dharma-realm. Second, accord with equality is the phenomenon Dharma-realm.
Third, impartially contemplating all is the unimpeded Dharma-realm of principle and phenomenon. Fourth, both are non-existent...
This is precisely the dharma-realm of the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena (*shishi wuai fajie*). Now, in the tenth stage, the nature-virtues are perfectly accomplished;

the measure of the dharma-realm ceases, and only then is one unconditioned by anything. Only then does one emerge from the entanglements of the coverings (*gachen*). Only then does one correspond with the original dharma.

Since it is already the original dharma, how could there be any measurable quantity to be reckoned? Therefore, it is called the "Infinite Dedication of the Dharma-realm. 6. The Stage of Applied Practice (*prayogamārga*).
Ānanda, these good sons (up to) next accomplish the four kinds of wondrous and perfect preparatory practices (*prayoga*).
From the time they previously attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) through the third gradual stage, they have passed through the forty-one minds;

because they perceive the unobstructed interpenetration [of all phenomena], they now emerge from the ten stages of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) into the four preparatory practices, intending to verify the reality of their conduct.
However, the stages and positions of the various vehicles are all established according to the specific meaning of their respective teachings; they are not a universal discourse.
The *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*, being a definitive teaching of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), merely sets forth these stages and positions to testify to the reality of what has been attained.
Thus, a single stage encompasses all stages, and all stages are likewise encompassed within one. Therefore, regarding faith...
At the beginning of the stages, it is called "the perfect and wondrous unfolding"; at the conclusion of the stage of dedication, it is called "the perfect fulfillment of inherent virtues.
Now, in the four stages of applied practice, it is further called "wondrously perfect applied practice.

Discussing these traces, from beginning to end, the single character "perfect" (yuan) serves as the guiding eye, pointing out that which is primordially complete—unlike other teachings, which remain entirely unaware of its existence.

This refers merely to the realization according to the stages (*bhūmi*). Furthermore, as for what is called the "preparatory stage" (*prayoga*), this also pertains to the meaning of the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*);
it involves adding four kinds of profound investigation to examine and verify the underlying reality of the meaning. Therefore, it is called the "preparatory stage.
