when the eye-consciousness turns back toward the mind, one again perceives this fire. This is what is called the "single intersection" of cause and effect. In the section beginning with "To illuminate," he clarifies the self.

These are transformations of their respective characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). First, the characteristic of light is "visible" (*sanidarśana*); because what is seen is different [from oneself], there is dread.
Second, the characteristic of darkness is "invisible" (*anidarśana*); because what is seen is non-existent, there is fear. This fear arises from the transformation of one's own characteristics.
Thus, below, the specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) that are transformed are clarified: the ear hears water; when boiled with fire, it becomes hot water or molten copper.
The breath of the nose is qi; when ignited by fire, it becomes smoke and flame. The tongue tastes flavors;
when struck by fire, they become pellets and gruel. The dust of the body is contact; when kindled by fire, it becomes ash and charcoal. The mental images are fire;
when augmented by fire, they become a fanning and stirring of the void. These sense-faculties and objects are thus distinct in their characteristics.
Regarding what is transformed: in general, that which is habituated within the cause is the faculty (*indriya*), while that which is transformed within the fruit is the object (*viṣaya*).
This, moreover, constitutes the first intersection of faculty and object. △ Second, the retribution of hearing.
Second, hearing reports that attract evil retributions (extending to) being struck by lightning and hail that shatters one’s heart and soul.
Second, the lower section indicates cause and effect: hearing of karmic deeds at the time of birth is the cause; encountering the surging waves at the moment of death is the effect.
This is because when the auditory consciousness turns back toward the mind, one again perceives this as water. This is what is meant by "cause and effect meeting."

Furthermore, the following section clarifies what is transformed by the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*). First, when opening the ears to listen, one hears various noises; therefore, the spirit becomes distracted.

Second, when closing the ears to listen, there is silence and nothing is heard; therefore, the soul becomes submerged. This sinking and distraction are both transformations resulting from specific characteristics.
Thus, the following clarifies the transformations of specific characteristics: what the ears hear is water, yet one pours water upon it as a reproach or a censure;
what the eyes see is fire, yet one rides upon the fire as a roar or a poison; what the nose breathes is air.
When water encounters it, it becomes rain or venomous insects; when the tongue tastes this flavor and stirs it with water, it becomes pus or filth;
when the body’s dust touches it and is doused with water, it becomes ghosts, beasts, excrement, or urine.
The mind is fire; when water is poured upon it, it becomes lightning and hail. These sense organs and their objects are transformations arising from their distinct characteristics.
Generally speaking, that which is habituated within the cause is the organ, while that which is transformed within the effect is the object.
This, moreover, is the mutual interaction between organ and object. △ Third, the retribution of smelling.
Third, the retribution for smelling invites the drawing forth of evil fruits, [extending] until one’s body is shattered by flying sand and gravel.
Third, the lower section indicates cause and effect: smelling karma at the time of birth is the cause; seeing poisonous vapors at the moment of death is the fruit.
This is because when the nose-consciousness turns back toward the mind, one again sees these poisonous vapors. This is what is meant by "cause and effect being one."

"Interacting. The passage beginning with "To reveal" clarifies what is transformed by the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*). The passage beginning with "In this way" clarifies what is transformed by the distinct characteristics (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*).

These should be understood according to the text. Furthermore, "substance" (*zhì*) refers to that which is obstructive; "to tread upon" (*lǚ*) means to pass through. When fish spoil, it is called "putrid" (*nǎi*); when soup spoils, it is called "stale" (*shuǎng*).
These signs of retribution are all caused by transformations of the vital energy (*prāṇa*). △ Fourth, the experience of retribution:
Fourth, the retribution of taste invites evil fruits (extending to) flying hot iron raining down from the sky.
Fourth, the section below indicates cause and effect. The tasting of food at the time of birth is the cause; the vision of the iron net and fierce flames at the moment of death is the effect.
This is because when the gustatory consciousness (*jihvā-vijñāna*) turns back toward the mind, one again perceives those fierce flames; this is what is meant by "the convergence of cause and effect.

The section beginning with "To manifest" clarifies that which is transformed by its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); the section beginning with "In this way" clarifies that which is transformed by its specific characteristic (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*).
One should reflect according to the text. However, the tongue faculty commits offenses to an extreme degree. First, there is the offense of craving flavors;

for hunting, trapping, and fishing are its primary occupations. Second, there is the offense of uttering speech; for false speech, frivolous talk, slander, and harsh words are its primary occupations.
Due to these, one is reborn in hells such as the Iron Net and Intense Flames—what is truly "given forth" by you.
This is the principle of "returning what you have done to others. The lower realms involve being a burden and enduring suffering. One may infer other cases by applying this same logic.
△ Fifth, the retribution of contact. Fifth, the retribution of contact that invites evil fruits (extending to) being cast down, being flown away, being boiled, and being roasted.
Fifth, the section below indicates cause and effect. Taking the contact with karma at the time of birth as the cause, one sees mountains closing in at the moment of death as the result.
This is because when the body-consciousness returns to the mind, one again perceives great mountains coming together to close in; this is what is meant by "cause and effect meeting once.

The section beginning "To manifest" clarifies that which is transformed by the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*); the section beginning "In this way" clarifies that which is transformed by the distinct characteristics (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*).
Reflect according to the text. Generally speaking, union and separation constitute the objects of bodily contact. In union, massive mountains press down upon one;
in separation, the heart and liver are torn asunder. Whether it be for the Way or for contemplation, whether it be a hall or a desk, all are places for administering the prisons of karma.
This is precisely what the body relies upon for tactile contact. △ Sixth, the retribution of volition (*cetanā*).
Sixth, the retribution of volition draws forth evil fruits, leading to ten thousand deaths and ten thousand births, being cast face down or face up.
Sixth, the section below indicates cause and effect. The karma of volition at the time of birth is the cause; the vision of the wind destroying the land at the moment of death is the effect.
This is because when the mental consciousness turns back toward the mind, one again perceives the blowing of the wind; this is what is meant by the "convergence of cause and effect.

The section beginning with "Manifesting" clarifies that which is transformed by the specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa); the section beginning with "In this way" clarifies that which is transformed by the distinct characteristics (viśeṣalakṣaṇa).
Reflect according to the text. Generally speaking, arising and ceasing are the objects of the mental consciousness (*manas*).

Since the mind must necessarily be driven by the wind of the *ālayavijñāna*, consciousness and wind revolve and fall together. "Location" refers to the place where one undergoes retribution. "Witnessing" refers to the final adjudication.
Whether one lies face down or face up, all of this is nothing other than the result of chaotic conceptualization (*vikalpa*). △ Fourth, concluding the previous response.
Question Two: First, a summary of the characteristics of the hells.
Ānanda, these are called the ten causes and six effects of the hells... such a person shall enter one hundred and eight hells.
First, Ānanda’s section concludes the summary. In Sanskrit, this is called Avīci; here it is translated as "Without Interval" (Mújiàn). However, there are five kinds of "without interval":

first, the without interval of destination; second, the without interval of suffering; third, the without interval of time; fourth, the without interval of life; and fifth, the without interval of form.
If sentient beings, among their six sense faculties, fully cultivate the ten habitual causes, they will enter these five kinds of without interval.
Because body, life, time, and place all endure for immeasurable kalpas, it is called the Great Avīci Hell.

Next, regarding the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*), there is a fourfold analytical explanation: each of the six faculties is created by its own corresponding consciousness and does not involve the other faculties;
thus, they do not fulfill the ten causes. Being slightly lighter than the former [Great Avīci], one enters the Eight Avīci Hells. This is the first category.
1. Sañjīva (Reviving), 2. Kālasūtra (Black String), 3. Saṃghāta (Crushing), 4. Raurava (Crying Out), 5. Mahāraurava (Great Crying Out), 6. Tapana (Heating), 7.

Pratāpana (Extreme Heating), and 8. Avīci (Unrelenting), and so forth. Furthermore, if one ceases the three branches of body, speech, and mind among the six sense faculties, and ceases the three karmas of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct among the ten habitual causes, it is even lighter than the former; thus there are eighty-eight hells.

This refers to the eight hot hells and the ten cold hells. Third, among the three types of karma, if one commits only a single act of killing or a single act of stealing, it is lighter than the previous cases and thus one enters thirty-six hells.

Fourth, if one commits a single karma within a single sense faculty—for example, seeing that which invites the karma of seeing with the eyes while the body never moves, or speaking with the mouth such that the deed is accomplished—[one likewise enters these hells].
Yet, in reality, they have no [fixed] mind; being lighter than the previous state, they enter the one hundred and eight hells.

These one hundred and eight hells are precisely the aforementioned eight *avīci* (uninterrupted) hells. Each hell has four gates, and each gate has four minor hells; thus, one major hell comprises sixteen minor hells.
Consequently, the eight hells together total one hundred and twenty-eight hells. This is according to the scripture.
To avoid prolixity, it is said there are one hundred and eight hells. However, there are also eight cold and eight hot hells. The eight cold hells have already been explained in the preceding text.
As for the eight hot hells: first, the Pit of Charcoal; second, Boiling Excrement; third, the Forest of Flames; fourth, the Forest of Swords; fifth, the Path of Blades;
sixth, Iron Thorns; seventh, the Salt River; and eighth, Copper Stakes. When these are added to the eight cold hells, they constitute sixteen hells.
Generally speaking, those with heavy offenses but few instances of imprisonment refer to major cases; those with light offenses but many instances of imprisonment refer to minor cases.
Minor cases are easily resolved as they approach liberation, whereas major cases extend far, lasting through immeasurable kalpas.
Furthermore, these differ in terms of small and large, much and little, light and heavy. △ Second, the conclusion answering the question:
"Because sentient beings act and create separately... (up to)... delusive thoughts arise; they do not exist from the beginning."
Regarding the terms "separate making" and "separate creating": if one completes ten causes of habitual practice (*vāsanā-hetu*), one enters the Great Avīci Hell;
if one does not complete ten causes of habitual practice, but instead commits one, two, or three separately, one enters the four subsequent sections of hell.

Furthermore, since the nature of the offenses of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct among sentient beings is the same, the retribution received in hell is likewise the same; therefore, they are said to be of the same category (*sabhāga*).
Section on the Grounds. Previously, Ānanda asked whether the hells have fixed locations or arise spontaneously.
The Buddha’s exposition of the ten causes of habitual practice was precisely his answer that these hells arise spontaneously. How is this known? For example, suppose one sees with one's own eyes...
As for the matter that does not pertain to body or speech—where one ultimately speaks with the mouth but acts with the body—is this not the natural emergence from hell?
The subsequent explanation of the sixfold mutual retribution is precisely the answer to the question regarding whether hell has a fixed location.
How do we know this? Suppose a person, while alive, creates karma through views; at the time of death, as they traverse the various sense faculties, they receive retribution in hell.
Is it not the case that hell has a fixed location? It is the same for each individual faculty.
The same applies to all six sense organs. Each person initiates karma through them and each privately undergoes its retribution.
To investigate this thoroughly, one must ask: did this hell exist from the beginning? It is entirely created by the deluded ignorance of sentient beings. It is just like a dream;
the dream is fundamentally empty, yet while one is dreaming, one cannot say it does not exist. Why is this? Because for this person, the dream has not yet...
Because one awakens, so too it is with the karma created by humans. It is not that the Way does not exist. Why is this? Because these people have not yet realized the emptiness of intrinsic nature;
they are just like those in a dream. Therefore, it is said that the hells have fixed locations and that their emergence occurs spontaneously.
All these arise from deluded thoughts; they do not exist inherently from the beginning. △ Second, the realm of hungry ghosts (preta-gati), in three parts. First, the general heading:
Furthermore, Ānanda, these sentient beings... [until] later, when their retribution for sins is exhausted, they receive the forms of various hungry ghosts.

Among all the most heinous offenses for accusing others of transgressions, none surpasses slandering the Triple Gem. Having burned one's own roots of goodness, one also causes immeasurable sentient beings to sever their roots of goodness.
For this reason, throughout kalpas, one enters the Great Avīci Hell of Uninterrupted Suffering.

Only when the nature of that karma has been completely consumed by fire will one emerge to be born in the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*). Within the realm of hungry ghosts there are also ten types; these follow from the ten causes mentioned above, augmented by others.
This is the retribution for mixed karma. △ Second, the specific manifestation:
If, due to the original cause, one commits the offense of coveting another's property (up to the point where), upon encountering people, one takes on their form and name to be sent forth as a ghost.

First, by committing the offense of greed for material things, one becomes a *guǐguǐ* (strange ghost) after the retribution is exhausted. "Strange" (*guǐ*) refers to the transformation of the ordinary.

Because their greed does not cease, they immediately attach themselves to objects whenever they see them; people thus regard them as strange and constant phenomena. Second, by committing the offense of greed for sexual beauty, one becomes a *póguǐ* (drought ghost) after the retribution is exhausted.
"Drought" (*pó*) refers to the vapors of a drought. Because the fire of lust has not yet been extinguished, they still stir up winds to oppress the world.
Third, through greed and delusion one incurs sin; when the retribution for that sin is exhausted, one emerges as a *mèi* ghost. A *mèi* is a seductive spirit.

Because the deceitful mind has not yet ceased, it is still able to borrow the form of a domestic animal to seduce and delude people. Fourth, through greed and resentment one incurs sin; when the retribution for that sin is exhausted, one emerges as a *gǔdú* (poisonous charm) ghost.
*Gǔ* means ruin. Because the habitual tendencies of enmity still persist, one becomes a type of insect; such beings are also capable of ruining others.
The *Shi* (Record) says: "Those who commit the fifth greed through recollection incur sin; when their sin is exhausted, they emerge as *li*-ghosts. A *li* is a spirit of discordant qi.
Because their mind of anger has not been pacified, they still ride upon their decline to act as a *li*; this constitutes discordance. Those who commit the sixth greed through arrogance incur sin;
when their sin is exhausted, they emerge as hungry ghosts (*preta*). Hungry ghosts take a hollow stomach and a haughty mind as their habitual practice."

This is like becoming a ghost who still relies on its hollow breath to overcome others. Seventh, through greed for deception one commits a transgression; when the retribution for that transgression is exhausted, one emerges as a *yan-gui* (demon of nightmares).
A *yan* is a thing of darkness and obscurity. When one’s deceptions fail to succeed, one then rides upon the profound darkness to oppress and subdue the human mind with nightmares.
Eighth, through greed for brilliance one commits a transgression; when the retribution for that transgression is exhausted, one emerges as a *wangliang-gui* (demon of shadows). A *wangliang*...
This is the dependence of a shadow. Because one's own vision is not clear, one borrows from other things to obscure the people and dazzle the world.

When the nine types of greed are fully realized, they constitute a transgression; when the transgression is completed, one emerges as a servant-ghost. A servant-ghost is one who is employed by others.

Previously, they constructed falsehoods upon the void and fabricated realities to deceive others; now, as retribution for their service, they are made to manifest the fulfillment of mandates and are dispatched to perform such duties.
When the ten types of greedy factions commit crimes, once their punishment is complete, they emerge as "transmission ghosts.

These transmission ghosts are those who report matters of good fortune and misfortune; they were previously accustomed to forming cliques and engaging in malicious litigation, and thus they now serve as ghosts.
One can still act as a messenger for others, conveying words and transmitting messages. △ Third, the conclusion and demonstration:
Ānanda, all these people have fallen due to their pure passions... (until)... then this wondrous, perfect, and luminous [nature] fundamentally possesses nothing at all.
If we refer to the previous discourse, those of pure emotion enter hell; those with seven parts of emotion and three parts of thought belong to the realm of ghosts.
This refers to their initial place of descent. Now, emerging from hell, their emotional habits have dried up, yet residual thoughts still remain, causing them to enter the realm of ghosts.
These thoughts of the ghost realm are not comparable to the emotional thoughts of the previous time; they are, in fact...
This is merely the residue of the fires of karma. Other sources describe the appearance of hungry ghosts as resembling charred wood when they first emerge;
is this not the burning of the fires of karma? Generally speaking, the karma of ghosts is mostly summoned by habitual delusions from past lives.
If one observes with the wondrous, perfect, and luminous mind, these things are exactly like dreams—they do not exist inherently from the beginning. △ Three: The Realm of Animals.
Three. First, the general heading:
Furthermore, Ānanda, when the karmic retribution of the hungry ghost is exhausted, they take on the body of an animal to repay their past debts.

Through the path of hell, their emotions (*citta*) are disciplined; through the path of ghosts, their perceptions (*saṃjñā*) are disciplined. When emotions are exhausted and perceptions are emptied, one is liberated.
Emerging from the realm of darkness into the sphere of luminosity, yet karma remains without a presiding master;
one flows into other classes of beings, and with no correct awakening in the mind, returns once more to dependence upon others. This dependence results in encountering one's original debt;

as such, these other classes of beings naturally must repay their past obligations. Generally speaking, the animal realm is the residue of emotional and conceptual attachments, governed by both [the realms of] desire and form.
These are not yet exhausted. This category is vast and extensive; filling debts and repaying lives can only be described by citing its general outline.
△ Second, the specific manifestation:
from "the ghosts of material anomalies" (wùguài zhī guǐ) through "their retribution is exhausted" (bào jìn), they are born into the world and mostly follow their respective species.
The *wuguai* (object-monster) is a ghost that transforms into a *xiaoxiao* (owlet) and carries clods of earth to raise its young; this is still the mind of greed.
The *fengbie* (wind-demoness) is a drought-ghost whose retribution manifests as portents of calamity; it is provoked by the sight of beautiful forms, and its omens are deduced from the hexagrams.

The *chumei* (beast-seducer) is a seductive ghost that shifts into the form of a fox; its seductive heart does not change, and its habitual deceit remains solemn. The *chonggu* (insect-poison) is a ghost of toxic venom.
They return as a class of venomous creatures—vipers, snakes, vipers, and scorpions; their resentful energy still persists, and they become decaying, malevolent ghosts.
Yet again, they become a class of parasites, entering the bodies of humans; only when their anger subsides do they receive the breath of hungry ghosts. Then they are born as a class of food.
To fill the kitchen and be swallowed down is the result of the habit of arrogance; this is the "Mian-you" (綿幽) *yan-gui* (魘鬼). Now it belongs to the category of clothing;
fond of deception, it conceals its body and remains ultimately unrevealed. This is the "He-ling" (和精) *wang-liang-gui* (魍魎鬼). It transforms into the category of responses;

it regulates the seasonal cycles, yet its habitual manifestations remain as they were. This is the "Ming-ling" (明靈) *yi-shi-gui* (役使鬼). Its retribution is manifested as auspicious omens: the auspicious qilin and the majestic phoenix.

"To correct a crookedness by going too far in the opposite direction" and "relying on others to transmit the ghosts" are, in fact, instances of following their own kind; even the keeping of auspicious birds as domestic animals is no different from this partisan bias.
What has been clarified above does not exceed the common perceptions of ordinary people. However, if one extends this principle to touch upon all related categories, [the truth becomes clear].
This is indeed infinite. △ Third, the concluding indication:
"Ānanda, all these are dried up by the fires of karma... (until)... all are the congealed solidification of floating, empty, and false imaginings."
Ānanda concludes the summary below: From the previous section on the ghost hells onward, his emotional attachments (*saṃjñā*) were dissolved;
from the animal realm onward, his karmic debts were repaid. For the reason that sentient beings transmigrate in saṃsāra is precisely because they possess emotional attachments.
Even if those attachments were dried up today, he could not forget them, as they existed simultaneously with him. Once—
If we encounter one another, you shall naturally submit to my command. Nevertheless, if one awakens to true illumination, these sentient beings are entirely illusory;

their thoughts and appearances are unreal. As you answered previously in your response, regarding the crimes of lust and murder committed by those such as Bao-lianxiang—were these brought down by Heaven, or were they produced by humans?
"Give it to him. If one awakens to Bodhi and clearly understands that [suffering] is summoned by one's own delusions, then within the original mind, it has never existed from the very beginning.
△ Section on the Four Destinies: First, the general heading.
Furthermore, Ānanda, from this state of being an animal (until) the appearance of a Buddha in the world, one cannot rest.
Furthermore, the initial inquiry below [begins with] "Or perhaps," which follows the preceding discourse: having been born as an animal, one repays one's past debts.
Consequently, one might claim that animals may be killed and eaten; one even beats them with clubs without realizing they are dying, and exhausts their labor without recognizing its hardship.

One regards humans as noble and animals as base to such an extreme that it becomes difficult to act otherwise. One fails to realize that although the life-force of a creature may be minute, its karma has fixed limits.
Should one exceed what is rightfully owed, that being—though now an animal—will likewise become a human and demand back the surplus. (As stated in the preceding text.)
It is said that when a person eats a sheep, the sheep dies and becomes a human being; this is a principle of the world that cannot be known.

As in those two lower treatises concerning merit and demerit, it may be that although one's animal karma has been exhausted, what remains to be repaid is not yet finished, and thus the retribution manifests in the human realm.
One who honors merit and cultivates goodness may, conversely, suffer violence and injustice; for no reason and without cause, they encounter robbery and murder.

This means that one does not abandon the human body to repay that labor; or, although one may be reborn among humans, lacking both merit and virtue, the debt remains unpaid and one returns as an animal to compensate for the remaining balance. This is the most difficult matter to understand in the dark realm of the afterlife.
Ānanda, the three arguments below illustrate its inexhaustible difficulty. In a previous life, one’s labor may have exceeded the required effort, or...
Having exhausted their wealth or even lost their lives, they now exist as animals or humans to repay each debt in full;
thus, in this world, there would be no lingering mutual obligations, and the karmic obstacles of retribution would naturally cease. But now it is not so;

instead, resentment is compounded and hatred is deepened, leading to mutual slaughter and even devouring and extermination, revolving like a well-drawing wheel as one party repays another in an endless cycle.
They never cease. These [beings] cannot rest, neither through the cultivation of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) nor because a Buddha has appeared in the world.
This is the most difficult aspect to clarify regarding the saṃsāra of the three miserable realms. Furthermore, *śamatha* is called "cessation" (*zhi*) and also "wondrous concentration.
Concentration can destroy delusions and demons, thereby perfecting the path to *samyak-saṃbodhi*. Contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) can contemplate the mind and contemplate phenomena, thereby perfecting...
Cultivate practice. If you do not do so, when will there ever be a day of rest? △ Second, the specific manifestation:
"You should now know that those of the owl species... [until]... are born into the human realm and join the ranks of the enlightened."
The habituation of greed takes the grasping for objects as its nature. When one descends to the rank of the *xiāo* (owls), objects become useless;
consequently, the greedy mind ceases, and one returns to the human realm as a dull-witted being. That those who are now ignorant and lack discernment are the retribution for this.

The habituation of lust takes the craving for beauty as its nature. When one descends to the rank of the *jiùzhēng* (ominous portents), beauty becomes useless; consequently, [the lustful mind ceases...]
This fire of lust was extinguished, and he returned to the human realm as one of the ignorant class; his present state as a dull-witted and unknowing person is the retribution for that.
Having practiced deception, he took greed and delusion as his nature, descending to the level of a fox; such delusion is utterly useless.
Because of this, his deceitful mind has perished, and he has returned to the human realm as one of the mediocre class; his present state of being coarse, parsimonious, and base is the result.
Such people are the retribution for this. The habit of resentment has greed and hatred as its nature; it descends to the realm of the most venomous creatures. Hatred is useless;
because of this, the heart of resentment does not arise. Furthermore, those who return to the human world as a class of the stubborn and headstrong are the retribution for this.
The habit of anger has greedy recollection as its nature; it descends to the realm of intestinal worms.
Recollection is useless; by this, the mind of anger is worn away. Returning again to the human realm as a lowly being, such a person of inferior and humble status is the retribution for that.
The habitual tendency of pride has greed and arrogance as its nature. Descending to the level of the hungry ghosts, arrogance is useless;
by this, the mind of pride does not arise. Returning again to the human realm, one becomes gentle.
The retribution for this is that one becomes a person of weak character and cowardice, now rendered useless. The habit of deception takes greed and delusion as its nature;
descending to the level of the human realm, "delusion" (wang) means being useless. Consequently, the deceptive mind is extinguished, and one returns to the human world as a class of laborers.
The retribution for this is that one becomes a person who exerts physical toil with great hardship. The habit of views takes greed and clarity as its nature...
It constitutes one's nature. Descending to the level of the "Response to Cycles" (Yinglun), it is revealed to be useless.

From this, habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) do not arise; one returns to the human realm as a literary type. That there are now people capable of producing fine literature yet lacking right view (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*) is the retribution for this.
Habitual tendencies of perversity, perfected through greed, constitute one's nature. Descending to the level of the "Auspicious Omens" (Xiuzheng), they become useless. From this...
This is the result of the habituation to perversity, which did not manifest in that life; they return to the human realm as beings of clear intelligence.

That one now possesses a clever and intelligent nature yet acts without sincerity is the retribution for this. The habituation to litigation has partisanship through greed as its nature; descending to the human level, it results in following the worldly conventions.
The faction is thus rendered useless. Consequently, the habit of litigation cannot be established, and they return once more to the human realm as beings of the enlightened class.
This is the retribution for those who today maintain their proper station and understand their destiny. △ Third, the conclusion and demonstration.
Ānanda, all these have fully repaid their past debts... these types of people are called those who are to be pitied.
These ten kinds of persons—whether possessed of clarity or wisdom, or whether dull-witted or foolish—all come from various realms of existence.
Having fully repaid their past debts, they again take form within the human realm; yet, due to differences in their habitual practices, they subsequently fall into various grades of good and evil.
Viewed from the present perspective, these classes of beings are all caught in the cycle of delusive thoughts and inverted views.
Were it not for the Buddha’s arising of compassion to reveal, inspire, awaken, and lead them, by what means could they ever escape the three realms? △ Five: The Immortals (Xian).
Destinations. First, a general heading:
Ānanda, furthermore, there are ten kinds of *ṛṣis* among the followers who do not rely on perfect enlightenment (up to) places where humans cannot reach.
Some contemplate that birth and death are empty and illusory, and thus seek the permanent; others perceive the cyclic nature of the world and [distinguish it] separately.
They cultivate liberation, yet do not rely upon true awakening; they take deluded conceptualization as their practice and fail to awaken to their own minds.

They regard the preservation of the physical form as the subtlety of the Way. Although they may move to mountain valleys and hide their traces in forests and springs, in essence they do not rely on their fundamental nature and thus ultimately remain outsiders.
Above, they do not accord with the heavens; below, they do not follow the world. Therefore, they are called—
Immortals. There are also ten kinds of immortals, which will be distinguished in the text below. △ Second, the specific manifestation:
"Ānanda, those sentient beings who firmly take medicinal elixirs... [until] they awaken to the perfection of their name as 'Transcendent Immortals of Exquisite Practice'."
"Those who are firm in taking medicinal elixirs without ceasing" refers to following the method of abstaining from grain (*pi-gu*), concentrating the spirit and emptying the mind;
this uses the refinement of the mind to manifest supernatural powers (*tong*) to accomplish the Way, and they are called "earth-walking immortals" (*di-xing-xian*).

"Those who are firm in consuming plants and trees without ceasing" refers to eating pine resin and ingesting fungi to prolong life and preserve the physical form; this uses the refinement of the body to lift oneself far aloft.

Having accomplished the Way, one is called a Flying Immortal (*khecarī-ṛṣi*). Regarding "firm as metal and stone, never ceasing": this refers to the ninefold transformation of the inner and outer elixirs (*neidan* and *waidan*);

that is, internally transforming the bones and externally transforming matter. This is the practice of alchemy through which one wanders the world to accomplish the Way, and is thus called a Wandering Immortal (*vihāra-ṛṣi*).
Regarding "firm in movement and stillness, never ceasing": this refers to the heart presiding over vitality and the lungs... [text truncated]
"Guarding the host" means regulating the *wei* (protective essence) to facilitate its entry and exit, and regulating the *rong* (vital luster) to ensure its coming and going;

this is what it means. This attains harmony with Heaven (*tianhe*). Truly, one is able to practice emptiness (*kongxing*) to accomplish the Way, and is thus called a "Space-Walking Immortal" (*Kongxingxian*).

As for "making the vital fluids firm and unceasing," this refers to stirring the "Heavenly Pond," swallowing the vital fluids, and circulating them throughout the upper and lower parts of the body, thereby being able to nourish and moisten the entire person.
Those who sever desire and practice in common with the heavens to accomplish the Way are called *devacara-ṛṣis* (Heaven-Walking Immortals).

Those who are firm and steadfast in their vital essence and radiance without ceasing—specifically, those who swallow the solar essence in the morning, hold the lunar brilliance at night, inhale the wind, and drink the dew—are [the latter].
These spirits communicate with Heaven and Earth to accomplish the Way; they are called *viśvācara-ṛṣis* (All-Pervading Immortals). They are firm and steadfast in their incantations and prohibitions.

"Without ceasing" means that one practices *bùxū* (stepping-void) and knocks the teeth; for incantations (*zhòu*), one invokes their spiritual efficacy, and for prohibitions (*jìn*), one restrains what has been transgressed.
This involves cultivating the Way through the application of immortal arts (*xiānshù*), and such a person is called a "Way-practicing Immortal" (*dàoxíng xiān*).

Regarding "firmly maintaining contemplation without ceasing," this refers to visualizing the Yellow Court (*huángtíng*) above and binding the *tiāndān* below, while quieting the mind and focusing on a single thought.

Furthermore, this refers to the aspiration that the mind shall certainly give rise to wisdom to accomplish the Way. Wisdom is illumination; such a one is called an "Illuminating Practice Immortal" (*zhàoxíng xiān*).
Regarding "firmly maintaining the union without ceasing," this means the heart and kidneys interact, the *kan* and *li* trigrams meet, and water and fire assist each other.
This involves gathering the yin to consolidate the yang to accomplish the Way; such a one is called a "Essence Practice Immortal" (*jīngxíng xiān*). Firmly maintaining the transformation...

Regarding "transformation without ceasing": this refers to entrusting oneself to external objects and focusing one's thoughts upon them; as the thought solidifies, the object is transformed, and the Way of transformation is accomplished.

Once the Way has been formed through transformation, both mind and object are severed to perfect that Way; this is called the "Transcendent of Severed Practice" (Juexing-xian). △ Third, the conclusion and demonstration.
Ānanda, all these individuals refine their minds among human beings; when their retribution is exhausted, they return once more to be scattered into the various realms of existence.
There is no separate realm for immortals (*ṛṣi*); they cultivate while remaining as humans. Upon completing their cultivation, there arise ten types of destinies.

Because these destinies differ, they receive the title of "immortal. Thus it is said: "An immortal (*ṛṣi*) is one who migrates. They migrate to dwell in deep mountains or reside on islands in the sea.
Although these beings obtain the principle of life, it is ultimately a product of deluded thought; though they may live for ten million years, they will inevitably fall.
This is because, while practicing while still burdened by karma, once that karma is exhausted, they return to sink into the various realms of existence. △ Sixth, the Realm of Devas.
First, the Desire Realm. Second, detailed explanation.
Ānanda, those people in the world who do not seek the permanent [state]—[continuing until:]—such a class is called the Heaven of the Four Great Kings (*Cāturmahārājakāyika*).
"Desire" (*kāma*) refers to what the mind desires. That which sentient beings desire is form (*rūpa*); therefore, it is called the Realm of Desire (*kāmadhātu*).

However, desires have degrees of lightness and heaviness, and the realms have their sequential order. First, within the Realm of Desire, there are persons who, although they remain within form, are not subject to perverse defilement.
Although one loves one’s wife, one does not engage in illicit lust; this is called purity of desire. When the mind’s desires are thus purified, that is clear wisdom;
when the mind does not wander or stray, that is virtuous discipline. Therefore, one is reborn in the Four Heavenly Kings’ realm, adjacent to the sun and moon.
This retribution lies at the waist of Mount Sumeru, which is the first heaven of the Desire Realm.
Their sensual desire for their own wives is slight (up to: this class of beings is called the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Next, not only are they unstained by external forms, but even regarding their own wives, such desire is diminished and rare.
Not only is their mind free from wandering, but they do not even relish the Pure Abodes. This is the purity of desire. Since the desire of the mind is thus pure...

Furthermore, having attained the nourishment of the Pure Abodes, they transcend the sun and moon and are born in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; their retribution lies upon the summit of Mount Sumeru, which is the second heaven of the Desire Realm.
When encountering desire, they engage briefly and depart without thought or recollection; such a class is called the Suyāma Heaven.
As for these three [classes], "encountering desire and engaging briefly" refers to having a mind; "departing without thought or recollection" refers to being without a mind.

Because they are without a mind, they are mostly quiescent; because they engage briefly, they are slightly active. Being slightly active and mostly quiescent, they surpass the previous two [levels] and are thus born in Suyāma.
The Heaven of the Time-Portions (Nirmāṇarati). "Time-portion" (yāmā) means a period of time. The deities of this heaven possess their own radiance and do not require the sun or moon;

they distinguish day and night by the opening and closing of lotus flowers, hence it is called the Heaven of the Time-Portions. This retribution resides among those who dwell in space; it is the third heaven of the Desire Realm.
At all times there is tranquility, yet contact comes to touch [the senses]; such a class of beings is called the Tuṣita Heaven.

What was previously described as having little movement and much tranquility implies that there are still intervals [of activity]. Now, describing it as tranquil at all times implies that it is purely pure.
Previously, it was said that they encounter desire and briefly engage in union, which implies the presence of defilement. Now, it is said that contact has not yet... [occurred].
If one deviates from this, then although one should indeed be without mind, this practice is superior to the former;
therefore, one is born in Tuṣita Heaven. "Tuṣita" means "Contentment. Beings in this heaven realize contentment within their own minds and thus lack defiled desire.

Because they perceive the subtle essence of their own minds, they do not descend to the lower heavens. Not descending to the lower heavens means not engaging with external objects. The mind is without...
This is the excellence of the meditative power of those with desire-taints. Furthermore, this heaven consists of an inner court and an outer court;
the outer court is where the original devas reside, while the inner court is where the Bodhisattvas reside. This retribution exists in a place free from the three calamities;
it is the fourth heaven of the Desire Realm.
"I have no mind of desire, yet I respond to your actions"—up to this point—this class of beings is called the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (*nirmāṇarati-deva*).
"I have no mind of desire" means that it is indeed a state of no-mind. "The flavor is like chewing wax" means that the flavor is itself flavorless.

Previously, one merely subdued the mind; here, one simultaneously subdues the objects of experience. Therefore, one is born in the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations. This is because one transforms desire.

Purifying [the environment], they transform that purity into pleasure; therefore, they are called "Those Who Delight in Transformations. This retribution exists beyond the Realm of Transformation (Nirmāṇarati), namely, the fifth heaven of the Desire Realm.
Without a worldly mind, they perform actions identical to those of the world; such a class is named the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Transformations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin).

The former was a state of non-mentation through mental attention; therefore, its flavor was described as being like chewing wax. The present is a state of non-mentation within the very phenomena themselves;
therefore, it is said to be "clearly transcendent. As for what is called "transcendence," it refers to surpassing the previous fifth stage, which takes the transformation of objects as pleasure.

Surpassing the former three and four heavens of non-conceptualization as bliss—in short, surpassing each state whether with mind or without mind—one is thus born in the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations (*Paranirmita-vaśavartin*). This heaven does not create its own pleasure;

rather, whatever pleasure it enjoys is derived from the emanations produced by others, hence it is called "Mastery over Others' Emanations. This retribution resides in the Great Sovereign Heaven (*Maheśvara*).
This refers to the sixth heaven of the desire realm. △ Third, the summary and indication:
"Ānanda, these six heavens, although their forms manifest movement... (omitted)... from this point downward is called the desire realm."
In the human realm, the mind is constantly agitated by desires, and the lifespan is extremely short;

at most, it does not exceed a hundred years. In the celestial realms, distinct objects of perception restrain such agitation; although the lifespan is long, at most it does not exceed ten million years.
Now, these six heavens transcend both types of agitation; their lifespan, merit, and bliss increase in excellence beyond all comparison. Nevertheless, they still possess the sphere of coarse desire.
Alternatively, [the objects] may be absent, yet the mind of subtle perception has not been severed; the traces of the mind still remain, and this is not yet true mindlessness.
Therefore it is said: "Though the form moves outward, the traces of the mind still intermingle. Because one has not yet completely severed desire, it is called the Desire Realm (kāmadhātu).
The Correct Vision of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra, Scroll Eight.
The Śūraṅgama Sūtra on the True Meaning of the Secret Cause and Realization of the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Tathāgata, and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas, Scroll Nine.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Jishi of the Ancient Xingfu Chan Monastery in Ludong.
△ Second, the six [heavens] of the Form Realm (Rūpadhātu). "Form" (rūpa) refers to material substance. "Brahma" (brahma) has the meaning of purity.

This means that, having departed from the coarse form of the afflictive obstacles of the Desire Realm, one attains the superior and wondrous pure form of the Brahma world. This pure form is the fruit of the four dhyānas.

The *lakṣaṇas* (marks) are the common destination of the eighteen heavens; therefore, it is called the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*). However, since there is still the substance of form, it clearly constitutes a defilement of the mind.
This is because, as one has not yet attained single-mindedness, one takes provisional, manifest form (*vijñaptirūpa*) as a cause.

Thus, while there are meditative wisdoms (*dhyānajñāna*), these are not the untainted (*anāsrava*) wisdom-meditations of the Noble Vehicle (*āryayāna*), but rather the tainted (*sāsrava*) wisdom-meditations of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). Now, regarding the fruit:
There are also distinctions in the analysis of these meanings, which will be explained below.
Ānanda, when all those in the world who cultivate the mind reach a state where they are unmoved by any outflows (*āsrava*), this is called the first dhyāna.
"Ānanda," [the Master] said, "the following excludes what is not true dhyāna. 'But those who can... and so forth clarifies the practice of the Brahma-multitude dhyāna.
This means that one studying the Path must possess right knowledge and right view. To directly and thoroughly understand one's own mind is precisely wisdom (*prajñā*).

Because one understands the mind, delusions do not arise; this is precisely meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Now, it is not like this: you do not rely on the factors of dhyāna (*dhyānāṅga*) and do not cultivate wisdom."

Wisdom. Merely clinging to the body while being free from desire, up to the point where both thought and recollection are entirely absent—this constitutes the severing of the fetters of the desire realm and birth in the Brahma-world as a member of the Brahmakāyika heaven. "Brahmakāyika" (Brahma-folk) refers to the common multitude of that celestial realm.

Having previously explained the practice of dhyāna for the Brahma-purohita heaven below, it was stated that when thought and recollection are both absent, the mind itself is concentration; now, however, it is not merely that.

The mind is concentrated. It further encompasses the *vinaya* (restraint); *vinaya* is precisely the precepts (*śīla*). With internal concentration and external precepts, one delights in and accords with them, becoming capable of assisting the "Mind-King";
thus it is named the Brahmā-purohita Heaven. "Brahmā-purohita" means the assistants or ministers of the devas.

The following passage clarifies the meditative practice of Mahābrahmā: body and mind are wondrously perfect—this is concentration (*samādhi*). One's dignified deportment is without deficiency—this is the precepts (*śīla*). Furthermore...
"Enlightened understanding" (*vidyā*) is wisdom (*prajñā*). When the three trainings are complete, one is able to lead the assembly of Brahmās;
thus they are called "Great Brahmā," which is the lord of the first dhyāna heaven. Ānanda concludes by showing that the first dhyāna is called the "ground of joy and bliss born of seclusion":

because it arises from being secluded from sensual thoughts, it is said that suffering and affliction cannot oppress it; because the mind attains purity, it is said that the outflows (*āsrava*) do not [arise].
Although this capacity for movement is not yet the actual cultivation of samādhi, when compared to the lower realms, it has already transcended them;

because one has attained the immovability from all outflows (*āsrava*), it is called "superior flow" (*viśeṣa-bhāgīya*). Question: Since the three trainings are now complete, is this not indeed the actual cultivation? Answer: No.
Not so. This superior stream [of practitioners] all possesses attachments. First, they are attached to the immobility of the body;
second, they are attached to the immobility of conduct; third, they are attached to the immobility of views. Since the ground of the mind thus possesses attachments, how can it be true?

This merely attains the coarse, scattered immobility of the desire realm and has not yet reached the stage of the "unborn" (anutpattika-dharma-ksanti); therefore, it is said that this is not correct cultivation.
△ Second Dhyāna Heaven.
Ānanda, the next Brahmā heaven governs the Brahmās (up to the point where) coarse outflows have already been subdued; this is called the Second Dhyāna.
Ānanda, below this it clarifies the practice of the Limited Light Dhyāna. "Governing the Brahmās" refers to the aforementioned Mahābrahmā. Because of his greatness...

Brahmā is one who has perfected the three trainings and is able to preside over the Brahma host. Now, as the characteristics of concentration become increasingly superior, the function of light is manifested;

hence it is said that "tranquil stillness gives rise to light. Previously, because there were the hindrances of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), the light could not manifest its function.

Now, being free from applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), they take light as their sound. Because the meditative light first emerges here, it is named the Heaven of Limited Light (*Parīttābha*).

As for the meditative practice of the Heaven of Immeasurable Light (*Apramāṇābha*), its light shines downward with immeasurable brilliance. Furthermore, since they take light as their function, that function is inexhaustible.
When this inexhaustible light reflects throughout the worlds of the ten directions, one then perceives the excellence of that light.

Regarding the statement that it is "universally composed of lapis lazuli," this refers to the purity of the light of Right View. Because its light is thus supreme and its clarity is thus pure, it is named the Heaven of Immeasurable Light (*Apramāṇābha*).
It absorbs and sustains the meditative practices of the Heaven of the Sound of Lower Radiant Light (*Parīttābhāsvara*).
Previously, one merely allowed the light to function outwardly, unable to turn the light back to reflect upon itself in order to achieve the benefit of teaching.

Now, having attained the ability to turn the light back to reflect upon itself so as to clarify its principle, it is said: "Absorbing and sustaining the perfect light to accomplish the substance of the teaching.
This is what is meant by the "benefit of teaching. Why? Because the light serves as the revelation, yet it is not through verbal expression; therefore, it is called "pure. By means of this—
Light serves for transformation; since this transformation is inexhaustible, it is called "infinite. To attain such pure and infinite function—what else could it be but the Light-Sound Heaven?
Therefore, it is named "Light-Sound. Ānanda, the following concludes and indicates the second dhyāna heaven.
It is called the stage of "joy and bliss born of concentration" because light arises from concentration; thus, it does not depend on other factors.
Because the supreme joy attained is such, anxiety cannot oppress it. Although this is not yet the actual cultivation of *samādhi*, compared to the first dhyāna, it is already superior.
Because one has subdued and obtained [freedom from] coarse outflows (*āsrava*), it is called "the superior flow. Question: As for the previously mentioned grasping of the mind...
"It is not that these are not truly excellent and correct. Now you say that light arises from meditative concentration (*samādhi*); how could this also not be true?

He replied, "Not so. Concentration is the mind; light is a mark (*nimitta*). Where there is a mind that can be conceptualized and marks that can be delighted in, since there is a mind and marks to be deliberated upon and delighted in, how can it be 'true'?
This merely suppresses coarse outflows (*āsrava*); it has not yet attained true non-existence."
Because there are still outflows (*āsrava*), it is said that this is not yet correct cultivation.
△ Third Dhyāna Heaven. Ānanda, when such celestial beings (up to) fully possess joy, it is called the Third Dhyāna.
Ānanda, the following clarifies the meditative practice of the Parīttābha (Limited Light) heaven. As indicated above, this refers to the Ābhāsvara (Luminous) heaven.

Light arises from concentration; because of that light, the subtle (miao) is revealed. "Subtle" refers to principle (li). By advancing through the application of this principle, one accomplishes the practice. This cessation is the factor of joy (prīti-aṅga).
The penetration into tranquil bliss is the characteristic of this dhyāna. Generally speaking, once the mind-ground is stilled, even the mark of cessation does not arise;

as a pure realm manifests before one, it is therefore called the Heaven of Limited Purity (*Parītta-śubha*). The following section on "Pure Emptiness" clarifies the dhyāna practice of the Heaven of Immeasurable Purity (*Apramāṇa-śubha*):
the body being free from false movement is called "lightness," and the mind not being conditioned by objects is called "tranquility. This arises because pure emptiness has manifested before one.
Seeing this as boundless, one attains the bliss of immeasurable purity of nature; this is the mark of dhyāna. Therefore, it is called the Heaven of Immeasurable Purity (*Apramāṇaśubha*).
Next, the world below clarifies the meditative practice of the Heaven of Universal Purity (*Śubhakṛtsna*). "World" refers to the pure void. "Body and mind" [refer to the practitioner].
It is the bliss of tranquility (*śānti-sukha*). If one perceives the world as pure emptiness and the body and mind as tranquil bliss, these are two distinct characteristics;
they are partial rather than complete. Now, seeing that the body, mind, and world are entirely one in perfect fusion, there is nothing that is not thus.

Through this, the virtue of purity is perfected, and one attains the bliss of universal purity (*viśuddhi-sukha*). This is the mark of dhyāna, and therefore it is called the Heaven of Universal Purity (*Śubhakṛtsna-deva*).

Thus it is. Ānanda concludes the demonstration below: "The third dhyāna is called the stage of sublime bliss detached from joy. This is because in the first dhyāna there is joy due to being detached from the birth of the desire realm;
in the second dhyāna there is joy due to the birth of meditative concentration; and in the third dhyāna there is bliss due to being detached from joy.

Because one is detached from this factor of joy and gives rise to pure and sublime bliss, it is said that it "possesses great conformity," which means it accords with what is naturally settled in its nature.
It is for the sake of bliss. Thus, although it is not the direct cultivation of *samādhi*, compared to the previous two stages, it is already transcendent;
because one sees with complete joy, it is called the "superior flow" (*viśeṣāgama*). Question: In the third dhyāna, neither sorrow nor joy reach it, and one dwells solely in the unity of mind.
Why, then, is it not considered the direct cultivation [of *samādhi*]? Answer: It is not so. One perceives the world as pure emptiness, and perceives the body and mind...
This is quiescent bliss. If one perceives this integration yet still clings to a single mind, how can it be considered true?
This merely involves perceiving that bliss is inherently present within the mind, rather than generating a further mind to seek bliss;
because what is perceived is still [the objectified] mind, it is said not to be correct cultivation. △ Fourth Dhyāna Heaven.
Ānanda, furthermore, when gods and humans are not oppressed in body or mind... [up to] ...when their application is fully matured, it is called the Fourth Dhyāna.

Ānanda, the following clarifies the meditative practice of the "Birth of Merit" (Puṇyaprasava). Now, wherever there is a cause within the mind-ground, there must be birth; and whatever is born must be suffering.

This is the characteristic of the lower realms. In the third dhyāna, the causes of suffering have been exhausted; thus, there is no affliction of body or mind, and one attains the bliss of quiescence.
Nevertheless, suffering and bliss are relative phenomena; that extreme bliss gives rise to sorrow is the natural law.
Based on this, even the factor of bliss attained in the third dhyāna is not permanent; therefore, it is said that "bliss is impermanent."

Abiding for a long time, it will inevitably give rise to decay. Now, in the fourth dhyāna, the two factors of suffering and pleasure do not arise, and the characteristics of coarseness and heaviness have already been extinguished;
this is called the purity of equanimity and mindfulness. Because one attains mindfulness, equanimity, and the arising of merit, it is named the Heaven of Merit-Birth (Puṇyaprasava).
The "Equanimity Mind" section below clarifies the dhyāna practice of "Blessed Love" (Puṇyaprasava). A pure mind constitutes peace; a peaceful mind constitutes blessing.

Generally speaking, where there is thought, there is obstruction; where one is free from thought, there is no obstruction. Now, with both suffering and pleasure absent, the ground of the mind is pure and harmoniously integrated with meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
This peace of mind is blessing; therefore, it is called the Heaven of Blessed Love (*Puṇyaprasava*). As for the phrase "reaching the limits of the future," it refers to...
This refers to the explanation of the latter two heavens. It means that the merit and love generated today are the cause, while being born in those heavens in a future life is the result.
Since the result is inexhaustible, it is said to extend to the "limits of the future" (*aparānta*). Below, Ānanda, the practice of the *Bṛhatphala* (Great Fruit) dhyāna is explained.
Furthermore, within this merit and love there are two paths: one is the direct path, proceeding from the first dhyāna to the fourth dhyāna.
In the interim, they do not intermingle with heterodox views. Taking pure radiance as the cause, they attain the manifestation of vast merit as the fruit;

thus, they are named the Heaven of Vast Fruit (*Bṛhatphala*). If, in the two lower [stages], one follows a circuitous path—intermingling with heterodox views from the initial subduing of afflictions, longing for the higher while loathing the lower, and maintaining a continuity of equanimity—one investigates until the body and mind are extinguished; thus, it is named the Realm of Non-conception (*Asaṃjñin*).
"O Deva, the lifespan of this deva is five hundred kalpas. During the first half-kalpa, there remains a mind of longing and aversion;
it is only during the second half-kalpa that the mind finally subsides and ceases. Yet, even though it ceases, it is not yet true cessation.

This is because one has not awakened to the fact that one's own mind is unborn, and thus takes birth and cessation as its cause. Ānanda, [the Buddha] concludes by showing that the fourth dhyāna is called "equanimity" (upekṣā).
Regarding the purification of mindfulness: the desire realm is suffering, while the three dhyānas are pleasure. The fourth dhyāna is where neither suffering nor pleasure reach;
this is the stage of immovability (*aniñjya-bhūmi*). Although it is not yet the direct cultivation of samādhi, compared to the third dhyāna, it is already supreme.

Because one has attained the equilibrium of concentration and wisdom and its application has become fully matured, it is called "the superior flow" (*viśeṣa-ogha*). Question: Why do suffering and pleasure not reach it?
If no thoughts arise, why would this not be correct cultivation? It is not so. Because taking arising and ceasing as the cause, one enters a superior meditative concentration;

this is because it is based on a mind that grasps at existence. Even if one attains a state of no-mind, it merely suppresses coarseness and agitation for a time, as it is entirely composed of deluded conceptualization.

This is merely a practice involving effortful application (*sābhoga-prayoga*), not the path of effortless spontaneity (*anābhoga-mārga*). Therefore, it is said that this is not the correct [cultivation].
This is the cultivation. △ Fifth, the heavens of the Non-returners (Anāgāmin).
Ānanda, within this there are further five heavens of the Non-returners... [up to] ...which cannot be seen by the coarse people of the world.
Ānanda, the following provides a general definition. In Sanskrit, *dhyāna* means "meditative concentration" (*ting-lü*);
it is like a solitary lamp in an empty room—something of ultimate stillness. However, there is the meditation of the noble ones (*ārya*) and the meditation of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
Ordinary beings do not perceive the principle; they merely suppress the coarse desires of the lower realms and practice while harboring a mind of longing and aversion. This is called...
This is the dhyāna with outflows (*sāsrava*). If a noble one (*ārya*) first realizes the principle, it is called the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna-phala*).

Progressing further to sever the six grades of afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm, it is called the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmi-phala*). Further severing the remaining three grades of afflictions, it is called the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmi-phala*).
The five heavens of non-returners today are precisely such persons. These five heavens of non-returners constitute the third fruit.

Exhausting the nine grades of the desire realm constitutes the branch of the absence of suffering. Exhausting each of the nine grades of the form realm constitutes the branch of the absence of pleasure.
Having attained the simultaneous forgetting of both suffering and pleasure, the mind has no further attachments; thus, there is no fixed dwelling place.

Because the afflictions of the fourth dhyāna have not yet been fully exhausted, one proceeds within the stage of equanimity and mindfulness to cultivate and sever them individually; this is called "cultivating dhyāna by borrowing a stage. Therefore...
It is said: Within the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*), abodes are established; however, there are five distinct grades, namely:
inferior, middling, superior, excellent, and supreme. These are the five grades. Ānanda, suffering and pleasure are distinguished separately below.
The first is the Heaven of No Affliction (*Avṛha*). When mind and objects intersect, it is called "strife" (*yudh*); when the mind is heated by this strife, it is called "affliction" (*vṛha*).

Furthermore, when it is intense, it is called "affliction," and when slight, it is called "heat. Now, the two factors of suffering and pleasure are ultimately and forever severed; since the striving mind no longer intersects with its objects, it is "No Affliction.
Therefore, it is named the Heaven of No Affliction. The second is the Heaven of No Heat (*Atapa*). Although there is no affliction above [in the previous heaven], it still...
This was established in opposition to what preceded it. Now, however, the mechanism functions independently; thus, there is no opposition. When arising without opposition, it arises alone;
when functioning, it functions alone. This single path of pure emptiness is precisely "without heat" (anabhraka).

Therefore, it is named the Heaven Without Heat. Third is the Heaven of Good Vision (sudarśana): its essence is perfect clarity and illumination, and its function is wondrous vision. It is appropriate for this function...
It illuminates immediately; as it illuminates, it functions. This is being skillfully able to see, and thus it is named the Heaven of Good Vision (*Sudṛśa*).

Furthermore, sensory objects are obstacles to wisdom (*prajñā*), and deep-seated defilements are obstacles to meditative concentration (*samādhi*). This heaven does not lean exclusively toward concentration, and thus lacks obstacles to concentration;
it does not lean exclusively toward wisdom, and thus lacks obstacles to wisdom. This is precisely the mutual integration of concentration and wisdom. These are its four virtues.

The Heaven of Manifestation (*Sudṛśa*). Furthermore, since concentration and wisdom have already merged, there is wondrous clarity free from partiality; because one attains a refined vision that manifests before one, it is named the Heaven of Good Manifestation (*Sudṛśa*).
Moreover, molding clay is called "pottery," and melting gold is called "casting"; both involve refining until the ultimate state of purity is reached.
It is redefined as "unimpeded molding and casting. As for the "ultimate heaven of the five colors," "ultimate" (*jìngjiù*) carries the sense of pushing to the limit.
"Ji" refers to the subtle and minute; when one pushes to the furthest point of the subtle and minute, that is emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
When one pushes to the very boundary of emptiness, that is the nature of form (*rūpa-dharmatā*). Only emptiness and form are both ungraspable; it is not that the nature is entirely absent.

Why is it called the Heaven of Ultimate Form (*Akaniṣṭha*)? Ānanda, the following concludes the demonstration: these five heavens of the Non-returners (*anāgāmin*) are all abodes of the noble ones (*ārya*);
they cannot be seen by the tainted minds (*sāsrava-citta*) of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*). Moreover, it is not only that humans cannot see them;
even the Four Kings of the Fourth Dhyāna, who share the same rank and realm, can only hear of them with reverence.
How much more so for those others? Generally speaking, that which is cultivated and subdued within the realms is coarse substance;

that which is cultivated and severed by the sages is subtle consciousness. Because their coarseness and subtlety differ, the sages and ordinary beings are far apart, such that [the latter] cannot perceive [the former]. △ Sixth, the summary.
Ānanda, from the eighteen heavens where beings dwell alone without companions (up to this point) is what is called the Realm of Form (*rūpadhātu*).
"Without companions" means they do not associate with worldly minds. "Dwelling alone" means they are uniquely able to investigate and exhaustively realize the principles of the sages.
Among these eighteen heavens, whether ordinary beings or sages, their practices differ and their realizations vary.
They are distinct. Yet, as they have not yet emerged from the cage of form and have not exhausted the burdens of the physical body, they are collectively termed the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*).
This is what is called the mind that grasps at existence. △ Third, the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Furthermore, Ānanda, from this Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) down to what is called the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

Next, a general summary below: at the Heaven of the Peak of Form (*rūpāvacara-bhavāgra*), two divergent paths are distinguished. That which illuminates alone within meditative concentration is "possessing form" (*rūpin*);
because form is adjacent to space, two routes are divided. First, those with sharp faculties immediately transcend the three realms (*tridhātu*). Second...
Those of dull faculties enter the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). Regarding those who turn their minds from the lower levels of clarity:

first, as for those of sharp faculties, they attain wisdom through the inspiration of others; they perceive the perfect penetration of their own nature and dwell neither in existence nor in emptiness.

They abandon the minor fruits and hasten toward the Mahāyāna; these are called those who have turned their minds. This applies to those at the lower level of clarity in the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).

Regarding concentration, there are also two types of those with dull faculties. First, those who take aversion toward discursive thought as their obstruction, extinguishing the body and returning to non-existence;
these are the śrāvakas of fixed nature. Second, those who take aversion toward form as a affliction, suppressing delusions and entering emptiness;

these are the ordinary beings of external paths. Although their destinations differ, their retribution is the same: both extinguish the aggregate of form. Thus it is said: ... [omitted] ... because they both extinguish the aggregate of form.
Taking emptiness as its support, it is therefore called the concentration of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana-samādhi*).

To clarify the concentration of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana-samādhi*), it is stated that "there is no obstruction," meaning it does not rely on form (*rūpa*); and it is stated that "there is no cessation," meaning it does not rely on emptiness (*ākāśa*).
Since it relies neither on form nor on emptiness, only the *ālayavijñāna* and the *manas* remain. Why is this? Because the seventh *manas* takes [the *ālayavijñāna*] as its object.

At the stage of the eighth ālayavijñāna, one does not take as objects the coarse characteristics of form and space belonging to the sixth [consciousness], but rather takes as its object the subtle consciousness that constitutes half of the sixth.
This is because the sixth is what is stored within the eighth, and thus the manas-vijñāna is able to take it as its object; therefore, it is called the *vijñānānantyāyatana-samādhi*.
Below this, the *ākiṃcanyāyatana-samādhi* is explained: although the space and form of the preceding stage have ceased, there still remains...

It abides within consciousness (*vijñāna*). One does not realize that consciousness is also an obstruction. Now, when the conscious mind is entirely extinguished, then the three dharmas of emptiness, form, and consciousness are all absent.
Because these three dharmas are all absent, it is called "tranquil" (*jiran*). Since the characterized (*lakṣya*) is already non-existent, the characterizer (*lakṣaṇa*) also perishes;
therefore, it is called "no going. Thus, the ten directions are tranquil, and the mind has nowhere to go; it is utterly non-existent.
Because a single dharma accords with the mind, it is called the concentration of the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana-samādhi*).

Because the nature of consciousness is further clarified below, it is not the concentration of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana-samādhi*). Since it does not follow conditions such as form or emptiness, it is said that "the nature of consciousness is immovable.

Yet, because subtle perceptions still remain and cause the mind to extinguish consciousness, it is said that "one exhausts investigation through extinction. Furthermore, the non-exhaustion of this is perception; the exhaustion of its nature is emptiness. It does not persist.
This is non-existence; it is not that all things exist. By taking the thought of inexhaustibility as the totality, one exhausts the emptiness of the nature of existence.

Therefore it is said: "As if existing, yet not existing," which constitutes the perception of non-existence (*asaṃjñā*). Furthermore, being originally without perception, one achieves the ultimate perception of existence. Therefore it is said:
"If exhausted, yet not exhausted," which constitutes the perception of non-non-existence (*naivasaṃjñā*). Hence it is named "Non-."
The meditative absorption of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. △ Fourth, the general analysis:
These [beings] exhaustively reach emptiness yet do not fully realize the principle of emptiness (up to: the *pudgalas* each follow their own kind).
The following section distinguishes between ordinary beings and sages. Regarding the four heavens mentioned above: first, one extinguishes form and returns to emptiness;

second, one extinguishes emptiness while preserving consciousness; third, one extinguishes consciousness so that there is nothingness; fourth, it is neither perception nor non-perception—this is called the ultimate limit of emptiness.
Generally speaking, emptiness and nothingness are not things that can be ultimately reached. If they are reached, they are merely manifestations of the mind. How could they ever be exhausted?
Therefore, it is said that they have not exhausted the principle of emptiness. However, there are two ways of exhausting emptiness. The first is the Path of the Sages (*āryayāna*):

coming from the Heaven of No-Return (*anāgāmin*), one realizes that the body is an obstruction; by dissolving this obstruction, one enters emptiness and reaches the stage of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*). This is the exhaustion of the path of the sages.

Yet, those [beings] do not realize that although the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) has been eliminated, the other four aggregates still remain. Thus, they take this as the realization of the principle of the sages, and ultimately...
The one with the small fruit is a person of dull faculties. The second belongs to the vehicle of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana-yāna*);

having come from the Bṛhatphala Heaven, they have suppressed their afflictions to realize emptiness and reach the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). These are those who exhaust emptiness and do not return. They do not realize that although the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) has been suppressed, [it remains].

The four aggregates [of form, sensation, perception, and formations] are not distinguished; they are deluded, leaking, and without hearing. Reaching beyond five hundred kalpas, when karma is exhausted, they continue to revolve in saṃsāra—these are the followers of external paths.
Ānanda, the correct teaching on the Heavenly Kings below begins with the general outline of the Four Formless Heavens (catur-ārūpya-dhātu).
These are the ultimate fruits of virtuous karma and the highest station for devas and humans. When that karma matures, the manifested realm becomes pure and elevated. If that karma...

When their merit is exhausted, they shall fall from their celestial wheel. Thus, throughout a single kalpa, their manifestations—whether ascending or descending, entering or exiting—are all governed by specific causes.

Other sutras clarify that Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages frequently reside as celestial kings, borrowing these positions to practice and thereby verify the signs of emerging from and entering into dhyāna, playing within samādhi, and accomplishing Buddha-work. Viewed in this light, those various...
The Heavenly Kings and others likewise cannot be indiscriminately categorized as ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
Ānanda, these four heavens of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) are thus explained. These four heavens of the formless realm are called the "formless" because they lack form and consciousness.

This means that because they do not take form as an object, they have no physical characteristics; because they do not take consciousness as an object, they have no mental characteristics. Furthermore, since they possess neither...
If body and mind possess the fetters of the realms (*dhātu-bandhana*), would this not be the characteristic of the aggregates (*skandha*)?

[One might argue] that in the four formless [attainments], while there is no aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), the other aggregates still remain; while there is no coarse consciousness (*vijñāna*), subtle consciousness remains;

and while there is no form resulting from karma (*karmaphala-rūpa*), there is form resulting from meditative concentration (*samādhiphala-rūpa*). This is not so. For those four heavens would lack a basis and thus become subject to annihilation. Therefore, it is certain...
One knows that this heaven takes the formless realm as its domain. Yet there is still bondage to a realm; such severance is not the ultimate truth.

Because one does not understand one's own mind, one pursues deluded karma and gives rise to it; through false views, one wanders through the three realms and falsely sinks into the seven destinies, from the human realm up to the heavens.
From the realm of desire up to the realm of emptiness, these are collectively termed the "three realms" and the "twenty-five states of existence.
*Pudgala* is translated here as "one who repeatedly takes on a course of existence. △ Seventh, the realm of *asura*.
Furthermore, Ānanda, within these three realms (up to) there are those included in the realm of animals due to moisture.
Asuras are sometimes called *Xulun*; both are erroneous. Their correct name is *Asura*. The old translation was "Lacking Uprightness," because while the males are ugly, the females are beautiful.
The new translation is "Non-Gods" (*Feitian*); their retribution is similar to that of the gods, yet they are not truly gods.
Indeed, there are four types of differences which the full text of the sutra does not discuss; it only addresses their remaining karma.
Asuras correspond to the affliction of anger (*dveṣa-anuśaya*) among the ten fetters (*daśānuśaya*). Suppose, for instance, one possesses the power of virtue, merit, wealth, and sovereignty.
Such a person is upright. However, if they happen to encounter an adverse circumstance and their mind is provoked, they immediately give rise to evil.
Riding on this momentum, they harbor jealousy and suspicion; consequently, they forget what they have received and are driven by the habituation of anger, thereby becoming unupright.
Furthermore, as this is not a single type but is possessed by all sentient beings alike, four categories are distinguished to determine their retribution, so as to exhaustively [categorize them].
