This is their karma. Furthermore, the asuras share the same karmic retribution of conceptual discrimination; though they belong to the same category, they differ in their destinies.
This is nothing other than being driven entirely by the movement of karma. △ 8. Summary of the Main Meaning (in two parts). 1. Conclusion answering the previous question.
Ānanda, such are the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals... (up to) why would one further follow the acts of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct?
Ānanda, the following concludes by demonstrating the false arising [of these states]. This is because previously Ānanda had asked: "The Buddha’s essence is true and real;
how then can there be the various paths of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, asuras, humans, and devas? World-Honored One, regarding these paths—

Furthermore, these originally exist of themselves, yet they arise through the habitual delusions of sentient beings. Now, in the concluding response, it is said that regarding these seven realms of rebirth:
if one minutely investigates their origin, they have no fundamental basis; they are fundamentally created by the self-delusions of sentient beings.
This does not concern anything else; it arises from the habituation of delusion and revolves according to deluded karma.

If one looks toward the wondrously luminous, perfect mind, these seven realms of existence are just like flowers in the sky—how could they have any root or source? Second, Ānanda, this section concludes by pointing out the causes of karma:
it is truly because sentient beings do not recognize that their own minds are unborn, and thus they follow after deluded thoughts.
Once born, even if one were to pass through aeons as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, one could not return. How then can it be known that delusive thoughts (*vikalpa*) are likewise without cause?
Nevertheless, although delusive thoughts are without cause, if one observes them through the lens of the karmic fruits of worldly sentient beings, they also appear as if they have a cause.

Did I not say before? It is solely because of the three—killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct—that they serve as the root. By reason of these causes and conditions, karmic results continue in succession.
Judging by this, if one possesses the three causal natures of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct that are heavy, one sinks into the dark realms to become a ghost;
if one lacks the three causal natures of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct and they are light, then one ascends to the luminous realm to become a deva. When the karma of a deva is exhausted...
Descending again to the lower realms, the ghost-fire, like dry wood, must rise upward; thus descending and ascending in succession, how could there ever be an end?
This is precisely what constitutes saṃsāra. Third, if one attains the wondrous [state], this concludes by indicating the true cause:
if one attains the genuine development of the wisdom of samādhi-observation, not only are existence and non-existence both absent, but even this non-duality—
The mind, too, does not exist. Why? If both existence and non-existence are absent, then birth and death are severed. If even the absence of duality is absent, then nirvana is empty.

Since both birth-and-death and nirvana are already empty, why would one further engage in the affairs of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct? △ Second, the conclusion answering the subsequent question.
"Ānanda, the three karmas are not severed; each has its own private [consequences]... (up to)... if anyone else were to speak thus, it would be the speech of Māra.
Below this, [the text] shows that there are fixed locations for the hells as well as those where beings are born spontaneously. This follows from the question previously asked by Ānanda.

As for this hell, does it have a fixed location, or is it spontaneous? Now, in the concluding answer, it is said that because the three karmas are not severed, each has its own private [retribution], yet these private instances share a commonality (*sabhāgatā*); thus, it is not that there is no fixed location.

Since killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct are individually committed by sentient beings, they might seem to lack a fixed attribution; however, the karma they have created is identical. This identity...
Thus, there must truly be a fixed locus. Since karma possesses a fixed locus, it must have existed inherently from the beginning.

If the karma created by many individuals is identical, then the retribution of suffering will likewise arise spontaneously. Furthermore, the collective private delusions of the multitude are themselves causeless;

how could they possibly be traced or investigated? "Exhort" (勗) refers to the act of admonishing and encouraging. This concludes the section on the demonstration of gain and loss. "Exhort" means to warn and urge toward virtue.

Killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct—these three afflictions must be restrained and diligently avoided by one who studies the Path. Only by severing these three afflictions does one truly accomplish the study of the Path.
Why is this? When the three afflictions are eliminated, the ground of the mind becomes pure, and one naturally attains entry into the stage of *samādhi*;

this is what is gained. Conversely, if one does not exercise restraint and fails to sever the three afflictions, yet practices killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct as one's cultivation, [one will fail].
Even if one attains supernatural powers (ṛddhi), one will inevitably fall into the path of Māra. Why? Because the habitual tendencies (vāsanā) of the three delusions have not been eliminated;
since one practices through worldly, conditioned effort (saṃskṛta-kriyā), how could one possibly succeed? This is what is lost.

Although one may wish to demonstrate the falsity of the lower fetters (avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana), if one does not sever the three delusions while attempting to remove delusive thoughts, one does not realize that this involves killing and stealing.
Sexual desire is the very root of delusion. To practice with delusion is to increase one's falsehood twofold. Why?
Because taking deluded thought as the foundation, even if one were to attain Bodhi, it would still turn out to be delusion; this is truly pitiable.

You have now concluded the section on delusion to demonstrate the distinction between the heterodox and the orthodox. If one observes with the eye of truth, this illusory cycle of saṃsāra ultimately has no bearing upon Bodhi.
Regarding the matter: because awakening is unborn, there nevertheless exists the karmic fruit of the world, for it is originally created by the delusions of sentient beings themselves.
This concludes the section below, as in the text.
△ The Section on Circulation is divided into three parts. First, the Manifestation of the Realm of Dhyāna, which has four sections. The first is the Spontaneous Discourse Without Inquiry.
At that time, the Tathāgata was about to conclude his teaching at the Dharma-seat... (until) ...with joy they prostrated themselves and listened humbly for his compassionate instruction.
The following is now recorded by the scribe of the scripture. The golden mountain represents the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); the precious desk represents wondrous enlightenment (*samyagbodhi*).
For wondrous enlightenment transcends words, yet words must have a basis; the Dharma-body is without form, yet form must have a manifestation.
Now that the formal teaching has been completed and the dharma-assembly is about to conclude, [the Buddha] again turns his purple-gold body toward the desk of the seven treasures as a support.

This reveals the characteristics of right concentration and demonstrates the path of wondrous enlightenment. This is the sūtra-master’s detailed narration, showing that the scene at that time was such as this.

"You all," and so forth, is the Tathāgata’s address; for Ānanda and the others had initially practiced the Hīnayāna as śrāvakas, but having subsequently passed through the Vaipulya period and resolved their minds toward the Mahāyāna, he therefore bestowed [this teaching] upon them.
This is the teaching of the perfect and sudden definitive meaning; it is the method for true cultivation.
As for what is called the method of cultivation, it refers to the aforementioned sublime *śamatha*, *samāpatti*, and *dhyāna*, which are the initial expedient means.
This dharma is easy when revealed by a teacher, but difficult for a student to realize. Why is this? Because the Great Dharma...
Although you are clear [in your understanding], there still remain subtle demonic activities within *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
If these are not exposed and explained, the harm they will bring in the future will not be slight. Therefore, without waiting for a question, I specifically inform you:

*śamatha* means "stopping" (*zhi*) and *vipaśyanā* means "contemplation" (*guan*). Regarding the demonic realms, the objects will be distinguished below; first, the *skandha-māra* (the demon of the aggregates).
These are transformations of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*): the celestial Māras are transformations of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*);

ghosts and spirits are transformations of the aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*); and *chimei* (goblins and specters) are transformations of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).

For a beginner whose meditative concentration is not yet deep and whose power of the Path is still shallow, when such demonic realms appear before them, if they cannot discern them, they will be captured by these thieves. How could this be...?

How lamentable! Furthermore, some are satisfied with a mere modicum of discernment. Some do not distinguish the characteristics of the various dhyāna practices, nor do they investigate the principles of the sūtras and śāstras;
they merely delight in and cling to samādhi, taking a little attainment as sufficient.

They are like the unlearned bhikṣu of the fourth dhyāna, who knew nothing at all, yet claimed, "I have already realized the Noble Vehicle and attained the fruit of arhatship. Up to the fifth [dhyāna]...

After a hundred kalpas, the signs of decline appeared once more. Seeing that there was still a place of birth, he began to doubt the Buddha’s teaching that Nirvana is birthless and false, while believing that the Arhat’s subsequent existence is real.
Consequently, he gave rise to slander and fell into the Avīci Hell. You should now listen attentively with a humble mind, as the text describes.
II. A General Explanation of the Great Meaning, in four parts: 1. A Comprehensive Clarification of Reality and Delusion.
The Buddha addressed Ānanda and the great assembly... (up to) "...how much more so for all worlds existing within empty space.
From "The Buddha addressed" downward, he establishes the reality; from "Because of you" downward, he establishes the delusion.

To begin with, the twelve classes of living beings and the Buddhas of the ten directions are of one and the same mind, fundamentally without distinction. Because they were deluded regarding this mind, they subsequently gave rise to ignorance and craving. Ignorance...
When craving arises, this mind becomes universally deluded. Because of this delusion, it fails to awaken; failing to awaken, it becomes empty.

Thus, by being utterly deluded regarding the wondrously enlightened mind, one comes to possess the nature of stubborn emptiness. Consequently, one gives rise to successive births and falls into successive delusions.
Now, these impure lands of the ten directions and all sentient beings therein all dwell in dependence upon deluded thoughts regarding inert emptiness;
they have no other basis. This should be understood through the following illustration: it is like empty space being produced within the awakened mind.
It is also like the appearance of a fragment of cloud appearing in the great void.
One should know that the fragment of cloud is without reality, and the void itself is likewise without reality. If even the void is unreal, how much more so the world, which exists within the void?
△ Second, giving rise to the True to dissolve the delusory.
"If even one among you gives rise to the True and returns to the Source" (up to) "...all lands will not be torn asunder.

This section below [the heading] provides a double reminder. The preceding section explained how delusion regarding this One Mind results in emptiness; that emptiness is immeasurable, and so too are the worlds.
Sentient beings are likewise immeasurable; this is called the ceaseless transformation of delusion.
Now, setting aside the discussion of immeasurable sentient beings, let us consider only one person who awakens to the truth and returns to the source.

Upon realizing this single mind and attaining enlightenment, the empty space of the ten directions is entirely dissolved. If even empty space is dissolved, then all lands that exist within that space must likewise perish.
"And yet, why does it not shatter? Question: "When one person awakens to the truth, how can it cause the ten directions to dissolve and perish?
Furthermore, at the very moment of dissolution, do the other realms and other sentient beings exist or not? If they exist, where are they placed?
If they do not exist, what then is being dissolved and accounted for before our eyes? Answer: "This is precisely the sentient beings' clinging to a self."
This is what is meant by "mine. Because of the conception of a self (*ātman*), there are sentient beings;

because of the conception of "mine" (*ātmīya*), there is the world. It is like a person who dreams; while dreaming, they ask another person, "Do these worlds and sentient beings exist, or do they not?
Even if one says they exist, it does not depart from this dream-consciousness; even if one says they do not exist, it likewise does not depart from it.
This is dream-consciousness. Why? Because this person has not yet awakened and not yet realized, which is what is meant by universal delusion.
If they were indeed able to awaken and realize, how could there be a world or sentient beings? Even if one were to say they exist, it does not depart from this awakening;
even if one says they do not exist, it likewise does not depart from this awakening. This is because this person has already awakened.
Because of awakening; that is to say, universal awakening. △ Third, the reason for the movement of Māra:
"When you practitioners cultivate dhyāna and adorn samādhi... at the time of samādhi, they will all come to harass you."
"You all should now understand the underlying principle. What was previously described as the empty space of the ten directions and all existing lands refers to the container-world (*bhājana-loka*).

This container-world is the locus upon which the practitioner relies. If one can give rise to the true mind and no longer allow views to arise following the six sense-faculties or the four great elements, then the empty space will naturally dissolve and the world will tremble."
It is split. Now, when one speaks of the bodhisattvas of the ten directions and the outflow-free arhats, this refers to the world of Perfect Enlightenment (samyaksambuddha).
Perfect Enlightenment is the objective realm for the practitioner.
If one cultivates dhyāna and adorns the samādhi, one will naturally achieve mental communion with the bodhisattvas and arhats of the ten directions. All that follows clarifies this.
The Māra is agitated. Furthermore, the mention of the Māra King and the various ordinary devas refers to the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*).
Sentient beings are the common retribution for practitioners. Should one enter the Great Śūraṅgama Samādhi, the Māra King and the various ordinary devas will naturally be unable to remain at ease.
This is because the Māra King is the lord of the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Those who are attached to these worldly afflictions are the ones who dwell therein.

Now, though this world is without cause for its violent rending and sentient beings are without cause for their terror, although ordinary people, shrouded in darkness, do not perceive it, the devas, māras, ghosts, spirits, and others all possess the five supernormal powers and great strength—save only for those who have attained the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows. How could such as these suffer your crushing and tearing apart?
Thus, within the samādhi of stillness, they all come to harass you. △ Fourth, showing the method for subduing them:
Although those various māras may be filled with great rage (up to) they will roll about and fall apart, beyond any possibility of pity or rescue.
However, the following passage provides extensive illustrations through metaphors: "Like wind blowing upon light, its nature is unmoving; like a knife cutting through water, the mind does not arise.
These illustrate the characteristics of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). "Hard ice and boiling water are easily melted and transformed;

the host is old and the guest is new, and the latter must eventually depart. These illustrate the function of concentration. Furthermore, *dhyāna* (meditation) is concentration, while awakening is wisdom (*prajñā*). Wisdom...

One is able to nourish concentration (*samādhi*); concentration can give rise to wisdom (*prajñā*). Wisdom is the luminosity of the mind. The various aggregates (*skandhas*) constitute the obscure; the multitude of evils constitutes the dark.

If the ground of the mind is luminous, the obscurity and darkness are instantly shattered. Although that [evil] may possess power, how would it dare to cause disorder? Furthermore, Buddhas and Māras do not coexist;
the heterodox and the orthodox do not interfere with one another. One dwells in the dust of worldly toil; the other dwells in wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). That—
Even if there is anger, how could it reach [the mind]? This is precisely the method for subduing demons. If one does not attain clear awakening, one cannot cite other matters as proof.
Essential to the cultivation of dhyāna is a gate of awakening; without a gate of awakening, the mind-ground remains unenlightened.
Deluded by the five aggregates, Ānanda has today become a son of Māra through his study of the Way. How do we know this? Take, for example, Dhanagarga;
she was but a single aggregate of form. She possessed neither the supernatural powers of a celestial Māra nor the great strength of a ghost or spirit;
she was exceedingly insignificant and inferior. Yet, solely by means of illusory incantations, she cast a spell upon you for eighty thousand kalpas.
While practicing, one violates a single precept; because there is no other [refuge], the entire body of precious awakening is utterly destroyed.

It is like a high minister’s family committing a crime: their official registers are stripped away and their family assets confiscated, until they fall into ruin with no one to rescue them—how tragic!
Those who study the Way do not expect clear enlightenment, yet they are deluded by the *skandhas* and sink into [suffering].
Regarding the evil destinies, how could they differ from this? It is simply the fault of the mind-ground being unclear and failing to achieve awakening.
△ Third, the explanation of the demon of the aggregates (*skandha-māra*). First, the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*). Initially, a general clarification.
"Ānanda, you should know that from your sitting at the site of enlightenment [up to] 'taking firm delusive thoughts as its basis.
Ānanda, the following clarifies the characteristics of the phenomenal world. This is because, since beginningless time, the various sense faculties have apprehended the shadows of the six objects;
thus, there is the characteristic of thought. However, this characteristic of thought is a law of arising and ceasing, which obscures the true nature."
Therefore, if one is free from the marks of thought, one immediately attains purity. As the preceding text states:

"If one abandons arising and ceasing and maintains the true permanence, the light of permanence will manifest before you, and the faculties, objects, consciousness, and mind will dissolve accordingly. Now it says: "You sit at the site of enlightenment."
"To dissolve all thoughts" means that this is precisely the abandonment of arising and ceasing. Furthermore, it is said, "Then all that is free from thought is entirely lucid and penetrating";
this refers to the constant radiance manifesting before one. Having attained this manifestation of constant radiance, it is thus whether in motion or at rest;
therefore, it is said that "motion and stillness do not shift. This arises from being free from the arising and ceasing of all thoughts. Recollection...
It is also like this. Forgetting is also like this. Therefore, it is said that "recollection and forgetting are as one.
Only when you reach such a state can you enter samādhi. Thus it is said: "One should abide in this place and enter samāpatti.

Generally speaking, although the mind is free from thought, one has not yet transcended the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha). It is like a person with clear vision situated in profound darkness; for the mind has not yet...

"Radiant Light. Ultimately, one still falls within the domain of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*). If the eyes are clear and bright, this is the sign that the obscuration of form is being exhausted.
Previously, one merely detached from discursive thought but could not destroy darkness; now, with the mind settled, light is emitted, illuminating the ten directions through and through.

This is the piercing of ignorance and the total casting off of worldly burdens; this is precisely the exhaustion of the aggregate of form. As for the "Dust-Turbidity" (*kalpa-kaṣāya*), it is simply the most... [text ends]
At the very first thought, there is emptiness without substance and seeing without cognition; these interweave delusively to form what is called the *kalpa-turbidity*.
Furthermore, that which is "solid" refers to ignorance enveloping the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), serving as the root of birth and death; thus it is called "solid.
Now, once this aggregate of form is entirely exhausted, one perceives the original cause and the root of ignorance, and immediately—
This transcends the characteristics of the kalpa-turbidity. △ Second, the detailed explanation has ten parts. First, the body can transcend obstructions:
"Ānanda, you should within this state investigate the wondrous clarity" (up to) "if you take this as a realization of sainthood, you will immediately fall prey to various heterodoxies."
Ānanda, the following clarifies the characteristics of the manifested realm. The two characters here refer back to the preceding discussion of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).
Through the development of that prior concentration and wisdom, one investigates and exhaustively examines the subtle principle and realizes that the four great elements do not interweave.
"Not interweaving" means they do not combine. Because the mind does not harmonize with various delusions, the sensory objects cannot coalesce. Because of these objects...
Because they do not combine, the mind is thus able to emerge from obstruction. This is termed "distinguishing the false from the wholesome" below;

it is the superior function of the mind’s sharp concentration, which forces beyond the refined essence and overflows as a transformation. Even if one is able to clearly perceive the objects before one, [it remains a state of mental fluctuation].
To know the events of a past life is merely a temporary crossroads; if one takes this to be the realization of sainthood, then one has succumbed to delusion.
△ Second, [the story of] Ti Shi finding the *ārśas* worms.
Ānanda again took this mind and investigated its subtle brilliance... (until) "if you take this as a realization of sainthood, you will immediately be possessed by various demons.
Below, Ānanda clarifies the characteristics of the manifested realm. *Ji* and *hui* are intestinal worms.

Because of the previous meditative state, the light of the mind shone back, enabling the four elements within to merge; thus, he was able to pick out the intestinal worms from the belly without causing them injury. This...
The name "Below" distinguishes it from false goodness. This is the exertion of effort that forces the vital essence beyond its bounds, overflowing into the physical form as a transformation.
If one regards this as the realization of sainthood, one will instead receive what is false. △ Third, preaching the Dharma within emptiness.

Furthermore, one should investigate this mind with precision both internally and externally (up to the point where it says): "If you take this as a realization of sainthood, you will immediately succumb to various demonic influences.
Next, [the text] clarifies the characteristics of the manifested realms: the "appropriated body" refers to that which is governed by the five viscera, such as the *hun* and *po* souls.
With the exception of the appropriated body, which remains unmoving, the other four viscera and so forth are all capable of entering [the realms]; they may either separate from or merge with them.

Yet there is no fixed singularity. Because of the previous stages—first emerging from obstruction, then penetrating within, and now refining both within and without—one attains the state where each acts as both guest and host.
Furthermore, regarding the hearing of the sound of the Dharma being preached within emptiness:

because the mind, intellect, and consciousness have, since beginningless time, perfumed the faculty of hearing to form seeds, now that the spirit has departed from its abode and lost its former constancy, one hears again.
Because old acquaintances have appeared, there is something heard being preached within the void. This is termed "distinguishing below" the heterodox from the wholesome, as in the text.
△ Fourth, the manifestation of Buddhas upon the flower pedestals.
Furthermore, with this mind clear, exposed, bright, and penetrating—up to—if one forms a saintly interpretation, one will immediately succumb to various heterodoxies.
Next, the following clarifies the characteristics of the manifested realm. The phrase "clear, exposed, bright, and penetrating" is the general description.
"Internal light shines forth, pervading the ten directions" refers to the state where the internal and external are a single color. Because that color is red and yellow, it is so named.
Jambūnada. Vairocana—this is translated as "Pervading All Places," meaning that he is universally present within all states of awakening.

Yet, awakening is without marks and without visibility. Now, because one perceives Vairocana within the preceding meditative concentration, seated upon the Terrace of Celestial Light, he appears to possess marks.
Since he possesses marks and can be seen, is this not perhaps a māra? Generally speaking...
When clarity reaches its ultimate limit, there is no presiding subject; yet, being drawn by the牵引 (karmic attraction) of former habits, views, and learning, such objects appear.
This is termed "distinguishing the false from the wholesome below," as in the text. △ Fifth, the manifestation of precious colors within emptiness.

Furthermore, by using this mind to scrutinize the wondrous clarity (up to the point where it says): "If one takes this as a realization of sainthood, one will immediately be possessed by various demons.
Furthermore, the following explains the manifestations of the objective realm: "Observation without ceasing" refers to excessive discrimination regarding clarity;
"restraint and transcendence" refers to over-pursuing the depths of investigation. Not knowing that excessive depth loses the middle way, and excessive clarity loses reality.
Thereupon, as the suppression becomes excessive, one then perceives the empty space of the ten directions entirely transformed into the color of the seven treasures.
Furthermore, regarding those that appear purely as individual colors: if it is blue, the entire realm is uniformly blue; if yellow, the entire realm is uniformly yellow, and so forth.
Yet, this does not lose its quality of being obstructive and tangible. What else could this be? It is nothing other than the mind’s restless seeking failing to cease. This is called...
The following section, "Distinguishing False Goodness," is as in the text. △ Sixth, "Seeing Objects in a Dark Room.

Furthermore, investigate this mind until it becomes clear and transparent... (up to)... if you take this to be a realization of sainthood, you will immediately fall prey to various demonic influences.

The mind is truly formless. In meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it is fundamentally without characteristics (*animitta*); yet now one can see objects in a dark room, no different from the light of day.

If this were the mind having form and concentration having characteristics, how could it be considered correct? It is simply that when the mind is extremely subtle and utterly clear, objects are able to be reflected through it.
However, objects are substantial entities that do not shift with the state of concentration; therefore, it is said that they are not eliminated.
△ Being burned by the seven fires and cut by knives, there is no sensation.
Furthermore, when this mind enters perfectly into the void and the harmonious (until: "if one takes this as a realization of sainthood, one will immediately succumb to various heresies").

When the mind is pure, external objects cannot invade it; when meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is supreme, sensory dust (*rajas*) cannot overwhelm it. Therefore, fire cannot burn it and a blade cannot cut it.
This is because one has departed from both the grasper (*grāhaka*) and the grasped (*grāhya*), entering exclusively into emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
The nature of emptiness is void and harmonious; for a time, one attains such a state, though it is not yet true meditative absorption (*samāpatti*). △ Eighth: Transformation into the Supreme Realm.
Furthermore, with this mind, one achieves purity (up to the point where) if one forms a holy understanding, one will immediately fall under the sway of various heterodoxies.
One-sidedly, one views mountains, rivers, and the great earth as inferior, and the palaces and halls of the Buddha-lands as superior; one views the hells as suffering and the heavens as bliss.
Consequently, one rejoices in bliss and loathes suffering, yearning for the superior and despising the inferior. Now, however, this is the function of stillness.

Reaching the ultimate perfection of meditative concentration, one enters the profound; through the accumulation of thought, it is transformed into manifestation. To attain such a state for a time does not mean it was originally present.
△ Ninth: The Distant Person’s Obstructed Vision.
Furthermore, when one uses this mind to investigate the profound (up to the point where), if one forms a holy understanding, one will immediately succumb to various heterodoxies.
When the investigation reaches its ultimate limit and the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is about to be exhausted, one is thus able to see people at a distance and hear their voices.
All of this occurs because the mind, having reached its extreme limit, soars forth and sheds its original aggregate. △ Ten: The Specific Manifestations of Consciousness Transformation.
Furthermore, if one uses this mind to investigate until reaching the ultimate refinement, yet interprets this as an attainment of holiness, one will immediately succumb to various demonic influences.

One may refine the investigation until form is exhausted, thereby perceiving the consciousness of others as a basis for existence. Although it serves as a basis, it is nonetheless manifold and unstable;
at times joyful, at times angry, at times beautiful, at times ugly—changing and shifting in an instant, never remaining constant.
This person may have previously possessed seeds of perverse defilement from past habituation, or an external demon may have taken advantage of an opportunity to enter.
Generally speaking, when the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) first ceases, the mind loses its support; for this reason, the demon is able to penetrate the core of their heart and belly.
△ Third, the conclusion and indication.

Ānanda, these ten kinds of meditative states (*dhyāna*) that manifest (up to) the stage of maintaining and protecting [the practice] to achieve the Unsurpassed Way—these ten types above are all transformations of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*). The preceding stages are transformations of its original characteristics, because the aggregate of form has not yet been exhausted;
the tenth stage, however, is a transformation of its external characteristics, because the aggregate of form has been exhausted.

Regarding "the mind and objects interacting": when a practitioner cultivates dhyāna, they focus solely on the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the object and do not focus on the characteristics of the thought (*nimittalakṣaṇa*).

Although they do not focus on the characteristics of the thought, because the fundamentally lucid and alert mind nevertheless flows back toward the preceding object, and because the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) may occasionally erupt surreptitiously—this is what is meant by "interaction.
If this is not explained and exposed, one will mistakenly take these experiences to be the realization of sainthood (*āryatva*), thereby ruining one's meditative cultivation.
This is a matter of profound importance, not a trivial one; therefore, I urge you to reveal it for future generations, so that the celestial Māras may find no opportunity to exploit them.
△ Second, the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha). First, a general explanation.
"Ānanda, for that good man who cultivates samādhi—[up to]—the root of this is false imagination of empty luminosity. Ānanda, the following clarifies the characteristics of the phenomenal realm.
When the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) is exhausted, the ground of the mind opens up and becomes expansive, like images appearing in a clear mirror.
Although there is comprehension, its function cannot be fully realized; it remains obscure as if something were still obstructing it. This is [the obstacle of the aggregate of sensation]."

The aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is its domain. It is like being oppressed by a ghost; though one’s seeing and hearing are perfectly clear, the hands and feet cannot move because they are struck by an external, malevolent spirit.
This is because the aggregate of sensation covers the mind. If one explains the signs of the exhaustion of the aggregate of sensation after the aggregate of form has ended:
although the mind possesses the faculty of reception, it is obstructed by this as if by a ghost oppressing the body. Suppose, however, that the mind’s reception were extinguished...
Having accepted this, the calamity of nightmares subsides, and one attains unimpeded freedom in both going and staying; this is the exhaustion of the *vedanā-skandha* (the aggregate of sensation).
As for "turbidity of views" (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*): it refers to that very first moment when one seizes upon phenomena to form cognition and consolidates a physical body to form awareness.

This aware, cognizing mind-nature is entirely a false weaving of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and possesses all manner of obstructions; therefore, it is called the turbidity of views. Furthermore, as for "empty luminosity," it is because the multitude...
Birth originally possesses the wisdom of luminous clarity; however, due to ignorance and non-awakening, it forms delusive appearances.
Thus, this luminosity is empty of substance. Therefore, it is called "empty luminosity. Now that the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is entirely exhausted, the mind attains mastery.
To observe the original source from which [the aggregates] arose and the root of deluded thought is precisely to transcend the characteristic of the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kāṣāya*). △ Second.
The ten distinct explanations: first, the demon of sorrow.
Ānanda, that son of good family, while in this state, shall lose right concentration and fall into ruin.
Ānanda, the following clarifies the characteristics of the manifest realm. Here, the two characters [“this” and “within”] refer to the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*).
"Attaining great radiance" refers to the clarity of the mind. Because one perceives through this clear mind that the aggregate of sensation is a fault, one then suppresses and subdues it.
However, if this suppression goes too far, the mind cannot maintain its composure; upon seeing objects, one immediately gives rise to sorrow.
This is the manifestation of the seeds of sorrow and grief. This is termed "Correctly Distinguishing the Right from the Wrong" within the section on Benevolence (*maitrī*).

Because [benevolence] is suppressed to excess, the demon of compassion (*karuṇā-māra*) enters one's heart and viscera. If one awakens to it, it becomes wholesome; if one does not awaken, it becomes unwholesome.
△ Second, the Demon of Madness (*unmāda-māra*).
Ānanda, furthermore, when those sons of good family within that samādhi (up to) lose their correct reception and are about to fall away, they perceive the principle within this state;
this is precisely the "clear and bright mind. Because this clear and bright mind is overly intense, they see that three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas do not exceed this single thought-moment.
Yet, by means of this single thought-moment, they can surpass Śākyamuni and outstrip Maitreya.
"There is no one superior to me. Because of this, he becomes deranged; whenever he sees someone, he immediately boasts of it to them.
△ Third, the recollection of Māra:
Furthermore, those good sons within that meditative concentration (until) they lose right reception and shall fall into ruin.

Observing the prior state of emptiness, there is nothing to be seen; thus, there is no new realization. Observing that one has already detached from the subsequent aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), one returns to lose the former dwelling.
Thus, observing both before and after, there is nothing at all to be obtained as a whole; this is called the "ground of collapsing in the middle" (*madhyavipatti-bhūmi*).

Furthermore, because there is no further progress, it is called "sinking"; because there is no regression, it is called "recollection. Striking the mind upon a single point all day long—this is what is meant.
This is the summary of the "Hanging" [samādhi]. △ Fourth, the demon of being easily satisfied with little:
Furthermore, those sons of good family within that state of concentration (until) they lose their right reception and shall fall into ruin.
Generally, concentration can nourish wisdom, and wisdom can nourish concentration. When concentration and wisdom are balanced and harmonious, it is called attaining the Middle Way.
Now, however, this is not the case. If wisdom exceeds concentration, one becomes mired in intellectual views (*jñāna-dṛṣṭi*).
If the mind neglects careful examination, one loses its sharp intensity. Sharp intensity is the superior mind; intellectual views are merely frantic wisdom (*unmatta-prajñā*). Such a person...
To perceive oneself as Vairocana is deluded wisdom (*mādhya-prajñā*); to no longer seek further progress and to take little as sufficient is intellectual view (*jñāna-dṛṣṭi*).
If one does not awaken in this way, the demon of "easily satisfied contentment" will surely enter one's heart and viscera in the future.
△ Fifth, the demon of sorrow and anxiety.
Furthermore, those sons of good family within that meditative concentration (until) they lose their right absorption and fall into ruin.

Having not yet attained new realization, the mind that previously gained [attainment] has already perished. With no basis for either advancing or retreating, they encounter hardship and conclude that practicing the Way is of no benefit.
They no longer wish to live and seek only a swift death. This is the loss incurred by practicing concentration.
Regarding skillful means, it causes the seeds of regret and affliction to manifest. 6. The Mara of Joy:
Furthermore, within that meditative concentration, those sons of good family (up to) lose their correct reception and shall fall away from it.

When the mind has obstructions, it sinks; when the mind has no obstructions, it floats. Now, within meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one perceives pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) and purity, giving rise to joy (*prīti*).
However, pliancy belongs to concentration, whereas joy belongs to floating. Because of this buoyancy, [the mind] becomes unstable.
Because wisdom cannot maintain and sustain [the mind], the factor of joy (prīti-aṅga) arises. △ Seventh, the Mara of Pride:
Furthermore, those sons of good family within that meditative concentration (from... until) lose their right absorption (samāpatti) and shall fall into ruin.

There are seven types of pride (*māna*). To treat those of equal virtue with arrogance is called pride. To rely on oneself and look down upon others is called the pride of self (*asmimāna*). To compete for superiority among equals is called excessive pride (*adhimāna*).

To compete for superiority among those who are already superior is called the pride beyond pride (*mānātimāna*). To claim one has attained what one has not attained is called overweening pride (*abhimāna*).

To boast of oneself despite being inferior is called the pride of inferiority (*ūnamāna*). To fail to pay reverence to stupas and temples, or to destroy scriptures and images, and so forth [is also categorized under these forms of pride].
It is called "false pride" (*mithyāmāna*). The first six types are mentioned collectively, while the last type is the primary manifestation.
If one still holds oneself in contempt even toward the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, how much more so toward śrāvakas of lower rank? This is precisely false pride.

Furthermore, not prostrating to stupas and temples, or destroying scriptures and images, constitutes "self-pride" (*asmimāna*). This arises from seeing within meditative concentration that one's own mind is non-existent.

The Buddha has no sentient beings; there is neither self nor other—this is called supreme vision (*vijaya-dṛṣṭi*). When this supreme vision arises, wisdom is unable to sustain it, and thus the demon of pride (*māna-māra*) emerges.
△ Eighth, the demon of lightness and purity (*laghu-viśuddhi-māra*).
Furthermore, those sons of good family within that meditative concentration (may) lose their right absorption and fall into decline.
Clarity and vigor constitute concentration; perfect realization constitutes wisdom. However, wisdom and concentration are most difficult to bring into accord.
Now, having perfectly realized the subtle principle, the principle accords with gnosis; this is what it means to attain accord. Because of this accord, one attains lightness and tranquility.
Arrogantly claiming to have realized the state of a sage—is this not a delusion? Furthermore, to fail to seek further advancement is to lack learning.
To have no learning yet to delight in what is light and pure—is this not the work of Māra? △ Ninth: The Mara of Emptiness.
Furthermore, those good sons within that state of meditative concentration (until they) lose their right absorption and fall into ruin, perceive a realm of empty luminosity in the midst of space.
They then cling to this emptiness as being correct, saying, "What holding or violating can there be in emptiness?
Consequently, they give rise to false views within and summon the demons of emptiness from without; they destroy the Buddha’s disciplinary code and do not avoid censure or suspicion.
That which causes people not to suspect [the danger] is actually sustained by Māra. △ Ten: The Mara of Desire.
Furthermore, those sons of good family within that meditative concentration (until) they lose their right absorption and shall fall into ruin.
"Flavor" refers to craving and attachment. One becomes attached to the realm of empty clarity; "empty clarity" is emptiness.
Because emptiness lacks the discernment of wisdom, demons enter one's heart and bones, preaching that desire is bodhi and that practicing sexual misconduct is the way of a Dharma-son.
This is precisely the work of Māra. △ Third, the conclusion and instruction.

Ānanda, these ten kinds of manifested states during *dhyāna* (extending to) maintaining and protecting [the mind] so as to achieve the Unsurpassed Way—these ten aforementioned types are transformations of the *vedanā-skandha* (aggregate of sensation).
They are like stains and scars; although the mental impurities have been removed, the traces of the objects still remain.
Wisdom cannot discern them, yet the *vedanā-skandha* takes advantage of this to manifest them. This is what is meant by "the interaction of the mind's application."

This is because when concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are balanced, demons cannot enter. Now, however, it is not so. Sometimes wisdom is excessive while concentration cannot maintain stability;
at other times, concentration is superior while wisdom lacks the power of discernment. For this reason, external demons take advantage of these conditions to arise.

If one does not expose and break through this, they will mistakenly recognize [delusions] as sagehood, thereby disturbing meditative absorption (*dhyāna-samādhi*). The harm caused is no small matter; therefore, I urge you [to do so].
He reveals this for future generations so that the heavenly Māras may find no opportunity. △ Third, the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*). First, the general explanation:
"Ānanda, those good sons... [up to] ...take the delusion of mutual fusion as its basis."
Ānanda, the following clarifies the characteristics of the physical realm. Now, the two aggregates of form and sensation are but illusory shadows of things;
sentient beings have consistently and delusively clung to them as their bodies, much like a bird confined within a cage.

Now that the aggregate of sensation has been exhausted and the attachment to the body has perished, it is like a bird escaping its cage—the mind has departed from its physical form. At this juncture, if it is...

Those of sharp faculties do not engage in other thoughts; they traverse the stages of sainthood within their ordinary bodies and attain the mind-born body (*manomayakāya*) to ascend the ranks of the Way.
This is precisely the realization of unimpeded wisdom (*anāvaraṇaprajñā*). If one is of dull faculties, it is not so;

although the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*) may have ended, there is still movement of thought, whereby one falls into the domain of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*). It is like the manner of speaking in one's sleep while in deep slumber.
The semblance-cause (sādṛśya-hetu) of clinging to a self is likened to deep sleep; the movement of thoughts arising from that cause is likened to talking in one's sleep.

This is because the noble ones who have attained the stages (bhūmi) know that they have exhausted the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) and possess the portion of the noble state, yet they are merely covered by the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha).
Lacking self-mastery—this is the domain of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).

If one moves the mind to clarify the characteristics of the exhaustion of this aggregate, generally speaking, when there is thought, one lacks self-mastery; when there is perception, one is obstructed by it.

If thought ceases and perception is removed, one attains the perfect illumination of awakened clarity, and thereby perceives both the root and the branches. Furthermore, the "root" is birth, and the "branches" are...
This is precisely cessation. For when conceptualization exists, there is birth; when conceptualization is absent, there is cessation.
Since birth and cessation are entirely false conceptualizations, if you now can illuminate them from beginning to end, root to branch, you will naturally not follow their arising and ceasing.

Once arising and ceasing have ceased, this is the exhaustion of the aggregate of conceptualization (*saṃjñā-skandha*). What is called affliction is simply the deluded thoughts, memories, and cognitions of beginningless time.
To recite and study [the scriptures] while agitating the pure mind is what is called "affliction" (*kleśa*).

Now, by means of the perfect illumination of awakened clarity, one contemplates and perceives the origin of birth-and-death and the root of delusive thought; this is precisely to transcend the turbidity of afflictions.
△ Second, the detailed explanation of the ten [turbidities], the first being the transformation resulting from craving for objects.
Ānanda, those good men, while the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is empty and subtle, become deluded and fail to realize this, thereby falling into the Avīci Hell.

Ānanda, what follows clarifies the essence and function [of this state]: when the aggregate of sensation is exhausted, the ground of the mind becomes empty and pure; thus, one perceives it as empty and subtle.
Because the perfect concentration is profound, perverse thoughts do not encounter it; thus, illumination is manifested. This refers to the essential substance of samādhi.
*Samādhi* means "contemplative observation. From concentration arises illumination; from illumination arises attachment.

The mind becomes attached to this illumination and sharpens its refined thinking to seek skillfulness. Skillfulness is the inclination toward gaining profit; it is the residual habit of greed for material objects.
Because objects constitute its domain, the practitioner’s mind becomes greedy; by skillfully attaining the path, it is called "skillful" (*kauśalya*). This refers to the application of concentration.
The passage beginning with "At that time" clarifies the signs of the manifestation of Māra. "That person" refers to the individual possessed by Māra.
"He seeks skill" refers to the person practicing concentration; because the practitioner's mind craves such skill, Māra then takes possession of them.
For some people, he may appear as a bhikṣu or as Śakra; these are precisely the manifestations of Māra.
Those who practice meditative concentration fail to realize this and, being deluded, place their trust in him; thus they fall into his clever stratagems and become his partisans.

In their mouths, they delight in speaking of the subtle and profound matters of Māra’s teachings. This is because people are fond of the strange; he speaks of calamities, auspicious signs, and miraculous transformations.
This serves to stir up their desires. People are fond of the perverse; thus, he preaches of the kalpa of swords and the fire at the end of the age to terrify their hearts.
This, moreover, is a skillful device of Māra that accords with human nature. This concludes the section on "Naming. As for "strange things," these are physical anomalies.
When the power of such things declines, they will inevitably be exposed, which is why they bring about calamities. You should immediately exhort them to act first.
Awakening: To awaken first is good; not to awaken leads to downfall. △ Second, the transformation caused by craving for form:

These are precisely the signs manifested by the *māra*. The practitioner of concentration, not recognizing this, becomes deluded and believes him; thus, he falls into that realm and completes [the cycle of rebirth].
They form a faction. In their mouths, they delight in speaking of the demonic teachings of "Lower Illumination. This is because people are fond of such realms;

This is yet another skillful device of Māra used to flatter and accommodate people. This is termed "Concluding Judgment by Association. As for *pó* (魃), it refers to the wind-demon (*vātābhra*). Wind...

yet it can cause the person to attain prior realization, which is a mental resonance and accord. Alternatively, one may obtain the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*), or obtain the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).
As for the mind, even when reciting sutras or chanting verses to cause each person to rejoice, if it accords with [their] principles, this is a manifestation of Māra.
A practitioner of meditative concentration who fails to perceive this will be deluded and believe it;
thus they fall into his scheme and become part of his faction. His mouth is fond of speaking of matters that appear to clarify the teachings of Māra, for the human heart desires...
Seeking to harmonize with that Way, he then asserts that the Buddha has great and small [teachings], and that there is a sequence of before and after; even regarding the Bodhisattvas, it is the same.
This, moreover, is the skillful device of Māra, used to ingratiate himself with people. This is termed "concluding the judgment. As for "mèi" (魅), it refers to a generic term for a malevolent spirit.
When the power of such a spirit declines, it inevitably leads to its exposure. This is why such difficulties arise. You should descend immediately.
The exhortation to awaken first is as stated in the text. △ Fourth, the transformations resulting from greed and resentment:

Generally speaking, although form and sensation have ceased, the fundamental element of perception (saṃjñā) still remains. Now, within this meditative concentration, one exhaustively examines the emptiness of the nature of things to refresh the mind.

They incline their hearts with reverence and submission. They take pleasure in speaking of the demonic teachings that claim to clarify the future—of calamities and blessings that shall never fail to manifest.

Those of great power harbor a spirit of empty arrogance; when this empty vigor declines, they will inevitably meet with ruin and destruction, which is why they encounter such difficulties.
You should now exhort those who have first awakened according to the text. (7) The Transformations of Greed and Deceit.

Furthermore, when the son of good family experiences the subtle emptiness of the *skandha* of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*)—up to the point where he is deluded and unaware and falls into the Avīci Hell—the essence and function of this state are clarified as follows.
The essence of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is as previously described. One knows that [sensation] belongs to the mind (*manas*), while seeing belongs to the eye (*cakṣus*).

When the mind craves knowledge and vision, this is the transformation of the residual habits (*vāsanā*) of greed and delusion. Indeed, there is nothing that delusion does not know; now, in seeking knowledge, there is nothing that delusion does not [obscure].
To see is now to seek to see. By means of this, one investigates and seeks after past lives (*pūrvanivāsa*), which is one of the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*).
At that time, the manifestation of Māra appears as a lower light. A precious jewel is a thing difficult to see;
a sealed document is a book difficult to see. [The teaching] causes all these to be seen: the hidden treasures beneath the earth, matters difficult to know, and medicinal herbs of excellence.
"Delicacies—flavors difficult to perceive—causing all to know them; this is a manifestation of Māra. He uses such excuses to bring about this state.
In his mouth he delights in speaking of matters taught by Māra as being 'subtle and clear. When he speaks of 'treasures in other lands,' it is to cause people to delight in seeking knowledge of them.
When he speaks of 'extraordinary persons,' it is to cause people to delight in seeing them. This is the skillful means of Māra."

The capacity for response meets with this; this is called the concluding judgment of the section below. You should now exhort and awaken [the practitioner] according to the text. △ Eight: Greed for the Manifestations of Luminosity.
Furthermore, son of good family, when the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becomes empty and subtle... (up to) ...being deluded and ignorant, they fall into the Avīci Hell.

Furthermore, this skillfully clarifies the essence and function [of luminosity]. The essence of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is as previously described. As for supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), they are one of the six powers; here, it refers specifically to the power of the mind (*manas*).
This is because it relies on the mind rather than consciousness (*vijñāna*), and relies on the spirit (*shen*) rather than form. This is what is called supernormal power.
If one seeks such powers through the attachment of the heart, this is merely a transformation of the residual habit of craving for luminosity. By using a mind that craves luminosity to investigate...

Because one investigates the source of transformation, and that source of transformation is the mind (*manas*). What is transformed by it is a "penetration" (*abhijñā*), yet this is a false penetration and not true supernatural power (*ṛddhi*).

At this point, the text clarifies the characteristics of the Māras manifesting supernatural powers; it briefly distinguishes between the false and the correct solely regarding the phrase "weapons" (*śastra*).
This means that if it is correct, weapons cannot cause obstruction; if it is false, one does not attain mastery. This is the false [penetration].
This is the correct verification. The mouth constantly speaks of what is inferior; this clarifies that it is the speech of Māra regarding supernatural powers (*abhijñā*).
This is termed the "concluding judgment. You should now exhort and awaken [the practitioner] according to the text, point by point. △ Ninth: Greed accomplishes what is transformed.

Furthermore, when the son of good family experiences the subtle emptiness of the *skandha* of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*)—up to the point where he becomes deluded and fails to recognize it—he falls into the Avīci Hell.

Furthermore, the lower section clarifies the essence and function [of concentration]. The essence of concentration is as previously described. As for "the mind loving entry into cessation": cessation is simply non-existence.

To investigate the transformative nature of the myriad things and find it to be only non-existence, and thus to negate everything as being utterly non-existent in order to enter emptiness—this too is a residual habit of craving for accomplishment. This is because the transformative nature of things is established by means of emptiness;
therefore, one craves that profound emptiness. At this point, the text below clarifies the signs of the manifestation of Māra: within the great assembly, his form suddenly becomes empty.
That which manifests the appearance of entering extinction, yet suddenly emerges again from emptiness, manifests the nature of empty transformation.
Because those who practice the Way harbor a deep craving for emptiness, Māra seizes this opportunity to delude them.
His mouth constantly speaks of inferior, demonic teachings, claiming that "emptiness is signless" and that one should return to extinction within emptiness immediately upon arising from it.
"How could there be cause and effect, or a future life? This is precisely the nihilistic emptiness of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas).

Furthermore, to clarify the essence and function [of samādhi]: the essence of concentration is as previously described. As for the mind’s longing for longevity, this is the hope that one shall not perish.
The segmented [existence] is the coarse aspect of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*); the transformational [existence] is the subtle aspect of consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Now, to transform the coarse aspect of the five aggregates and instead seek the transformation of the subtle aspect of consciousness, thereby attaining what is imperishable and seeking permanence, is the lingering habit of partisan attachment.
This is because the subtle consciousness of the mind is its own kindred. At this point, the following clarifies this.
Regarding the manifestations of Māra: that he may appear from ten thousand *li* away in a mere instant is "the same within the different.
Because it is the same, he arrives as soon as one lifts the eyes. That he does not arrive for many years despite being only a few paces away is "the different within the same.

Because it is different, the characteristics of a single room vary. All of the above are signs of transformation; the following, which are constantly spoken of in the mouth, clarify the speech of Māra.

Regarding these matters: to say that the Buddhas of the ten directions arise from me manifests transformation; to say that I am the primordial Buddha manifests permanence. This is called the "concluding judgment.
The Deva Īśvara is the sixth heaven of the desire realm, subsumed under the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*);
it is the Heaven of the Māra King. Cāmuṇḍā refers to the servant-demon (*yakṣa*). Piśāca refers to...

Those who consume vital essence and qi, seeking permanence through the consumption of vital essence and qi, yet seek changeability through the employment of spirits—this is precisely the dharma of the Mara King.
You should immediately exhort and awaken them according to the text. △ Third, the conclusion and demonstration, in two parts.

[They] act as spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). Since the master has become a demon, his disciples cannot be otherwise. When master and disciple both become demons, it is called "passion transmitted from passion.
Even those with good intentions who study the Way, if they lack the awakening of wisdom, will all fall into their faction and become the retinue of demons;
this is truly a great pity. Why is this so? It is generally because they take the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) as [their basis].

This is the harm [of the aggregate of perception]. There are two types of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*): first, that of the distracted state; second, that of the concentrated state. It is because of the distracted state [that this harm arises], not because of the concentrated state.
For example, it is like wind causing ripples on water. The subtle wind is the cause; the ripples on the water are the perceptions (*saṃjñā*).
When one practicing meditative concentration is either too buoyant or too sunken, concentration and wisdom are unbalanced, and thus the old habitual tendencies are aroused.
This is because it results in the fault of forming conceptual thoughts. Thus, Māra seizes this opportunity to respond accordingly.
Therefore, it is said that the cause lies in the harm wrought by the *saṃjñā-skandha* (the aggregate of perception). You should now issue an edict to exhort Ānanda. Previously, Ānanda made this vow:

"Just as one does not enter *nirvāṇa* here until every single sentient being has attained Buddhahood, I now command Ānanda that even if he attains the stage of *aśaikṣa*, he need not yet enter extinction.
This is because remaining to vow to deliver sentient beings is the primary duty of one who studies the Way.
To be able to deliver sentient beings is sufficient to repay the Buddha’s kindness. △ Second, the conclusion and exhortation to transmit and demonstrate this.

Generally speaking, the *saṃjñā-skandha* is like the wind, and the ocean of the mind is like the waves;
