Narrated by the Śramaṇa Jishi, residing at the Ancient Xingfu Chan Monastery in Ludong. △ Fourth:
The Aggregate of Volitional Formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). First, the general explanation:
"Ānanda, that good man who cultivates *samādhi*... [up to] ...takes profound and hidden delusions as its root."
Ānanda, the following clarifies the benefits of the preceding signs. Now, as long as the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) has not been exhausted, it is like a turbid wave;
when one is awake, it becomes thought, and when one sleeps, it becomes a dream, because it is conjoined with various illusions. If the aggregate of perception is exhausted, it is like a clear sky.

"Waking is also like this; sleeping is also like this" means that they are unified within a single awakening (*jue*). Furthermore, clarity is a metaphor for illumination, and emptiness is a metaphor for awakening.
When there is awakening, not a single dharma remains; when there is illumination, all phenomena are fully reflected. It is like a mirror:
regarding all objective realms (*viṣaya*), things come without sticking to it, and they depart without leaving a trace. This is the empty reception of reflections.
When one realizes this, how can there be old habits? How can there be floating thoughts? There is only the single, refined truth.

The "birth and extinction" section clarifies the characteristics of the phenomenal realm: form and sensation are coarse and heavy characteristics; the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is the shadow of all dharmas;
and it is the mind that pursues birth and extinction without being aware of it. Now that the coarse and heavy [characteristics] have been removed.

The reflected images have already vanished. Although the life-continuum of sentient beings has not yet been fully restored, the fundamental source of their arising and ceasing is entirely revealed herein.

How is this known? What we now see—this flickering, shimmering light that at times appears bright and at times dark, like a mirage—is it not the very arising and ceasing of sentient beings? We see that it sometimes moves...
At times it is still; it is indistinct, obscure, and fleeting, as if bound by a thread—is this not the fundamental source of all sentient beings?
Because all ten classes of beings possess it, it is called the "common basis of life. Because its movement and stillness are not constant, it is called "clarity and agitation."

Furthermore, the pivot of a door is called a *shu*, and the socket of a door is called a *xue*. The floating sense-faculties (*āyatana*) resemble the door pivots, while the ultimate sense-faculties (*indriya*) resemble the door sockets.
This is stated in reference to the overall mode of activity (*ākāra*), because all movement is governed by these.

When a practitioner of meditative concentration reaches this state, it is precisely the domain of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). What follows below clarifies the signs of the exhaustion of the aggregates. [This concludes] the section on perception (*saṃjñā*).
It is entirely like water; therefore, it is called "clear. Its movement is like waves; therefore, it is called "agitated. This is the original nature, the nature first born.
Once its active manifestations are settled, the original nature returns to oneness, just as waves subside into the sea;

this is the sign of the exhaustion of the *skandhas*. What is called the "turbidity of sentient beings" refers to the single thought-moment from time immemorial, wherein the mind gives rise to cognition.

Seeing constitutes birth. The karmic movement and flux constitute going; because the mind and its characteristics combine provisionally, it is called the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*).

Regarding the term "profoundly hidden" (*āvila*): because the mind of arising and ceasing is extremely deep and subtle, it appears as if seen yet not seen; therefore, it is said to be profoundly hidden.
Now, with the characteristics of activity fixed, one contemplates the cause of the ultimate movement and the root of deluded thought. Thus...
This transcends the turbidity of sentient beings. △ Second, the detailed explanation of the ten [heresies] has ten parts. First: the theory of no cause.
Ānanda, you should know that this refers to the first heterodox teacher who establishes the theory of no cause (up to the point where it says "attains right knowledge").
Ānanda, you should know that the single phrase "in summary" introduces the following heading on "right reception" (*samyaksamādhi*).
The term "right knowledge" (*samyagjñāna*) serves to distinguish this state from the presence of floating thoughts. "Concentrated clarity" refers to *śamatha* concentration;

by the power of *śamatha*, floating thoughts do not arise and external demons cannot enter—this is what is called "right reception. The subsequent section introduces the heading on "false calculations," beginning with the word "refined."
"Researching" refers to wild wisdom (*kudṛṣṭi*). "The source of birth" refers to the common basis of birth. "Profound clarity" is the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

Because the aggregate of formations has not yet been exhausted, wild wisdom suddenly arises; within the fundamental nature, one perceives the root of all classes of living beings as being entirely without cause.
From this speculative calculation, two theories of non-causality are established.

The first is the inferior view that there is no fundamental cause. How is this known? This person’s *saṃjñā-skandha* (perception aggregate) has already been exhausted, and their faculty of discernment has become penetrating.
Relying on this mind of wisdom, they see everything within eighty thousand kalpas and know each detail; yet beyond eighty thousand kalpas, it is dark and there is nothing to be observed.
By this, one knows that sentient beings arise from a state fundamentally without cause. They do not know [this absence of cause].

Since beginningless time, because of the habitual conditioning of karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*), there is nothing that is not known. When this karmic consciousness is exhausted, then [the perceived object] ceases to exist.
This is like seeing a person at night carrying a torch while walking; when they have walked far and it is no longer seen, one concludes that the fire has been extinguished and is no more.
What is seen within this person’s meditative concentration is precisely analogous to this. From this point downward, the faults are summarized as in the text.
Second, regarding the view that the end has no cause: how is this known? This person, by means of the power of this wisdom, sees that it was thus eighty thousand kalpas ago;
they see that it will be thus after eighty thousand kalpas as well. They see that there is no cause at the beginning, and they see that there is likewise no cause at the end.
This includes everything from the mountains, rivers, and great earth before one’s eyes, to the sun, moon, and stars, down even to the blades of grass.
Humans and animals each remain unchanged; it is not that they are incapable of changing, but rather because there is no distinct cause for change.
Since there is no distinct cause, how could *bodhi* (enlightenment) ever be realized at some future time?

By this, one knows that all phenomena are fundamentally without cause and likewise without cause in their final manifestation. It is simply that from beginningless time, they have been sustained by the power of habitual karmic conditioning. Karmic...

When power declines, it must undergo transformation. This is like looking up at the sky and seeing flowers appear; the flowers cannot transform [the sky], yet one might conclude that there is no other cause.
What this person perceives within meditative concentration is precisely analogous to this. From this point on, the conclusion of the faults follows the text.
The two types mentioned above both fall into the heterodox calculation that things arise without a cause.

This is also like the Confucian scholars of this land who calculate that "the alternation of Yin and Yang is called the Way," or the followers of Laozi who take "spontaneity" (*ziran*) as their fundamental tenet.
If one takes spontaneity as the fundamental tenet, it is arising without a cause; if one calculates that Yin and Yang constitute the Way, it is arising from a false cause. Why?
It is truly a pity that this essence of spiritual clarity and perfect awakening is deludedly taken to be causeless or produced by false causes.
Consequently, one loses right knowledge and falls into the ranks of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas). Is this not truly lamentable?

The "Eight Hundred Merits" section of the *Śāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra* (or relevant commentary), Volume Four, identifies the "winding currents of karma" as specifically referring to the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations). II. The Four Theories of Universal Permanence.

Ānanda, these good sons within the state of *samādhi*—[from here] up to—"the second heterodox teacher who establishes the doctrine of pervasive permanence"—the phrase "Ānanda" below marks the correct meditative attainment as previously described;
"exhausting the inferior" below marks the false calculations. Regarding the statement "the source of constant agitation," it is because the source of movement is like water;
that waves constantly arise even when there is no wind is due to the influence of one's nature and habitual tendencies. [This is] the practice.

The same applies to the *āyatanas*. Although floating thoughts have ceased, the fact that their active characteristics (*ākāra*) remain constantly disturbed is likewise brought about by the influence of one's nature and habitual tendencies.
Through this exhaustive investigation, he observed within that profound clarity that the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena (*dharmas*) is eternal;
he thus established the Fourfold Doctrine of Perfect Eternity.
First, one must thoroughly investigate the two domains of mind and object. It is said that these two domains lack the cause for floating thoughts;

they are merely what follows from their own characteristics. For the mind does not exist independently—it must rely on objects to arise—and objects do not perceive themselves—they must depend on the mind to exist.
Thus, while objects undergo arising and ceasing, the mind remains ever-present. Therefore, it is known that throughout twenty thousand kalpas...
That all sentient beings follow the cycle of birth and death without losing their continuity is because their nature is eternal.
Second, by investigating down to the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), one finds that each of these four elements is eternal.
If even one were not eternal, then heaven, earth, and the myriad things could not be established or maintained. Since the Great Nature is eternal, one thereby knows the four [elements].
Throughout ten thousand kalpas, all sentient beings undergo birth and extinction without interruption because their substance is eternal.
Third, [the text] exhaustively investigates the eight consciousnesses down to the lowest level: *manas* is the seventh consciousness; "appropriation" (*upādāna*) refers to the eighth consciousness.

The accumulation [of seeds] is called *citta* (mind); the deliberation is called *manas* (intellect); the discernment is called *vijñāna* (consciousness). Furthermore, the eight consciousnesses are called *citta*;
the seven consciousnesses are called *manas*; and the six consciousnesses are called *vijñāna*. These eight consciousnesses are each and every one of them eternal.

If even one were not eternal, the phenomena of the three periods of time could not be established, and one would fall into nihilistic emptiness (*uccheda-śūnyatā*). Because these consciousnesses are eternal, it is known that they have existed for eighty thousand kalpas.
Among these, the reason all sentient beings undergo birth and death in continuous succession without interruption is that their consciousness (*vijñāna*) is eternal.
Fourth, by investigating the principle of birth and death to its ultimate limit: if the source of ideation (*saṃjñā*) is exhausted, distinct objects of perception will not arise.
Since there is no arising, there is likewise no ceasing. This principle is precisely what is meant by "eternal. If this were not eternal, [it would be otherwise].

What else could be permanent? Therefore, we know that within the midst of the myriad transformations, that which attains spontaneity (*ziran*) without exhaustion does so because its principle (*li*) is permanent.
From this point downward, the errors are summarized as in the text. △ This concludes the discussion on the four inversions.
Furthermore, among the various good sons within *samādhi* (up to) the third type of externalist theory of partial permanence.
Again, "within *samādhi*" indicates the correct attainment as previously described; "exhausting the inferior" indicates the false calculations. Regarding "self and other":

these refer to the two dharmas of the "other" and the "self. Since these two dharmas of the other and the self must necessarily have distinct portions, one establishes the doctrine of partial permanence based on this. One.
The division [of the self] is impermanent.
First, there is the "lower self" which is impermanent; that which is profound and still is the "spiritual principle" (*shenli*).
This spiritual principle is precisely what is called the "self. This principle of the spiritual self pervades the ten directions, and all sentient beings are born from this self.
In that case, those [beings] undergo arising and ceasing, whereas I am without arising and ceasing. That which is without arising and ceasing is permanent;
that whose nature involves arising and ceasing is impermanent.

Regarding these two—the destruction during a kalpa and the non-destruction of the kalpa—one does not contemplate their underlying principle while in meditative absorption, but contemplates only the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*).

One observes that those in the third dhyāna and below, who possess form and color, are subject to destruction; one observes that those in the fourth dhyāna and above, who are formless and colorless, are not subject to destruction.
That which is not subject to destruction is beyond the reach of the three calamities of the kalpa; that which is subject to destruction is reached by the three calamities of the kalpa.
Therefore, it is known that that which is not destroyed by the kalpa possesses the nature of permanence, while that which is destroyed by the kalpa possesses the nature of impermanence.

Furthermore, there are three aspects: the inferior consists of the refined and the coarse. The refined is the mind; the coarse is the body. The body undergoes birth and extinction, whereas the mind does not change or shift.
That which does not change or shift is my nature; therefore, it is indestructible. All things that undergo birth and extinction—

It is because they flow forth from my mind that they perish. Thus, that which does not perish is of a permanent nature (*nityatā*), whereas that which perishes is of an impermanent nature (*anityatā*).

Fourth, the lower [realms] are permanent, while the rest are impermanent; that is to say, form (*rūpa*), sensation (*vedanā*), and perception (*saṃjñā*) are of an impermanent nature, as their cessation is directly perceived.

Because [the former] has been exhausted, the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is of a permanent nature, for it is seen to flow continuously in the present. That which flows continuously is the nature of true permanence;
that which is extinguished is the nature of true impermanence. From this point downward, the faults are summarized as in the text.
The four types mentioned above all arise from the view of self and other within a single body; therefore, they posit that one part is eternal and one part is impermanent.
This is called false view. Why? To establish "other" upon one's own body does not constitute [the reality of] the self;
for another being to be born within one's own body does not constitute [the reality of] the other. In this way, it is entirely a matter of external phenomena existing apart from the mind.
Because they naturally give rise to contradiction, they are called "inverted. △ Fourth: The Discourse on the Existence of Limits.
Furthermore, among the various good sons within *samādhi* (up to) the fourth non-Buddhist who establishes the theory of the existence of limits.
Furthermore, "again, samā" [in the original text] indicates correct realization as previously described; "exhausting the lower" indicates false conceptualization.
As for "states," existence is one extreme and non-existence is another extreme; therefore, the four theories of finitude are established.
First, regarding the inferior view that fails to see the two extremes: the past has already passed, and the future is yet to come;
since neither is seen, they are called "having limits" (*sānta*). The present functions without ceasing, continuing without end, and is clearly visible;
this is called "without limits" (*ananta*). "Continuity" is spoken of in terms of substance, while the "two limits" are spoken of in terms of time, because time exists.
"Limitation" refers to the fact that the essence has no limitations.

Second, there are the two extremes of "having hearing and seeing" and "lacking hearing and seeing. This means that within eighty thousand kalpas, there is hearing and seeing, which is called the extreme of existence;
prior to eighty thousand kalpas, there is neither hearing nor seeing, which is called the extreme of non-existence.
Furthermore, those who possess hearing and seeing are sentient beings; those without hearing and without seeing are emptiness and stillness (*śūnyatā-viśrānti*).
Emptiness and stillness constitute one extreme, while sentient beings constitute the other extreme.
Third, there are the two extremes of "knowing" and "not knowing" regarding that which is below. Non-limitlessness (anantatva) is "not knowing.
As for my universal knowledge, because I do not see anyone who perceives non-limitlessness, they are "not knowing" due to their ignorance. Limitlessness (antavattva) is "knowing."
I have never known anyone who, perceiving that things possess a finite nature, yet possesses knowledge;
for it is precisely because they possess knowledge that they are said to perceive a finite nature. That which I do not know is called the infinite nature.
Fourth are the two extremes of arising-and-ceasing and non-arising-non-ceasing. To have cognition in one moment is arising; to forget that cognition in one moment is ceasing.
Thus, within a single body, one perceives half-arising and half-ceasing. Furthermore, places where sentient beings reside are the extreme of existence, which is arising;
places where no sentient beings reside are the extreme of non-existence, which is ceasing. Thus, regarding the world—
In the midst [of samādhi], one perceives things as half-arising and half-ceasing. From this point downward, the faults are summarized as in the text.

△ Fifth, the Discourse on Evasive and Confused Answers Regarding Immortality. Furthermore, among the various good sons within samādhi... (up to) ...the evasive and confused answers regarding immortality, which are pervasive false speculations.
Furthermore, "Again, *samādhya*... indicates right attainment as previously described. "Exhausting inferiority... indicates false views.

Regarding "the indecisive evasion of immortality" (*amarā-vikṣepa*), it is explained in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* that non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) reckon the eternal nature of heaven to be "immortality," and they maintain that answering without confusion constitutes this [view].
One may thus be reborn in that heaven. If one were to answer impulsively when actually lacking knowledge, it would likely constitute evasive equivocation (*amarā-vikṣepa*).

Therefore, when questioned, one might reply, "It is secret," or claim that it should not be disclosed, or provide an indefinite answer. The Buddha’s teachings condemn this, stating: "This is true evasive equivocation.
Hence, it is called "evasive equivocation regarding immortality" (*amarā-vikṣepa*). This will be seen separately below, which clarifies the nature of such evasive answers.
The first [point] sets forth eight aspects: namely, permanence and change, arising and ceasing, increase and decrease, existence and non-existence.

Regarding the subsequent inquiry, the response provided consists of only six points; this is not due to a textual omission, but because the detailed meaning of those [remaining two] was not the subject of the question.

Regarding the phrase "losing the chapters and sentences": this refers to when a question is not answered directly, causing the interlocutor to fail to grasp the underlying meaning within the sentences;
hence it is called "losing the chapters and sentences."

Second, by observing downward that all phenomena are non-existent—since they perish moment by moment as soon as they arise and are thus non-existent the very instant they are produced—one comes to know that all phenomena are non-existent.
Because there is nothing to be realized due to this non-existence, the answer given is solely "non-existence."
Third, when observing downward, one sees that all phenomena exist; each and every one arises moment by moment, for as soon as the mind is directed toward them, they are present.
Thus, one knows that all phenomena are [thus]. Because this is realized through such means, the answer given is exclusively this.
Fourth, when one looks downward at all phenomena as being both existent and non-existent, because their objects are manifold, the mind also becomes distracted.
This means that as each thought-moment arises, it immediately perishes; thus, it is difficult to establish a fixed meaning.

Therefore, one knows that all phenomena are simultaneously both existent and non-existent, as this is realized through two proofs. Consequently, the answer given is that they are "both existent and non-existent. However...

Furthermore, "not being" is not "non-existent," and "non-existence" is not "being. Since existence and non-existence are ultimately distinct from one another, the answers provided mutually negate and protect [the position], rendering it impossible for others to exhaustively interrogate it. From this point downward, the faults are summarized as in the text.
△ Sixth, the sign of existence after death.
Furthermore, among the various sons of good family within *samādhi* (up to) the inverted discourse on the sign of existence after death.
Again, "within *samādhi*" indicates the correct attainment as before; "exhausting birth" indicates the false calculations; "inexhaustible flow" refers to—

This refers to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). Because the aggregate of formations is permanent and does not cease even after death, it is said that there is a "sign" (*nimitta*) after death.
Alternatively, from this point downward, one calculates that the four aggregates possess signs: first, form (*rūpa*) is the self, because one currently perceives the physical body as the self.
1. The self possesses form (*rūpa*), because it can pervade the entire realm. 2. Form belongs to the self, because the self returns to its former conditions. 3.
The self is within form, because it continues through the succession of activities. These four propositions constitute the four permutations for this aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).

Feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and formations (*saṃskāra*) each likewise have four permutations, thus forming sixteen aspects. All of these involve the grasping of signs (*nimitta*) that persist after death.

This concludes the section on the arising of conditions. From here below, the characteristics of various dharmas are individually examined. That is to say, just as it is with the characteristics of the aggregates (*skandha*), so it is with all dharmas.
"Afflictions" (*kleśa*) refers generally to all dharmas; "bodhi" specifically refers to awakened clarity. Bodhi and afflictions are driven together without distinction.
[The text] revises [the previous point], which also maintains that there is a mark after death. From this point downward, the faults are summarized as in the text. △ Seven:
No Mark After Death.
Furthermore, among the various good sons within samādhi... (up to) ...the inverted discourse on the mind being without mark after death.

Furthermore, "Again, *samā*... [and so on] marks the correct realization (*samyak-samādhi*) as previously described. "Exhausting the inferior... marks the false conceptualization (*mithyā-kalpanā*). This should be understood according to the text. "Seeing that...

refers to the calculation that the four aggregates (*skandha*) are extinguished. Now, where there is form (*rūpa*), one knows there is perception (*saṃjñā*); where there is perception, one knows there is feeling (*vedanā*).
If the present form is now extinguished, then one knows the aggregate of perception is likewise extinguished. Perception...

When the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is extinguished, one knows that the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is likewise extinguished. The principle of life is precisely the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
Although there is the impulse of vitality, it is the same as that of grass and trees; after death, how could it possess any marks of existence?

Furthermore, regarding the "eight absences," since the four marks of the present causal bond (*hetu-bandhana*) are extinguished, one knows that the four marks of the future resultant bond (*phala-bandhana*) are likewise [extinguished].
This is cessation; therefore, the eight [categories] become non-existent.
From this point downward, the individual calculations regarding the causes and effects of nirvana all depend upon the present aggregates (*skandha*) for their arising.
Since the present aggregates have already ceased, how could the future possibly exist? These are merely names in vain. From here downward, the faults are summarized as in the text.
△ 8. The Theory of Neither [Existence nor Non-existence].
Furthermore, among those good sons within samādhi... (up to) the theory of the post-mortem state of neither [existence nor non-existence] which is a perverted mind.

"Furthermore, within samādhi" indicates correct attainment (*samyaksamāpatti*). "Exhausting the lower" indicates false calculation. "Within the persistence of activity" refers to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*).
Thus it is said. To know that the currently existing aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) exists is to know that form (*rūpa*), feeling (*vedanā*), and perception (*saṃjñā*) have ceased.
Because form, feeling, and perception have ceased, one knows that the existence of the currently existing aggregate of formations is also not [truly] existent.

Because the aggregate of formations is not existent, one knows that form, feeling, and perception are not non-existent. By thus calculating these four aggregates in pairs, eight fallacies are established. Therefore, one knows death.
Finally, both are negated.

Regarding form (*rūpa*) and feeling (*vedanā*), one doubly calculates them as being neither existent nor non-existent. This means that form, feeling, and perception (*saṃjñā*) were previously existent, but now they are not;
therefore, it is called "seeing existence as non-existence. Furthermore, by analogy with the preceding [analysis of] form and so forth, one regards the formations (*saṃskāra*) as non-existent. By...

Regarding form and the other aggregates, their present modes of activity (ākāra) are neither existent nor non-existent; therefore, it is said that when observing them, they are not non-existent. As for the "eight non-characteristics" (aṣṭa-asallakṣaṇa):

within each of the five aggregates there are two non-characteristics, thus forming eight non-characteristics across the four [remaining] aggregates. This is called the exhaustive analysis of the aggregates and elements.
Regarding "having characteristics" and "lacking characteristics": since the present is neither existent nor non-existent, one thereby knows [the state] after death.
This is also neither existent nor non-existent; this is called the dual reckoning of existence and non-existence. Furthermore, one separately reckons the "neither" below.
This is because the present manifestations of mental activity flow and shift from moment to moment: within arising there is ceasing, and within ceasing there is arising.
Arising and ceasing are unstable; through this, one universally awakens to the fact that all dharmas are neither existent nor non-existent, hence they are called "neither both.

Furthermore, the preceding eight negations are not empty, while the eight affirmations are real; yet even emptiness and reality are difficult to establish as fixed standards, hence they are called "beyond reckoning."

The following concludes the critique: regarding the statement that "the future limit is obscure and indefinable," this means that concerning the present, one cannot say it exists, nor can one say it does not exist;
both extremes of existence and non-existence are unattainable. How much more so for that which is obscure after death—how could there be cognition?
The rest is as in the text. △ Ninth: The Theory of Annihilationism.
Furthermore, among those good sons within samādhi... [up to] the heterodox theories of the inverted mind regarding annihilation after death.
Again, "within samādhi" indicates the correct attainment as before; "exhausting the inferior births" indicates false calculations. Regarding the seven types of annihilation:
This refers to the two realms of humans and devas, the four dhyānas as four realms, and the formless realm; together these constitute seven stations.
As for "successive cessation," it means ceasing moment by moment in the present; even if one is born in these seven stations, one knows that they will all eventually be severed and extinguished.
Alternatively, one may calculate that the "extinction in seven places" refers to the extinction of the body, which consists of the two realms of humans and devas;

the exhaustion of desire, which refers to the first dhyāna; the exhaustion of suffering, which refers to the second dhyāna; supreme bliss, the third dhyāna; and supreme equanimity, the fourth dhyāna as well as the formless realms.
Regarding these seven places of extinction, it does not mean that extinction occurs only after advancing to a higher stage; rather, one attains it in the present moment, moment by moment.
It ceases. Later, one realizes that it also ceases moment by moment, and thus it no longer arises. From this point downward, the faults are concluded as in the text.
△ Fifteen: The Treatise on Manifesting Nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, regarding the "various good sons within samādhi" (up to) "the five inverted theories of manifesting nirvāṇa":
the phrase "furthermore, within samādhi" indicates correct realization as per the text; the phrase "exhausting the arising" indicates false conceptualization.

As for those who calculate that there is arising in each subsequent moment: because the preceding moments perish, one knows that each subsequent [moment] perishes; because they now arise in each moment, one knows... [that they arise].
Regarding "subsequent existence," if one discusses it in its entirety from beginning to end, it is merely the arising and ceasing of a single thought-moment.
Alternatively, this may explain the locus of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*). The desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is a place where the five destinies dwell together;

if one awakens to the principle of perfect luminosity, then the desire realm itself is the locus of the transformation of the basis. As for "the nature of the first dhyāna being free from sorrow," this means that one is detached from...

Sorrow (*daurmanasya*) is the locus for the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*). In the second dhyāna, suffering is absent by nature; thus, the departure from suffering is the locus for the transformation of the basis.

In the third dhyāna, there is the following of extreme joy (*prīti*); this joy is the factor of joy (*prīti-aṅga*), and it is the locus for the transformation of the basis. In the fourth dhyāna, both suffering and pleasure have vanished;

this is the factor of equanimity (*upekṣā-aṅga*), and it is indeed the locus for the transformation of the basis. This is called the fruit of the fivefold manifest nirvāṇa (*pañca-dṛṣṭa-dharma-nirvāṇa-phala*). This [attainment] is not yet thorough awakening.
Originally, upon obtaining a small measure of lightness and ease (*praśrabdhi*), one takes this to be the ultimate.

Thus, one falls into the erroneous views of "limb-dhyāna" (*aṅga-dhyāna*) and does not realize that this is precisely delusion regarding the heavens of outflows (*sāsrava*). To falsely construct an interpretation of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is to mistakenly grasp at *nirvāṇa*.
From this point on, the conclusion of the error is as stated in the text. △ Third, the summary and indication. First, the indication of the error.

Ānanda, these ten kinds of *dhyāna* (up to the point where they become great falsehood and result in falling into the Avīci Hell)—the above ten types are transformations of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (aggregate of formations).
Because the *saṃskāra-skandha* is shifting and moving, and because false calculations are triggered by it, the mind becomes unbalanced and cannot abide in right absorption (*samāpatti*).
As for "the mind and its application interacting," the mind that cultivates meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) is the correct one.
When deluded understandings suddenly arise, they are false; when the correct and the false are intermingled, it is called "interchange. As the saying goes:
"To err by a hair's breadth leads to a deviation of a thousand li. If these are not exposed, one may mistakenly take them as realization of the holy, which constitutes a great falsehood.
How can you not be cautious? △ Second, the exhortation to proclaim [the teaching]:
"You must take the words of the Tathāgata... (until) ...to serve as the pure pointing finger of the Great Awakened King."

Indeed, when the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is exhausted, there are no external demons. Yet, the inner obstruction of the mental demon leads to many errors and delusions, which conversely become a profound calamity for the study of the Way.
This was the hidden concern of the World-Honored One and the urgent intent behind his teachings.
Therefore, he commanded and exhorted its wide dissemination, repeatedly and earnestly admonishing it so that practitioners might realize this meaning and not fall into secondary entanglements.
To diverge and propagate the Great Way, and to ascend to Perfect Enlightenment—this is the guiding mark of purity. △ Five:
The Aggregate of Consciousness. First, a general explanation:
"Ānanda, that good man who cultivates samādhi... [up to] ...takes inverted false thoughts as its root."
Ānanda, the following clarifies the preceding benefit of the signs. "Faculty" (*mēi*) refers to the essential faculty. The "main rope" of a net is called the *gang*; the "knot" is called the *niu*.
*Pudgala* means "one who repeatedly takes up [existence]. This collectively indicates the characteristics of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
For the aggregate of formations is the essential faculty of all sentient beings; it is by means of this that they are born, and it is also the thread of their life.
It is the binding cord; because it connects and links all things, and because it serves as the point of convergence for all dharmas, sentient beings possess the nature of karma.
This skandha of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) acts as their vital circulation; thus, sentient beings possess the nature of delusion.
This skandha of formations acts as the medium of resonance; therefore, it is called the "nature of all worlds," wherein the profound stillness and the turbulent movement coexist.
The single characteristic of "activity" (saṃskāra) serves as the thread that interconnects them; it shifts and flows to constitute its karma.
Now, however, the aggregate of activity has been exhausted. The foundation of birth has crumbled, the binding cords have been untied, and all objects of grasping no longer function.
Since there is no longer any volitional action, who could trigger a response? This is like the dawn in the east, following the crowing of the rooster.
The sound fades; darkness will not long remain, for the great light is about to break through. This moment is the sign that the [previous] stage has reached its end.

When the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) are empty and still, one correctly enters the domain of the consciousness-aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*). Since there is no form, sensation, perception, or mental formations, the faculties themselves become empty and still.
Since there are no active volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), the mind does not wander or stray. Internally, it is limpid and luminous; therefore, it is called "internal."

"Externally serene and luminous. As for "internal and external," this refers to the profound meaning of contemplative observation (*vipaśyanā*). Generally, when the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) intersect, there is that which enters.

Now, with both perception (*saṃjñā*) and mental formations (*saṃskāra*) extinguished, the faculties and objects do not intersect; thus, there is no entry. Therefore, it is said: "entering where there is nothing to enter.
Only when one’s practice has reached such a state can one then contemplate the life-receiving of all sentient beings.

The Buddha told Ānanda, "The subtle, true, wondrous clarity... (up to) the fundamental causes of the five aggregates are all equally false thoughts."
The Buddha’s discourse below reveals the truth and clarifies delusion. The preceding text states, "The nature of awakening is wondrously luminous; fundamental awakening is luminously wondrous.
The present text states, "The essence of reality is wondrously luminous; fundamental awakening is perfectly pure. These are one and the same meaning, differing only slightly in their phrasing.
By comparing these, once the substance of the nature of awakening is understood to be luminous, how could there be birth and death?
Once the mind of essential purity is cleansed, how could there be any defilement? If even the defilements of birth and death do not exist, how could there be empty space?
Furthermore, "birth and death" encompasses the aforementioned meanings of subject and object; as previously stated, "the nature of awakening is necessarily luminous."

To falsely conceive of this as "clarity and awareness" is an error; awareness itself is not that which is clarified. Because there is clarity, an object is established. Once that object is falsely established, your false subjectivity arises.

This refers to the meaning of "dust and defilement" containing both identity and difference. What was previously stated—that within the absence of identity and difference, things blaze forth as different—refers to how, distinct from those differences, identity is established because of those differences. This refers to the meaning of "empty space" containing the world. As for what was previously stated...
Thus it is said that such disturbances interact and give rise to weariness; through long-standing weariness, dust is stirred up, and they become turbid within themselves.

From this, the afflictions of dust and toil are incited. That which arises becomes the world, while that which subsides into stillness becomes empty space—this is the delusion upon the fundamental substance.
Furthermore, "empty space" carries the meaning of containing the world; "dust and grime" carry the meaning of containing karmic fruits; and "birth and death" contains...
The meaning of "sentient beings" refers to delusion at the level of the fruit (*phala*). Furthermore, empty space represents the delusion of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*);

dust and grime represent the delusions of the *paryavasthāna* (dust-like afflictions); and birth and death represent the delusions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*). This refers to delusion within the cause (*hetu*).

While these were extensively elucidated in the preceding text, they are here presented in a concise and implicit manner. Now, I shall clarify them through these two aspects—cause and fruit—to show that they are nothing other than a single delusion.
That which is produced is thus. Therefore it is said that all are produced from the false and illusory.
Viewed in this light, a single wondrously bright, pure, and true mind possesses the marks of the false and illusory. Thus, because of delusion there is birth; because of delusion there is death;
and because of delusion there are the dust and dregs of the empty space-world and so forth. This is just like [the story of] Yanruo.
Dartā, being deluded regarding his own head, failed to perceive it and instead perceived the reflection in the mirror; consequently, various signs of madness and terror arose.

It is likewise like being deluded regarding the luminosity of original enlightenment (mūla-bodhi), whereby one perceives the falsity of that which is illuminated, and thus the various signs of the mundane world arise.
This is no different from the delusion of Yaññu (Evil Yakṣa). Delusion fundamentally arises from delusion;

it is like Yaññu’s head, which was never lost, yet he was terrified by its absence without cause. The nature of original enlightenment is never lost, yet one gives rise to false conceptualization without cause.
Falsehood is originally without cause, yet one establishes causes and conditions; furthermore, not recognizing these causes and conditions, one clings to them.
This is "natural. This is called a successive delusion. It is like Yajñadatta who, being confused about his own head, mistakes the reflected image in a mirror for a real head;
this too is a successive delusion. He does not know that the reflected image and the false head are both produced by the illusory workings of a frantic mind;
how could they ever be real? One does not realize that both "causal conditions" and "nature" are merely calculations of the conscious mind.
[If there is] no cause, how can there be a causal factor? This means that from delusion, delusion is produced. Ānanda, below [the text] correctly refutes the absence of cause.

Above, it was said that madness and terror are without cause, and that deluded thought is likewise without cause; this was stated precisely because one must know that even the claim of "no cause" constitutes a delusion.
Why is this? If one knows the origin of delusion, one may say there is a cause. But as for the primordial source of delusion...
It does not exist. As for what it could take as a cause: since even causes and conditions do not exist, how much less can there be anything that arises spontaneously?

To speak of existence and to speak of non-existence are both equally false; therefore, it is said that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are likewise all false. II. A detailed explanation of the five aggregates, in six parts:
1. The characteristic of form (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*).
"Your body was originally produced from the conceptualization of your parents... (up to) it is called the first solidified false imagination.

This section below marks the characteristics: when sentient beings perceive the red and white [semen and blood] from their parents, they may see it as light, or see it as a house, or smell its fragrance and purity, or smell its foulness and impurity; thus, the mind immediately gives rise to defilement.
It enters; having entered, it then covers [the body] and takes up its abode therein. Therefore it is said that "perception" (saṃjñā) means "image" (bimba).
Perception arises by taking on an image according to one's wholesome or unwholesome karma. Thus, if there were no perception of parents, one would not be born.
If there is no thought of a self-mind, then [consciousness] does not arise. It is only when the three conditions harmoniously combine that consciousness is produced.
By this, one knows that this body is entirely composed of deluded thoughts. As I shall demonstrate below through an experiment: vinegar is insentient.
Saliva and acidity are not the self. That which causes water to flow from the mouth and a sourness to arise in the feet—is this not due to your own deluded thoughts?
It is not so; what entity comes forth belonging to that same category? The passages concerning vinegar, cliffs, and so forth are fully seen at the end of the third fascicle.
Therefore, the names are concluded below. Thus, one should know that in the present there are forms that can be pointed out, and there are characteristics.

This is visible; it is called the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*). This aggregate of form, which arises from the inheritance of the parents and coalesces with the defilements of one's own mind to abide as a solidified mass, is precisely your own stubborn false conceptualization (*vikalpa*). II. The Characteristics of Feeling (*vedanā*).
This aforementioned state of mind, which imagines itself as standing on a high precipice, is called the second delusion, "empty clarity.
This follows upon the previous discussion of the vinegar cliff to clarify the delusion of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*). How is this known?

When discussing the emergence of the vinegar-water, the imagination of height that results in acidity is actually the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*). However, form cannot move of its own accord; it must necessarily depend upon...
The mind moves. The mind has that which it receives. It is the mind that drives and impels movement. Verifying this through experience:
when the body encounters the two conditions of compliance and resistance, it is entirely driven by the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*).

This is because the body benefits from compliance and suffers loss from resistance; its essential nature is illusory and thus easily moved. Furthermore, because the deluded mind is pervasive and lucid, it acts first.

Feeling (*vedanā*). Because it has been received from the beginning, it is able to move the physical body; this is called delusive discrimination (*parikalpita-vikalpa*). △ Third, the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*):
"By your thoughts and reflections, you cause your physical body... (up to) "...is called the third delusive discrimination of pervasive integration."
Examining the movements of the physical body, they must necessarily arise from thought and deliberation. Is thought not, indeed, ideation? How is this known?
It is because the body does not belong to the category of thought; thought must be ideation. Ideation gives rise to form, for it takes the entire external object as its mind.
Thereupon, the body moves in accordance with it. Is not the preceding object the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*)? Is not the movement of the body the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*)?
That which arises from the melting away of the material substance of that form-aggregate through the faculty of conceptual thought is a transformation produced by deluded thought (*vikalpa*).
△ Fourth, the characteristics of activity (*ākāra*).
The principle of transformation does not abide, but shifts subtly and incessantly; this is called the fourth deluded thought, which is profound and hidden.

While the first three aggregates (skandhas) all manifest as external objects, the present aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) manifests according to its own specific characteristics. Therefore, it is said that "the principle of transformation does not abide.
As for "shifting subtly and incessantly," this conveys the sense of flowing spontaneously and effortlessly; it explains the preceding phrase "does not abide."
The three phrases beginning with "the fingernails grow" reveal the characteristics of the activity. The phrase "never having any awareness" judges that this, too, is a false conception.
From "Ānanda" onwards, [the text] specifically points out that the activity belongs to Ānanda; it says:
if it were not you, who would cause your fingernails to grow and your hair to sprout, thereby causing your body to undergo change? If the activity were you, why would there be no awareness?
Awakened! Have you not been chasing after all that arises and ceases, unable to turn the light back to reflect upon itself? Its mode of activity is most subtle and dense;
therefore, it is called "profoundly hidden. Because one is unaware of its profound hiding, one knows it to be deluded thought. △ The Characteristics of the Five Consciousnesses.
Furthermore, from "the place where your clarity and brilliance are profound and unshakable" up to "the fifth inverted subtle and refined perception," [the text proceeds].
Moreover, your three subsequent phrases cite what Ānanda has calculated. The single phrase "regarding the body" specifically points to the characteristics of consciousness.
However, fearing that Ānanda’s calculation might imply, "I have no concern for the mind, and therefore I lack such perceptions; my mind is essentially true and real," [the text clarifies this].
"Therefore, it has no activity; the substance of the mind is eternal, exquisite and unshakable—this is my true mind.

The Buddha now refutes this, saying: "Your body is present here; do you not have seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing? Since this mind belongs to seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, it is clearly the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).
How can it be the true mind? If [you claim] it is truly exquisite and true, [the following passage from the scripture] is cited below:
This refutes your position. You claim that the nature which is still and unshaken is your true mind.
If it were truly pure and real, and could not tolerate the adventitious delusions, would this not be fortunate? Yet, I fear it is not so. Why? Suppose in years past you once saw a strange object;

many years have passed since then, such that you can neither recall nor forget it. Now, upon seeing it again, you suddenly remember it. [If your mind were inherently pure and incapable of delusion, how could such memory arise?]
Is this not the present consciousness-aggregate? This is not merely a single instance;
within the state of profound stillness and immobility, it is perfumed moment by moment, ever-new and never-abiding. How can one calculate this and reckon it to be the subtle, true mind?
Ānanda, you should know that the following uses an analogy to refute [your position].

That is to say, Ānanda, if you reckon that the state of being still and unmoving is truly like a rapid current appearing to be tranquil—where "rapid current" refers to a subtle flow that is not seen because the flow is so fine, yet it does not mean there is no flow at all—the state of being still and unmoving reckoned by the Śrāvakas of the Two Vehicles is exactly like this flow; it appears to be pure.
"Profound stillness" (*zhan*) is likewise a subtle flow that is not perceived; it is not, however, the absence of flow.

If one attains true non-flow, which truly severs birth and death, it must be through the mutual functioning of the opening and closing at the gates of the six sense faculties; only then can it be recognized as the True Mind.
If you cannot distinguish between opening and closing, and allow them to be used interchangeably, when will the deluded thoughts of birth and death ever come to rest?

Therefore, I shall now conclude by defining the names based solely on the events of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing within your present state of profound stillness and immovability—how many such things are there that you do not know?
Yet, when they are for a moment not manifest before you, you immediately reckon them to be real; you fail to realize that this profound stillness [is merely a temporary state].
The nature of this realization—when called "existent," it is yet empty; when called "non-existent," it seems to possess form.

Among all things, this is the most extremely subtle; therefore, it is named the "phantom-like, non-substantial, subtle conception. △ Sixth, a general conclusion summarizing the preceding five aggregates.
Ānanda, these five aggregates of clinging are formed by five kinds of false imagination... [up to] ...knowing that there is nirvāṇa and no longer craving for the three realms.
Previously, Ānanda asked whether the five aggregates are eliminated all at once or exhausted sequentially. Thus, regarding these five layers, what constitutes their boundaries?
Now, first I shall answer the final question. Generally, realms differ in their depth; if we discuss the realm of form (*rūpa*)...
Superficial. To discuss emptiness as profound—why is this? People know that form is identical to emptiness, yet they do not realize that form is itself emptiness, because emptiness is precisely form.
Therefore, by citing both form and emptiness, all that possesses form is exhausted. That which is the point of exhaustion is the limit.
Therefore, it is called the "limit of form. Hereafter, whenever the term "limit" (paryanta) is used, it should be understood according to this principle.

People know that contact is a characteristic of feeling (*vedanā*), but they do not know that separation is also a characteristic of feeling. Why? For who could know of a separation if there were no feeling?

People know that having an object and recollecting it is perception (*saṃjñā*), but they do not know that forgetting an object and losing its mark is also perception. Why? Because not forgetting is precisely...
To "recollect" means that failing to recollect is simply forgetting. People know that the arising of a single thought-moment is birth and the passing away of a single thought-moment is cessation;
yet they do not realize that every instance of birth and cessation belongs to the characteristic of conditioned activity (*saṃskāra*).

Because these characteristics flow and shift without staying still, people perceive the absence of the first four aggregates as stillness. Having realized this clearly, they take this stillness to be their entry into the profound stillness. This is why...

There is no dharma of arising and ceasing. Not knowing that the profound entry merges with the profound is the characteristic of consciousness (*vijñāna*). Because it involves conscious mental awareness, it is likewise a dharma of arising and ceasing.
Thus, this distinction between the deep and the shallow constitutes the limit of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

Once one knows this limit, one knows the boundaries of the realms (*dhātu*). The above answers the question, "What constitutes a realm? This section on the five aggregates below answers [the subsequent questions].
The first two lines concern the necessity of knowing the cause of arising; that is, arising originates from consciousness. Why is this?
Because all phenomena are transformations of consciousness alone; therefore, it is said that the cause of arising exists through consciousness. One must also know the method for their cessation.
This means that cessation is the removal from form (*rūpa*). Why? Because if form is extinguished and removed, all phenomena (*dharma*) have no basis;
therefore, it is said that cessation is the removal from form. Generally speaking, arising proceeds from within, while cessation proceeds from without;

this is explained according to their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). This is because one does not realize that they are entirely empty and false. If one speaks according to principle (*tattva*), it is not so: there is neither arising nor cessation. There is no...

There is no before or after. One thing fully understands all; one realization verifies all realizations. The *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra* says: "To know that it is an illusion is itself to be free from it;
no expedient means need be employed. To be free from illusion is itself awakening; there is also no gradual sequence. The preceding text states:

"The precious awakening of the Vajra King transcends the stage of No-More-Learning with a mere snap of the fingers. This is precisely the principle of sudden enlightenment. If we speak in terms of phenomenal characteristics, furthermore—
However, this is not so. This matter requires one to stand firmly on solid ground.
One must study through gradual stages, taking faith as the entrance and proceeding step by step, such as the ten faiths, the ten abidings, the ten practices, and the ten dedications.

Together with the four stages of application (*prayoga*) and the ten stages (*bhūmi*), one reaches the ocean of wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), where one finally exhausts the source of all phenomena. The text states:

"It is like a clean vessel from which poisonous honey has been removed; by using various hot waters and mixed ashes and incense to wash and cleanse that vessel, one subsequently stores ambrosia (*amṛta*) within it.
This is the principle of exhausting [the defilements] to the very bottom in successive order. The above response addresses whether [the defilements] are eliminated simultaneously or sequentially.
This concludes the sequence. From "I have already... below, the text summarizes and rebukes the questions asked.
This refers back to the previous discourse to reprimand Ānanda; the passage is found in the fifth fascicle. The text says: "According to your own mind, choose among the six faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*).

If the knots of the faculties are untied, the appearances of sense objects will naturally cease. When all delusions are extinguished, what need is there to wait for the unreal? This demonstrates the sudden teaching (*tun-fa*). [The word] "choose" [is used].
Regarding the selection of the six sense organs: it is as with Avalokiteśvara, who entered the perfect penetration through the ear organ. Furthermore, it is said:

"When this organ is first understood, one first attains the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). When the nature of emptiness is perfectly luminous, one achieves liberation regarding phenomena (*dharma-vimukti*).

Once liberated from phenomena, both [person and phenomenon] are empty and do not arise. This demonstrates the gradual method (*anupūrva-dharma*). Within this, the method of the three types of liberation is like that of the various Bodhisattvas, and...
The Arhats of the Two Vehicles first follow the provisional methods and subsequently enter perfect penetration;
this has already been clearly explained through two meanings. What is there that is not understood that you must inquire about again? This reproach is for Ānanda’s persistent questioning.

You should descend to offer encouragement and proclaim this teaching. People are like physicians and the Dharma is like a prescription. If a person lacks medical understanding yet clings to a prescription, they will surely kill the patient.
Likewise, if one does not personally awaken to their own delusions while attempting to eliminate the delusions of others, it is rare that they can provide salvation.
Therefore, I urge Ānanda: you must first awaken to the mind-ground yourself so that it becomes open and unobstructed, and only then transmit and reveal it to others.

The World-Honored One causes those of later generations to know that there exists the Way of the Self. What is there in the three realms to be attached to? What is there in Nirvana that cannot be attained?

This is called the Way of self-awakening and awakening others. △ Third, the comparative evaluation of merits and benefits, in three parts: first, the comparative evaluation of the benefits of the sutra.
"Ānanda, if there were someone who filled the ten directions... (up to) "...beyond what can be reached by calculation or analogy.

Ānanda, the passage beginning with "If there were another person" below cites inexhaustible giving to manifest inexhaustible merit. Generally, there are three things for which the merit of giving is said to be inexhaustible:
first, the empty space of the ten directions, which is inexhaustible in its measure and number; second, [the second point...]* *Note: The provided source text appears to be truncated at this point.*

The wealth bestowed as gifts of the seven precious gems is superior and inexhaustible; the third offering, which consists of making offerings to Buddhas as numerous as atoms, is the inexhaustibility of the initial resolve.
These are what are known as the three kinds of inexhaustibility. Briefly stated, the first two belong to external giving, while the latter one belongs to internal giving.
Taken together, these represent the exhaustion of both internal and external giving; the merit thereby obtained is truly immeasurable.
This is the measure. Following the passage where Ānanda replies, "The light is cited to manifest the heavy":
seven coins represent the lightest possible gift, while a wheel-turning monarch represents the heaviest possible reward. Thus, by means of the lightest gift, one obtains the heaviest reward.

It is clear that the merit of the aforementioned inexhaustible giving cannot be compared [to the merit of upholding this sutra]. From the passage "The three Buddhas told Ānanda" onwards, the heavy is cited to manifest the light.
The four grave offenses and ten abandonments are the ultimate evils among sins; the Avīci hell of the ten directions is the heaviest among retributions.
That ultimate heaviness of suffering is infinite, whereas a single thought-moment of propagating this sutra is finite. By means of...
Finite merit, conversely, results in infinite suffering; it not only fails to evoke inexhaustible joy, but further causes those in the ten directions to become lands of ultimate suffering.
Now, by reciting this sutra for a single thought-moment, one may compare that to maintaining the recitation in every subsequent thought-moment.
How could the calculation of its merit ever be compared?
Thus far, in weighing the benefits of the sutra, we have first proceeded from the broad to the narrow, and then from the narrow back to the broad.
"Broad" refers to the empty space of the ten directions; "narrow" refers to the merit of seven coins. "Broad" also refers to the ten directions of the Avīci hell.

One attains extreme suffering; yet by reciting this Sūtra for even a single thought-moment, one attains ultimate bliss. Thus, as these states are compared against one another, nothing can equal its excellence;
this collectively demonstrates that this Sūtra alone is supreme. Its uniquely superior merit is unsurpassed; please allow me to illustrate it with a brief analogy.
Suppose a person, in a single thought-moment, gives rise to a desire for sensual pleasure—they are already utterly deluded. How could it stop at being merely "utterly" [deluded]?
The deluded will inevitably create inexhaustible evil and undergo inexhaustible suffering. This inexhaustible suffering cannot be compared to the desire of that initial thought;
it is said that they differ by degrees of magnitude. Suppose a person were to awaken to the principle in a single thought—that would be universal enlightenment.
Not only would it be universal enlightenment, but they would surely realize the fruit of ultimate holiness.
The station of the Ultimate Sage and its most supreme fruit, as well as that station of the Ultimate Sage and the initial thought of awakening—these cannot be fathomed by ordinary sentiments.
As one progresses through these successive stages of excellence, one realizes that this ultimate evil and the ultimate fruit are not two separate things;
they are but a single thought-moment. Even this single thought-moment is the ultimate fruit. Furthermore—
Treatise: To expound the sutras for even a single moment of thought, its merit is truly unsurpassed.
Why is this? The ultimate fruit [of Buddhahood] pertains to the side of self-benefit; however, the propagation of the sutras pertains to the side of benefiting others.
Since there is no end to benefiting others, its merit and its blessings are immeasurable. This is also a progressively superior attainment; it is through this that one gains faith.
Know that this sutra is inconceivable; its karmic retribution is likewise inconceivable. How could one possibly treat it with negligence?
△ Second, the comparison of benefits for persons:
"Ānanda, if there are sentient beings who can recite this sutra... (until) they directly achieve Bodhi and no longer have demonic activities."
The foregoing comparison of the merit of this sutra has shown it to be uniquely supreme and unsurpassed.
Now, I exhort those who are able to recite this sutra or maintain this mantra: their merit shall likewise be uniquely supreme and unsurpassed.

Furthermore, it is not only the case that the benefits of being able to recite and maintain it are thus; if one truly practices according to my teachings, one will directly realize the ultimate fruit. Moreover—
There are no demonic obstacles. How can such merit be measured? Furthermore, being able to recite this sutra refers to the explicit teaching;
being able to uphold this mantra refers to the esoteric teaching; and directly realizing Bodhi refers to those of sudden capacity.
The absence of further demonic interference refers to those of gradual capacity. In sum, whether manifest or esoteric, the merit of one who can recite and uphold [this scripture] is beyond compare.
Whether sudden or gradual, the blessings of one who can receive its transformative influence are likewise beyond compare.
Thus, by extensively extolling these inexhaustible merits, it is revealed that the profound depth of this scripture’s penetration is such as this. △
The three groups of disciples performed prostrations.
After the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, and so forth, up to the entire assembly, were filled with great joy; they performed prostrations and departed.

The mention of "bhikṣus" below refers to the four assemblies who are the primary audience for the teaching. The mention of "devas and humans" below refers to the eight classes of beings who constitute the immediate retinue. As for "bodhisattvas from other directions,"...

The Bodhisattvas and the sages of the Two Vehicles constitute the assembly of those who have distanced themselves from the multitudes. Those who have first resolved their minds [for enlightenment] and the powerful spirits and deities constitute the assembly that protects the Dharma.

Furthermore, the Bodhisattvas and those of the Two Vehicles constitute the world of correct awakening. The eight classes of gods and humans constitute the world of sentient beings. All such worlds constitute the receptacle world.
As for the intention behind these classifications, once the meaning is exhausted, there is no need for further elaboration. This concludes the [discussion on] the assemblies.
Contemplation.
*The Scripture of Śūraṅgama Samādhi: Right View*, Fascicle Ten (End).
Postscript to *The Scripture of Śūraṅgama Samādhi: Right View*.

I have often heard venerable elders discuss the Great Canon, noting that only the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* is able to awaken the wondrous insight of sentient beings and serve as a guide for entering the Way.

However, while commentaries and sub-commentaries are numerous, those that point directly to the enlightened nature and provide an immediate resolution for the path of delusion are truly few and far between.
In the winter of the year Yihai, I first attended upon Master Jiufeng; day and night I followed him, listening to his every word.
He was commanded to face [the assembly] and speak upon the principles of the Mahāyāna; his discourse flowed forth like rivers that never run dry.
Within his satchel were ten scrolls of the *Lengyan Zhengjian* (Correct Vision of the Śūraṅgama), which were the Master’s own lifelong compositions.

In them, he established topical divisions and sections, providing detailed and clear commentaries that truly elucidate the ultimate truth. He brought forth what our Buddha had not yet revealed, opening wide the path for the masses of the deluded and illuminating [the Way].

Before the teachings of the successive sages were clarified, it could cause the ashes of kalpas as numerous as motes of dust to rise in dance, and the rubble beyond worlds as vast as the sands of the Ganges to radiate brilliance.
It is truly a precious raft for saving the world and benefiting living beings. Even if one wished not to transmit it, how could that be possible?

Whenever someone raised this point, saying, "The two paths of Chan and Teaching seem to be outside the scope of the Chan school," I smiled and replied, "One may distinguish between the Path of the School (Zong) and the Path of the Teachings (Jiao), but the Yellow-Faced Gautama would not have them follow separate tracks.

Formerly, there was a monk who asked Chan Master Baling Jian, "Are the intent of the Patriarchs and the meaning of the Teachings the same or different? Jian said, "When a rooster is cold, it climbs up..."
"The tree. "The duck, cold, plunges into the water. How can these two phrases be distinguished? Here, I ask you to offer a turning word. Alas!
It is a pity that they do not examine the principles of the Buddha or awaken to their own minds; they peer at the heavens through a tube and measure the ocean with a seashell.
Are the heavens and the oceans truly like this? Our Honored Master propagated the wind of the school and resided at Lou for many years, never seeking patronage or support.
He sought no worldly fame, but instead secluded himself in deep mountains, delighting in the company of fellow practitioners who came and went to him.
He instructed them with earnest and repeated guidance, never begrudging his compassionate heart. This sūtra remained within his chest for over twenty years, unknown to anyone.
Once I had seen it, how could I bear to regard it as something outside my own concern, merely as a bridge for awakening the world? Thus, I made a vow to entrust it [to others].
With carving tools in hand, he sought out like-minded companions to assist in this undertaking. After two cycles of winter and summer, the work was finally completed.
Throughout this process, the miraculous responses and karmic conditions that arose were manifold. This truly demonstrates the Buddha’s desire to propagate his teachings widely;
will it not endure forever, as eternal as heaven and earth? Indeed, the immortality of these scriptures is the immortality of the Buddha himself.
The lamp of wisdom shall endure; thus, the wondrous enlightenment of my Preceptor shall likewise remain imperishable.

Therefore, I have inscribed the names of all my fellow practitioners one by one at the beginning of this brief record, while also recounting the full account of its origins and conclusion. Written with reverent devotion by the student Dao Yi.
Bowing in prostration.
Postscript:
When Daoyi was a young child, he entered the monastic life and began studying the various scriptures. This was much like the lessons on the Four Books in a village school;

the sole requirement was to memorize them by heart, without investigating their underlying meanings. Upon reaching the age for tonsure, receiving full ordination, and becoming a monk, he occasionally took up the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
Having recited the scripture once, he was utterly bewildered and knew nothing of it; he could do no more than chant "Oṃ udauṣṭi kṛṣṇaśukla. Alas, how lamentable!
From this he began to harbor doubts, wondering what made this scripture so venerable that devas and nāgas would protect it and the underworld authorities would hold it in such high esteem.
Furthermore, he did not know what made this scripture so precious that its influence reached from kings, dukes, and great men above... down to [the commoners].
The common people of the neighborhood were murmuring in respectful agreement with this. Thereupon, he sighed deeply and said: "The Buddha is not a person of the world;
the Dharma is not a teaching of the world. How can I attempt to resolve this through the ordinary perceptions, understandings, and consciousnesses of the mundane world?
Nevertheless, though I am born of dull and ignorant nature, I must seek to clarify it. For now, I shall harbor this thought and preserve my resolve. Thus he spoke for several times.

Many years have passed, yet in the end I have been unable to explain my mind to others. Is this not my own stupidity? In the winter of the year Yihai, I first had an audience with the Elder of Jiufeng.
While casually reading the *Jingang Jing Tiyao* (Essentials of the Diamond Sutra) in his quarters, I thought, "How wonderful! How wonderful!"
It causes those who read it to feel as if they were lifting up the sun and moon to behold the azure sky, or as if they were standing by a clear stream to recognize their own true countenance.
With its chapters divided and meanings analyzed, the path is carved with such clarity that it appears exactly like the golden mouth of the Tathāgata, cast forth in perfect form.
Upon surveying other editions of the commentaries and sub-commentaries, they were found to be overly prolix and disordered in their topical divisions (*kepan*).

It was as if setting a dining table before one who is already full; though the flavors may be exquisite, there is only fear that the meal will not be cleared away soon enough. Thus, my joy and gratitude are immeasurable.

A mixture of sorrow and joy welled up within me. Alas! How could this sutra and its meaning not be disseminated throughout the world, so that every person might open this radiance to see their own mind and see the Buddha-mind? Would this not be a truly great and auspicious event?

"Samādhi-vipaśyanā" (Lengyan Zhengjian) is an alternative designation for meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). *Śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna* represent the equilibrium of concentration and wisdom.
Asaṅga emphasizes "stopping" (*śamatha*) to demonstrate the Great Samādhi of Samādhi-vipaśyanā; Nāgārjuna emphasizes "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*) to reveal the correct view of samādhi.
When Zhiyi of Tiantai presents both "stopping" and "contemplation" together, they likewise do not deviate from the equilibrium of concentration and wisdom.

Ānanda was widely learned, yet he fell into perverse thoughts and views, inviting the calamity of licentious arts. This was solely because he possessed wisdom but lacked concentration, and had not yet attained *samādhi* or right view.

The Tathāgata refuted him seven times; when Ānanda sought his mind and found no place for it, the Buddha immediately pointed out to Ānanda that he should clarify his own original nature to enter ultimate right concentration.
From this point, he took up the practice and established his footing. Later, there were eight more [refutations].

Returning to the ten manifestations, he untied the knots and refolded the cloth. Pointing directly to the great assembly, they attained the samādhi of right view; they recognized their fundamental nature and reached the source.
From this point on, practitioners of Zen turned the pivot of their understanding. Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra realized that all is originally pure and did not enter the fixed positions of the stages.
Falling into various categories, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva realized that Mañjuśrī is ungraspable and that all myriad phenomena are empty.

The "Superior Flow of the Realms" (dhātu-srotas) relies upon the four dhyānas and eight samādhis, ultimately returning to the realm of inert emptiness.

The "Sixty Holy Stages" rely upon precept, concentration, and wisdom to enter the ocean of the nature of nirvāṇa. The "Hearingless Bhikṣu" dwells in the samādhi of cessation, severing all thought and reflection;

he achieves a withered dhyāna and enters a dead-like contemplation, like a fish trapped in ice or grass covered by a stone. Although his life-faculty is not yet severed, it subsequently invites the [retribution of] earth.
The miserable realms of hellish suffering all arise from having concentration (*samādhi*) without wisdom (*prajñā*); this is not true concentration.

If concentration and wisdom are in equilibrium, the demons of the aggregates (*skandha-māra*) cannot enter. If concentration and wisdom are not in equilibrium, one will inevitably encounter demonic realms.
